knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized network flows with arc gains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines gain-adjusted balances, generalized-network optimization, cycle-gain classes, and a bounded-divergence variant, including a failure boundary for the usual accumulation-node reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ be a directed network with an arc gain $g_{ji}>0$ for every $(j,i)\in\mathcal A$. Flow $x_{ji}$ sent from $j$ arrives at $i$ as $g_{ji}x_{ji}$, and the gain-adjusted balance equations are
\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}g_{ji}x_{ji}=s_i,\qquad i\in\mathcal N.
\]
Minimizing $f(x)$ subject to these equations and $x\in X$ is a network problem with gains, or generalized network problem; a network problem without gains is called pure. For a cycle $C$, with positively and negatively traversed arc sets $C^+$ and $C^-$, its gain is
\[
G_C=\frac{\prod_{(i,j)\in C^+}g_{ij}}{\prod_{(i,j)\in C^-}g_{ij}}.
\]
The cycle is passive if $G_C=1$, active if $G_C\ne1$, flow generating if $G_C>1$, and flow absorbing if $G_C<1$. In the bounded-divergence variant,
\[
\underline s_i\leq\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}g_{ji}x_{ji}\leq\overline s_i,\qquad i\in\mathcal N.
\]
Unlike in pure networks, these inequalities cannot generally be converted to circulation equalities using artificial accumulation nodes, because with gains the sum of node supplies need not be zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a generalized network, each arc has a positive gain, so flow may be amplified or diminished and node balance uses gain-weighted incoming flow. A cycle is passive when its gain product ratio is one, generating when it exceeds one, and absorbing when it is below one. Node divergences may instead lie within bounds; the usual pure-network reduction using artificial accumulation nodes can then fail because gains remove the zero-total-supply property.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is a directed network}
g_{ji}>0\quad\forall (j,i)\in\mathcal A
x\in X
\underline s_i\leq\overline s_i\quad\forall i\in\mathcal N\text{ in the bounded-divergence variant}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}g_{ji}x_{ji}=s_i\quad\forall i\in\mathcal N,\qquad G_C=1\Leftrightarrow C\text{ is passive},\quad G_C>1\Rightarrow C\text{ is flow generating},\quad G_C<1\Rightarrow C\text{ is flow absorbing}.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear minimum-cost circulation with lower and upper arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. For each arc \(a\in A\), let \(c_a\in\mathbb R\) and \(-\infty<\ell_a\le u_a\le+\infty\). A feasible circulation is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) satisfying \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every arc and \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=0\qquad(v\in V).\] The minimum-cost circulation problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a:x\text{ is a feasible circulation}\right\}.\] An instance is infeasible if no such \(x\) exists and unbounded below if feasible circulations have arbitrarily negative cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-cost circulation minimizes linear arc cost subject to flow conservation at every vertex and prescribed lower and upper arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(c_a\in\mathbb R\) and \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\inf\{c^\top x:Bx=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Circuit Optimality Criterion for Minimum-Cost Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality characterization for a feasible circulation with lower and upper arc bounds using its residual digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph, let \(d,c,k:A\to\mathbb R\) be lower bounds, upper bounds, and arc costs, and let \(f\) be a feasible circulation. Then \(f\) has minimum cost among all feasible circulations if and only if every directed circuit of the residual digraph \(D_f\) has nonnegative cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible bounded circulation is minimum-cost exactly when its residual digraph has no negative-cost directed circuit.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear transshipment with the convention that positive balance denotes supply.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, with arc costs \(c\in\mathbb R^A\), bounds \(\ell\le u\), and balances \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). A feasible transshipment is \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) such that \(\ell\le x\le u\) and \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\qquad(v\in V).\] The minimum-cost transshipment problem minimizes \(c^\top x\) over these vectors. Thus \(b_v>0\) specifies net supply, \(b_v<0\) specifies net demand, and \(b_v=0\) imposes ordinary flow conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-cost transshipment sends specified supplies to specified demands at minimum linear cost while respecting all arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
\(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\inf\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme bounded flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines extremality as minimum cost among bounded flows having the same vertex-excess vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(d,c,k:A\to\mathbb R\), and let \(f:A\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(d\le f\le c\). The flow \(f\) is called extreme if, for every \(f':A\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(d\le f'\le c\) and \(\operatorname{excess}_{f'}=\operatorname{excess}_f\), one has \(\operatorname{cost}(f')\ge \operatorname{cost}(f)\). Equivalently, with \(b:=\operatorname{excess}_f\), \(f\) is a minimum-cost bounded \(b\)-transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded flow is extreme when it has minimum cost among all bounded flows with the same excess vector; equivalently, it is a minimum-cost transshipment for the demand vector equal to its excess.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph}
d,c,k:A\to\mathbb R
f:A\to\mathbb R
d\le f\le c
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is extreme}\iff \forall f'\,[d\le f'\le c\ \land\ \operatorname{excess}_{f'}=\operatorname{excess}_f\Rightarrow \operatorname{cost}(f')\ge\operatorname{cost}(f)].

knowledge_statements.title: Prescribed-Value Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source, single-sink flow with fixed throughput.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct, and fix \(F\ge 0\). Let \(c\in\mathbb R^A\), and let the arc bounds satisfy \(-\infty<\ell_a\le u_a\le+\infty\) for every \(a\in A\). If \(B\) is the node-arc incidence matrix using net outflow, a feasible flow of prescribed value \(F\) is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) satisfying \[Bx=F\mathbf e_s-F\mathbf e_t,\qquad \ell\le x\le u.\] The prescribed-value minimum-cost flow problem has extended optimal value \[\operatorname{OPT}=\inf\{c^\top x:Bx=F\mathbf e_s-F\mathbf e_t,\ \ell\le x\le u\}.\] It is the transshipment instance with supply \(F\) at \(s\), demand \(F\) at \(t\), and zero balance elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among all bounded source-to-sink flows having exactly the prescribed throughput, minimize linear arc cost; the instance may be infeasible or unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(s\ne t\).
\(c\in\mathbb R^A\) and \(-\infty<\ell_a\le u_a\le+\infty\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\inf\{c^\top x:Bx=F\mathbf e_s-F\mathbf e_t,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).

children.title: Minimum-Cost Maximum Flow
children.top_down_role: Throughput optimization followed by cost minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic optimization of throughput first and cost second.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct, let \(u\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^A\) be finite arc capacities, and let \(c\in\mathbb R^A\) be arc costs. With \(B\) denoting the node-arc incidence matrix using net outflow, define \[\mathcal F=\{x\in\mathbb R^A:0\le x\le u,\ (Bx)_v=0\text{ for every }v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\}.\] For \(x\in\mathcal F\), define \(|x|=(Bx)_s=-(Bx)_t\), and let \[F^*=\max\{|x|:x\in\mathcal F\}.\] A minimum-cost maximum flow is any \[x^*\in\arg\min\{c^\top x:x\in\mathcal F,\ |x|=F^*\}.\] Thus throughput is maximized first, and cost is minimized only among maximum-value flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First maximize source-to-sink throughput under finite arc capacities; among all maximum flows, select one having minimum linear cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(s\ne t\).
\(u\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^A\) has finite components.
\(c\in\mathbb R^A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((|x^*|,c^\top x^*)\) is lexicographically optimal with throughput ordered decreasingly and cost increasingly.

notation.meaning: Net flow value from source s to sink t.
Node-arc incidence matrix using the outflow-minus-inflow convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Value Circulation Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-preserving reduction of the fixed-maximum-value cost phase to minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After determining \(F^*\), add a zero-cost return arc \(a_0=(t,s)\) with \(\ell_{a_0}=u_{a_0}=F^*\). A flow \(x\) on the original arcs has value \(F^*\) if and only if its extension with \(x_{a_0}=F^*\) is a feasible circulation. The extension preserves objective value, so minimum-cost maximum flows correspond bijectively to minimum-cost circulations in the augmented network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed zero-cost return arc from the sink to the source converts the maximum-value cost phase into an equivalent minimum-cost circulation.
assumptions_latex: \(F^*\) is the maximum feasible source-to-sink flow value.
The return arc \(a_0=(t,s)\) has zero cost and fixed flow \(F^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\longleftrightarrow (x,x_{a_0}=F^*)\text{ is a cost-preserving bijection between value-}F^*\text{ flows and feasible augmented circulations.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rejected as a duplicate restatement of the accepted lexicographic definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First compute the maximum feasible flow value \(F^*\). Then solve \(\min\{c^\top x:x\in\mathcal F,\ |x|=F^*\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute maximum throughput and then minimize cost among flows having that value.
assumptions_latex: \(F^*\) is the maximum feasible source-to-sink value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal F,\ |x|=F^*}c^\top x\text{ is the set of minimum-cost maximum flows.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hitchcock Labeling Routine
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routine A of a primal–dual algorithm for a transportation-flow tableau.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current transportation flow $(r_{ij})$, label every row $i$ with positive residual supply $\varepsilon_i=a_i-\sum_j r_{ij}$. Repeatedly scan a labeled row across admissible cells $(i,j)$ to label previously unlabeled columns, and scan a labeled column backward across cells with $r_{ij}>0$ to label previously unlabeled rows, propagating the bottleneck value $\min\{r_{ij},\varepsilon_j\}$. If a labeled column has $\sum_i r_{ij}<b_j$, declare breakthrough and invoke the flow-change routine; if no further label can be assigned, declare nonbreakthrough and invoke the dual-change routine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from every row with unused supply and alternately label reachable columns through admissible cells and reachable rows through positive-flow cells, propagating bottleneck amounts. A labeled column with unmet demand triggers flow augmentation; exhaustion of the labeling process without such a column triggers a dual-variable change.
assumptions_latex: r_{ij}\ge 0
\varepsilon_i=a_i-\sum_j r_{ij}>0\text{ for each initially labeled row }i
\text{Row-to-column scans use admissible cells; column-to-row scans require }r_{ij}>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The routine returns either a breakthrough label path for Routine B or a nonbreakthrough labeled set for Routine C.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Admissible-Arc Labeling and Node-Potential Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimum-cost flow routine operating on the admissible residual subnetwork.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Beginning with the current flow $f$, perform labeling on admissible residual arcs. A node $y$ may be labeled from $x$ when either $(x,y)$ is admissible and $f(x,y)<c(x,y)$, or $(y,x)$ is admissible and $f(y,x)>0$. On breakthrough, change the flow along the labeled path and relabel. On nonbreakthrough, let $f'$ be the current flow and $X$ the labeled-node set, and define
\[
\pi'(x)=\begin{cases}
\pi(x),&x\in X,\\
\pi(x)+1,&x\notin X.
\end{cases}
\]
Repeat the routine from $f'$ using the admissible arcs defined by the updated node integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Label through unsaturated admissible arcs forward and positive-flow admissible arcs backward. A breakthrough causes a path flow change; otherwise increase each unlabeled node integer by one and repeat from the current flow with the newly admissible arcs.
assumptions_latex: \text{$f$ is the current capacitated flow.}
\text{Forward labeling requires $(x,y)$ admissible and }f(x,y)<c(x,y).
\text{Backward labeling requires $(y,x)$ admissible and }f(y,x)>0.
\text{$\pi$ consists of the current node integers defining admissibility.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each pass either changes the flow after breakthrough or updates }\pi\text{ after nonbreakthrough and repeats.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hitchcock Dual-Variable Change after Nonbreakthrough
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routine C updates potentials when the admissible-cell labeling search cannot reach an unmet-demand column.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $I$ and $J$ be the labeled rows and columns after nonbreakthrough, and set $\delta=\min\{a_{ij}+\alpha_i- eta_j:i\in I,\ j
otin J\}$. Define $\alpha_i'=\alpha_i$ for $i\in I$ and $\alpha_i'=\alpha_i+\delta$ for $i
otin I$; define $ eta_j'= eta_j$ for $j\in J$ and $ eta_j'= eta_j+\delta$ for $j
otin J$. Redefine admissible cells using $(\alpha', eta')$ and repeat the labeling process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a failed labeling search, choose the minimum slack from a labeled row to an unlabeled column, shift the unlabeled row and column potentials by that amount, recompute admissible cells, and relabel.
assumptions_latex: I=\{i:i\text{ is labeled}\}
J=\{j:j\text{ is labeled}\}
\text{The labeling process ended without breakthrough}
\delta=\min_{i\in I,\,j\notin J}(a_{ij}+\alpha_i-\beta_j)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The updated potentials }(\alpha',\beta')\text{ define the admissible cells for the next labeling pass.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Demand-Weighted Maximal Dual Change
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects a larger dual step by ordering column slacks and accumulating their demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each column $j$, compute $\lambda_j=\min_{i\in I}(a_{ij}+\alpha_i-\beta_j)$ and order the $\lambda_j$ increasingly. Accumulate the associated demands $b_j$ until their sum first exceeds $b(J)-a(T)$, and let $\varepsilon$ be the corresponding $\lambda_j$. Set $\alpha_i'=\alpha_i$ for $i\in I$ and $\alpha_i'=\alpha_i+\varepsilon$ for $i\notin I$, then set $\beta_j'=\min_i(a_{ij}+\alpha_i')$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order each column's minimum slack from the labeled rows, attach the column demand, and choose the slack where cumulative demand first exceeds the stated residual threshold. Shift the unlabeled row potentials by this value and recompute every column potential as its minimum reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: \lambda_j=\min_{i\in I}(a_{ij}+\alpha_i-\beta_j)
\text{The values }\lambda_j\text{ are ordered increasingly with their associated demands }b_j
\text{The cumulative-demand threshold is }b(J)-a(T)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon\text{ is the first ordered }\lambda_j\text{ whose cumulative associated demand exceeds }b(J)-a(T),\quad \beta_j'=\min_i(a_{ij}+\alpha_i').

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal-flow recovery from optimal node potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a capacitated minimum-cost flow with optimal node potentials and a feasible completion of the induced zero-reduced-cost network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given optimal node potentials $\pi$, compute $c_{ij}^{\pi}$. Fix $x_{ij}=0$ when $c_{ij}^{\pi}>0$, fix $x_{ij}=u_{ij}$ when $c_{ij}^{\pi}<0$ and adjust the endpoint supplies accordingly, and retain capacity interval $[0,u_{ij}]$ when $c_{ij}^{\pi}=0$. Construct the auxiliary source–sink maximum-flow instance for the modified balances. If its flow satisfies all modified supplies and demands, combining it with the fixed arc flows yields an optimal flow for the original minimum-cost-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify arcs by reduced-cost sign: positive-cost arcs carry zero flow, negative-cost arcs are saturated, and zero-cost arcs remain free within capacity. After updating node balances, solve an auxiliary maximum-flow problem to complete a feasible flow. Any completion satisfying all balances is optimal for the original minimum-cost-flow problem.

\pi\text{ is an optimal set of node potentials}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrality and Labeling-Pass Bound for the Hitchcock Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guarantee for the algorithm composed of Routines A, B, and C.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $a_i>0$ $(i=1,\ldots,m)$, $b_j>0$ $(j=1,\ldots,n)$, and $a_{ij}\ge0$ be integers defining a feasible Hitchcock transportation problem. The algorithm composed of Routines A, B, and C produces integral optimal solutions of the primal problem and its dual after at most
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n b_j+\left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j-1\right)(\min\{m,n\}+1)
\]
applications of Routine A.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer Hitchcock transportation instance, the three-routine primal–dual algorithm returns integral primal and dual solutions. The number of labeling passes is at most total demand plus total demand minus one times one more than the smaller tableau dimension.
assumptions_latex: a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
b_j\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
a_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
\text{The corresponding Hitchcock transportation problem is feasible}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_A\le \sum_{j=1}^n b_j+\left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j-1\right)(\min\{m,n\}+1),\quad\text{with integral primal and dual outputs.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Node–Arc and Return-Arc Formulations of Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity, single-commodity directed maximum flow with zero lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network with source $1$, sink $m$, and arc capacities $u_{ij}$, maximum flow is formulated by maximizing $f$ subject to $\sum_j x_{ij}-\sum_k x_{ki}=f$ for $i=1$, $0$ for $i\notin\{1,m\}$, and $-f$ for $i=m$, with $0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}$. Equivalently, introducing a return arc $(m,1)$ with flow $x_{m1}=f$, lower bound $0$, and cost $-1$ converts the problem into a zero-balance minimum-cost circulation with all other arc costs zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flow maximizes the source-to-sink flow value subject to node conservation and arc capacities. Treating that value as flow on a return arc from the sink to the source gives an equivalent zero-balance circulation formulation, with cost −1 on the return arc and zero cost elsewhere.

0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\quad((i,j)\in E),\qquad u_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{<\infty}.
\ell_{ij}=0\quad((i,j)\in E).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max f\ \text{subject to flow conservation and capacities is equivalently represented by a circulation with }x_{m1}=f\text{ and }c_{m1}=-1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hitchcock Flow-Change Routine
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow adjustment following breakthrough at a labeled column with unsatisfied demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a breakthrough column $j$, set
\[
\varepsilon=\min\left\{\varepsilon_j,\ b_j-\sum_i r_{ij}\right\}.
\]
Follow the path specified by the labels, alternately adding and subtracting $\varepsilon$, beginning by adding $\varepsilon$ to the cell entering column $j$, and stop upon reaching an initially labeled row. If all column demands are then satisfied, terminate; otherwise discard the labels and restart Routine A from the resulting flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augment along the alternating labeled path by the smaller of its propagated amount and the breakthrough column's unmet demand. Terminate if all demands are satisfied; otherwise erase the labels and restart labeling from the new flow.

\varepsilon_j>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cheapest flows, k-braids, potentials, and reduced costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and equivalences for bounded minimum-cost flows and the unit-capacity fixed-value specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D=(V,A), |V|\ge 2, and let f:A\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}, g:A\to\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\} satisfy f\le g. A function x:A\to\mathbb R is feasible when f\le x\le g; given a node-imbalance vector m admitting a feasible m-flow and costs c:A\to\mathbb R, a cheapest feasible m-flow minimizes cx. For c:A\to\mathbb R_+ and unit capacities g\equiv1, a feasible integer s-t flow of value k is a (0,1)-valued k-braid, identified with k edge-disjoint s-t walks, and is cheapest when it minimizes cz among all k-braids. A potential is a function \pi:V\to\mathbb Z_+ with \pi(s)=0\le\pi(v)\le\pi(t) for all v; its tension is \Delta_\pi(uv)=\pi(v)-\pi(u), and c_\pi(uv)=c(uv)-\Delta_\pi(uv). Every flow of value k has \Delta_\pi-cost k\pi(t), so a flow is c-minimum if and only if it is c_\pi-minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded flow is feasible when it lies between its arcwise lower and upper bounds, and a cheapest feasible flow minimizes total cost. With unit capacities, an integer flow of feasible value k is a 0–1 k-braid representing k edge-disjoint source-to-sink walks. Subtracting the tension of a node potential from every arc cost changes every value-k flow's cost by the same amount, so it does not change which such flows are cheapest.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A),\quad |V|\ge 2
f:A\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\},\quad g:A\to\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\},\quad f\le g
m\text{ admits a feasible }m\text{-flow}
k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\text{ is feasible}
c:A\to\mathbb R_+,\quad g\equiv1\text{ in the }k\text{-braid specialization}
\pi:V\to\mathbb Z_+,\quad \pi(s)=0\le\pi(v)\le\pi(t)\ \forall v\in V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_\pi(x)=k\pi(t)\text{ for every value-}k\text{ flow }x,\qquad x\in\arg\min cx\iff x\in\arg\min c_\pi x.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine substitution converting finite lower bounds to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) with finite \(\ell\). Set \(y=x-\ell\), \(b'=b-B\ell\), and \(u'=u-\ell\). Then \[Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad By=b',\ 0\le y\le u'.\] The objectives satisfy \(c^\top x=c^\top y+c^\top\ell\). Consequently the substitution is a bijection between feasible sets, preserves the ordering of feasible solutions, and changes the optimal value only by the known constant \(c^\top\ell\). If the original data are integral, the map also preserves integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract each arc's lower bound, adjust vertex balances by its incidence, and retain costs; feasibility and optimal solutions correspond up to a constant cost.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the node-arc incidence matrix.
\(\ell\in\mathbb R^A\) is finite and \(\ell\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\leftrightarrow y=x-\ell\) bijects the two feasible regions and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{x}=\operatorname{OPT}_{y}+c^\top\ell\).

notation.meaning: Net outflow induced by the vector of lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-reversal substitution eliminating finite upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an arc \(a=(i,j)\) constrained by \(0\le x_a\le u_a<\infty\), introduce the reverse arc \(\bar a=(j,i)\) with unbounded nonnegative flow \(y_{\bar a}=u_a-x_a\) and cost \(-c_a\). Delete \(a\), replace balances by \(b'_i=b_i-u_a\), \(b'_j=b_j+u_a\), and leave other balances unchanged. Then feasible solutions correspond bijectively through \(x_a=u_a-y_{\bar a}\), and \[c_ax_a=c_au_a-c_ay_{\bar a}.\] Applying this independently to every finitely upper-bounded arc removes all such upper bounds, while preserving minimizers after adding the known constant \(\sum_a c_au_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a bounded arc by an unbounded reverse arc carrying unused capacity, adjust endpoint balances, and account for a constant objective shift.
assumptions_latex: The balance convention is \(Bx=b\) with net outflow positive.
Each transformed arc satisfies \(0\le x_a\le u_a<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_a\leftrightarrow y_{\bar a}=u_a-x_a\) preserves feasibility and changes cost by the constant \(c_au_a\).

notation.meaning: Reverse arc replacing the original finitely capacitated arc.
Unused capacity of the original arc.

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of balanced transshipment to circulation using fixed-flow auxiliary arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Bx=b\) be a transshipment instance with \(\sum_v b_v=0\), where positive \(b_v\) denotes supply. Add a new vertex \(r\). For each \(v\) with \(b_v>0\), add a zero-cost arc \((r,v)\) whose lower and upper bounds both equal \(b_v\); for each \(v\) with \(b_v<0\), add a zero-cost arc \((v,r)\) fixed at \(-b_v\). Retain every original arc and require zero balance at every vertex. Restriction to the original arcs bijects feasible circulations with feasible transshipments and preserves their costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attach fixed zero-cost arcs to a new vertex so prescribed supplies and demands become ordinary circulation conservation equations.
assumptions_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
Fixed-flow arcs are permitted through equal lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Bx=b\) on original arcs holds exactly when the augmented flow is a circulation.

notation.meaning: Prescribed net outflow at vertex v.

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Viewing circulation as the zero-balance transshipment case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a minimum-cost circulation instance \(Bx=0\) with bounds \(\ell\le x\le u\), form a transshipment instance on the same graph, with the same bounds and costs, by setting \(b_v=0\) for every vertex. The feasible regions and objective functions are identical. More generally, after fixing auxiliary arcs in a circulation reduction, deleting those arcs and moving their incidence contributions to the right-hand side produces \(Bx=b\). Thus circulation and balanced transshipment formulations convert into one another without changing the original decision variables or their costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circulation is exactly a transshipment with zero balances; deleting fixed auxiliary arcs conversely recovers nonzero prescribed balances.
assumptions_latex: The same outflow-minus-inflow incidence convention is used in both formulations.
Any deleted auxiliary arc has a fixed flow value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:Bx=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\}=\{x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) when \(b=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-Bound Shifting from Circulation to Transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a lower-bounded circulation to a zero-lower-bound transshipment on the same graph.

Thus \(y\) is a transshipment with balance \(b'=-B\ell\). The objective is \(c^{\mathsf T}y+c^{\mathsf T}\ell\), so \(x=y+\ell\) is a feasible-solution bijection and preserves minimizers up to the constant \(c^{\mathsf T}\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting lower bounds turns a circulation into a zero-lower-bound transshipment, adjusts balances, and adds only a constant to the objective.

\(\ell\le u\).

children.title: Canonical-Form Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Preservation of feasibility, objective values, capacities, and recoverable solutions across the two forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-Form Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization equivalence of circulation and balanced transshipment canonical forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite balanced transshipment instance with \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), fixed-arc augmentation produces a circulation instance whose feasible circulations restrict bijectively to the original feasible transshipments and have equal cost. Conversely, every circulation instance is a transshipment instance with \(b=0\). These reductions preserve feasibility, finite optimal values, minimizers, and unboundedness. When bounds and balances are integral, the reductions use only integral fixed flows and preserve integral feasible solutions. The augmentation adds one vertex and at most \(|V|\) arcs and is computable in time linear in the augmented instance description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced transshipment and circulation are mutually reducible while preserving costs, feasibility, optimality, integrality, and linear instance growth.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(b\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfies \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
Equal lower and upper bounds may encode fixed auxiliary flows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{transshipment}}=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{augmented\ circulation}}\), with a cost-preserving bijection of feasible solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transportation as minimum-cost flow on a layered bipartite network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For supplies \(a_i\ge0\), demands \(b_j\ge0\), and costs \(c_{ij}\), assume \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\). Construct a network with source \(s\), supply vertices \(i\), demand vertices \(j\), and sink \(t\). Give \((s,i)\) capacity \(a_i\), \((i,j)\) cost \(c_{ij}\) and sufficient capacity, and \((j,t)\) capacity \(b_j\); all other costs are zero. A flow of value \(\sum_i a_i\) corresponds to the transportation plan \(x_{ij}=x_{(i,j)}\), satisfying \(\sum_jx_{ij}=a_i\) and \(\sum_ix_{ij}=b_j\), with identical cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent a transportation table as flow through source, supply, demand, and sink layers; transportation quantities are the middle-arc flows.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i,b_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\).
Every permitted shipment pair has a corresponding middle arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}=c^\top x\), and feasible transportation plans biject with full-value network flows.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dummy-Node Balancing Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balancing a standard unequal-total transportation variant by one zero-cost dummy margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\sum_{i\in I}s_i\) and \(D=\sum_{j\in J}d_j\). If \(S>D\), add a dummy demand node \(j_0\) of demand \(S-D\) and zero-cost arcs \((i,j_0)\) from every origin. If \(D>S\), add a dummy supply node \(i_0\) of supply \(D-S\) and zero-cost arcs \((i_0,j)\) to every destination. Deleting dummy shipments gives a cost-preserving correspondence with the variant in which all margins on the smaller-total side are met exactly and margins on the larger-total side are upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-cost dummy origin or destination balances the standard unequal-total transportation variant with inequality margins on the larger-total side.
assumptions_latex: Original shipments are nonnegative.
Margins on the smaller-total side are equalities and margins on the larger-total side are upper bounds.
All required dummy arcs exist, have zero cost, and have sufficient capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented instance is balanced, and deleting its dummy shipments preserves feasibility and original-route cost for the stated unbalanced variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment as unit-supply, unit-demand transportation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite sets with \(|I|=|J|\), and let \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) be the cost of assigning \(i\in I\) to \(j\in J\). Form the transportation problem with \(a_i=1\) for every \(i\in I\), \(b_j=1\) for every \(j\in J\), and variables \(x_{ij}\ge0\). Its constraints are \[\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in I),\qquad \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\quad(j\in J).\] Its integral feasible points are precisely perfect assignments, with \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\). The bipartite transportation constraint matrix is totally unimodular, so with the integral right-hand side the linear relaxation has an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set every transportation supply and demand to one; perfect assignments are the integral feasible plans, and total unimodularity makes the linear relaxation exact.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite and \(|I|=|J|\).
\(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) for every \((i,j)\in I\times J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{\sum_{i\in I,\,j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:x\text{ is a perfect assignment}\}\) equals the unit-transportation linear-programming optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Network Expansions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clone expansion from integral transportation to assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integral transportation instance with \(a_i,b_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and total mass \(N=\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\). Replace each supply vertex \(i\) by \(a_i\) clones and each demand vertex \(j\) by \(b_j\) clones. Join every permitted supply clone of \(i\) to every permitted demand clone of \(j\), assigning each such edge cost \(c_{ij}\). A perfect assignment of clones induces \(x_{ij}\) equal to the number of matched clone pairs of types \((i,j)\). Conversely, every integral transportation plan expands to such a perfect assignment, with equal total cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clone each origin and destination according to its integral multiplicity; perfect assignments between clones encode integral transportation plans with unchanged cost.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i,b_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j=N\).
Clone edges reproduce exactly the permitted transportation pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integral transportation plans and perfect clone assignments correspond cost-preservingly, although the expanded graph may have size polynomial in \(N\), not its bit length.

notation.meaning: Total transported mass and number of clones on each side.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rollout Iteration for Arc-Flow Decisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies one iteration and the finite completion of the rollout procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from a partial solution \(P=\{x_{ij}:(i,j)\in S\}\), choose a nonempty subset \(T\subseteq\mathcal A\setminus S\). For every admissible assignment \(y\in F_T\) on \(T\), form \(P_y^+=P\cup y\) and evaluate \(H(P_y^+)\) using the base heuristic. Select \(\bar y\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\in F_T}H(P_y^+)\), replace \(P\) by \(P_{\bar y}^+\), and repeat until all arc flows are assigned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each rollout iteration, select some unassigned arcs, enumerate their admissible flow assignments, complete each resulting partial solution with the base heuristic, and permanently choose an assignment minimizing heuristic cost. Repeat until the solution is complete.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x_{ij}:(i,j)\in S\}\text{ is the current partial solution}.
T\subseteq\mathcal A\setminus S\text{ is the selected set of unassigned arcs}.
F_T\text{ is the collection of admissible assignments on }T.
H(P_y^+)\text{ is computable for every }y\in F_T.
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\in F_T}H(P_y^+)\neq\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\leftarrow P_{\bar y}^+,\qquad \bar y\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\in F_T}H(P_y^+),\quad\text{with iteration continuing until }S=\mathcal A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise-requirement network synthesis model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility and the cut-indexed linear formulation for an undirected capacitated network supporting pairwise flow requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=(r_{ij})\) be a symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix of nonnegative pairwise flow requirements. A capacitated network is feasible if, for every pair \(i,j\), it can support an \(i\)-to-\(j\) flow of value \(v_{ij}\ge r_{ij}\). For arc-capacity costs \(a_{ij}\), the synthesis problem minimizes \(\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}c_{ij}\) subject to the cut inequalities \[\sum_{i\in S,\,j\in T}c_{ij}\ge \max_{i\in S,\,j\in T}r_{ij}\] for every bipartition \((S,T)\) of the node set and to \(c_{ij}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given symmetric nonnegative pairwise flow requirements, a network is feasible when it can support at least the required flow between every node pair. Minimum-cost synthesis is a linear program whose constraints require the capacity across every cut to be at least the largest pairwise requirement separated by that cut.
assumptions_latex: R=(r_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}
r_{ij}=r_{ji}
c_{ij}\ge0
(S,T)\text{ ranges over all bipartitions of the node set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{c\ge0}\left\{\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}c_{ij}:\ \sum_{i\in S,\,j\in T}c_{ij}\ge\max_{i\in S,\,j\in T}r_{ij}\ \forall(S,T)\right\}\text{ models minimum-cost feasible network synthesis.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial Solutions and Heuristic Cost in Network Rollout
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the partial-solution evaluation supplied by a base heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite feasible set of flow vectors on arc set \(\mathcal A\), with objective \(f\). For a proper subset \(S\subset\mathcal A\), a partial solution is \(P=\{x_{ij}:(i,j)\in S\}\); a complete solution assigns every arc. A base heuristic completes \(P\) with \(\bar P=\{x_{ij}:(i,j)\notin S\}\), producing \(x=P\cup\bar P\). The heuristic cost is \(H(P)=f(x)\) if \(x\in F\), and \(H(P)=\infty\) otherwise. For a feasible complete solution \(P=x\), \(H(P)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite feasible set of network flows, a partial solution assigns flows on only some arcs. A base heuristic assigns the remaining arcs, and the partial solution's heuristic cost is the completed flow's objective value when feasible and infinity otherwise. A feasible complete solution has heuristic cost equal to its true cost.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is a finite feasible set of flow vectors on }\mathcal A.
f:F\to\mathbb R\text{ is the objective function}.
S\subset\mathcal A\text{ is a proper subset for a partial solution}.
\text{A base heuristic supplies values on }\mathcal A\setminus S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(P)=\begin{cases}f(P\cup\bar P),&P\cup\bar P\in F,\\ \infty,&P\cup\bar P\notin F.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and dual integrality of minimum-cost flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusions are conditional on attainment of an optimum; primal and dual integrality have distinct data assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathrm{MCFP}_0\) has an optimal solution. If \(\bar c:A\to\mathbb{Z}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(\underline c:A\to\mathbb{Z}\cup\{-\infty\}\), and \(x:V\to\mathbb{Z}\), then there exists an integer-valued optimal flow \(\xi:A\to\mathbb{Z}\). Moreover, \(\Pi^*=\{p\mid p\text{ is an optimal potential}\}\) is an L-convex polyhedron. If \(\gamma:A\to\mathbb{Z}\), then \(\Pi^*\) is an integral L-convex polyhedron and contains an integer-valued optimal potential \(p:V\to\mathbb{Z}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming the conventional minimum-cost-flow problem attains an optimum, integer lower and upper capacities and integer vertex balance data guarantee an integer optimal flow. The optimal-potential set is L-convex; when arc costs are integer, it is an integral L-convex polyhedron and contains an integer optimal potential.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathrm{MCFP}_0\) has an optimal solution.
For primal integrality, \(\bar c:A\to\mathbb{Z}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(\underline c:A\to\mathbb{Z}\cup\{-\infty\}\), and \(x:V\to\mathbb{Z}\).
For integrality of \(\Pi^*\) and existence of an integer-valued optimal potential, \(\gamma:A\to\mathbb{Z}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the primal data assumptions an integer-valued optimal flow exists; \(\Pi^*\) is an L-convex polyhedron, and under integer arc costs it is integral and contains an integer-valued optimal potential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tight-arc contraction and dual lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the failure boundary separating dual lifting from primal-flow lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let I=(G,c,b) be a transshipment instance and let f=pq carry positive flow in some optimal solution. Then every optimal dual solution y satisfies \bar c_f=0, equivalently y_q-y_p=c_f. Substituting y_q=y_p+c_f yields the dual of the contracted instance I/f. Every optimal dual solution y' of I/f lifts to an optimal dual solution of I by y_v=y'_v for v\ne q and y_q=y'_p+c_f. One cannot conclude merely from the stated assumption that every optimal flow of I/f determines an optimal flow of I; that conclusion would require, at minimum, that f carry positive flow in every optimal flow of I.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an arc carries positive flow in some optimal transshipment solution, it is tight in every optimal dual solution. Eliminating its tight dual constraint produces the dual of the contracted instance, and every contracted optimal dual solution lifts to an original optimal dual solution. The corresponding primal-flow lifting conclusion does not follow from positivity in only some optimal flow.

f=pq\in E
\exists x^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(I)\text{ such that }x_f^*>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall y^*\in\operatorname{OptDual}(I),\ \bar c_f=0;\qquad \operatorname{OptDual}(I/f)\text{ lifts into }\operatorname{OptDual}(I)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Consistency and Rollout Improvement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines sequential consistency of the base heuristic and states its monotonicity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A base heuristic is sequentially consistent if, whenever its completion from \(P\) is \(\bar P\), then for every extension \(P^+\) fixing an additional arc set \(T\), its completion \(\bar P^+\) agrees with \(\bar P\) on every arc outside \(S\cup T\). Under this condition, every rollout iteration satisfies \(H(P^+)\le H(P)\). Consequently, the completed-solution costs are monotonically nonincreasing, and if \(x_0\) is the base heuristic's initial completed solution and \(x_t\) is the rollout output, then \(f(x_t)\le f(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A base heuristic is sequentially consistent when fixing additional decisions from its current completion does not change its remaining decisions. With such a heuristic, every rollout step has no greater heuristic cost than the preceding step, so the final rollout solution costs no more than the initial base-heuristic solution.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x_{ij}:(i,j)\in S\}\text{ is a partial solution completed by the base heuristic as }P\cup\bar P.
T\subseteq\mathcal A\setminus S\text{ is the next set of fixed arcs}.
\forall(i,j)\notin S\cup T,\;\bar x^+_{ij}=\bar x_{ij}\text{ whenever }P^+\text{ extends }P\text{ using the corresponding decisions}.
\text{The rollout iteration minimizes }H(P_y^+)\text{ over its considered assignments}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(P^+)\le H(P)\text{ at every iteration},\qquad f(x_t)\le f(x_0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic characterizations of basic solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizations for equality-inequality systems, standard-form systems, and nonnegative inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}P\\Q\end{pmatrix}\). (A) A feasible \(z\) for \(Px=b_0,\ Qx\le b_1\) is basic if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(M)=\operatorname{rank}(M_z^{=})\). (B) A feasible \(z\) for \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\) is basic if and only if the columns of \(A\) indexed by \(\{j:z_j>0\}\) are linearly independent. (C) A feasible \(z\) for \(Bx\le b,\ x\ge0\) is basic if and only if there exists a nonsingular square submatrix \(B'\) such that \(z\) is obtained by extending the unique solution of \(B'x'=b'\) with zero components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic solutions admit equivalent rank and support characterizations: active rows have full system rank in mixed equality-inequality form; positive-support columns are independent in standard form; and in a nonnegative inequality system the solution comes from a nonsingular square subsystem, extended by zeros.
assumptions_latex: z\text{ is feasible for the respective displayed linear system}
M=\begin{pmatrix}P\\Q\end{pmatrix}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}z\text{ basic for }(Px=b_0,Qx\le b_1)&\iff \operatorname{rank}(M)=\operatorname{rank}(M_z^{=}),\\ z\text{ basic for }(Ax=b,x\ge0)&\iff \{A_j:z_j>0\}\text{ is linearly independent},\\ z\text{ basic for }(Bx\le b,x\ge0)&\iff \exists B'\text{ nonsingular with }B'x'=b'\text{ uniquely and }z\text{ its zero extension}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced flow, feasible flow, and tree solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes equality-balanced flows from nonnegative feasible flows and spanning-tree-supported balanced solutions; a tree solution is not required to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flow \(x\) is balanced if it satisfies the balance equation at every node, without a sign restriction on its arc values. It is feasible if it is balanced and \(x_a\ge 0\) for every arc \(a\). Given a spanning tree \(T\), it is a tree solution if it is balanced and \(x_a=0\) for every arc \(a\notin T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced flow satisfies every node-balance equation and may have negative arc values. A feasible flow is a nonnegative balanced flow. Relative to a spanning tree, a tree solution is a balanced flow that is zero on every non-tree arc; it need not be feasible.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ assigns a real flow value to every network arc.}
T\text{ is a spanning tree when the tree-solution definition is applied.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is feasible}\iff x\text{ is balanced and }x_a\ge 0\ \forall a;\qquad x\text{ is a tree solution for }T\iff x\text{ is balanced and }x_a=0\ \forall a\notin T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Big-M equivalence theorem for minimum-cost flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A path-cost condition ensuring status and optimizer correspondence between an original flow problem and its artificial-arc Big-M version.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the original minimum-cost flow problem with $x\ge 0$ and its Big-$M$ version, suppose that for every simple path $P$ in the original graph, with forward and backward arc sets $P^+$ and $P^-$, respectively, $$2M>\sum_{(i,j)\in P^+}a_{ij}-\sum_{(i,j)\in P^-}a_{ij}.$$ If the original problem is feasible and not unbounded, the Big-$M$ problem has an optimum, every Big-$M$ optimum has zero flow on artificial arcs and restricts to an original optimum, and every original optimum extends by zero artificial flows to a Big-$M$ optimum. If the original problem is unbounded, the Big-$M$ problem is unbounded. If the original problem is infeasible, every feasible Big-$M$ solution has positive flow on at least one artificial arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If twice M exceeds the signed cost of every simple path, the Big-M reformulation preserves all optima when the original problem is feasible and not unbounded: artificial flows vanish, and extension or restriction gives the optimizer correspondence. Original unboundedness implies Big-M unboundedness, while original infeasibility forces every feasible Big-M solution to use an artificial arc positively.
assumptions_latex: 2M>\sum_{(i,j)\in P^+}a_{ij}-\sum_{(i,j)\in P^-}a_{ij}\quad\text{for every simple path }P
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}\text{Optimizer equivalence with zero artificial flow},&\text{if the original problem is feasible and not unbounded},\\\text{Big-$M$ unboundedness},&\text{if the original problem is unbounded},\\\text{positive artificial flow in every feasible Big-$M$ solution},&\text{if the original problem is infeasible}.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong basic solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, invariance, pointed case, and extension to mixed equality-inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R=\{x:Qx\le b\}\), a basic solution \(z\) is strong if the columns \(Q_j\) with \(z_j\ne0\) are linearly independent. This notion depends only on the nonempty polyhedron \(R\), since equivalent descriptions have the same nullspace, equal to the translation subspace of \(R\). If \(R\) is not pointed, it has infinitely many basic solutions; in particular, every solution of a system of linear equations is basic. If \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=n\), equivalently \(R\) is pointed, every basic solution is strong and the basic solutions are precisely vertices of \(R\). More generally, for \(Px=b_0,\ Qx\le b_1\), with \(M=\begin{pmatrix}P\\Q\end{pmatrix}\), a basic solution \(z\) is strong if and only if the columns of \(M\) indexed by \(\{j:z_j\ne0\}\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic solution is strong when the constraint-matrix columns on its nonzero support are linearly independent. The property is invariant under equivalent descriptions. A nonpointed polyhedron has infinitely many basic solutions, while in the pointed full-column-rank case every basic solution is strong and is a vertex. The same support-independence test uses the stacked matrix for mixed equality-inequality systems.
assumptions_latex: R=\{x:Qx\le b\}\ne\varnothing
z\in R\text{ is basic}
M=\begin{pmatrix}P\\Q\end{pmatrix}\text{ for the mixed-system characterization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{gathered}z\text{ strong}\iff \{Q_j:z_j\ne0\}\text{ is linearly independent},\\ R\text{ nonpointed}\Rightarrow R\text{ has infinitely many basic solutions},\\ \operatorname{rank}(Q)=n\iff R\text{ pointed}\Rightarrow \text{every basic solution is strong and is a vertex},\\ z\text{ strong for }(Px=b_0,Qx\le b_1)\iff \{M_j:z_j\ne0\}\text{ is linearly independent}.\end{gathered}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) prescribe node supplies, with positive entries denoting net production. The supply regime is balanced precisely when
\[\sum_{v\in V} b_v=0.\]
If a flow satisfies the conservation equations
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\qquad(v\in V),\]
then its prescribed supplies are balanced. Supply balance is necessary but, in the presence of arc bounds or missing connections, not sufficient for feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Supplies are balanced when their total is zero. This is necessary for flow conservation, although capacity restrictions or network connectivity may still make the model infeasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have weakly connected components \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\), and let \(B\) use the outflow-minus-inflow convention. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced minimum-cost network flow formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasible flows, records aggregate balance as necessary but not sufficient for feasibility, and distinguishes capacitated from uncapacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A) be directed, with supplies b_i, capacities u_{ij}\in[0,+\infty], and costs c_{ij}. A flow f is feasible if b_i+\sum_{j\in I(i)}f_{ji}=\sum_{j\in O(i)}f_{ij} for every i and 0\leq f_{ij}\leq u_{ij} for every arc. Every feasible flow satisfies \sum_i b_i=0; hence \sum_i b_i\neq0 implies infeasibility. Assuming \sum_i b_i=0, minimum-cost flow minimizes \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}c_{ij}f_{ij} over feasible flows. It is uncapacitated if all u_{ij}=+\infty and capacitated otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow satisfies node conservation and its nonnegative arc-capacity bounds. Aggregate supply must equal aggregate demand, although this condition alone need not ensure feasibility. Minimum-cost flow minimizes total linear arc cost; it is uncapacitated exactly when every upper capacity is infinite.
assumptions_latex: G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is directed}
u_{ij}\in[0,+\infty]\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A
\sum_{i\in\mathcal N}b_i=0\text{ for the stated minimum-cost model}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_f\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}c_{ij}f_{ij}:b_i+\sum_{j\in I(i)}f_{ji}=\sum_{j\in O(i)}f_{ij}\ \forall i,\ 0\leq f_{ij}\leq u_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacitated b-flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a capacitated flow realizing balanced vertex supplies and demands, together with the circulation and vertex-role terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a digraph, $u:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$, and $b:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\sum_{v\in V(G)}b(v)=0$. A $b$-flow in $(G,u)$ is a function $f:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ such that $f(e)\leq u(e)$ for every $e\in E(G)$ and $\sum_{e\in\delta^{+}(v)}f(e)-\sum_{e\in\delta^{-}(v)}f(e)=b(v)$ for every $v\in V(G)$. A $b$-flow with $b\equiv0$ is a circulation. If $b(v)>0$, then $v$ is a source and $b(v)$ is its supply; if $b(v)<0$, then $v$ is a sink and $|b(v)|$ is its demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a directed graph with nonnegative arc capacities and vertex balances summing to zero, a b-flow is a nonnegative capacity-feasible arc flow whose net outflow at each vertex equals that vertex's balance. Zero balances yield a circulation; positive-balance vertices are sources and negative-balance vertices are sinks.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). If
\[\sum_{v\in V}b_v\ne0,\]
then no vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) can satisfy
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\qquad(v\in V).\]
Thus an unbalanced supply vector makes the standard equality-constrained flow model infeasible, independently of costs and arc bounds. The converse fails: a balanced vector may remain infeasible because of lower bounds, upper bounds, or network cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero total supply makes exact node conservation impossible, regardless of costs or capacities. Zero total supply removes this obstruction but does not guarantee feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Node Balancing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Star augmentation that converts arbitrary supplies into a balanced extended instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), set \(B=\sum_{v\in V}b_v\) and add an auxiliary node \(r\) with supply \(b_r=-B\). Add an artificial arc \((v,r)\) for every \(b_v>0\) and \((r,v)\) for every \(b_v<0\), each with zero lower bound and capacity at least \(|b_v|\). Then
\[\sum_{v\in V\cup\{r\}}b_v=0,\]
and the artificial flow \(x_{vr}=b_v\) for \(b_v>0\), \(x_{rv}=-b_v\) for \(b_v<0\), with original arcs set to zero, satisfies every augmented balance equation. Artificial costs may be assigned separately to penalize their use.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one node with the opposite aggregate supply and suitable star arcs produces a balanced, feasible augmented instance; penalties can discourage artificial flow.

\(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) is arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented supply vector is balanced and admits the displayed artificial-star flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Circulation Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hoffman-type cut certificate under the outflow-minus-inflow balance convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, let \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(l\le u\), and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(b(V)=0\). A flow \(x\) with \(l\le x\le u\) and \(\operatorname{div}x=b\) exists if and only if, for every \(S\subseteq V\),
\[l(\delta^+(S))-u(\delta^-(S))\le b(S)\le u(\delta^+(S))-l(\delta^-(S)).\]
Consequently, any set \(S\) violating either inequality is a directly checkable infeasibility certificate; if no set violates them, the bounded-flow system is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded flow exists exactly when every vertex cut can carry its required net supply. Any cut violating the displayed lower or upper inequality certifies infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to the two cut inequalities for every \(S\subseteq V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Flow Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-vertex theorem for a finite capacitated network-flow polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. Suppose \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\) and \(l,u\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\) with \(l\le u\), and define
\[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:\operatorname{div}x=b,\ l\le x\le u\}.\]
If \(P\ne\varnothing\), then every vertex of \(P\) is integral. Hence, for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), whenever \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\) is finite, it has an optimal solution in \(\mathbb{Z}^{A}\). In particular, continuous relaxation does not destroy the existence of an integral optimum for integral network data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integral supplies and arc bounds, every vertex of the feasible flow polytope is integral, so every finite linear-cost optimum has an integral representative.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
\(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\) and \(l,u\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\) with \(l\le u\).
\(P\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{A}\), and every finite linear-cost minimum over \(P\) has an integral optimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fractional-Data Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the integral-flow conclusion when prescribed balances are fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{s,t\}\), \(A=\{a=(s,t)\}\), \(0\le x_a\le1\), and prescribe \(b_s=\tfrac12\), \(b_t=-\tfrac12\) under the net-outflow convention. The balance equations force \(x_a=\tfrac12\). Hence the feasible flow polytope is the singleton \(\{\tfrac12\}\) and contains no integral flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single arc required to carry one half unit gives a feasible polytope whose unique point is fractional, so fractional balance data need not admit an integral flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\{1/2\}\quad\text{and}\quad P\cap\mathbb Z^A=\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total-Unimodularity Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural matrix reason for integrality of bounded network-flow polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be the node-arc incidence matrix of a finite directed graph. Then \(B\) is totally unimodular, and adjoining signed identity rows preserves total unimodularity. Consequently the equality-and-bound system \[Bx=b,\qquad \ell\le x\le u\] has a totally unimodular coefficient matrix after equalities are written as paired inequalities. For integral \(b,\ell,u\), every basic feasible solution is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed incidence matrices remain totally unimodular when arc-bound rows are added, which makes every basic feasible network flow integral for integral data.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(b\in\mathbb Z^V\) and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^A\) with \(\ell\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ and the full equality-and-bound coefficient matrix are totally unimodular, so every basic feasible solution is integral.}
knowledge_statements.title: Total-Unimodularity Mechanism

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite \(G=(V,A)\), supplies \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), and finite bounds \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfying \(l\le u\), define \(b(S)=\sum_{v\in S}b_v\) for \(S\subseteq V\), and define \(q(F)=\sum_{a\in F}q_a\) for \(q\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) and \(F\subseteq A\). The system
\[\operatorname{div}x=b,\qquad l\le x\le u\]
is infeasible if and only if either \(b(V)\ne0\), or \(b(V)=0\) and some \(S\subseteq V\) satisfies
\[b(S)<l(\delta^+(S))-u(\delta^-(S))\]
or
\[b(S)>u(\delta^+(S))-l(\delta^-(S)).\]
Thus aggregate imbalance and a violated capacity cut are the two obstruction forms for this model. Costs play no role in determining feasibility.

Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), and suppose the minimum-cost flow model is feasible, with finite lower bounds and upper bounds \(u_a\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). Define
\[A_\infty=\{a\in A:u_a=+\infty\}.\]
Then

knowledge_statements.title: Pathology Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutually exclusive feasibility and boundedness classification for linear minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph, consider
\[\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:\operatorname{div}x=b,\ l\le x\le u\},\]
where \(l\) is finite and \(u\) may contain \(+\infty\). Exactly one of the following holds: the feasible set is empty; the feasible set is nonempty and the infimum is \(-\infty\); or the feasible set is nonempty and a finite minimum is attained. Hence infeasibility concerns only the constraints, whereas unboundedness presupposes feasibility and is witnessed by a negative-cost recession circulation. The two pathologies are logically disjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every linear minimum-cost flow instance is exactly one of infeasible, feasible but unbounded below, or feasible with an attained finite optimum. Infeasibility and unboundedness cannot coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(l_a\in\mathbb{R}\), \(u_a\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and \(l_a\le u_a\).
\(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of infeasibility, feasible unboundedness, or attainment of a finite optimum occurs.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncapacitated Transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear transshipment with nonnegative flows and no finite upper arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An uncapacitated transshipment instance consists of a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), and balanced supplies \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). Its optimization problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}}\ \sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_a\ge0\ (a\in A),\qquad \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\ (v\in V).\]
No arc has a finite upper bound. Nodes may supply, demand, or transship flow according as \(b_v\) is positive, negative, or zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncapacitated transshipment minimizes linear routing cost subject to nonnegative flows and node balances, with no finite upper arc capacities and zero aggregate supply.

\(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncapacitated minimum-cost transshipment model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static transshipment through intermediate cities, with nonnegative shipment variables and no finite arc upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For cities \(j=1,\ldots,n\), let \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) denote the amount shipped from \(i\) to \(j\) for \(i\ne j\), let \(a_j^*\) and \(b_j^*\) denote production and consumption at city \(j\), and let \(c_{ij}\) denote shipment cost. The transshipment problem is
\[
\min_{x\ge 0}\;\sum_{i\ne j}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{i\ne j}x_{ij}+a_j^*=\sum_{k\ne j}x_{jk}+b_j^*,\qquad j=1,\ldots,n.
\]
The net available and required amounts are
\[
a_j=a_j^*-\min\{a_j^*,b_j^*\},\qquad b_j=b_j^*-\min\{a_j^*,b_j^*\}.
\]
Each shipment-variable column of the balance matrix has one \(+1\) and one \(-1\); a slack column representing permitted surplus or shortage has one nonzero coefficient. The classical transportation model is a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-cost transshipment model allows goods to pass through intermediate cities. At each city, incoming shipments plus local production equal outgoing shipments plus local consumption. Cancelling local production against local consumption gives the net available and required amounts. Each shipment column has one plus-one and one minus-one balance coefficient. This formulation does not impose finite arc capacities, and the classical transportation model is a special case.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be a finite set of supply nodes, let \(J\) be a finite disjoint set of demand nodes, let \(A\subseteq I\times J\) be the permitted shipping arcs, and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\). For supplies \(s_i\ge0\) and demands \(d_j\ge0\), a balanced transportation problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}}\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=s_i\ (i\in I),\quad \sum_{i:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=d_j\ (j\in J),\quad x_{ij}\ge0\ ((i,j)\in A),\]
with \(\sum_{i\in I}s_i=\sum_{j\in J}d_j\). This is transshipment on a bipartite graph whose arcs run from supply nodes to demand nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transportation network is a bipartite transshipment model shipping prescribed supply to prescribed demand at minimum linear cost, with total supply equal to total demand.

\(A\subseteq I\times J\) is the permitted-route set.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-supply, unit-demand transportation model on a balanced bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite sets with \(|I|=|J|\), and let \(A\subseteq I\times J\) contain the allowed assignments. The linear assignment model is
\[\min\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=1\ (i\in I),\quad \sum_{i:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=1\ (j\in J),\quad x_{ij}\ge0.\]
It is a transportation problem with every supply and demand equal to one. Whenever feasible, its vertices are incidence vectors of perfect matchings, so a finite optimum has a binary optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assignment network is unit-supply transportation. Its feasible vertices encode perfect matchings, so the linear relaxation yields a binary optimum whenever one exists.
assumptions_latex: \(I,J\) are finite with \(|I|=|J|\).
\(A\subseteq I\times J\).
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment program is unit transportation, and every feasible vertex lies in \(\{0,1\}^{A}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Costed residual network and feasible-increment correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-network representation for capacitated minimum-cost flows, including cycle correspondence and the stated per-iteration search bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible flow $f$ on $G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ with $0\le f_{ij}\le u_{ij}$, an original arc $(i,j)$ of cost $c_{ij}$ induces a forward residual arc of capacity $u_{ij}-f_{ij}$ and cost $c_{ij}$ and a reverse residual arc of capacity $f_{ij}$ and cost $-c_{ij}$; zero-capacity arcs are deleted and residual supplies are zero. If $f+\bar f$ is another feasible flow, then $\bar f$ admits a representation as a nonnegative feasible residual circulation $\widetilde f$ of equal cost. Conversely, every feasible residual circulation induces an increment $\bar f$ for which $f+\bar f$ is feasible and costs are equal. Unsaturated cycles correspond, with equal cost, to directed residual cycles whose arcs have positive capacity. Consequently, negative unsaturated-cycle search reduces to negative directed-cycle search, giving $O(n^3)$ work per cycle-canceling iteration when the latter search is implemented in $O(n^3)$ time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow produces forward residual arcs for allowable increases and reverse residual arcs for allowable decreases, with the corresponding capacities and opposite costs. Every feasible flow change can be represented by a feasible residual circulation of the same cost, and every feasible residual circulation induces such a change; this need not be a unique representation. Unsaturated cycles correspond cost-preservingly to positive-capacity residual cycles, so an O(n^3) negative-cycle search gives O(n^3) work per cycle-canceling iteration.
assumptions_latex: $G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ is a capacitated costed network with the standard bounds $0\le f_{ij}\le u_{ij}$.
$f$ is feasible; for the forward construction, $f+\bar f$ is also feasible.
The directed negative-cycle subroutine has running time $O(n^3)$ for the stated iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f+\bar f\text{ feasible}\Rightarrow\exists\widetilde f\text{ feasible in the residual network with }c^{\mathsf T}\bar f=\widetilde c^{\mathsf T}\widetilde f;\quad \widetilde f\text{ feasible residual}\Rightarrow\exists\bar f:\ f+\bar f\text{ feasible and }c^{\mathsf T}\bar f=\widetilde c^{\mathsf T}\widetilde f.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Network for an Integer Convex-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction using discrete marginal costs and maximal constant-marginal-cost residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be an integer arc-flow vector satisfying \(0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\), with convex arc-cost functions \(C_{ij}\) defined on integer flow values. If \(x_{ij}<u_{ij}\), the residual network contains a forward arc \((i,j)\) of cost \(C_{ij}(x_{ij}+1)-C_{ij}(x_{ij})\). If \(x_{ij}>0\), it contains a reverse arc \((j,i)\) of cost \(C_{ij}(x_{ij}-1)-C_{ij}(x_{ij})\). Each residual arc receives the largest residual capacity over which its corresponding per-unit cost change remains constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Below capacity, an arc has a forward residual arc priced by the cost of adding one unit. Above zero flow, it has a reverse residual arc priced by the cost change from removing one unit. The residual capacity is the largest flow change over which that marginal cost remains constant.

0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in A
C_{ij}\text{ is a discrete convex arc-cost function}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(x)\text{ contains the stated marginal-cost residual arcs with maximal constant-marginal-cost capacities.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deficit of a Nonconservative Directed-Edge Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform lifting of a nonconservative cost function on a digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D=(V,A) and let c:A\to\mathbb R be nonconservative. A lift by \alpha replaces c with c+\alpha on every edge. The deficit \varepsilon(c) is the smallest positive \varepsilon such that c^+=c+\varepsilon is conservative; equivalently, the minimum-cost directed circuit under c^+ has cost zero. A directed circuit C has mean cost \widetilde c(C)/|C|, and lifting by \alpha increases every directed-circuit mean by \alpha.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly lifting a directed-edge cost adds the same value to every edge. The deficit of a nonconservative cost is the smallest positive lift that makes it conservative, equivalently the lift at which the cheapest directed circuit has cost zero. A circuit's mean is its total cost divided by its length, and a uniform lift raises every circuit mean by that amount.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)
c:A\to\mathbb R\text{ is not conservative}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon(c)=\min\{\varepsilon>0:c+\varepsilon\text{ is conservative}\},\qquad \operatorname{mean}_{c+\alpha}(C)=\operatorname{mean}_c(C)+\alpha

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible-Flow Correspondence through a Residual Network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the feasibility equivalence and additive cost identity relative to a baseline feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^{\circ}\) be a feasible baseline flow and let \(G(x^{\circ})\) be its residual network. For each original arc \((i,j)\), define the corresponding residual flow \(x'\) by \[x'_{ij}-x'_{ji}=x_{ij}-x_{ij}^{\circ},\qquad x'_{ij}x'_{ji}=0.\] Then \(x\) is feasible in \(G\) if and only if \(x'\) is feasible in \(G(x^{\circ})\), and \[cx=c'x'+cx^{\circ}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a feasible baseline flow, an original flow is feasible exactly when its corresponding residual adjustment is feasible; the original cost is the baseline cost plus the residual-adjustment cost.
assumptions_latex: \(x^{\circ}\) is a feasible flow in \(G\), and \(G(x^{\circ})\) is its costed residual network.
\(x'_{ij}-x'_{ji}=x_{ij}-x_{ij}^{\circ}\) and \(x'_{ij}x'_{ji}=0\) for every original arc \((i,j)\).
Forward and reverse residual arcs have costs \(c_{ij}\) and \(-c_{ij}\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible in }G\iff x'\text{ is feasible in }G(x^{\circ}),\qquad cx=c'x'+cx^{\circ}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Path Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint imbalance transfer induced by augmenting along a residual path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a feasible bounded flow \(x\), form its residual network by assigning a forward residual arc capacity \(u_a-x_a\) and cost \(c_a\), and a reverse residual arc capacity \(x_a-l_a\) and cost \(-c_a\), whenever the respective capacity is positive. If \(P\) is a directed residual path from \(s\) to \(t\) and
\[0<\varepsilon\le\min_{e\in P}r_e,\]
augmenting \(\varepsilon\) along \(P\) preserves all arc bounds and every internal node balance, increases divergence at \(s\) by \(\varepsilon\), decreases divergence at \(t\) by \(\varepsilon\), and changes cost by \(\varepsilon\sum_{e\in P}\bar c_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmenting within a residual path transfers a chosen flow amount from its start to its end, preserves internal balances and bounds, and changes cost by path cost times the amount.

\(P\) is a directed residual path from \(s\) to \(t\).
\(0<\varepsilon\le\min_{e\in P}r_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual-path augmentation preserves bounds and internal balances while changing endpoint divergences by \(+\varepsilon\) and \(-\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a directed cycle in the residual network of \(x\), and let \(r_e>0\) be the residual capacity of each \(e\in C\). For any \(0<\theta\le \min_{e\in C}r_e\), augment \(\theta\) on forward residual arcs of \(C\) and subtract \(\theta\) on reverse residual arcs. The resulting flow \(x'=x+\theta\chi_C\) satisfies \(Bx'=Bx=b\) and \(l\le x'\le u\). Moreover, \[c^{\mathsf T}x'-c^{\mathsf T}x=\theta\sum_{e\in C}c_e^R=\theta c^R(C).\] Thus residual-cycle augmentation is circulation-preserving, and a negative-cost residual cycle gives a feasible strict cost decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmenting within residual capacities around a directed residual cycle preserves feasibility; its cost change equals the augmentation amount times the cycle's residual cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an oriented augmenting path P, let P^{+} and P^{-} be its forward and backward arcs. An augmenting cycle is a closed augmenting path, and its cost is computed by the same signed sum with respect to the chosen orientation.

An augmenting cycle is a closed augmenting path and uses the same signed rule for a chosen orientation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal potentials from residual shortest-path distances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to an optimal minimum-cost flow when the required residual shortest-path distances are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x^*$ be an optimal minimum-cost flow, let $G(x^*)$ be its residual network with residual-arc costs $c_{ij}$, and suppose shortest-path distances $d(v)$ from a fixed node are defined for every relevant node. Then $G(x^*)$ has no negative-cost cycle. Setting $\pi(v)=-d(v)$ gives $c_{ij}^{\pi}=c_{ij}-\pi(i)+\pi(j)\ge 0$ for every $(i,j)\in G(x^*)$, and $\pi$ is an optimal set of node potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an optimal minimum-cost flow, compute shortest-path distances in its residual network using arc costs as lengths and negate those distances. The resulting potentials have nonnegative reduced cost on every residual arc and are optimal.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is an optimal feasible minimum-cost flow}
G(x^*)\text{ is the residual network of }x^*
d(v)\text{ is a finite shortest-path distance from a fixed node to every relevant }v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi=-d\implies c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge 0\ \forall(i,j)\in G(x^*),\quad \pi\text{ is optimal}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conformal path component of \(d\) is a vector \(h=\theta\chi_P\), where \(\theta>0\) and \(P\) is a simple directed path from \(s\) to \(t\) using only residual arcs selected by the sign of \(d\): a forward residual copy of \(a\) may occur only if \(d_a>0\), and a reverse copy only if \(d_a<0\). It must satisfy \(|h_a|\le |d_a|\) for every original arc \(a\). Consequently, \(h_a d_a\ge0\), \(|h_a|\le|d_a|\), and \[Bh=\theta(\mathbf e_t-\mathbf e_s).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conformal cycle component of \(d\) is a vector \(h=\theta\chi_C\), where \(\theta>0\) and \(C\) is a simple directed cycle in the signed residual support of \(d\). Thus a forward residual copy of an original arc \(a\) can occur only when \(d_a>0\), and a reverse copy only when \(d_a<0\); additionally, \(|h_a|\le |d_a|\) for every \(a\). Since \(C\) is a cycle, \[Bh=0.\] Hence the component is a circulation and is conformal to \(d\) arcwise.
