children.top_down_role: Support and orientation restrictions governing decomposition of flows or flow differences.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite, \(B\) is its node-arc incidence matrix, and \(d\in\mathbb R^A\).
The positive and negative entries of \(d\) are represented on forward and reverse copies in a directed signed-support graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist finitely many conformal path components \(p^1,\ldots,p^k\) and conformal cycle components \(z^1,\ldots,z^m\) such that \[d=\sum_{i=1}^k p^i+\sum_{j=1}^m z^j.\] Every component \(h\) is sign-compatible with \(d\), meaning \(h_a d_a\ge0\) and \(|h_a|\le|d_a|\) for all \(a\in A\). Each \(z^j\) satisfies \(Bz^j=0\), while the path boundaries sum to the total imbalance: \[\sum_{i=1}^k Bp^i=Bd.\] If \(Bd=0\), the decomposition may be chosen with cycle components only.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite signed arc adjustment decomposes into arcwise sign-compatible path and cycle flows; paths realize its node imbalance, while cycles are circulations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constructive Support-Elimination Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive decomposition in the finite directed signed-support graph, with component-count, runtime, and integrality guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Orient one copy of every arc \(a\) with \(d_a\ne0\) according to the sign of \(d_a\), and give it amount \(y_a=|d_a|\). Repeatedly subtract the bottleneck amount from a directed simple cycle in the positive support. After the support becomes acyclic, repeatedly subtract the bottleneck amount from a maximal directed path in the positive support. Each extracted vector is conformal to \(d\), and every extraction deletes at least one currently positive arc. Thus \[d=\sum_{i=1}^{q}h^i,\qquad q\le |\operatorname{supp}(d)|,\qquad h^i\sqsubseteq d.\] A direct implementation that searches the current support for each component runs in \(O(|\operatorname{supp}(d)|(|V|+|A|))\) time. If \(d\in\mathbb Z^A\), every bottleneck and component can be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated bottleneck extraction of supported cycles and then maximal paths constructs a conformal decomposition, removes an arc at every step, uses at most one component per initially nonzero arc, and preserves integrality.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(d\in\mathbb R^A\).
Each nonzero coordinate of \(d\) is represented by a nonnegative arc in its signed direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d=\sum_{i=1}^{q}h^i,\quad q\le |\operatorname{supp}(d)|,\quad h^i\sqsubseteq d;\qquad d\in\mathbb Z^A\Longrightarrow h^i\in\mathbb Z^A.

notation.meaning: nonnegative vector on the directed signed-support graph
h is sign-compatible with and coordinatewise dominated by d
set of arcs where d is nonzero

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasible flow \(x\) is optimal if and only if \[c^R(C)\ge0\quad\text{for every directed cycle }C\text{ in }G_x^R.\] In particular, a directed residual cycle with \(c^R(C)<0\), together with any augmentation \(0<\theta\le\min_{e\in C}r_e\), is a directly checkable nonoptimality certificate because it produces a feasible flow of cost \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\theta c^R(C)<c^{\mathsf T}x\). Conversely, absence of such a cycle certifies global minimum cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow is minimum-cost exactly when its residual network has no negative-cost directed cycle; any such cycle certifies nonoptimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-cost cycle-canceling algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational algorithm for a capacitated minimum-cost flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a feasible flow $f$. While there is an unsaturated negative-cost cycle $C$, let $\delta(C)$ be its augmentation limit. If $\delta(C)<\infty$, replace $f$ by $f+\delta(C)h^C$ and repeat. If $\delta(C)=\infty$, terminate with optimal value $-\infty$. If no unsaturated negative-cost cycle exists, terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a feasible flow and repeatedly augment as far as possible around an unsaturated negative-cost cycle. A finite augmentation produces another feasible flow; an infinite augmentation limit certifies cost unbounded below; absence of such a cycle terminates the method.
assumptions_latex: $f$ is a feasible flow in a capacitated costed network.
$C$ is an unsaturated cycle of negative cost when an augmentation is performed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(C)<\infty\Rightarrow f+\delta(C)h^C\text{ is the next feasible iterate};\quad \delta(C)=\infty\Rightarrow \inf c^{\mathsf T}f=-\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary network and negative cycle for a feasible flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-network construction for the conventional linear-arc-cost minimum-cost-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible flow \(\xi:A\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(G_\xi=(V,A_\xi)\), where \(A_\xi=A_\xi^*\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_\xi^*\), \(A_\xi^*=\{a\in A\mid \xi(a)<\bar c(a)\}\), and \(B_\xi^*=\{\bar a\mid a\in A,\ \underline c(a)<\xi(a)\}\), with \(\bar a\) denoting the reverse of \(a\). Define \(\ell_\xi(a)=\gamma(a)\) for \(a\in A_\xi^*\), and \(\ell_\xi(a)=-\gamma(\bar a)\) for \(a\in B_\xi^*\) with \(\bar a\in A\). Then \((G_\xi,\ell_\xi)\) is the auxiliary network. A negative cycle is a directed cycle having negative total \(\ell_\xi\)-length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The auxiliary network of a feasible flow contains a forward arc when its upper capacity is not saturated and a reverse arc when the corresponding original arc is above its lower bound. Forward lengths equal the original costs and reverse lengths are their negatives. A negative cycle has negative total length.
assumptions_latex: \(\xi:A\to\mathbb{R}\) is feasible for the conventional linear-arc-cost minimum-cost-flow problem \(\mathrm{MCFP}_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G_\xi,\ell_\xi)\) is the associated auxiliary network, and its negative cycles are precisely its directed cycles of negative total \(\ell_\xi\)-length.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Difference of Two b-Flows as a Residual Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For two feasible b-flows, records their signed arcwise difference on the bidirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,u,b,c)$ be a minimum-cost-flow instance and let $f,f'$ be $b$-flows in $(G,u)$. For each $e\in E(G)$, define $g(e)=\max\{0,f'(e)-f(e)\}$ and $g(\overleftarrow e)=\max\{0,f(e)-f'(e)\}$. Then $g$ is a circulation on $\overleftrightarrow G$, $g(a)=0$ for every $a\notin E(G_f)$, and $c(g)=c(f')-c(f)$.

$f$ and $f'$ are $b$-flows in $(G,u)$.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an original arc \(a=(v,w)\), define \(\bar c_a=c_a+\pi_v-\pi_w\). Its forward residual copy, present when \(x_a<u_a\), has reduced cost \(\bar c_a\); its reverse copy, present when \(x_a>l_a\), has reduced cost \(-\bar c_a\). Hence a residual reduced-cost certificate consists of the verifiable inequalities \[x_a<u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\ge0,\qquad x_a>l_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\le0.\] Equivalently, \(\bar c_e^R\ge0\) for every residual arc \(e\), which certifies that \(x\) is minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute reduced costs on every available forward and reverse residual arc; their nonnegativity is an arcwise certificate that the feasible flow is optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Reduced-Cost Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following conditions are equivalent: \[(i)\quad c^R(C)\ge0\text{ for every directed cycle }C\subseteq G_x^R;\] \[(ii)\quad \exists\pi\in\mathbb R^V\text{ such that }\bar c_e^R=c_e^R+\pi_v-\pi_w\ge0\text{ for every }e=(v,w)\in G_x^R.\] For every directed residual walk \(W\) from \(s\) to \(t\), reduced costs satisfy \[\sum_{e\in W}\bar c_e^R=\sum_{e\in W}c_e^R+\pi_s-\pi_t.\] Thus potentials change path costs only by endpoint terms and leave every cycle cost unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual network has no negative directed cycle exactly when node potentials can make all residual reduced costs nonnegative; cycle costs remain unchanged.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shortest-Path Construction of a Feasible Potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive realization of the finite difference-constraint correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the finite residual digraph \(G_x^R=(V,E^R)\) has no negative directed cycle. Add a vertex \(s\) with a zero-cost arc \((s,v)\) to every \(v\in V\), and let \(d(v)\) be the shortest-path distance from \(s\) to \(v\). Then \(\pi_v=d(v)\) satisfies \[c_e^R+\pi_v-\pi_w\ge0\qquad\text{for every residual arc }e=(v,w).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When no negative residual cycle exists, shortest-path distances from an added zero-cost source construct a feasible reduced-cost potential.
assumptions_latex: \(G_x^R\) is a finite residual digraph.
\(G_x^R\) contains no negative-cost directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi_v=d(v)\implies c_e^R+\pi_v-\pi_w\ge0\quad\forall e=(v,w)\in E^R.

notation.meaning: shortest-path distance from the added source to vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Network Complementary Slackness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded linear-flow complementary slackness in reduced-cost form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonfixed arc \(a\) with \(l_a<u_a\), network complementary slackness requires \[x_a=l_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\ge0,\qquad l_a<x_a<u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a=0,\qquad x_a=u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\le0.\] If \(l_a=u_a\), that fixed arc imposes no reduced-cost sign restriction. A feasible flow \(x\) is minimum-cost if and only if there exists \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfying these conditions. Equivalently, every residual arc has nonnegative reduced cost under \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow is optimal exactly when suitable node potentials make reduced costs nonnegative at lower bounds, zero in arc interiors, and nonpositive at upper bounds on nonfixed arcs; fixed arcs impose no sign restriction.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\).
For \(a=(v,w)\), define \(\bar c_a=c_a+\pi_v-\pi_w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) and \(\pi\) certify optimality exactly when the reduced-cost sign matches each nonfixed arc's bound status, while fixed arcs impose no sign restriction.

notation.meaning: reduced cost of original arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network complementary slackness for bounded arc flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise complementary-slackness conditions for linear minimum-cost flow with lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A capacity-feasible flow-price pair (x,p) satisfies complementary slackness if, for every (i,j)\in\mathcal A, x_{ij}<c_{ij}\Rightarrow p_i-p_j\le a_{ij} and b_{ij}<x_{ij}\Rightarrow p_i-p_j\ge a_{ij}. Equivalently, x_{ij}\in\arg\min_{b_{ij}\le z\le c_{ij}}(a_{ij}+p_j-p_i)z for every arc. Consequently, b_{ij}<x_{ij}<c_{ij} implies p_i=a_{ij}+p_j; p_i>a_{ij}+p_j implies x_{ij}=c_{ij}; and p_i<a_{ij}+p_j implies x_{ij}=b_{ij}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacity-feasible flow and node-price pair satisfies network complementary slackness when each arc flow minimizes its reduced-cost term over its lower-to-upper capacity interval.
assumptions_latex: b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A,\quad x_{ij}\in\arg\min_{b_{ij}\le z\le c_{ij}}(a_{ij}+p_j-p_i)z.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary-slackness certificate for multicommodity path-flow optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible path flows satisfying positive commodity demands and shared arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be feasible for the capacitated path-flow formulation, with \(d^k>0\) for each commodity. Let \(w_{ij}\ge 0\) be shared arc-capacity prices and \(\sigma^k\) the demand-constraint dual variables, and define \(c_P^{\sigma,w}=c^k(P)+\sum_{(i,j)\in P}w_{ij}-\sigma^k\). Then \(f\) is optimal if and only if some \((w,\sigma)\) satisfies \(w_{ij}(\sum_k\sum_{P\in\mathbf P^k}\delta_{ij}(P)f(P)-u_{ij})=0\) for every arc, \(c_P^{\sigma,w}\ge 0\) for every commodity path, and \(c_P^{\sigma,w}f(P)=0\) for every commodity path. Consequently, \(\sigma^k\) is the \(s^k\)-to-\(t^k\) shortest-path distance under costs \(c_{ij}^k+w_{ij}\), and every positive-flow path for commodity \(k\) is shortest under those costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible multicommodity path flow is optimal exactly when capacity prices and commodity prices satisfy capacity complementarity, all path reduced costs are nonnegative, and every used path has zero reduced cost. With positive demand, each commodity price is its modified-cost shortest-path distance and every used path is shortest.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is feasible for the capacitated path-flow multicommodity formulation}
d^k>0\quad\forall k
w_{ij}\ge 0\quad\forall(i,j)\in A
c_P^{\sigma,w}=c^k(P)+\sum_{(i,j)\in P}w_{ij}-\sigma^k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is optimal}\iff\begin{cases}w_{ij}(\sum_k\sum_{P\in\mathbf P^k}\delta_{ij}(P)f(P)-u_{ij})=0,&\forall(i,j)\in A,\\c_P^{\sigma,w}\ge0,&\forall k,\ P\in\mathbf P^k,\\c_P^{\sigma,w}f(P)=0,&\forall k,\ P\in\mathbf P^k.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary-slackness characterization of optimal network flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient primal-dual optimality conditions for uncapacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem, \(\mathbf f\) and \(\mathbf p\) are respectively optimal primal and dual solutions if and only if \(\mathbf A\mathbf f=\mathbf b\), \(\mathbf f\ge0\), and, for every arc \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\), \(p_i-p_j\le c_{ij}\) and \(f_{ij}(c_{ij}-p_i+p_j)=0\). Equivalently, every positive-flow arc satisfies \(p_i-p_j=c_{ij}\), while an arc with \(p_i-p_j<c_{ij}\) carries zero flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow and feasible node-potential vector are jointly optimal exactly when every positive-flow arc has zero reduced cost, or equivalently every arc with positive reduced cost carries no flow.
assumptions_latex: The network-flow problem is uncapacitated.
\(\mathbf f\) and \(\mathbf p\) have the primal-flow and dual-potential dimensions of the problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mathbf f,\mathbf p)\text{ is primal-dual optimal}\iff \mathbf A\mathbf f=\mathbf b,\ \mathbf f\ge0,\ p_i-p_j\le c_{ij},\ f_{ij}(c_{ij}-p_i+p_j)=0\ \forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network Complementary-Slackness Optimality Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise primal-dual optimality characterization for capacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible flow \(x^*\) is optimal for the minimum-cost flow problem if and only if there exist node potentials \(\pi\) such that, for every arc \((i,j)\in A\), \[c_{ij}^{\pi}>0\implies x_{ij}^*=0,\qquad 0<x_{ij}^*<u_{ij}\implies c_{ij}^{\pi}=0,\qquad c_{ij}^{\pi}<0\implies x_{ij}^*=u_{ij}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible capacitated minimum-cost flow is optimal exactly when some node potentials satisfy the arcwise complementary-slackness rules: positive reduced cost forces zero flow, an interior flow forces zero reduced cost, and negative reduced cost forces flow to capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is feasible for a minimum-cost flow problem with arc capacities \(u_{ij}\).
\(c_{ij}^{\pi}\) is the reduced cost induced by node potentials \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\text{ is optimal}\iff \exists\pi\;\forall(i,j)\in A:\;(c_{ij}^{\pi}>0\Rightarrow x_{ij}^*=0),\;(0<x_{ij}^*<u_{ij}\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}=0),\;(c_{ij}^{\pi}<0\Rightarrow x_{ij}^*=u_{ij}).\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary slackness for uncapacitated minimum-cost flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-specific complementary-slackness implications for a primal-feasible flow and dual-feasible node potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf f\) be primal feasible and \(\mathbf p\) dual feasible for an uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem. For every node \(i\), \(p_i\ne0\Rightarrow[\mathbf A\mathbf f]_i=b_i\), which is automatic because primal feasibility requires \(\mathbf A\mathbf f=\mathbf b\). For every arc \((i,j)\), \(f_{ij}>0\Rightarrow p_i-p_j=c_{ij}\). Equivalently, \(p_i-p_j<c_{ij}\Rightarrow f_{ij}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive-flow arc has zero reduced cost, while a strict dual inequality forces zero flow. The node-balance implication is automatic for a feasible flow.

\(\mathbf f\ge0\)
\(p_i-p_j\le c_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((x,\pi)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-price-optimal when \[\bar c_e^R:=c_e^R+\pi_v-\pi_w\ge-\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every residual arc }e=(v,w).\] For every feasible comparison flow \(y\), the signed adjustment \(y-x\) can be represented in the residual network, and the potential terms cancel because \(B(y-x)=0\). Consequently, \[c^{\mathsf T}x-c^{\mathsf T}y\le\varepsilon\lVert y-x\rVert_1.\] At \(\varepsilon=0\), this reduces to exact residual reduced-cost optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every residual reduced cost is at least minus epsilon, the flow's cost gap to any feasible comparison is bounded by epsilon times their arcwise distance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure at the Integral Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure boundary for the strict integral-cost exactness threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\ge2\), there is an \(n\)-vertex residual directed cycle of integral total cost \(-1\) and a potential vector for which every residual arc on the cycle has reduced cost \(-1/n\). Thus a feasible flow can be \((1/n)\)-price-optimal while remaining nonoptimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality at epsilon equal to one over the number of vertices does not guarantee exact optimality, even with integral costs.
assumptions_latex: The residual cycle has positive residual capacity and integral total cost \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon=1/n\text{ need not imply exact optimality.}

notation.meaning: number of vertices and arcs in the residual cycle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral-Cost Exactness Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict tolerance threshold converting approximate price optimality into exact optimality for integral linear costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n=|V|\). If all arc costs are integral and a feasible flow \(x\) admits potentials satisfying \(\bar c_e^R\ge-\varepsilon\) on every residual arc for some \(0\le\varepsilon<1/n\), then \(x\) is minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integral costs, epsilon-price-optimality implies exact optimality whenever epsilon is strictly less than one over the number of vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for a finite bounded linear minimum-cost flow problem.
All original arc costs are integral.
\(\bar c_e^R\ge-\varepsilon\) for every residual arc, where \(0\le\varepsilon<1/|V|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is minimum-cost.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-complementary slackness for capacitated flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate complementary-slackness conditions for a capacity-feasible minimum-cost flow and node prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A capacity-feasible flow vector \(x\) and a price vector \(p\) satisfy \(\epsilon\)-complementary slackness if, for every arc \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\), \[x_{ij}<c_{ij}\implies p_i-p_j\le a_{ij}+\epsilon,\qquad b_{ij}<x_{ij}\implies p_i-p_j\ge a_{ij}-\epsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacity-feasible flow and price vector satisfy epsilon-complementary slackness when every arc below its upper bound satisfies the approximate upper price inequality and every arc above its lower bound satisfies the approximate lower price inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-optimal flow or pseudoflow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate complementary-slackness conditions for capacitated minimum-cost flow, including the residual-network representation and exact-limit boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\epsilon>0\), a capacitated flow or pseudoflow \(x\) is \(\epsilon\)-optimal if there exists a node-potential vector \(\pi\) such that, for every arc \((i,j)\), \(c_{ij}^{\pi}>\epsilon\Rightarrow x_{ij}=0\), \(-\epsilon\le c_{ij}^{\pi}\le\epsilon\Rightarrow 0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\), and \(c_{ij}^{\pi}< -\epsilon\Rightarrow x_{ij}=u_{ij}\). Equivalently, \(c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge-\epsilon\) for every residual arc \((i,j)\in G(x)\). At the boundary \(\epsilon=0\), the conditions become exact network complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated flow or pseudoflow is epsilon-optimal if suitable node potentials make positive-reduced-cost arcs beyond epsilon empty, negative-reduced-cost arcs below minus epsilon saturated, and all remaining arcs capacity-feasible. Equivalently, every residual arc has reduced cost at least minus epsilon. At epsilon zero this becomes exact network complementary slackness.

0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\quad\text{for every arc }(i,j)
c_{ij}^{\pi}\text{ is the reduced cost under node potentials }\pi
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is }\epsilon\text{-optimal}\iff \exists\pi\;\forall(i,j)\in G(x),\ c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge-\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.title: Node–Arc Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Head-positive incidence convention for finite directed networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The node–arc incidence matrix of \(G\) is \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\). For a nonloop arc \(a\), its entries are \[B_{v,a}=\begin{cases}-1,&v=\operatorname{tail}(a),\\1,&v=\operatorname{head}(a),\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\] while a loop has a zero column. Thus, for every arc-flow vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\), \((Bx)_v\) is total inflow minus total outflow at \(v\), and \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}B=0\). If the underlying undirected graph has \(q\) connected components, then \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=|V|-q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonloop directed incidence column has minus one at its tail and plus one at its head, while a loop has a zero column. Matrix multiplication gives inflow minus outflow, all columns sum to zero, and a graph with q weakly connected components has incidence-matrix rank |V|-q.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph, and loops are represented by zero columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R^A\), \((Bx)_v\) equals inflow minus outflow at node \(v\), \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}B=0\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=|V|-q\) when \(G\) has \(q\) weakly connected components.

notation.meaning: tail and head of arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Image and Circulation Spaces of an Incidence Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise linear spaces represented by a finite directed node–arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the weak components of \(G\) have vertex sets \(V_1,\ldots,V_q\), then \[\operatorname{im}B=\left\{b\in\mathbb R^V:\sum_{v\in V_i}b_v=0\text{ for every }i\right\}.\] Its kernel \(\ker B=\{x:Bx=0\}\) is the signed circulation space, and \[\dim\ker B=|A|-|V|+q.\] Zero loop columns contribute independent circulation coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The image consists exactly of balance vectors summing to zero on every weak component, while the kernel is the circulation space of dimension arcs minus vertices plus components.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with \(q\) weakly connected components.
\(B\) has minus one at each nonloop arc tail and plus one at its head.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{im}B=\{b:\sum_{v\in V_i}b_v=0\ \forall i\}\) and \(\dim\ker B=|A|-|V|+q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transpose as the Node-Potential Difference Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjoint representation associated with the head-positive incidence convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every node vector \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) and nonloop arc \(a=(v,w)\), \[(B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_a=\pi_w-\pi_v.\] The coordinate of a loop is zero. Moreover, \[\ker B^{\mathsf T}=\{\pi:\pi\text{ is constant on every weak component of }G\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transpose maps node potentials to head-minus-tail differences, and its kernel consists of potentials constant on each weak component.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the head-positive incidence matrix of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_{(v,w)}=\pi_w-\pi_v\), and \(B^{\mathsf T}\pi=0\) exactly when \(\pi\) is componentwise constant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bidirected graph and bidirected network flow problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the signed incidence convention, including the optional same-node double-end case, and the associated capacitated integer minimum-cost flow model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bidirected graph permits each end of an arc to be independently a head or a tail. Its node--arc incidence matrix $A=(a_{ij})$ is given by $a_{ij}=1$ when arc $j$ has a tail at node $i$, $a_{ij}=-1$ when it has a head there, and $a_{ij}=0$ otherwise; an arc having two tails or two heads at the same node may instead contribute $2$ or $-2$. A bidirected network flow problem has the form $\min\{\sum_j \alpha_jx_j:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le c,\ x\in\mathbb Z^m\}$, where $\alpha_j$ is the unit arc cost, $c_j$ is the arc capacity, and $b_i$ is the net supply when nonnegative or net demand when nonpositive at node $i$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bidirected graph allows either endpoint of an arc to be a head or a tail. Its incidence entry is 1 for a tail, −1 for a head, and 0 otherwise; two coincident tails or heads may contribute 2 or −2. A bidirected network flow minimizes total arc cost over nonnegative integer flows satisfying the incidence balance equations and arc-capacity bounds, with each balance component representing net supply or demand.
assumptions_latex: A=(a_{ij})\text{ is the incidence matrix of a bidirected graph}
\alpha\in\mathbb R^m,\quad b\in\mathbb Z^r,\quad c\in\mathbb Z_+^m
x\in\mathbb Z_+^m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_jx_j:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le c,\ x\in\mathbb Z^m\right\}\text{ is a bidirected network flow problem.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Leaf-Elimination Construction of a Tree-Supported Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction for balanced node requirements on a directed spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $T$ be a directed spanning tree on $\mathcal N$, and let $s_i$ be node requirements satisfying $\sum_{i\in\mathcal N}s_i=0$. Initialize $R=T$, $x=0$, and $w_i=s_i$. While $R$ has more than one node, choose a leaf $i$ with neighbor $j$. If $(i,j)$ is its incident arc, set $x_{ij}:=w_i$ and $w_j:=w_j+w_i$; if $(j,i)$ is its incident arc, set $x_{ji}:=-w_i$ and $w_j:=w_j-w_i$. Delete $i$ and its incident arc from $R$. At termination, $x$ is the flow supported on $T$ corresponding to the node requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize each node's residual requirement with its given requirement. Repeatedly determine the flow on a leaf's only incident arc, transfer the residual to its neighbor with the appropriate sign, and delete the leaf. For balanced requirements, the resulting tree-supported flow satisfies the node balances.

\sum_{i\in\mathcal N}s_i=0.
R=T,\quad x=0,\quad w_i=s_i\quad\forall i\in\mathcal N.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Upon termination, }x\text{ is the flow supported on }T\text{ corresponding to the node requirements }s.

knowledge_statements.title: Total Unimodularity Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total unimodularity of directed node–arc incidence matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every square submatrix \(M\) of the directed node–arc incidence matrix \(B\), \[\det(M)\in\{-1,0,1\}.\] Therefore \(B\) is totally unimodular. Total unimodularity is preserved by deleting rows or columns, transposing, duplicating rows or columns, and multiplying a row or column by \(-1\). In particular, deleting one incidence row from each weakly connected component produces a full-row-rank totally unimodular reduced incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every square minor of a directed node–arc incidence matrix is zero, plus one, or minus one, so the matrix is totally unimodular; deleting one row per weakly connected component yields a full-row-rank totally unimodular reduced incidence matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the node–arc incidence matrix of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every square subdeterminant of \(B\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\); hence \(B\) is totally unimodular.

notation.meaning: an arbitrary square submatrix of B

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signed-Column Certificate for Total Unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural total-unimodularity certificate covering directed incidence matrices and their submatrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\{0,1,-1\}^{m\times n}\). If every column contains at most one \(+1\) and at most one \(-1\), then \(M\) is totally unimodular. In particular, every directed node–arc incidence matrix and every matrix obtained from it by deleting rows or columns satisfy this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-plus-minus-one matrix with at most one plus one and at most one minus one in each column is totally unimodular; directed incidence matrices satisfy this condition.
assumptions_latex: Every column of \(M\) has at most one \(+1\) and at most one \(-1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential Min-Max Formula for Minimum-Cost Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual potential representation with separate primal and dual integrality conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a digraph $D=(V,A)$ with bounds $f\le g$ and costs $c$, assuming a feasible circulation exists, define $c_\pi(uv)=c(uv)-\pi(v)+\pi(u)$. Then
$\min\{cx:f\le x\le g,\ x\text{ is a circulation}\}=\max_{\pi:V\to\mathbb R_+}\left(\sum_{c_\pi(uv)>0}f(uv)c_\pi(uv)+\sum_{c_\pi(uv)<0}g(uv)c_\pi(uv)\right).$
If $f,g$ are integral, a primal optimum may be chosen integral; if $c$ is integral, a dual optimum $\pi$ may be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum cost of a bounded feasible circulation equals a maximum over nonnegative vertex potentials, with lower bounds contributing on positive reduced-cost arcs and upper bounds on negative reduced-cost arcs. Integral bounds yield an integral optimal circulation, and integral costs yield an integral optimal potential.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph}
f,g,c:A\to\mathbb R
f\le g
\{x:f\le x\le g,\ x\text{ a circulation}\}\ne\varnothing
\pi:V\to\mathbb R_+
c_\pi(uv)=c(uv)-\pi(v)+\pi(u)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{cx:f\le x\le g,\ x\text{ a circulation}\}=\max_{\pi}\left\{\sum_{c_\pi>0}fc_\pi+\sum_{c_\pi<0}gc_\pi\right\},\quad f,g\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow x^*\in\mathbb Z^A,\quad c\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow\pi^*\in\mathbb Z^V\text{ may be chosen}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in P\), let \(F(x)=\{e\in E:\ell_e<x_e<u_e\}\). Then \(x\) is a vertex of \(P\) if and only if the columns of \(A_{F(x)}\) are linearly independent. For an incidence matrix, this is equivalent to the undirected edge set underlying \(F(x)\) containing no cycle. Thus every vertex has at most \(r\) arcs strictly between their bounds, while all remaining arcs are fixed at lower or upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow is a vertex precisely when its strictly non-bound arcs form an incidence-independent set, equivalently an undirected forest.

For disjoint \(L,U\subseteq E\), define
\[

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc-Bound Facet Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Codimension-one criterion for lower- and upper-arc-bound faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) have positive relative dimension \(d\). For an arc \(e\), a nonempty lower-bound face \(F_e^\ell=P\cap\{x_e=\ell_e\}\) is a facet exactly when \(\dim F_e^\ell=d-1\); the same criterion holds for \(F_e^u=P\cap\{x_e=u_e\}\). Using the active-bound dimension formula, this is equivalent to the remaining free incidence columns leaving exactly \(d-1\) feasible degrees of freedom. An empty tight set, a bound tight throughout P, or a tight set of dimension below \(d-1\) does not define a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc bound defines a facet exactly when its nonempty tight set has codimension one; empty, universally tight, and higher-codimension cases are not facets.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty and has positive relative dimension d.
Dimensions are taken in \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_e^\ell\text{ or }F_e^u\text{ is a facet}\iff \dim F=d-1.

notation.meaning: Lower- and upper-bound faces of arc e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A linear objective exposing any nonempty face specified by selected arc bounds.

\(L\cap U=\varnothing\) and \(F_{L,U}\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x,y)\) be the intersection of all faces of \(P\) containing distinct vertices \(x\) and \(y\). The vertices are adjacent in the one-skeleton of \(P\) if and only if
\[
\dim F(x,y)=1.
\]
Equivalently, within the \(d\)-dimensional affine hull of \(P\), the lower- and upper-bound constraints active at both \(x\) and \(y\) have rank \(d-1\). These common active bounds therefore leave exactly one feasible degree of freedom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two flow vertices are adjacent exactly when their smallest common face is one-dimensional, equivalently when common active bounds leave one feasible degree of freedom.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit Directions of Flow-Polytope Edges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-specific representation of one-dimensional flow-polytope faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), where \(A\) is a directed incidence matrix. Every edge direction of \(P\) is a nonzero scalar multiple of a circuit of \(A\). For a loopless directed network, the circuit support is an undirected simple cycle, including a two-edge parallel cycle when applicable, with signs describing a circulation around it. Hence adjacent vertices differ only along one signed cycle. Conversely, if fixing every coordinate outside such a circuit leaves a nondegenerate feasible segment, that segment is a one-dimensional face and its endpoints are adjacent vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every edge of a bounded flow polytope moves along one signed incidence circuit, or network cycle; a nondegenerate feasible circuit section is an edge.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty bounded flow polytope.
Dimensions and faces are relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a connected graph on \(n\) nodes, the reduced incidence matrix \(\bar A\) has rank \(n-1\). A set \(B\subseteq E\) with \(|B|=n-1\) satisfies
\[
\det(\bar A_B)\ne0
\]
if and only if the underlying undirected arcs in \(B\) form a spanning tree. Consequently, each network-simplex basis can be represented by a spanning tree, with every nonbasic arc assigned to one of its bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Basic Flow Determined by a Tree and Bound Assignments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic reconstruction associated with a bounded-flow tree basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the arcs into a spanning-tree basis \(T\) and nonbasic set \(N\), and prescribe each \(x_e\), \(e\in N\), at either \(\ell_e\) or \(u_e\). For the reduced incidence system \(\bar A x=\bar b\), the balances uniquely determine \[x_T=\bar A_T^{-1}(\bar b-\bar A_Nx_N).\] The resulting basis is primal feasible if and only if \(\ell_T\le x_T\le u_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree and bound assignments on all non-tree arcs uniquely determine the tree flows; the basis is feasible exactly when those flows satisfy their bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar A_T\) is a spanning-tree column basis of a reduced incidence matrix.
Every nonbasic arc is assigned one of its bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spanning-Forest Bases for Disconnected Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise extension of the spanning-tree basis correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite directed graph have \(q\) weakly connected components, and delete one incidence row from each component to obtain \(\bar A\). Then \(\operatorname{rank}(\bar A)=|V|-q\). A set \(F\subseteq E\) of \(|V|-q\) columns is a basis of \(\bar A\) if and only if its underlying undirected edges form a spanning forest containing one spanning tree in every weak component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After deleting one incidence row per weak component, column bases are exactly component-spanning forests and have vertices minus components arcs.
assumptions_latex: The directed graph is finite and has \(q\) weakly connected components.
One incidence row is deleted from each weak component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar A_F\) is nonsingular exactly when \(F\) contains one spanning tree of every weak component.

assumptions_latex: A feasible network-simplex basis consists of a spanning tree \(B\) and nonbasic arcs fixed at bounds.
The associated basic flow is \(x_B\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\) be a spanning-tree basis and fix each arc in \(E\setminus B\) at either its lower or upper bound. The balance equations uniquely determine \(x_B\). This feasible basis is degenerate if and only if at least one basic arc also satisfies
\[
x_e=\ell_e\quad\text{or}\quad x_e=u_e.
\]
Geometrically, the represented vertex then lies on more active bound hyperplanes than are required, so a basis pivot may change the tree without moving the flow vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network basis is degenerate precisely when a tree arc is itself at a bound, allowing basis changes that may leave the represented flow unchanged.

children.title: Basis Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of tree representations for the same flow-polytope point.

assumptions_latex: The feasible flow \(x\) is a vertex of a bounded network-flow polytope.
A basis representation uses a spanning tree and fixes every non-tree arc at a bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Basis representations of \(x\) are nonunique exactly when two distinct spanning trees satisfy the stated bound assignment and balance equations for \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal B(x)\) contain every spanning tree \(B\) such that each arc outside \(B\) is at a bound in \(x\), while the tree equations reproduce \(x_B\). Then the basis representation of \(x\) is nonunique if and only if
\[
|\mathcal B(x)|>1.
\]
Distinct members of \(\mathcal B(x)\) represent the same geometric vertex. Such nonuniqueness can occur only at a degenerate representation, because exchanging a basic arc without changing \(x\) requires a basic arc to be active at a bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow vertex has nonunique bases when distinct spanning trees, with their non-tree arcs fixed at bounds, reproduce the same flow; this requires degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degeneracy Does Not Imply Basis Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp converse boundary for the seed's necessary degeneracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two nodes joined by one nonloop arc \(e\), with \(0\le x_e\le1\) and zero balance at both nodes. The only feasible flow is \(x_e=0\), and \(\{e\}\) is the unique spanning tree. Its basis is degenerate because the basic arc is at its lower bound, but the vertex has only one tree-basis representation. Thus basis nonuniqueness implies degeneracy, whereas degeneracy need not imply basis nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-arc, two-node network has a unique degenerate tree basis, so degeneracy is necessary but not sufficient for basis nonuniqueness.
assumptions_latex: The graph has two nodes and one directed nonloop arc \(e\).
The bounds are \(0\le x_e\le1\), and both node balances are zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sole feasible vertex has a degenerate but unique tree-basis representation.

notation.meaning: the unique arc and unique spanning-tree edge

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis Forests as Completions of the Free-Arc Forest
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise combinatorial description of all incidence bases representing one bounded-flow vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) have \(q\) weak components, let \(x\) be a vertex of \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), and put \(F(x)=\{e:\ell_e<x_e<u_e\}\). A component-spanning forest \(T\) represents \(x\) as a bounded-variable incidence basis if and only if \[F(x)\subseteq T.\] Hence \[\mathcal B(x)=\{T:T\text{ contains one spanning tree of each weak component and }F(x)\subseteq T\}.\] In a weakly connected graph these are precisely the spanning-tree completions of \(F(x)\). Basis representations are nonunique exactly when this completion family has more than one member.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All incidence bases representing a flow vertex are exactly the component-spanning forests containing its strictly interior arcs; nonuniqueness is multiplicity of such completions.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite directed graph with \(q\) weakly connected components.
\(x\) is a vertex of the bounded flow polytope \(P\).
One redundant incidence row is removed from each weak component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B(x)=\{T:T\text{ is component-spanning and }F(x)\subseteq T\}\).

assumptions_latex: The feasible polytope \(P\) is nonempty and independent of the cost vector.
The flow \(x^*\in P\) minimizes \(c^Tx\) over \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The flow \(x^*\) remains optimal under \(c+\delta c\) exactly when \(c+\delta c\in\mathcal C_P(x^*)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the minimizing cost cone at \(x^*\) by
\[
\mathcal C_P(x^*)=\{q\in\mathbb R^E:q^T(y-x^*)\ge0\text{ for every }y\in P\}.
\]
For a cost perturbation \(\delta c\), the flow \(x^*\) remains optimal if and only if \(c+\delta c\in\mathcal C_P(x^*)\). Moreover, the optimal value
\[
v(c)=\min_{x\in P}c^Tx
\]
is a concave, piecewise-linear function of \(c\), and every optimal flow at \(c\) is a supergradient of \(v\) there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow remains optimal exactly while the perturbed cost stays in its minimizing normal cone; the optimal value is concave and piecewise linear in costs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Arc Cost Allowable Interval
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residual-cycle stability interval for changing one original arc cost while retaining a fixed optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) be optimal and change only the cost of original arc \(a\) from \(c_a\) to \(c_a+\delta\). For each residual directed cycle \(C\), let \(\sigma_a(C)\) be its number of forward residual copies of \(a\) minus its number of reverse residual copies. Define \[L_a:=\sup_{C:\,\sigma_a(C)>0}\frac{-c^R(C)}{\sigma_a(C)},\qquad U_a:=\inf_{C:\,\sigma_a(C)<0}\frac{c^R(C)}{-\sigma_a(C)},\] with an empty supremum equal to \(-\infty\) and an empty infimum equal to \(+\infty\). Then \(x^*\) remains optimal exactly when \(L_a\le\delta\le U_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact allowable change to one arc cost is the interval imposed by residual cycles using that arc forward or backward.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is feasible and optimal for a finite bounded linear minimum-cost flow problem.
Only the cost of one original arc \(a\) changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ remains optimal}\iff L_a\le\delta\le U_a.

notation.meaning: signed use of the perturbed original arc by residual cycle C

assumptions_latex: The value \(v(u)=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\) is finite near the capacity vector \(u\).
The set \(D^*(u)\) of optimal dual solutions is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For admissible \(d\), \(v'(u;d)=\max_{(\pi,\beta)\in D^*(u)}(-\beta^Td)\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value as a function of capacities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(A,b,c\), the finite value function
\[
v(u)=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}
\]
is componentwise nonincreasing and convex on each convex region where the problem is feasible. If \(D^*(u)\) is the set of optimal dual solutions and \(\beta\ge0\) denotes the multiplier of \(x\le u\), then every feasible directional derivative satisfies
\[
v'(u;d)=\max_{(\pi,\beta)\in D^*(u)}(-\beta^Td).
\]
When the optimal capacity multiplier is unique, this reduces to \(-\beta^{*T}d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum cost is convex and nonincreasing in capacities; optimal capacity multipliers give its directional marginal values.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Capacity Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacity-Only Optimizer Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact test for preserving a fixed optimal flow after arbitrary upper-capacity changes, with one-sided simplifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) be optimal under upper capacities \(u\), and change only the upper capacities to \(u'\). Then \(x^*\) remains optimal exactly when \(x^*\le u'\) and the residual network \(G_{x^*}^R(u')\) contains no negative-cost directed cycle. In particular, if \(u'\le u\) and \(x^*\le u'\), then \(x^*\) remains optimal. If \(u'\ge u\), feasibility is automatic, but newly available forward residual capacity can destroy optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After capacity-only changes, an old optimum is preserved exactly when it remains feasible and its updated residual network has no negative cycle; feasible capacity decreases preserve it automatically.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is optimal for fixed costs and balances under upper capacities \(u\).
Only upper capacities change, from \(u\) to \(u'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ remains optimal under }u'\iff x^*\le u'\text{ and }G_{x^*}^R(u')\text{ has no negative directed cycle.}

notation.meaning: residual network of the old optimum under the updated capacities

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Only Optimizer Preservation

The square matrix \(A_B\) is nonsingular, and the model has lower bounds \(0\) and perturbed upper bounds \(u'\in\mathbb R_+^E\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times E}\) have full row rank, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) be fixed, and let \(E=B\mathbin{\dot\cup}L\mathbin{\dot\cup}U\), where \(A_B\) is square and nonsingular. For perturbed data \(c'\in\mathbb R^E\) and \(u'\in\mathbb R_+^E\), set \(x'_L=0\), \(x'_U=u'_U\), and \[x'_B=A_B^{-1}(b-A_Uu'_U).\] For each \(e\in E\setminus B\), define \(\bar c'_e=c'_e-c_B'^TA_B^{-1}A_e\). The fixed bounded-variable basis \((B,L,U)\) is primal and dual optimal for the perturbed problem if and only if \[0\le x'_B\le u'_B,\qquad \bar c'_e\ge0\ \text{for every }e\in L,\qquad \bar c'_e\le0\ \text{for every }e\in U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed bounded-variable flow basis remains optimal under simultaneous cost and capacity perturbations exactly when its recomputed basic flow stays within its bounds and the reduced costs retain the signs required at lower- and upper-bound nonbasic arcs.

\[

is convex and piecewise linear on its feasible imbalance domain. Let \(\Pi^*(b)\) be the set of optimal node-potential vectors. Increasing supply at node \(s\) while decreasing it equally at node \(r\) gives the balanced direction \(h=e_s-e_r\), and

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible for \(b\), use the outflow-minus-inflow convention \(Ax=b\), and set \(h=e_s-e_r\). For \(\delta\ge0\), \(b+\delta h\) is feasible if and only if the residual network \(G_x\) admits an \(s\)-to-\(r\) flow of value \(\delta\). Hence \[\delta_{\max}=\operatorname{maxflow}_{G_x}(s,r)=\min_{S:\,s\in S,\,r\notin S}u_x^+(\delta^+(S)).\]

\(\delta\ge0\) and \(h=e_s-e_r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Residual Reoptimization for a Supply Increase
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite value response to a compensated supply increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) be optimal for \(b\), and give each residual arc its signed original cost. For every feasible \(\delta\ge0\), \[v(b+\delta(e_s-e_r))-v(b)=\min\{c_{x^*}^{\mathsf T}y:y\text{ is a residual }s\text{-}r\text{ flow of value }\delta\}.\] Augmenting \(x^*\) by an optimal residual flow yields an optimum for the perturbed imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite cost of a compensated supply increase equals the minimum cost of routing that amount from s to r in the old optimum's residual network.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is optimal for b.
\(b+\delta(e_s-e_r)\) is feasible.
Reverse residual arcs have negated forward-arc costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v(b+\delta(e_s-e_r))=v(b)+\operatorname{MCF}_{G_{x^*}}(s,r;\delta).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit supply–demand perturbation by residual shortest-path augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of an optimal minimum-cost flow to a one-unit transfer in the node-imbalance vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x^*$ be an optimal minimum-cost flow for node imbalances $b$ with $\sum_{i\in N}b(i)=0$. Replace $b(k)$ by $b(k)+1$ and $b(l)$ by $b(l)-1$. Then $x^*$ is a pseudoflow satisfying the reduced-cost optimality conditions. If the residual network $G(x^*)$ contains a directed $k$-$l$ path, augmenting one unit along a shortest such path produces an optimal flow for the modified problem and changes the objective value by $d(k,l)$. If no directed $k$-$l$ path exists, the modified problem is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an optimal minimum-cost flow, increase one node imbalance by one and decrease another by one. If the residual network has a path from the first node to the second, augment one unit along a shortest path; the resulting flow is optimal and its cost increases by the residual shortest-path distance. If no such path exists, the modified problem is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is an optimal minimum-cost flow for }b
\sum_{i\in N}b(i)=0
b'(k)=b(k)+1,\quad b'(l)=b(l)-1
d(k,l)\text{ is the shortest-path distance in }G(x^*)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\leadsto l\text{ in }G(x^*)\Rightarrow x^*+\text{one-unit shortest-path augmentation is optimal and }z'^*=z^*+d(k,l);\quad k\not\leadsto l\Rightarrow\text{infeasible}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Cut Characterization of a Feasible Balanced Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient feasibility test for a simultaneous balanced change of node imbalances, relative to a feasible bounded flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Use the outflow-minus-inflow incidence convention and let \(x\) satisfy \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\). Form the residual digraph with forward capacity \(u_{ij}-x_{ij}\) and reverse capacity \(x_{ij}-\ell_{ij}\). A perturbation \(d\in\mathbb R^V\) can be realized by some \(x'\) satisfying \(Ax'=b+d\) and \(\ell\le x'\le u\) if and only if \[d(V)=0\quad\text{and}\quad d(S)\le r\bigl(\delta^+(S)\bigr)\quad\text{for every }S\subseteq V,\] where \(r\) denotes residual capacity. Equivalently, the residual network admits a correction flow whose node imbalance is \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced node-imbalance change is feasible exactly when every vertex set can send its required net additional outflow through the current residual capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) uses the outflow-minus-inflow convention.
\(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
All residual capacities are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x'\in[\ell,u]\text{ with }Ax'=b+d\iff d(V)=0\text{ and }d(S)\le r(\delta^+(S))\ \forall S\subseteq V.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Basis Stability Under Balanced Imbalance Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stability region of an already dual-feasible bounded-variable basis when only node imbalances change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((B,L,U)\) be an optimal bounded-variable basis for \(Ax=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), with nonsingular \(A_B\). Keep costs, bounds, and nonbasic bound statuses fixed, and perturb the balance to \(b+d\). In a full-row-rank incidence representation, the recomputed basic variables are \[x'_B=x_B+A_B^{-1}d.\] Because costs and the basis are unchanged, all reduced costs and hence dual feasibility are unchanged. Therefore the fixed basis remains primal-dual optimal if and only if \[\ell_B\le x_B+A_B^{-1}d\le u_B.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed optimal basis, a compatible balanced imbalance perturbation preserves optimality exactly while the recomputed basic flows remain within their bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular in a full-row-rank incidence representation.
The original bounded-variable basis is primal and dual optimal.
Costs, arc bounds, and nonbasic bound statuses are unchanged.
The perturbation \(d\) is compatible with the row-reduced balance system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (B,L,U)\text{ remains optimal}\iff \ell_B\le x_B+A_B^{-1}d\le u_B.

notation.meaning: Basis submatrix of the full-row-rank incidence representation.
Compatible simultaneous perturbation of node imbalances.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Basis Stability Under Balanced Imbalance Changes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balancedness Does Not Imply Capacity Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal witness separating global balance compatibility from network realizability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the network consist of two vertices \(s,t\) and no arcs, with original balance \(b=0\). The perturbation \(d_s=1\), \(d_t=-1\) satisfies \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=0\), but no flow can realize \(Ax=b+d\) because \(A\) has no columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-sum perturbation between disconnected vertices is balanced but infeasible.
assumptions_latex: The network has vertices \(s,t\) and no arcs.
The original balance is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=0\quad\text{but}\quad \nexists x\text{ with }Ax=d.
knowledge_statements.title: Balancedness Does Not Imply Capacity Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Value Function for Balanced Imbalances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint value sensitivity for arbitrary balanced node-imbalance vectors; coordinate supply and demand specializations remain in sibling leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed costs and bounds, define \[v(\beta)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=\beta,\ \ell\le x\le u\},\] with value \(+\infty\) when infeasible. Then \(v\) is a proper convex polyhedral function on the feasible balance polytope and has the dual representation \[v(\beta)=\max_{p\in\mathbb R^V}\left[p^{\mathsf T}\beta+\sum_{e\in E}\min_{\ell_e\le z\le u_e}\bigl(c_e-(A^{\mathsf T}p)_e\bigr)z\right].\] If \(p^*\) is dual optimal at \(b\), then for every balanced perturbation \(d\), \[v(b+d)\ge v(b)+(p^*)^{\mathsf T}d.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum cost is a convex polyhedral function of the balanced node-imbalance vector, and optimal node prices give a joint subgradient bound for every balanced perturbation.
assumptions_latex: The finite network has fixed linear costs and finite arc bounds.
The balance vector \(b\) is feasible.
Strong linear-programming duality applies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*\in\partial v(b),\qquad v(b+d)\ge v(b)+(p^*)^{\mathsf T}d.

notation.meaning: Minimum-cost value for node-imbalance vector beta.
Optimal node-price vector at the original imbalance.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Value Function for Balanced Imbalances
Balanced Imbalance Perturbations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for perturbing node supplies in a capacitated transshipment model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have node-arc incidence matrix \(A\), with each column containing one \(+1\) and one \(-1\). A perturbation \(d\in\mathbb R^V\) of a balance vector \(b\) is balanced precisely when
\[\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=\sum_{v\in V}d_v=0.\]
Thus \(b+d\) preserves the necessary conservation identity \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}(b+d)=0\). Balancedness alone does not guarantee feasibility under arc bounds; feasibility additionally requires \(b+d\) to belong to \(\{Ax:\ell\le x\le u\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-imbalance change must sum to zero. This preserves global conservation but does not by itself ensure that capacities permit the perturbed balances.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is the incidence matrix of a directed graph.
\(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}b=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbation preserves global balance if and only if \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=0\).

notation.meaning: Original node balances and their perturbation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility condition and capacity-feasibility qualification are mathematically precise, but the record supplies no inspectable source locator.

children.title: Parametric Warm-Start Interface
children.top_down_role: Reuse of primal, dual, and basis information across related instances.

children.title: Parametric Flow Structure
children.top_down_role: Changes in optimal network structure across controlled parameter ranges.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Right-Hand-Side Parametric Flow Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-affine structure for a scalar affine balance family with fixed costs and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[v(\lambda)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b^0+\lambda d,\ \ell\le x\le u\},\qquad \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}b^0=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}d=0,\] with fixed \(A,c,\ell,u\). Its feasible parameter set is an interval, possibly empty or unbounded. On every subinterval where one dual-feasible bounded-flow basis remains primal feasible, its basic flow is affine in \(\lambda\), its nonbasic arcs remain at their bounds, and it is optimal. Because only finitely many bases and statuses occur, the finite value function is convex and piecewise affine on the feasible parameter interval. For a fixed basis, reduced costs are constant; basiswise intervals end through basic-flow bound events, although degeneracy may permit overlapping optimal bases or a basis change without a unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With affine node balances and fixed network data, stable bases give affine optimal flows and the value is convex piecewise affine. Reduced costs stay constant for each retained basis, so its interval is limited by primal bound events, subject to degeneracy.
assumptions_latex: The graph, incidence matrix, costs, and finite arc bounds are fixed.
The value is finite on the parameter interval considered.
Balances depend affinely on one scalar parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_B(\lambda)\text{ is affine on each stable-basis interval, and }v(\lambda)\text{ is convex piecewise affine}.

notation.meaning: Flow induced by a retained bounded-flow basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Right-Hand-Side Parametric Flow Structure
Parametric Flow Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-parameter right-hand-side sensitivity with fixed costs and capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[v(\lambda)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b^0+\lambda d,\ \ell\le x\le u\},\]
where \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}b^0=\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=0\). On every interval of parameters having a common optimal nondegenerate basis, the associated basic flow is affine in \(\lambda\), while its nonbasic arcs remain at bounds. The interval ends when a basic arc reaches a bound or an optimality condition becomes tight. Over any interval on which the problem is feasible, \(v\) is a convex piecewise-affine function of \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With affine node balances and fixed network data, each stable optimal basis yields an affine flow; basis events partition the feasible parameter range, and the value is convex piecewise affine.
assumptions_latex: The graph and \(A,c,\ell,u\) are fixed.
The minimum is finite throughout the parameter interval considered.
A basis is interpreted in the bounded network-linear-program sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimal flows are basiswise affine in \(\lambda\), and \(v(\lambda)\) is convex and piecewise affine.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex piecewise-affine value claim is standard, but no source is supplied. Moreover, with fixed costs and capacities, reduced costs for a fixed basis do not vary with the right-hand-side parameter, so the claimed optimality-condition breakpoint requires correction or a broader data-variation model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient of the Minimum-Cost-Flow Value Function with Respect to Arc Capacities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity sensitivity for a feasible minimum-cost-flow problem with nonnegative parametric arc upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z(q)=\min\{c^\top x:\mathcal N x=b,\ 0\le x\le q\}\). Suppose \(q^*\ge0\), \(x^*\) is optimal at \(q^*\), and \(x^*\) together with the reduced-cost vector \(c^\pi\) satisfies the minimum-cost-flow optimality conditions. Define \(\mu_{ij}=0\) if \(x^*_{ij}<q^*_{ij}\), and \(\mu_{ij}=c^\pi_{ij}\) if \(x^*_{ij}=q^*_{ij}\). For every \(q'\ge0\) for which the flow problem is feasible, \[z(q')\ge z(q^*)+\mu^\top(q'-q^*).\] Thus \(\mu\in\partial z(q^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an optimal minimum-cost flow, assign zero sensitivity to an arc below capacity and its reduced cost to an arc at capacity. Provided the stated flow optimality conditions hold, this vector gives a global affine lower bound on the optimal value for every other nonnegative capacity vector yielding a feasible problem, so it is a subgradient of the capacity-parametrized value function at the reference capacities.
assumptions_latex: q^*\ge0
x^*\in\arg\min\{c^\top x:\mathcal N x=b,\ 0\le x\le q^*\}
(x^*,c^\pi)\text{ satisfies the minimum-cost-flow optimality conditions}
\mu_{ij}=\begin{cases}0,&x^*_{ij}<q^*_{ij},\\c^\pi_{ij},&x^*_{ij}=q^*_{ij},\end{cases}
q'\ge0\text{ and }\{x:\mathcal N x=b,\ 0\le x\le q'\}\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z(q')\ge z(q^*)+\mu^\top(q'-q^*)\text{ for every feasible }q'\ge0,\qquad \mu\in\partial z(q^*).

children.title: Primal Warm Starts
children.top_down_role: Reuse of feasible or nearly feasible flow information across related instances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Repair of a Primal Warm Start
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact repair after a balanced change in node imbalances with fixed network and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) satisfy \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), and let \(d\) satisfy \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}d=0\). Build the capacitated residual network of \(x\) and find a signed residual flow \(y\) satisfying \(Ay=d\). If one exists, \(x'=x+y\) satisfies \(Ax'=b+d\) and the original bounds and is a feasible primal warm start. Such a correction exists if and only if the updated fixed-network, fixed-bound instance is feasible. It may be found by an auxiliary max-flow or feasible-circulation computation, after which any primal-feasible minimum-cost-flow method may reoptimize from \(x'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route the balance change through the old flow's residual network. A successful correction produces a feasible warm start; under unchanged bounds and network, correction failure exactly means the updated instance is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
The incidence matrix and arc bounds are unchanged.
\(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}d=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y\text{ residual with }Ay=d\iff \exists x'\text{ with }Ax'=b+d,\ \ell\le x'\le u.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Repair of a Primal Warm Start

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direct Primal-Flow Reuse Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition for carrying an old flow unchanged into a modified instance on a fixed arc set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a stored flow and let the updated instance on the same arc set have balances \(b'\) and bounds \(\ell',u'\). The unchanged flow is a valid primal warm start if and only if \[Ax=b',\qquad \ell'\le x\le u'.\] Failure rejects only unchanged reuse; it does not imply that the updated instance is infeasible or that x cannot be repaired.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old flow is directly reusable exactly when it satisfies every updated balance and bound. Failure means repair or replacement is needed, not that the new problem is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: The incidence matrix and arc-coordinate identification are unchanged.
Updated balances and bounds are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is directly reusable}\iff Ax=b'\text{ and }\ell'\le x\le u'.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Primal-Flow Reuse Test
Primal Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual correction of a previously feasible flow after balanced balance changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a flow \(x\) satisfying \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), together with a balanced perturbation \(d\). Construct the residual network of \(x\). Find a residual correction \(y\) whose signed arc flow satisfies \(Ay=d\), respecting every residual capacity. Set \(x'=x+y\). If no such correction exists, report that this warm-start repair failed. Otherwise use \(x'\) as the initial feasible flow for a minimum-cost-flow optimization method and stop when its usual residual optimality certificate holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair the old feasible flow by routing the changed balances through its residual network, then optimize from the repaired flow; failure to find a correction rejects this warm start.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for the old balances.
\(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A returned correction produces \(Ax'=b+d\) and \(\ell\le x'\le u\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual repair algorithm fits the leaf and its conditional feasibility conclusion is plausible, but the signed correction convention and warm-start procedure lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Dual Warm Starts
children.top_down_role: Reuse of potentials or reduced-cost information across related instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuse of node potentials after costs, capacities, or balances change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible for the updated instance and let \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) be inherited node potentials. For each residual arc \((i,j)\), define its updated reduced cost by \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\), using the residual arc's signed cost. If \(\bar c_{ij}\ge0\) for every residual arc, then every residual cycle has nonnegative cost, so \((x,\pi)\) certifies optimality for the updated instance. If some inequality fails, this particular reduced-cost test is inconclusive: \(\pi\) may still serve as an initialization, but it does not provide this certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every updated residual reduced cost is nonnegative, the inherited prices certify that the updated feasible flow is optimal. If the test fails, the prices may still initialize dual repair, but this certificate is unavailable.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) satisfies the updated balances and arc bounds.
Residual reverse arcs carry the negatives of their forward costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual reduced-cost nonnegativity makes \((x,\pi)\) an updated primal-dual optimality certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Right-Hand-Side Preservation of a Dual-Feasible Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-state reuse when only balances change and a network-simplex tree and bound statuses are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix arc costs, bounds, a spanning-tree basis \(T\), and the lower/upper statuses of nonbasic arcs. Potentials satisfying \(c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j=0\) on tree arcs are independent of the balance vector. Consequently, changing only balances leaves all nonbasic reduced costs and their required signs unchanged. An inherited dual-feasible basis remains dual feasible; after recomputing its tree flow, bound feasibility gives immediate optimality, while bound violations leave a dual-feasible initialization for dual network simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing only node balances preserves the reduced-cost feasibility of a retained tree basis. Its recomputed flow is either optimal immediately or provides a dual-feasible start for primal-feasibility repair.
assumptions_latex: Arc costs and bounds are unchanged.
The tree and nonbasic bound statuses remain structurally valid.
The inherited basis is dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Dual feasibility persists, and new primal feasibility implies optimality.}
knowledge_statements.title: Right-Hand-Side Preservation of a Dual-Feasible Basis

children.title: Basis Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Data changes that preserve or invalidate a reusable network basis.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Basis Transfer Region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and dual inequalities defining where a fixed bounded-flow basis remains optimal under affine data variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a network-simplex tree basis \(B\), its nonbasic lower/upper statuses, and a parameter interval on which the underlying arcs remain available. Let balances, bounds, and costs vary affinely with \(\lambda\). The basis is an optimal basis exactly at parameters for which its induced basic flow satisfies all current bounds and every nonbasic reduced cost has the sign required by its current lower or upper status. Thus its transfer region is the intersection of the corresponding scalar affine inequalities. An endpoint can occur when a basic flow meets a bound or a nonbasic reduced cost becomes zero; equality may create an alternative optimal basis and does not by itself imply loss of optimality until an inequality is crossed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A retained bounded-flow basis remains optimal exactly while its induced flow is primal feasible and its nonbasic reduced costs have the required signs. Bound hits and zero reduced costs delimit, but need not immediately invalidate, its transfer region.
assumptions_latex: The network structure and retained tree basis remain valid.
Balances, finite bounds, and costs vary affinely with a scalar parameter.
Nonbasic arcs retain specified lower or upper statuses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Lambda_B=\{\lambda:\ell(\lambda)\le x_B(\lambda)\le u(\lambda),\ \bar c_N(\lambda)\text{ has the required bound signs}\}.

notation.meaning: Retained bounded network-flow basis and nonbasic statuses.
Parameter region on which B is an optimal basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Basis Transfer Region

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Right-Hand-Side-Only Transfer Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Special boundary regime when only node balances vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If costs, bounds, the tree, and nonbasic statuses are fixed while only \(b(\lambda)\) varies, the tree-induced potentials and all reduced costs are constant. An initially dual-feasible basis therefore remains dual feasible throughout the parameter range; its optimal-basis transfer can fail only when the affine basic flow violates an arc bound or the retained network structure ceases to be valid. A zero reduced cost may already represent degeneracy, but it is not a newly varying breakpoint in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a balance-only change with a fixed tree, costs, bounds, and statuses, reduced costs do not move; only primal bound feasibility or structural validity can end basis transfer.
assumptions_latex: Only the node-balance vector varies.
Costs, bounds, tree arcs, and nonbasic statuses are fixed.
The retained basis is initially dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar c_N(\lambda)=\bar c_N\quad\text{and transfer persists exactly while }\ell\le x_B(\lambda)\le u.

notation.meaning: Tree-basic flow induced by the varying balances.

knowledge_statements.title: Right-Hand-Side-Only Transfer Boundary
Basis Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Events at which an inherited bounded network-flow basis ceases to remain optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a network basis and vary the instance data continuously. The basis transfers as an optimal basis while its induced basic flow satisfies every arc bound and the reduced costs of nonbasic arcs have the signs required by their active lower or upper bounds. A transfer boundary occurs when either a basic flow reaches a bound, making primal feasibility tight, or a nonbasic reduced cost reaches zero, making dual optimality tight. Beyond such an event, the inherited basis need not be feasible or optimal and a pivot or reoptimization is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old basis remains usable only while its basic flows respect bounds and nonbasic reduced costs have correct signs. Bound hits and zero reduced costs mark transfer boundaries.
assumptions_latex: The current basis is initially primal and dual feasible.
Data vary continuously along a scalar parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first violated primal-bound or reduced-cost sign condition ends guaranteed optimal-basis transfer.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of a nonbasic arc.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycle Canceling for Integer Convex-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-cost specialization using a discrete-marginal residual network, with an optional batching implementation for a persistent cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with a feasible integer flow \(x\) and construct its convex-cost residual network \(G(x)\). While \(G(x)\) contains a negative-cost directed cycle \(W\), augment the maximum amount permitted by the current residual capacities along \(W\), update \(x\) and \(G(x)\), and repeat. If no negative directed cycle exists, \(x\) is an optimal integer flow. As an implementation variant, repeated augmentations may remain on the same cycle until it is no longer a directed residual cycle or its cost becomes nonnegative; the total amount can be determined by repeated augmentation or binary search over \([0,U]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible integer flow, repeatedly augment as much as currently permitted around a negative cycle in the convex-cost residual network and update the network. No negative residual cycle certifies optimality. A cycle that remains negative may be reused until it disappears or becomes nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is a feasible integer flow}
C(x)=\sum_{(i,j)\in A}C_{ij}(x_{ij})\text{ with discrete convex arc costs}
G(x)\text{ uses the corresponding discrete-marginal residual costs and capacities}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(x)\text{ contains no negative directed cycle}\;\Longrightarrow\;x\text{ is an optimal integer convex-cost flow.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Fixed Arc
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of arc invariance across sufficiently accurate approximate optima, with its stated consequence for the maintained minimum mean cycle-canceling sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An arc \(a\) is \(\epsilon\)-fixed if, whenever \(\epsilon'\leq\epsilon\), all \(\epsilon'\)-optimal flows assign the same flow to \(a\). Because the minimum mean cycle-canceling algorithm maintains \(\epsilon(x)\)-optimal flows with nonincreasing \(\epsilon(x)\), the flow on an arc that is \(\epsilon(x)\)-fixed at the current iterate does not change subsequently and equals its flow in every optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc is epsilon-fixed if, for every epsilon-prime at most epsilon, all epsilon-prime-optimal flows assign it the same flow. Since the algorithm's maintained epsilon(x) values do not increase, an arc fixed at the current epsilon(x) never changes afterward and has the same flow in every optimal flow.
assumptions_latex: \forall\epsilon'\leq\epsilon,\;\text{the comparison is over all }\epsilon'\text{-optimal flows}.
\epsilon(x)\text{ is nonincreasing during the minimum mean cycle-canceling algorithm.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\text{ is }\epsilon\text{-fixed}\iff \forall\epsilon'\leq\epsilon,\;x_a\text{ is identical over all }\epsilon'\text{-optimal flows};\quad a\text{ currently }\epsilon(x)\text{-fixed}\Rightarrow x_a\text{ remains unchanged and agrees with every optimal flow.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Step Cycle-Cancellation Identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility and objective effect of one residual-cycle augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible and let \(C\) be a directed cycle in its residual network. For \(0<\delta\le\min_{e\in C}r_e\), augmentation by \(\delta\) around \(C\) produces a feasible flow \(x'\) with \(c^{\mathsf T}x'=c^{\mathsf T}x+\delta c(C)\). If \(\delta=\min_{e\in C}r_e\), at least one residual arc of \(C\) is exhausted; if \(c(C)<0\), the objective strictly decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual-cycle augmentation preserves feasibility, changes cost by the augmentation amount times the cycle cost, and at the bottleneck exhausts a residual arc.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible.
\(C\) is a directed residual cycle.
\(0<\delta\le\min_{e\in C}r_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'\text{ is feasible and }c^{\mathsf T}x'-c^{\mathsf T}x=\delta c(C).
