knowledge_statements.title: One-Step Cycle-Cancellation Identity
Generic Cycle Canceling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational residual negative-cycle algorithm for a feasible minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible flow \(x\) for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\). Construct its residual network with residual capacities and signed residual costs. While a directed residual cycle \(C\) has \(c(C)<0\), choose such a cycle, set \(\delta=\min_{e\in C}r_e\), and augment \(\delta\) units around \(C\). Stop when no negative-cost residual cycle exists and output \(x\). The output is optimal; with integral finite data, every augmentation preserves integrality and the procedure terminates after finitely many objective-decreasing iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment a feasible flow by the bottleneck amount around any negative-cost residual cycle. Absence of such a cycle certifies minimum cost.
assumptions_latex: The initial flow is feasible.
All residual capacities used for the termination claim are finite integers.
Arc costs are integers for the finite-decrease argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(x\) is a minimum-cost feasible flow.

notation.meaning: Signed residual cost of cycle C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generic Negative-Cycle Canceling Procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Improves a feasible fixed-value flow by repeatedly canceling negative-cost residual cycles; optimality holds when the procedure reaches a state with no such cycle.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Selection Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible and structured rules for choosing an improving residual cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cycle-selection rule is admissible if, whenever the residual network contains a negative-cost directed cycle, it returns one. Generic selection may return any such cycle. Minimum-total-cost selection minimizes \(c(C)\) over eligible cycles, whereas minimum-mean selection minimizes \(c(C)/|C|\). Each rule preserves feasibility when followed by bottleneck augmentation, and each strictly decreases the objective. Their iteration and running-time guarantees differ because admissibility alone controls neither the magnitude of the decrease nor the number of cancellations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any negative residual cycle gives a valid improvement, but arbitrary, minimum-cost, and minimum-mean selection rules can have substantially different convergence guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The current flow is feasible.
Every selected cycle has positive residual capacity on all its arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bottleneck augmentation along any admissibly selected cycle preserves feasibility and decreases cost.

notation.meaning: Total signed residual cost of cycle C.
Number of arcs in cycle C.

children.title: Cycle-Canceling Convergence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence on numeric data, cycle choice, and recession directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Negative-Cycle Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession certificate for minimum-cost flow with unbounded residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a feasible flow's residual network contains a directed cycle of negative total cost whose residual capacity is unbounded on every cycle arc, then the corresponding cycle circulation is a feasible recession direction and the minimum-cost objective is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative residual cycle with unlimited augmentation capacity certifies that the flow objective is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: A feasible flow exists.
Every arc of the directed residual cycle has unbounded residual capacity.
The cycle has negative total residual cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\text{ feasible}\}=-\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Negative-Cycle Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Objective-Gap Iteration Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Magnitude-dependent termination bound for bottleneck cancellation under integral data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^0\) be an integral feasible flow in a finite network with integral finite capacities and integral costs, and suppose the finite optimum value is \(z^*\). If every iteration augments by the residual bottleneck around a negative-cost residual cycle, then all iterates remain integral and the algorithm terminates after at most \(c^{\mathsf T}x^0-z^*\) cancellations. This bound is pseudopolynomial because it depends on numerical objective magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral bottleneck cycle cancellation terminates within the initial integer objective gap, a magnitude-dependent pseudopolynomial bound.
assumptions_latex: \(x^0\) is an integral feasible flow.
Capacities and costs are finite integers.
The optimum \(z^*\) is finite.
Each selected residual cycle has negative cost and is augmented by its bottleneck.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{cancel}}\le c^{\mathsf T}x^0-z^*.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Objective-Gap Iteration Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Unit Progress Without Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the integer objective-descent argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\delta>0\), a residual network may contain a unit-capacity directed cycle of total cost \(-\delta\). Bottleneck cancellation of that cycle decreases the objective by exactly \(\delta\). Therefore, without an integral objective lattice, no uniform unit-decrease bound—and hence no iteration bound derived solely from the unscaled objective gap—follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonintegral costs, a legal cancellation can improve the objective by an arbitrarily small amount, so integer unit-progress analysis no longer applies.
assumptions_latex: The selected negative cycle has residual bottleneck one and total cost \(-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf\{-\Delta(c^{\mathsf T}x):\text{legal improving cancellation}\}=0\text{ is possible}.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Unit Progress Without Integrality
Cycle-Canceling Convergence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination and boundedness limits for residual-cycle cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral finite capacities and integral costs, bottleneck cycle cancellation keeps flows integral and each iteration lowers the integer objective by at least one; hence it terminates after at most \(c^{\mathsf T}x^0-z^*\) iterations when the optimum \(z^*\) is finite. This bound depends on numerical magnitudes and is therefore only pseudopolynomial. Without integrality, arbitrary cycle choices can yield arbitrarily small decreases, so this argument gives no finite iteration bound. If a negative-cost residual cycle has unbounded residual capacity, it is a recession direction and the objective is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral data give finite but magnitude-dependent convergence. Real data and arbitrary choices lose that bound, while an unlimited negative residual cycle proves unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(x^0\) is a feasible initial flow.
The finite-termination bound assumes finite integral capacities and integral costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cycle cancellation is finitely bounded under integral finite data, but the bound is pseudopolynomial; an uncapacitated negative cycle certifies \(z^*=-\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integral objective-gap bound and unbounded negative-cycle criterion are plausible, but the convergence-boundary record lacks a source, especially for its contrast with arbitrary choices over real data.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Shortest Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical successive shortest residual-path augmentation from excess to deficit nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input integral balances \(b\) with \(\sum_v b_v=0\), capacities \(u\), costs \(c\), and a capacity-feasible pseudoflow \(x\) whose residual network has no negative-cost cycle. While some node \(s\) has positive excess and some node \(t\) has deficit, choose such an \(s\), find a minimum-cost residual path \(P\) from \(s\) to a reachable deficit node \(t\), and augment by the minimum of the excess at \(s\), deficit magnitude at \(t\), and residual bottleneck of \(P\). Stop when all imbalances vanish and output \(x\), or report infeasibility if no required path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly send as much flow as possible along a cheapest residual path from an excess node to a deficit node until balances are satisfied.
assumptions_latex: Balances and capacities are integral.
The initial residual network contains no negative-cost cycle.
Shortest paths are computed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful termination returns a feasible minimum-cost flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-Cycle Initialization Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of path-only termination when the initial capacity-feasible pseudoflow is not residual-cycle optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take two vertices a,b with zero balances and arcs a\to b and b\to a, each having capacity one and cost -1. At the zero flow all balances vanish, so an algorithm performing only excess-to-deficit augmentations stops with cost 0. Its residual network contains the negative cycle a\to b\to a; sending one unit around that cycle gives a feasible flow of cost -2. Thus balance-only termination is not an optimality certificate unless the initial residual network has no negative-cost cycle or negative cycles are handled separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced initial flow can make path augmentation stop immediately even though a residual negative cycle yields a cheaper circulation.
assumptions_latex: The implementation performs only excess-to-deficit augmentations and stops when all balances vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Balance alone does not certify optimality in the presence of a residual negative-cost cycle.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shortest-distance potential update preserves reduced-cost optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential-update invariant underlying the successive shortest-path method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a pseudoflow or flow \(x\) satisfy the reduced-cost optimality conditions with respect to node potentials \(\pi\). In \(G(x)\), let \(d(v)\) be the finite shortest-path distance from \(s\) to \(v\) with residual-arc lengths \(c_{ij}^{\pi}\). Then \(x\) satisfies the reduced-cost optimality conditions with respect to \(\pi'=\pi-d\). Moreover, every residual arc lying on a shortest path from \(s\) to another node has zero reduced cost under \(\pi'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting finite residual shortest-path distances from the current potentials preserves reduced-cost optimality. Arcs on the corresponding shortest paths have zero updated reduced cost.

d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G(x),c^{\pi}}(s,v)\text{ is finite for every node under consideration}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pseudoflow and node imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pseudoflows, node-imbalance classes, the aggregate balance identity, and the associated residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pseudoflow is a function \(x:A\to\mathbb{R}_+\) satisfying the arc-capacity constraints but not necessarily the mass-balance constraints. Its imbalance at \(i\in N\) is \[e(i)=b(i)+\sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji}-\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}.\] A node is an excess node if \(e(i)>0\), a deficit node if \(e(i)<0\), and balanced if \(e(i)=0\). For \(E=\{i:e(i)>0\}\) and \(D=\{i:e(i)<0\}\), if \(\sum_{i\in N}b(i)=0\), then \(\sum_{i\in E}e(i)=-\sum_{i\in D}e(i)\); consequently, an excess node can exist only if a deficit node exists. The residual network of a pseudoflow is defined as for a flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudoflow is a nonnegative, capacity-feasible arc assignment that need not satisfy node balance. Imbalance equals supply plus inflow minus outflow; its sign classifies excess, deficit, and balanced nodes. With zero total supply, total excess equals total deficit in magnitude, so an excess node implies a deficit node.
assumptions_latex: x:A\to\mathbb{R}_+
0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\quad\text{for all }(i,j)\in A
\sum_{i\in N}b(i)=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i\in E}e(i)=-\sum_{i\in D}e(i),\qquad E\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow D\ne\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Successive shortest-path algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-augmentation procedure using node imbalances, reduced costs, residual capacities, and potential updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x:=0\), \(\pi:=0\), \(e(i):=b(i)\), \(E:=\{i:e(i)>0\}\), and \(D:=\{i:e(i)<0\}\). While \(E\ne\varnothing\), select \(k\in E\) and \(l\in D\); compute reduced-cost shortest-path distances \(d\) from \(k\) in \(G(x)\), choose a shortest \(k\)-to-\(l\) path \(P\), set \(\pi:=\pi-d\), and augment \[\delta=\min\left\{e(k),-e(l),\min_{(i,j)\in P}r_{ij}\right\}\] units along \(P\). Update \(x\), \(G(x)\), \(E\), \(D\), and the reduced costs, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with zero flow and potentials. Repeatedly select an excess node and a deficit node, find a reduced-cost shortest residual path between them, update the potentials, and augment by the minimum endpoint imbalance or path residual capacity.
assumptions_latex: x=0\text{ satisfies the nonnegativity and capacity constraints}
E\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow D\ne\varnothing
\text{a shortest residual path from the selected }k\in E\text{ to }l\in D\text{ exists whenever an iteration is performed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E=\varnothing\quad\text{when the while-loop terminates}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-Cycle Elimination and Sequential Shortest-Path Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a minimum-cost flow of prescribed value, or reports that the requested value is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with a feasible s\text{-}t flow x of value v'\le v. While a negative-cost augmenting cycle exists, augment around it to decrease cost without changing v'. When none remains, return x if v'=v. Otherwise find a minimum-cost residual s\text{-}t augmenting path. If none exists, report that no flow of value v exists; otherwise augment by a feasible \delta>0 satisfying v'+\delta\le v and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from any feasible flow whose value does not exceed the target. Cancel negative-cost augmenting cycles until none remains. If the target value has been reached, stop. Otherwise augment along a cheapest residual source-to-sink path; if no such path exists, report that the target value is infeasible, and otherwise repeat.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Successive Shortest Paths for Convex-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-cost specialization maintaining a pseudoflow, a discrete-marginal residual network, and node potentials with nonnegative residual reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an integer pseudoflow \(x\), its convex-cost residual network \(G(x)\), and node potentials \(\pi\) for which every residual reduced cost is nonnegative. Initially set \(\pi(i)=0\) and choose each \(x_{ij}\) at a value minimizing \(C_{ij}(x_{ij})\). At each iteration select an excess node \(k\), compute residual shortest-path distances \(d(\cdot)\) from \(k\), update \(\pi\leftarrow\pi-d\), and augment the maximum possible amount along a shortest path from \(k\) to a deficit node \(l\). Repeat until \(x\) satisfies flow balance.

Repeatedly route the maximum possible amount from an excess node to a deficit node along a shortest residual path, updating the potentials by the computed distances, until the pseudoflow becomes a flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacity-Scaling Successive Shortest-Path Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balance-scaling variant for minimum-cost flow with integral balances, infinite arc capacities, and conservative costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $f=0$ and $b'=b$. If $b'=0$, return $f$; otherwise let $b_{\max}=\max_{v\in V(G)}b(v)$ and $\gamma=2^{\lfloor\log b_{\max}\rfloor}$. At scale $\gamma$, repeatedly choose reachable vertices $s,t$ with $b'(s)\geq\gamma$ and $b'(t)\leq-\gamma$, augment $\gamma$ units along a minimum-cost $s$-$t$ path in $G_f$, and update the two residual balances. If no such pair exists, halve $\gamma$; if this occurs at $\gamma=1$ while $b'\neq0$, report that no $b$-flow exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic shortest-path characterization of minimum-loss augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes augmenting paths in a capacitated gain/loss network by additive logarithmic arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be a flow in a capacitated network with positive arc multipliers \(m_{ij}>0\), capacities \(c_{ij}\), source \(s\), and sink \(t\). Define
\[
\bar a_{ij}=\begin{cases}
-\log m_{ij},&x_{ij}<c_{ij},\ x_{ji}=0,\\
\min\{-\log m_{ij},\ \log m_{ji}\},&x_{ij}<c_{ij},\ x_{ji}>0,\\
\log m_{ji},&x_{ij}=c_{ij},\ x_{ji}>0,\\
+\infty,&x_{ij}=c_{ij},\ x_{ji}=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then every shortest directed \((s,t)\)-path with respect to \(\bar a\) corresponds to a minimum-loss \((s,t)\)-augmenting path. Moreover, a negative directed cycle from which \(s\) or \(t\) is reachable yields an endogenous flow-augmenting path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each residual direction its logarithmic loss length, using the cheaper of forward augmentation and reverse cancellation when both are available. A shortest directed source-to-sink path then gives a minimum-loss augmenting path. A negative directed cycle from which the source or sink can be reached yields an endogenous augmenting path.
assumptions_latex: x_{ij}\le c_{ij}
s,t\in V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{Q:s\leadsto t}\sum_{(i,j)\in Q}\bar a_{ij}\ \Longrightarrow\ P\text{ is a minimum-loss augmenting path};\quad C\text{ negative and }(C\leadsto s\text{ or }C\leadsto t)\Longrightarrow C\text{ yields an endogenous flow-augmenting path}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Successive Shortest-Path Algorithm for Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical residual shortest-path augmentation algorithm, including its infeasibility stopping condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $f=0$ and $b'=b$. While $b'\neq0$, choose $s$ with $b'(s)>0$ and a reachable $t$ with $b'(t)<0$. If no such $t$ exists, report that no $b$-flow exists. Otherwise choose a minimum-cost $s$-$t$ path $P$ in $G_f$, set $\gamma=\min\{\min_{e\in E(P)}u_f(e),b'(s),-b'(t)\}$, augment $f$ along $P$ by $\gamma$, and update $b'(s)\leftarrow b'(s)-\gamma$ and $b'(t)\leftarrow b'(t)+\gamma$. When $b'=0$, return $f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly send the maximum admissible amount from a residual surplus vertex to a reachable deficit vertex along a shortest residual path; return the resulting minimum-cost flow, or report infeasibility when no required path exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Successive Shortest-Path Algorithm for Feasible Integer Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded specialization; the residual sets and condition (10.49) retain their source definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $\xi\in\mathbb Z^A$ satisfying (10.49) and $x\in B$. If $S^+=\varnothing$, return $\xi$ as feasible. If no path joins $S^+$ to $S^-$, certify that no feasible flow exists. Otherwise choose a shortest $S^+$--$S^-$ path $P$ and, for every $a\in P$, update $\xi(a)\gets\xi(a)+1$ when $a\in A_\xi^*$, update $\xi(\bar a)\gets\xi(\bar a)-1$ when $a\in B_\xi^*$, and update $x(\partial^+a)\gets x(\partial^+a)-1$, $x(\partial^-a)\gets x(\partial^-a)+1$ when $a\in C_x$; then repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an integer flow satisfying (10.49) and a base point x, repeatedly augment along a shortest path from the positive-deficit set to the negative-deficit set. An empty positive-deficit set yields a feasible flow, while absence of such a path certifies infeasibility.

x\in B.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^+=\varnothing\Rightarrow \xi\text{ is feasible};\qquad \nexists\,P:S^+\leadsto S^-\Rightarrow\text{ no feasible flow exists}.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Reweighted Residual Shortest Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential updates for repeated residual shortest-path searches when every residual vertex is reachable from the selected source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each residual arc \((i,j)\), let \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\). Suppose all residual reduced costs are nonnegative and every residual-network vertex is reachable from a source \(s\). Let \(d_v\) be the finite shortest reduced-cost distance from \(s\) to \(v\), and define \(\pi'_v=\pi_v-d_v\). Then
\[\bar c'_{ij}=\bar c_{ij}+d_i-d_j\ge0\]
for every residual arc \((i,j)\). Original and reduced costs of any fixed-endpoint path differ only by endpoint potentials, so they have the same minimizing paths; Dijkstra's algorithm is therefore applicable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When all residual reduced costs are nonnegative and every vertex is reachable from the source, subtracting shortest-path distances from the potentials preserves nonnegative reduced costs on every residual arc and preserves shortest-path minimizers.
assumptions_latex: All residual reduced costs before the search are nonnegative.
Every residual-network vertex is reachable from the source \(s\), so every distance \(d_v\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update \(\pi'_v=\pi_v-d_v\) preserves reduced-cost nonnegativity and shortest-path minimizers.

notation.meaning: Shortest reduced-cost distance from the source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Target-Capped Distance Reweighting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe potential reweighting when some residual vertices are unreachable from the selected source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\ge0, choose a source s and reachable target t, and let d(v) be the shortest reduced-cost distance from s, possibly +\infty. Set D=d(t), q(v)=\min\{d(v),D\}, with \min\{+\infty,D\}=D, and \pi'_v=\pi_v-q(v). Then \bar c'_{ij}=\bar c_{ij}+q(i)-q(j)\ge0 for every residual arc, and every arc on an s-t shortest path has zero updated reduced cost. Updating only finite-distance vertices can fail: if d(j)=2, i is unreachable, and an entering residual arc i\to j has \bar c_{ij}=0, leaving \pi_i unchanged while subtracting d(j) at j produces \bar c'_{ij}=-2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capping every distance at the target distance safely handles unreachable vertices and makes a shortest source-target path tight; ignoring unreachable vertices can create a negative reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: All residual reduced costs before the update are nonnegative.
The selected target t is reachable from s.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar c'_{ij}\ge0\text{ for every residual arc, and every arc of an }s\text{-}t\text{ shortest path is tight}.

notation.meaning: Finite reduced-cost distance to the selected target.

knowledge_statements.title: Successive Shortest-Path Complexity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantity-dependent bound for integral successive shortest-path augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=\sum_{v:b_v>0}b_v\) be the total integral supply. In successive shortest path, every successful augmentation sends at least one unit and eliminates at least one unit of remaining supply, so there are at most \(F\) augmentations. With nonnegative reduced costs and a binary heap, one residual shortest-path computation costs \(O(m+n\log n)\); hence the running time is
\[O\bigl(F(m+n\log n)\bigr).\]
Because \(F\) may be exponential in the binary encoding length of the balances, this is a pseudopolynomial bound rather than a strongly polynomial one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral successive shortest path uses at most total-supply many augmentations, giving a quantity-dependent pseudopolynomial time bound with heap-based shortest paths.
assumptions_latex: The network has \(n\) nodes and \(m\) residual arcs up to constant factors.
Balances and residual capacities are integral.
Reduced costs are nonnegative for each shortest-path search.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm runs in \(O(F(m+n\log n))\) time under the stated implementation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacity-Scaling Successive Shortest-Path Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard integral capacity-scaling regime replacing linear dependence on total supply by logarithmic magnitude dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard capacity-scaling successive shortest-path algorithm on integral data of magnitude at most U\ge1, let \Delta range over descending powers of two. In each \Delta-phase the algorithm maintains its \Delta-residual and feasible-potential invariants and performs O(m) shortest-path augmentations before halving \Delta. Hence it performs O(m\log U) shortest-path computations. If each search uses binary-heap Dijkstra on nonnegative reduced costs, the running time is O\!\left(m\log U\,(m+n\log n)\right). The bound is polynomial in the binary encoding length of U but is not strongly polynomial because it depends on \log U.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard capacity scaling reduces the number of shortest-path augmentations to O(m log U), giving a weakly polynomial rather than strongly polynomial bound.
assumptions_latex: Capacities and balances are integral and have absolute magnitude at most U.
The standard capacity-scaling residual and feasible-potential invariants are maintained.
Each shortest-path search has nonnegative reduced arc costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{sp}}=O(m\log U),\qquad T=O\!\left(m\log U\,(m+n\log n)\right).

notation.meaning: Bound on integral capacity and balance magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Ascent Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Price updates driven by the concave Lagrangian dual of capacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\), initialize node prices \(\pi\) and choose
\[x(\pi)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le x\le u}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}(c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j)x_{ij}.\]
The concave dual function is \(g(\pi)=b^{\mathsf T}\pi+\sum_{(i,j)}\min_{0\le z\le u_{ij}}(c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j)z\), and \(b-Ax(\pi)\) is a supergradient. Select an ascent direction from this imbalance, increase prices until a reduced-cost breakpoint is reached, recompute minimizing arcs, and repeat. Stop when a selected \(x(\pi)\) satisfies \(Ax=b\); output \(x(\pi),\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual ascent adjusts node prices using imbalance supergradients, stopping at reduced-cost events. A Lagrangian minimizer that also satisfies flow balance is primal-dual optimal.
assumptions_latex: Arc capacities are finite and nonnegative.
The primal problem is feasible.
Price steps produce nondecreasing dual values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(Ax(\pi)=b\) at termination, then \(x(\pi)\) is primal optimal and \(\pi\) is dual optimal.

notation.meaning: Dual supergradient represented by node imbalance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Superdifferential Stationarity and Feasible Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stationarity certificate for the polyhedral node-price dual, including nonunique bound minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X(\pi)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le x\le u}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\pi^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\} and g(\pi)=\min_{0\le x\le u}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\pi^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\}. Then \partial^+g(\pi)=\{b-Ax:x\in X(\pi)\}. Hence \pi maximizes g if and only if 0\in\partial^+g(\pi), equivalently if and only if some x^*\in X(\pi) satisfies Ax^*=b. Such x^* is primal optimal and \pi is dual optimal. A particular tie-broken minimizer can be imbalanced even when another minimizer in X(\pi) supplies the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A price is dual optimal exactly when its bound-minimizing face contains a balanced flow; an arbitrarily selected minimizer can remain imbalanced because of ties.
assumptions_latex: The bounded minimum-cost-flow primal is feasible.
All arc capacities are finite, so X(\pi) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi\in\operatorname*{argmax}g\iff0\in\partial^+g(\pi)\iff\exists x^*\in X(\pi):Ax^*=b.

notation.meaning: Face of capacity-bounded Lagrangian minimizers at price pi.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting-Path Characterization and Price Formula for a Primal-Dual Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of the augmenting paths generable by the iteration and representation of its resulting price vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a primal-dual iteration starts from $(x,p)$, and let $I=\{i\in\mathcal N:g_i>0\}$ be the initial positive-surplus set. An augmenting path $P$ can be generated in the augmentation step through some ordering of the preceding operations if and only if $P$ has minimum length among all augmenting paths with respect to $x$ that start at a node in $I$. If $\bar p$ is the price vector produced by the iteration, then $\bar p_m=p_m+\max\{0,\bar d-d_m\}$ for every $m\in\mathcal N$, where $\bar d$ is the length of the iteration's augmenting path and $d_m$ is the minimum length of an unblocked path with respect to $x$ from some node in $I$ to $m$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual iteration can generate exactly the minimum-length augmenting paths beginning at an initially positive-surplus node. Its new price at each node is the old price plus the positive part of the augmenting-path length minus that node's minimum unblocked-path distance from the initial surplus set.

I=\{i\in\mathcal N:g_i>0\}\text{ is the initial positive-surplus set}
d_m=\min\{\operatorname{len}(Q):Q\text{ is an unblocked path with respect to }x\text{ from some }i\in I\text{ to }m\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is generable}\iff P\in\arg\min\{\operatorname{len}(Q):Q\text{ is an augmenting path with respect to }x\text{ starting in }I\},\qquad \bar p_m=p_m+\max\{0,\bar d-d_m\}\ \forall m\in\mathcal N.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariants and Termination of the Sequential Shortest-Path Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality and complementary-slackness preservation, optimal termination, and infeasibility detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimum-cost-flow problem with integer $a_{ij},b_{ij},c_{ij}$ and $s_i$, and apply the sequential shortest-path method from an integral flow-price pair satisfying complementary slackness. Each iteration preserves integrality and complementary slackness. If the problem is feasible, the method terminates with an integer optimal flow vector $x$ and an integer optimal price vector $p$. If it is infeasible, the method terminates either with $g_i\le0$ for every $i$ and $g_i<0$ for at least one $i$, or because no augmenting path starts at a node of $I$ and ends at a node with negative surplus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integral minimum-cost-flow data and an integral complementary-slackness starting pair, every sequential shortest-path iteration preserves integrality and complementary slackness. Feasible instances terminate at an integral optimal pair; infeasible instances terminate through one of the two stated tests.
assumptions_latex: a_{ij},b_{ij},c_{ij},s_i\in\mathbb Z\quad\text{for all applicable arcs and nodes}.
(x,p)\text{ is initially integral and satisfies complementary slackness}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Shortest-Path Primal-Dual Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-length augmentation, node-price update, and the three stopping conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $I$ be a nonempty set of positive-surplus nodes. If an augmenting path exists from $I$, choose one, $P$, having minimum length and augment along it. Let $\bar d=L_P$, and let $d_m$ be the minimum length of an unblocked path from a node of $I$ to $m$, with $d_m=\infty$ if none exists. Update
\[\bar p_m=p_m+\max\{0,\bar d-d_m\},\qquad m\in\mathcal N.\]
Terminate optimally if $g_i=0$ for every node. Declare infeasibility if $g_i\le0$ for every node with strict inequality for at least one node, or if no augmenting path starting in $I$ exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a shortest augmenting path from the positive-surplus source set, augment along it, and update each price using the difference between the augmenting-path length and the node's shortest unblocked-path distance. Stop optimally at zero surplus everywhere and declare infeasibility under either stated failure condition.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne I\subseteq\{i\in\mathcal N:g_i>0\}.
d_m=\min\{L_Q:Q\text{ is an unblocked path from }I\text{ to }m\},\quad d_m=\infty\text{ if the set is empty}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar p_m=p_m+\max\{0,L_P-d_m\}\quad\forall m\in\mathcal N,\quad\text{followed by repetition or one of the stated stopping outcomes.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual successive shortest-path algorithm for square assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment specialization of primal-dual sequential shortest-path augmentation. Previously selected edges may be replaced; only the cardinality of the partial assignment is guaranteed to increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a complete $m\times m$ assignment problem, initialize $\bar x=0$ and $UO=UD=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. At each iteration, form a residual network having zero-cost arcs from a dummy root to origins in $UO$, forward arcs $(i,m+j)$ of cost $c_{ij}$ when $\bar x_{ij}=0$, and reverse arcs $(m+j,i)$ of cost $-c_{ij}$ when $\bar x_{ij}=1$. Compute a basic optimal shortest-path tree rooted at the dummy root and complement assignment values along eligible alternating paths to unassigned destinations. The resulting partial assignment remains complementary slack with dual node potentials feasible for the assignment problem, while $|UO|=|UD|$ decreases by at least one per iteration. Hence, after at most $m$ iterations, $UO=UD=\varnothing$ and complementary slackness certifies that $\bar x$ is optimal. If each shortest-path computation costs $O(m^3)$, the total running time is $O(m^4)$. For a noncomplete bipartite instance, infeasibility of an intermediate residual shortest-path problem implies infeasibility of the original assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the empty partial assignment. Build a residual network by keeping unselected assignment edges forward with their original costs, reversing selected edges with negated costs, and connecting a dummy root to every unmatched origin at zero cost. Solve the resulting shortest-path problem and complement edges along eligible alternating tree paths to unmatched destinations. Selected edges may change, but the number of matched origins and destinations increases by at least one per iteration. Dual node potentials remain feasible and complementary to the partial assignment, so a complete assignment is optimal. The method takes at most m iterations and O(m^4) time when each shortest-path computation takes O(m^3). On a noncomplete bipartite graph, an infeasible residual problem certifies infeasibility of the assignment instance.
assumptions_latex: m\in\mathbb{N}
c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\quad(i,j=1,\ldots,m)
\text{The unconditional residual-feasibility and termination claim assumes a complete bipartite assignment network.}
\text{A basic optimal shortest-path solution can be computed in }O(m^3)\text{ time.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is optimal after at most }m\text{ iterations, and the total running time is }O(m^4).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auction/sequential shortest path algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-epsilon algorithm for integral bounded minimum-cost flow, stated with its initialization and maintained path invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix $\epsilon>0$. Maintain an integral flow-price pair $(x,p)$ satisfying $\epsilon$-CS and a simple $\epsilon$-unblocked path $P$ whose start has positive surplus and whose nodes have nonnegative surplus, with an acyclic admissible graph. One valid initialization chooses arbitrary $p$, sets $x_{ij}=c_{ij}$ if $p_i\ge a_{ij}+p_j$ and $x_{ij}=b_{ij}$ otherwise, and takes $P$ to be one positive-surplus node. If the terminal node $i$ has price below the minimum eligible forward or reverse threshold, raise $p_i$ to that minimum and contract $P$ when $i\ne s(P)$. Otherwise extend $P$ along a minimizing admissible direction. If the new terminal has negative surplus, augment along $P$; terminate under the stated global surplus test, or restart from a one-node path at a positive-surplus node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With epsilon fixed, ASSP keeps an integral flow-price pair satisfying epsilon-complementary slackness, an acyclic admissible graph, and a simple admissible path beginning at positive surplus. At each iteration it either raises the terminal price to the next admissibility threshold and contracts the path, or extends the path along a minimizing admissible arc. Reaching a negative-surplus node triggers augmentation, followed by termination under the algorithm's global surplus test or a restart at another positive-surplus node.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon>0
x\text{ is integral}
(x,p)\text{ initially satisfies }\epsilon\text{-CS}
G^*(x,p)\text{ is initially acyclic}
P\subseteq G^*(x,p),\ g_{s(P)}>0,\text{ and every node of }P\text{ has nonnegative surplus}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each iteration performs a price-rise/contraction or an admissible extension, with augmentation upon reaching negative surplus.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Graph Implementation of the Primal-Dual Shortest-Path Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative residual lengths, shortest augmenting-path computation, and distances for the price update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a flow-price pair $(x,p)$ satisfying complementary slackness, construct a residual graph on $\mathcal N$ with a forward arc $(i,j)$ of length $r_{ij}$ whenever $x_{ij}<c_{ij}$ and a reverse arc $(j,i)$ of length $-r_{ij}$ whenever $b_{ij}<x_{ij}$. If this produces parallel arcs in the same direction, retain an arc of minimum length. Compute a shortest path from $I$ to a negative-surplus node and distances $d_m$ from $I$. Complementary slackness makes every residual-arc length nonnegative, so Dijkstra's algorithm applies. Residual paths correspond length-preservingly to unblocked paths, hence the computed path is a required shortest augmenting path and the distances determine $\bar p_m=p_m+\max\{0,L_P-d_m\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use reduced costs on usable forward arcs and negated reduced costs on usable reverse arcs, retaining only a shortest parallel copy. Complementary slackness makes all residual lengths nonnegative, so Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest augmenting path and the distances used in the price update.
assumptions_latex: (x,p)\text{ satisfies complementary slackness}.
r_{ij}=a_{ij}+p_j-p_i.
\varnothing\ne I\subseteq\{i:g_i>0\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Dijkstra's algorithm returns a minimum-length augmenting path and distances satisfying the stated price-update formula.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hungarian Algorithm and Its Assignment Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual assignment specialization with shortest-path and zero-reduced-cost flow steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On an assignment instance, the Hungarian algorithm repeatedly computes shortest-path distances from the transformed supply node $s^*$, updates node potentials, and sends a maximum $s^*$-$t^*$ flow over zero-reduced-cost arcs. Every iteration sends at least one unit and assigns at least one additional vertex of $N_1$, so there are at most $n_1=|N_1|$ iterations. If one nonnegative-length shortest-path computation costs $S(n,m,C)$, the shortest-path work is $O(n_1S(n,m,C))$; the labeling-based maximum-flow work totals $O(nm)$ and is dominated, yielding overall time $O(n_1S(n,m,C))$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hungarian algorithm applies a primal-dual minimum-cost-flow scheme to assignment: update potentials from shortest-path distances and then send as much flow as possible on zero-reduced-cost arcs. It assigns at least one new first-side vertex per iteration, uses at most n1 iterations, and runs in O(n1 S(n,m,C)) time; its stated maximum-flow work totals O(nm).
assumptions_latex: S(n,m,C)\text{ is the time for the required shortest-path computation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{iterations}\le n_1,\qquad T_{\mathrm{flow}}=O(nm),\qquad T_{\mathrm{total}}=O(n_1S(n,m,C)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-Dual Minimum-Cost-Flow Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Labeling, flow augmentation, dual-price changes, optimal stopping, and infeasibility detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a flow-price pair $(x,p)$ satisfying complementary slackness, choose a nonempty set $I\subseteq\{i:g_i>0\}$ and initialize $\mathcal L=I$ and $\mathcal S=\varnothing$. Scan labeled nodes and label nodes reachable through balanced residual arcs. Upon labeling a node $j$ with $g_j<0$, trace a path $P$ from some initial node $i\in I$ and augment by
\[\delta=\min\!\left\{g_i,-g_j,\min_{(m,n)\in P^+}(c_{mn}-x_{mn}),\min_{(m,n)\in P^-}(x_{mn}-b_{mn})\right\}.\]
If all labeled nodes have been scanned without reaching negative surplus, let $\gamma$ be the minimum reduced-cost slack of an eligible forward or backward residual arc crossing from $\mathcal S$ to its complement, increase $p_i$ by $\gamma$ for every $i\in\mathcal S$, and label the nodes reached through minimizing arcs. If no node has positive surplus, terminate optimally when $g_i=0$ for every $i$ and otherwise declare infeasibility. If no eligible residual arc crosses from $\mathcal S$ in the price-change step, declare infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from positive-surplus nodes, scan balanced residual arcs. Augment when a negative-surplus node is reached; otherwise increase the prices of scanned nodes just enough to balance another residual arc. All-zero surplus gives an optimal flow-price pair, while the stated surplus-sign and residual-cut failures certify infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: (x,p)\text{ satisfies complementary slackness for the minimum-cost-flow problem}.
b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad\text{for every arc }(i,j).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each iteration either augments the flow, performs a dual-price change, returns an optimal pair, or terminates with one of the stated infeasibility conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced Costs and Unblocked-Path Lengths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and the complementary-slackness sign property used in the primal-dual sequential-shortest-path method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a pair $(x,p)$ satisfying complementary slackness, define $r_{ij}=a_{ij}+p_j-p_i$. A path $P$ is unblocked with respect to $x$ when $x_{ij}<c_{ij}$ for every forward arc $(i,j)\in P^+$ and $b_{ij}<x_{ij}$ for every backward arc $(i,j)\in P^-$. It is augmenting when its initial node has positive surplus and its terminal node has negative surplus. Define
\[L_P=\sum_{(i,j)\in P^+}r_{ij}-\sum_{(i,j)\in P^-}r_{ij}.\]
Complementary slackness implies $r_{ij}\ge0$ on the forward arcs and $r_{ij}\le0$ on the backward arcs of an unblocked path, and therefore $L_P\ge0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced cost equals arc cost plus head price minus tail price. An unblocked path has residual capacity in every traversed direction, and it is augmenting if it joins positive to negative surplus. Under complementary slackness its signed reduced-cost length is nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: (x,p)\text{ satisfies complementary slackness}.
P\text{ is unblocked with respect to }x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_{ij}\ge0\ \forall(i,j)\in P^+,\qquad r_{ij}\le0\ \forall(i,j)\in P^-,\qquad L_P\ge0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Labeling Implementation of a Primal-Dual Sequential Shortest-Path Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate-list residual shortest-path computation, augmenting-path recovery, and price updating within the primal-dual sequential shortest-path method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $(x,p)$ satisfying complementary slackness and a set $I$ of positive-surplus nodes, initialize $V=I$, $\bar d=\infty$, $d_i=0$ for $i\in I$, and $d_i=\infty$ otherwise. While $V\neq\varnothing$, remove $i\in V$. Relax each forward residual arc $(i,j)$ with $x_{ij}<c_{ij}$ when $d_i+r_{ij}<\min\{d_j,\bar d\}$, and each backward residual arc $(j,i)$ with $b_{ji}<x_{ji}$ when $d_i-r_{ji}<\min\{d_j,\bar d\}$. Record the corresponding predecessor label, update $d_j$, and add $j$ to $V$ if necessary. Whenever $g_j<0$, set $\bar d=d_j$ and $\bar j=j$. If $\bar d<\infty$ at termination, tracing labels backward from $\bar j$ to a node in $I$ yields an augmenting path of length $\bar d$, and $\bar p_m=p_m+\max\{0,\bar d-d_m\}$ for every $m\in\mathcal N$. Choosing a minimum-label node from $V$ gives Dijkstra's method; SLF, threshold, and other selection rules may instead be used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a complementary-slackness pair and a chosen set of positive-surplus nodes, relax forward and backward residual arcs using a candidate list and predecessor labels. If a negative-surplus node is reached, the labels recover an augmenting path and the distance labels determine the price update. Minimum-label extraction specializes the computation to Dijkstra's method, while other candidate-list rules are permitted.
assumptions_latex: (x,p)\text{ satisfies complementary slackness}
I\subseteq\{i\in\mathcal N:g_i>0\}
x_{ij}<c_{ij}\text{ for each usable forward residual arc }(i,j)
b_{ji}<x_{ji}\text{ for each usable backward residual arc }(j,i)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar d<\infty\implies\left(P\text{ is recovered by predecessor labels with length }\bar d\ \land\ \bar p_m=p_m+\max\{0,\bar d-d_m\}\ \forall m\in\mathcal N\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Iteration of the ASSP Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration rule using a surplus-rooted path, candidate arcs, price rises, path contraction, extension, and augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a positive-surplus node and initialize \(P\) to that node; terminate if none exists. At terminal node \(i=t(P)\), if its candidate list is empty, raise \(p_i\) by the maximum amount preserving \(\epsilon\text{-CS}\), contract \(P\) when \(i\ne s(P)\), and repeat. Otherwise extend \(P\) along a candidate forward or backward arc to node \(j\). If \(g_j<0\), augment along \(P\) by \(\delta=\min\{g_{s(P)},-g_{t(P)},\min_{a\in P}\operatorname{flowmargin}(a)\}\), increasing forward-arc flows and decreasing backward-arc flows by \(\delta\); then begin the next iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start a path at a positive-surplus node. At its terminal node, either maximally raise the price while preserving epsilon-complementary slackness and contract the path when possible, or extend it along a candidate arc. Upon reaching a negative-surplus node, augment by the minimum of the source surplus, sink deficit, and path arc flow margins, then begin the next iteration. Stop when no positive-surplus node remains.
assumptions_latex: (x,p)\text{ is the current flow-price state for which candidate lists and }\epsilon\text{-CS are defined.}
g_i\text{ denotes the surplus of node }i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure either detects that no positive-surplus node remains or performs the prescribed price, path, or augmentation update.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential least-cost-path buildup algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a prescribed-value minimum-cost flow while maintaining optimality at each attained, possibly smaller, flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: While the current flow value f is less than v_0, find a least-cost s\text{-}t augmentation path P in the residual network N'(f), and augment along P until either the flow value reaches v_0 or P ceases to be a least-cost augmentation path because an associated original arc is saturated or emptied. Residual arcs may have negative costs, so the shortest-path routine must handle negative arc costs. Because the current flow is maintained as optimal for its attained value, N'(f) has no negative-cost cycle. The method produces a flow of the prescribed value v_0 only upon termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment an optimal current flow along a cheapest residual source-to-sink path. Continue until the target value is reached or the path loses its cheapest-path status when an arc is saturated or emptied. Negative residual arc costs are allowed, but the maintained optimality invariant excludes negative-cost residual cycles. Before termination, the flow need not have the prescribed target value.
assumptions_latex: v_0\text{ is the prescribed flow value}.
f<v_0\text{ and the current flow is optimal among flows of value }f.
N'(f)\text{ is the residual network of the current flow}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At termination, the procedure has an optimal flow of value }v_0;\text{ before termination, it need not have value }v_0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relaxation Iteration for Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A flow-and-price relaxation iteration using balanced residual arcs, augmenting paths, and price changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\bar i\) with \(g_{\bar i}>0\), initialize \(\mathcal L=\{\bar i\}\) and \(\mathcal S=\varnothing\), and scan labeled nodes through balanced arcs having residual capacity. If a labeled node \(j\) with \(g_j<0\) is reached, trace an augmenting path \(P\) and set \[\delta=\min\!\left\{g_{\bar i},-g_j,\min_{(m,n)\in P^+}(c_{mn}-x_{mn}),\min_{(m,n)\in P^-}(x_{mn}-b_{mn})\right\};\] increase flow by \(\delta\) on \(P^+\) and decrease it by \(\delta\) on \(P^-\). If scanning instead requires a price change, place balanced arcs leaving \(\mathcal S\) at their appropriate upper or lower bounds, choose the least positive breakpoint \[\gamma=\min\!\left(\{p_j+a_{ij}-p_i:(i,j)\in\mathcal A,\ x_{ij}<c_{ij},\ i\in\mathcal S,\ j\notin\mathcal S\}\cup\{p_j-a_{ji}-p_i:(j,i)\in\mathcal A,\ b_{ji}<x_{ji},\ i\in\mathcal S,\ j\notin\mathcal S\}\right),\] and replace \(p_i\) by \(p_i+\gamma\) for every \(i\in\mathcal S\). If no node has positive imbalance, terminate: \((x,p)\) is optimal when every \(g_i=0\), and otherwise the problem is infeasible. If no eligible arc crosses the scanned cut after the boundary-flow adjustments, terminate as infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a node with positive imbalance and scan balanced residual arcs. Reaching a negative-imbalance node produces an augmenting path; send the largest amount allowed by the endpoint imbalances and residual arc bounds. If augmentation is unavailable, move all balanced arcs crossing the scanned cut to their relevant bounds and increase the scanned-node prices to the next arc breakpoint. Absence of positive imbalance certifies optimality when all imbalances vanish and otherwise certifies infeasibility; absence of an eligible cut arc after adjustment also certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad\text{for every arc }(i,j)
\text{Balanced arcs and node imbalances }g_i\text{ are defined for the current flow-price pair }(x,p).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each iteration performs either a residual-path flow augmentation or a dual price change, with the stated optimality and infeasibility termination conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Node Relaxation Iteration for Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single-node specialization of the flow-and-price relaxation method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a node \(i\) with \(g_i>0\) and define \[B_i^+=\{j:(i,j)\text{ is balanced and }x_{ij}<c_{ij}\},\qquad B_i^-=\{j:(j,i)\text{ is balanced and }b_{ji}<x_{ji}\}.\] While possible, choose \(j\in B_i^+\) or \(j\in B_i^-\) with \(g_j<0\) and transfer \(\delta=\min\{g_i,-g_j,c_{ij}-x_{ij}\}\) on an outgoing arc or \(\delta=\min\{g_i,-g_j,x_{ji}-b_{ji}\}\) on an incoming arc, updating the two endpoint imbalances and deleting an arc from the corresponding set when its bound is reached. If \[g_i\ge \sum_{j\in B_i^+}(c_{ij}-x_{ij})+\sum_{j\in B_i^-}(x_{ji}-b_{ji}),\] first move all arcs indexed by \(B_i^+\) and \(B_i^-\) to their upper and lower bounds, respectively, subtract those adjustments from \(g_i\), and increase \(p_i\) to the smallest strictly larger value among \(p_j+a_{ij}\) for outgoing arcs and \(p_j-a_{ji}\) for incoming arcs. If the breakpoint set is empty and \(g_i>0\), the primal problem is infeasible because the dual cost is unbounded along \(p_i\); if it is empty and \(g_i=0\), leave \(p\) unchanged and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a positive-imbalance node, repeatedly send flow along balanced incident arcs toward negative-imbalance neighbors, limited by endpoint imbalances and residual arc bounds. When the available balanced residual capacity does not exceed the remaining imbalance, saturate those arcs and raise the node price to the next incident-arc breakpoint. An empty breakpoint set certifies primal infeasibility if positive imbalance remains; if the imbalance is zero, the price is left unchanged.

b_{uv}\le x_{uv}\le c_{uv}\quad\text{for every arc }(u,v)
B_i^+\text{ and }B_i^-\text{ consist of balanced incident arcs with positive residual adjustment capacity.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration performs admissible single-arc flow transfers or a single-node price increase, with the stated empty-breakpoint infeasibility and zero-imbalance boundary cases.}

children.title: Dual Stalling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Degenerate or weak-progress price configurations in dual-driven methods.

assumptions_latex: The concave flow dual is \(g(p)=\inf_{\ell\le x\le u}\{c^Tx+p^T(Ax-b)\}\).
An implementation supplies an allowed direction \(d\), step interval \([0,\alpha_{\max}]\), and a selected minimizer \(x(p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stalled state need not provide a feasible primal flow: \(Ax(p)\ne b\) may hold even though the prescribed dual step makes no progress.

notation.meaning: Direction proposed by the dual-ascent rule.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational definition of stalling for restricted dual-ascent rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational stalling condition relative to a specified dual-ascent rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual iteration is stalled at \(p\) when its prescribed nonzero direction \(d\) satisfies \(g(p+\alpha d)=g(p)\) for every \(\alpha\in[0,\alpha_{\max}]\), or when the rule returns \(d=0\), while its currently selected bound minimizer remains nonconservative: \(Ax(p)\ne b\). The definition is relative to the permitted directions and tie-breaking rule; it does not assert that \(p\) is globally dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual method stalls when its permitted update cannot improve the dual objective although its associated bound-minimizing flow still violates conservation.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Stalling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed stalling condition is algorithm- and tie-breaking-dependent and has no citation. Source support is needed to establish that this is a recognized regime for the parent method rather than a newly constructed operational definition.

children.title: Dual Reoptimization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Reuse of price information after controlled changes to network data.

assumptions_latex: The current prices \(p\) determine the bound-minimizer face \(X(p)=\arg\min_{\ell\le x\le u}(c+A^Tp)^Tx\).
The current dual-ascent rule has stalled while no selected \(x\in X(p)\) is conservative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recomputed pair is either primal-dual optimal, or it exposes a new ascent direction or admissible residual augmentation that leaves the stalled regime.

notation.meaning: Face of bound minimizers at current prices.
Residual network induced by the reselected flow.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reoptimization over a degenerate dual minimizer face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic recovery by globally reoptimizing the current dual minimizer face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On stalling, solve the restricted feasibility problem \(x\in X(p)\) and \(Ax=b\). If it is feasible, output such an \(x\) with \(p\). Otherwise choose a minimizer \(x\in X(p)\), rebuild \(G_x\), and recompute globally the shortest-path, cut, or block direction prescribed by the parent primal-dual method. Move \(p\) to the first breakpoint at which \(X(p)\) changes, reselect \(x\), and restart local relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reoptimization escapes a stall by reconsidering the entire current minimizer face and globally recomputing a residual path, cut, or price direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Reoptimization Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the claimed face-reoptimization procedure or the conclusion that it necessarily exposes an ascent direction or admissible augmentation. The statement also blends shortest-path, cut, and block variants without fixing their hypotheses.

children.title: Stall-Recovery Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions separating reusable dual states from states requiring substantial repair.

assumptions_latex: A stalled state \((x,p)\) and a set \(\mathcal U(p)\) of admissible dual updates are fixed.
The recovery merit is \(M(x)=\lVert Ax-b\rVert_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state is recoverable exactly when an allowed update yields strict dual ascent or reaches a new bound-minimizer face with smaller conservation violation; otherwise it lies on the stall-recovery boundary.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact operational boundary induced by allowed recovery steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-relative boundary between recoverable and persistent dual stalls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stalled pair \((x,p)\) is recoverable if some \((d,\alpha)\in\mathcal U(p)\) satisfies either \(g(p+\alpha d)>g(p)\), or \(X(p+\alpha d)\ne X(p)\) and contains \(x'\) with \(M(x')<M(x)\). The stall-recovery boundary consists of stalled pairs for which neither alternative holds. Persistent stalling is therefore possible only when every permitted step is dual-flat and every newly reachable minimizer face has conservation merit at least \(M(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery ends precisely where every allowed price step is dual-flat and cannot reach a bound-minimizing flow with less imbalance.
knowledge_statements.title: Stall-Recovery Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary is defined relative to an unspecified update set and parent algorithm, and no source establishes this merit-based characterization. The dual objective and minimizer-face map used in the statement are also not introduced within this record.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc-bound violation and primal penalty for the out-of-kilter method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific penalty representation used to analyze the primal phase of the out-of-kilter algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each arc $(i,j)$ with finite bounds $\ell_{ij}\le u_{ij}$, define
\[
P_{ij}(x_{ij})=\max\{0,\ell_{ij}-x_{ij}\}+\max\{0,x_{ij}-u_{ij}\}.
\]
Then $P_{ij}(x_{ij})=0$ if and only if $\ell_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}$, and $P_{ij}(x_{ij})>0$ otherwise. For a flow-conserving vector $x$ and a sufficiently large penalty parameter $M$, define
\[
f(x)=cx+M\sum_{(i,j)}P_{ij}(x_{ij}).
\]
If $Ax=0$ and $(wA)_{ij}=z_{ij}$, then
\[
f(x)=\sum_{(i,j)}(c_{ij}-z_{ij})x_{ij}+M\sum_{(i,j)}P_{ij}(x_{ij}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The violation of an arc's lower and upper bounds is measured by the sum of its two one-sided violations. It vanishes exactly when the arc flow lies within its bounds. Adding a sufficiently large multiple of total violation to the flow cost gives the primal penalty used in the out-of-kilter analysis. For a conserving flow, subtracting the zero term wAx yields an equivalent reduced-cost representation.
assumptions_latex: -\infty<\ell_{ij}\le u_{ij}<\infty\quad\text{for every arc }(i,j)
Ax=0
(wA)_{ij}=z_{ij}
M\text{ is sufficiently large for the intended penalty analysis}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{ij}(x_{ij})=0\iff \ell_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij},\qquad f(x)=cx+M\sum_{(i,j)}P_{ij}(x_{ij})=\sum_{(i,j)}(c_{ij}-z_{ij})x_{ij}+M\sum_{(i,j)}P_{ij}(x_{ij}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Strategy of the Out-of-Kilter Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-level strategy for bounded minimum-cost circulation; finite-termination hypotheses are recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with a conserving flow $x$, for example $x_{ij}=0$, and a feasible dual state obtained from arbitrary node potentials $w$ together with the associated arc variables $h_{ij}$ and $v_{ij}$. Compute the kilter state and kilter number of every arc. For a selected out-of-kilter arc, seek a conserving primal flow change that improves its kilter number without worsening any other arc. If no such change can be constructed, update the dual state without worsening any kilter number and repeat the primal phase. The alternatives at termination are an optimal flow and a determination of primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize a conserving flow and feasible dual state, classify all arcs by kilter status, and alternate nonworsening primal flow repairs with dual price updates. Termination yields either an optimal flow or an infeasibility determination.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Termination of the Integral Out-of-Kilter Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness under integral network data and the rule of retaining a selected arc until it becomes in kilter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume $\ell,u,c\in\mathbb Z^{|A|}$ and retain a selected out-of-kilter arc until it becomes in kilter. Each primal circuit augmentation through the selected arc decreases its kilter number and the total network kilter number by a positive integer. After a finite dual update, either the reachable set $X$ gains a node or, if $X$ is unchanged, the new sets satisfy $S_1'\subseteq S_1$ and $S_2'\subseteq S_2$, with at least one inclusion strict. Therefore only finitely many primal augmentations and dual updates can occur before all arcs are in kilter or $S_1\cup S_2=\varnothing$ and $\theta=\infty$. Hence the algorithm terminates finitely with an optimal solution or an infeasibility determination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integer lower bounds, upper bounds, and costs, and while retaining one selected arc until repaired, primal steps make positive integral progress. Dual steps either enlarge the reachable set or strictly shrink the finite cut sets. These measures force finite termination at an optimum or an infeasibility finding.
assumptions_latex: \ell,u,c\in\mathbb Z^{|A|}
\text{the selected out-of-kilter arc is retained until it becomes in kilter}
\text{the primal and dual phases use the stated nonworsening updates}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The out-of-kilter algorithm terminates after finitely many updates with an optimal solution or an infeasibility determination.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual formulation of bounded minimum-cost circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The network-flow dual representation used by the out-of-kilter method, including optimal arc-multiplier completion for fixed node potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the minimum-cost circulation problem with flow conservation and bounds \(\ell_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\) on \((i,j)\in A\), its dual is
\[
\max\ \sum_{(i,j)\in A}\ell_{ij}v_{ij}-\sum_{(i,j)\in A}u_{ij}h_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
w_i-w_j+v_{ij}-h_{ij}=c_{ij},\qquad h_{ij},v_{ij}\ge0,
\]
where each \(w_i\) is unrestricted. For any fixed integer vector \(w\), the choices
\[
v_{ij}=\max\{0,c_{ij}-w_i+w_j\},\qquad h_{ij}=\max\{0,-(c_{ij}-w_i+w_j)\}
\]
form a dual-feasible completion and maximize the dual objective over \((h,v)\) conditional on that \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded minimum-cost circulation dual has unrestricted node potentials and nonnegative lower- and upper-bound multipliers. For fixed integer node potentials, taking the positive and negative parts of each adjusted arc cost gives a feasible and conditionally optimal choice of the arc multipliers.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is the set of existing directed arcs.}
\ell_{ij}\le u_{ij}\quad((i,j)\in A).
w\in\mathbb Z^m\text{ is fixed for the multiplier-completion claim.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (w,h,v)\text{ is dual feasible, and }(h,v)\text{ maximizes the dual objective for the fixed }w.

knowledge_statements.title: Kilter Classifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise linear-cost kilter classification using reduced-cost sign conventions, including fixed arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Arc \(a\) is in kilter for \((x,p)\) if \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) and one of the following mutually exclusive cases holds: \(\ell_a=u_a=x_a\); \(\ell_a<u_a\), \(x_a=\ell_a\), and \(r_a\ge0\); \(\ell_a<x_a<u_a\) and \(r_a=0\); or \(\ell_a<u_a\), \(x_a=u_a\), and \(r_a\le0\). It is out of kilter otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc is in kilter when its flow respects its bounds and its reduced-cost sign agrees with whether it is at the lower bound, in the interior, or at the upper bound; a fixed arc is automatically in kilter.
assumptions_latex: The bounded flow problem is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\).
For each arc \(a\), let \(r_a=c_a+(A^Tp)_a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An arc is in kilter exactly when its flow and reduced cost satisfy the stated bound-complementarity cases; otherwise it is out of kilter.

notation.meaning: Lower and upper bounds on arc a.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent scalar stationarity formulation of the arcwise kilter cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(I_a=[\ell_a,u_a]\), arc \(a\) is in kilter for \((x,p)\) if and only if \(x_a\in I_a\) and \(0\in r_a+N_{I_a}(x_a)\), where \(r_a=c_a+(A^{\mathsf T}p)_a\) and \(N_{I_a}(x_a)=\{g:g(y-x_a)\le0\ \forall y\in I_a\}\). This gives \(r_a\ge0\) at a nonfixed lower bound, \(r_a=0\) in the interior, \(r_a\le0\) at a nonfixed upper bound, and no restriction for a singleton interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The kilter table is the scalar normal-cone stationarity condition for minimizing reduced cost over an arc's bound interval.

\(r_a=c_a+(A^{\mathsf T}p)_a\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kilter Conditions for a Submodular Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines arcwise and vertex-pair kilter status, its negation, the associated characteristic curve, and the all-in-kilter optimality implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a submodular flow \(\varphi\in\mathcal N_{SS}\) and a potential \(p:V\to\mathbb R\), an arc \(a\in A\) is in kilter when condition (12.2) or condition (12.3) holds. For distinct \(u,v\in V\), the ordered pair \((u,v)\) is in kilter when \(p(u)\ge p(v)\) or \(u\notin\operatorname{dep}(\partial\varphi,v)\). An arc or pair is out of kilter exactly when it is not in kilter. If every arc and every ordered pair of distinct vertices is in kilter, then \(\varphi\) is optimal. For each \(a\in A\), its characteristic curve is the set of points \((\varphi(a),p(\partial^-a)-p(\partial^+a))\in\mathbb R^2\) for which \(a\) is in kilter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a submodular flow and vertex potential, arc kilter status is determined by either of the two one-sided derivative and capacity conditions, while a distinct ordered vertex pair is in kilter if its potential is nonincreasing in the stated order or the first vertex is absent from the relevant dependence set. Failure of these conditions is out-of-kilter status. If all arcs and all distinct ordered vertex pairs are in kilter, the flow is optimal. The arc's characteristic curve records the flow and potential-difference points at which it is in kilter.

p:V\to\mathbb R
a\in A
u,v\in V,\ u\ne v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\text{all arcs and all ordered pairs of distinct vertices are in kilter}\bigr]\implies \varphi\text{ is optimal}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Arc Kilter Number
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise kilter classification in a minimum-cost-flow residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a residual arc $(i,j)\in G(x)$ with residual capacity $r_{ij}$ and reduced cost $c_{ij}^{\pi}$, define
\[
k_{ij}=\begin{cases}0,&c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge0,\\r_{ij},&c_{ij}^{\pi}<0.
\end{cases}
\]
A residual arc with nonnegative reduced cost satisfies the residual reduced-cost optimality condition. If its reduced cost is negative, sending $r_{ij}$ units on it exhausts its residual capacity and removes that violating arc from the residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual arc has kilter number zero when its reduced cost is nonnegative; otherwise its kilter number is its residual capacity, which is the flow needed to exhaust the violating arc.
assumptions_latex: (i,j)\in G(x)
r_{ij}\ge0
c_{ij}^{\pi}\text{ is the residual-arc reduced cost}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_{ij}=0\text{ if }c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge0,\qquad k_{ij}=r_{ij}\text{ if }c_{ij}^{\pi}<0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: In-Kilter Arcs and Kilter Numbers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise primal-dual classification for a capacitated minimum-cost-flow arc with zero lower bound; the current flow may violate its bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an arc $(i,j)$ with capacity $u_{ij}\ge 0$, flow value $x_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}$, and reduced cost $c_{ij}^{\pi}$, the arc is in-kilter when $(x_{ij}=0\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge0)$, $(0<x_{ij}<u_{ij}\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}=0)$, and $(x_{ij}=u_{ij}\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}\le0)$. Equivalently, its kilter number—the magnitude of the flow change required to become in-kilter while holding $c_{ij}^{\pi}$ fixed—is
\[
k_{ij}=\begin{cases}|x_{ij}|,&c_{ij}^{\pi}>0,\\|u_{ij}-x_{ij}|,&c_{ij}^{\pi}<0,\\-x_{ij},&c_{ij}^{\pi}=0\text{ and }x_{ij}<0,\\x_{ij}-u_{ij},&c_{ij}^{\pi}=0\text{ and }x_{ij}>u_{ij},\\0,&c_{ij}^{\pi}=0\text{ and }0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}.
\end{cases}
\]
The aggregate kilter number is $K=\sum_{(i,j)\in A}k_{ij}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc is in-kilter when its flow position and reduced-cost sign satisfy the arcwise complementary-slackness conditions. Its kilter number is the flow change needed to reach an in-kilter position at fixed reduced cost, and the aggregate kilter number sums these violations over all arcs.
assumptions_latex: (i,j)\in A
u_{ij}\ge0
x_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}
c_{ij}^{\pi}\text{ is the reduced cost under node potentials }\pi

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc kilter state and kilter number
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the arcwise primal-dual status and distance measure, with the source's sufficient monotone-progress condition for finite termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an arc \((i,j)\), let \(r_{ij}=w_i-w_j-c_{ij}\). The arc is in kilter when \(\ell_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\) and
\[
r_{ij}<0\Rightarrow x_{ij}=\ell_{ij},\qquad r_{ij}>0\Rightarrow x_{ij}=u_{ij}.
\]
The kilter number—the minimum change in \(x_{ij}\) required to obtain an in-kilter flow while \(r_{ij}\) is fixed—is
\[
K_{ij}=\begin{cases}
|x_{ij}-\ell_{ij}|,&r_{ij}<0,\\
|x_{ij}-u_{ij}|,&r_{ij}>0,\\
\ell_{ij}-x_{ij},&r_{ij}=0\text{ and }x_{ij}<\ell_{ij},\\
0,&r_{ij}=0\text{ and }\ell_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij},\\
x_{ij}-u_{ij},&r_{ij}=0\text{ and }x_{ij}>u_{ij}.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence \(K_{ij}\ge0\), and \(K_{ij}=0\) exactly when the arc is in kilter. On a finite network, an out-of-kilter procedure terminates after finitely many progress events if no arc's kilter number increases and, whenever some \(K_{ij}>0\), some kilter number decreases by a positive integer after finitely many intervening operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc is in kilter when its flow is within its bounds and agrees with the sign of its reduced-cost expression. Its kilter number is the smallest flow change needed to reach that state. It is nonnegative and equals zero exactly in kilter. Finite termination follows under the stated continuing, monotone positive-integer progress condition.
assumptions_latex: \ell_{ij}\le u_{ij}.
r_{ij}=w_i-w_j-c_{ij}.
\text{For the termination claim, the arc set is finite and progress continues whenever some }K_{ij}>0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K_{ij}\ge0,\qquad K_{ij}=0\iff(i,j)\text{ is in kilter};\text{ the stated monotone integer-progress condition ensures finite termination.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Cycle-Repair Phase of the Out-of-Kilter Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of an admissible-change network and a conserving cycle augmentation for a selected out-of-kilter arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\bar x$ be a conserving flow, so $A\bar x=0$, and let $(p,q)$ represent a selected out-of-kilter arc in the admissible-change network $G'$. Include $(i,j)$ in $G'$ when $x_{ij}$ may be increased without worsening its kilter number, and include $(j,i)$ when $x_{ij}$ may be decreased without worsening it; assign each included arc its permitted change bound. Search for a directed path from $q$ to $p$. If one exists, it and $(p,q)$ form a directed circuit. Change the corresponding original-network cycle flow by the minimum permitted change on the circuit. The new flow is conserving, no kilter number worsens, and the selected arc improves. If no such path exists, let $X$ be the nodes reachable from $q$ and enter the dual phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build a directed network of flow changes that do not worsen kilter numbers. A path from the selected arc's head back to its tail closes an augmenting circuit; augment by its smallest permitted change. If no path exists, pass the reachable set to the dual phase.
assumptions_latex: A\bar x=0
(p,q)\text{ represents a selected out-of-kilter arc in }G'
\text{each arc of }G'\text{ represents a permitted nonworsening flow change}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}\text{a conserving, nonworsening circuit augmentation improves the selected arc},&q\leadsto p\text{ in }G',\\\text{enter the dual phase with reachable set }X,&q\not\leadsto p\text{ in }G'.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Out-of-Kilter Repair Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path price updates and residual-cycle augmentations starting from a feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $\pi:=0$, establish a feasible flow $x$, form $G(x)$, and compute residual-arc kilter numbers. While an out-of-kilter arc $(p,q)$ exists, set $\ell_{ij}:=\max\{0,c_{ij}^{\pi}\}$ on every residual arc. In $G(x)\setminus\{(q,p)\}$, compute shortest-path distances $d(i)$ from $q$ and a shortest path $P$ from $q$ to $p$, and update $\pi'(i):=\pi(i)-d(i)$ for all $i\in N$. If $c_{pq}^{\pi'}<0$, set $W:=P\cup\{(p,q)\}$, choose $\delta:=\min\{r_{ij}:(i,j)\in W\}$, augment $\delta$ units along $W$, and update $x$, $G(x)$, and the reduced costs. Continue while an out-of-kilter arc remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible flow, repeatedly select an out-of-kilter residual arc, perform the prescribed shortest-path potential update, and, when the selected arc remains negative, augment by the bottleneck residual capacity around the resulting directed cycle.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is an initially feasible flow}
G(x)\text{ is the residual network}
\pi=0\text{ initially}
P\text{ is a shortest }q\text{-}p\text{ path in }G(x)\setminus\{(q,p)\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure repeatedly applies the specified price update and conditional residual-cycle augmentation while out-of-kilter arcs remain.}
