knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Phase Out-of-Kilter Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual arc-status repair procedure for a minimum-cost network flow or circulation with lower and upper arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a conserving integer flow \(x\) and integral node potentials \(w\), and compute \(z_{ij}-c_{ij}=w_i-w_j-c_{ij}\). In the primal phase, determine every arc's kilter state. If all arcs are in kilter, stop with an optimal solution. Otherwise, select an out-of-kilter arc \((p,q)\) and construct the auxiliary network from permitted forward increases and reverse decreases. If an auxiliary circuit containing \((p,q)\) exists, let \(\Delta\) be the minimum permitted change on the circuit, augment the corresponding cycle by \(\Delta\), and repeat the primal phase. If no such circuit exists, let \(X\) be the nodes reachable from \(q\), let \(\bar X=V\setminus X\), define \(S_1=\{(i,j):i\in X,\ j\in\bar X,\ z_{ij}-c_{ij}<0,\ x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\}\) and \(S_2=\{(i,j):i\in\bar X,\ j\in X,\ z_{ij}-c_{ij}>0,\ x_{ij}\ge \ell_{ij}\}\), and set \(\theta=\min\bigl(\{|z_{ij}-c_{ij}|:(i,j)\in S_1\cup S_2\}\cup\{\infty\}\bigr)\). If \(\theta=\infty\), stop because no feasible solution exists. Otherwise set \(w_i'=w_i+\theta\) for \(i\in X\) and \(w_i'=w_i\) for \(i\in\bar X\), update the crossing reduced-cost values accordingly, and return to the primal phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with a conserving integer flow and integral node potentials. If every arc is in kilter, return an optimal solution. Otherwise, try to repair a selected out-of-kilter arc by augmenting through an admissible auxiliary circuit using its smallest permitted flow change. If no such circuit exists, compute the smallest eligible potential adjustment across the reachability cut. An infinite adjustment certifies infeasibility; a finite adjustment updates the potentials and crossing reduced-cost values before the primal phase resumes.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is a directed costed network with arc bounds }\ell_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}.
x\text{ is an initial conserving integer flow, not necessarily satisfying every arc bound, and }w\text{ is an integral node-potential vector}.
z_{ij}-c_{ij}=w_i-w_j-c_{ij}\text{, with permitted flow changes determined by the arc kilter states}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{All arcs in kilter imply optimality; }\theta=\infty\text{ implies infeasibility; otherwise the method performs a primal augmentation or dual update and continues.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Labeling procedure for the out-of-kilter algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-flow and dual-potential repair procedure for a capacitated minimum-cost network-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each labeled node \(j\), use \(L(j)=(\pm i,\Delta_j)\), where \((+i,\Delta_j)\) permits increasing \(x_{ij}\) and \((-i,\Delta_j)\) permits decreasing \(x_{ji}\), without increasing any arc's kilter number. Begin with a conserving flow \(x\) and node potentials \(w\). If all arcs are in kilter, terminate with an optimal solution. Otherwise select an out-of-kilter arc, label the endpoint in the direction of its required correction, and propagate labels through admissible arc changes, setting each new bottleneck to \(\Delta_j=\min\{\Delta_i,\Delta_{ij}\}\) for a forward increase or \(\Delta_j=\min\{\Delta_i,\Delta_{ji}\}\) for a backward decrease. If the opposite endpoint \(p\) is labeled, augment by \(\Delta_p\) around the resulting cycle and repeat. If labeling stops with labeled set \(X\), define \(S_1=\{(i,j):i\in X,\ j\in\bar X,\ z_{ij}-c_{ij}<0,\ x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\}\) and \(S_2=\{(i,j):i\in\bar X,\ j\in X,\ z_{ij}-c_{ij}>0,\ x_{ij}\ge \ell_{ij}\}\), and set \(\theta=\min\{|z_{ij}-c_{ij}|:(i,j)\in S_1\cup S_2\}\), taking \(\theta=\infty\) if the union is empty. If \(\theta=\infty\), terminate with infeasibility; otherwise replace \(w_i\) by \(w_i+\theta\) for \(i\in X\), leave the other potentials unchanged, update the crossing reduced-cost differences accordingly, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Label nodes with predecessor directions and bottleneck flow changes that do not worsen any arc's kilter number. Starting from a conserving flow and node potentials, terminate optimally if every arc is in kilter. Otherwise propagate admissible labels from an out-of-kilter arc. Reaching the opposite endpoint yields a cycle augmentation. If propagation stalls, change the potentials of all labeled nodes by the smallest eligible crossing reduced-cost magnitude. If there is no eligible crossing arc, terminate because no feasible solution exists.
assumptions_latex: \text{A minimum-cost network-flow problem is given with arc costs }c_{ij}\text{ and bounds }\ell_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}.
x\text{ is a conserving flow, and }w\text{ is a current vector of node potentials.}
\text{Kilter states and admissible flow changes are evaluated from the current }x\text{ and reduced-cost quantities }z_{ij}-c_{ij}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure repeatedly performs a kilter-nonworsening cycle augmentation or a node-potential update, and terminates either with all arcs in kilter and an optimal solution or with }\theta=\infty\text{ and infeasibility.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Cut-Price Update in the Out-of-Kilter Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual repair after the admissible-change network contains no circuit through the selected out-of-kilter arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose no circuit of $G'$ contains the selected out-of-kilter arc $(p,q)$. Let $X$ be the nodes reachable from $q$ in $G'$ and $\bar X=V\setminus X$, so $q\in X$ and $p\in\bar X$. Define
$S_1=\{(i,j):i\in X,j\in\bar X,7_{ij}-c_{ij}<0,x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\}$ and $S_2=\{(i,j):i\in\bar X,j\in X,7_{ij}-c_{ij}>0,x_{ij}\ge \ell_{ij}\}$. Let $\theta_r=\min_{(i,j)\in S_r}|z_{ij}-c_{ij}|$, with $\theta_r=\infty$ when $S_r=\varnothing$, and set $\theta=\min\{\theta_1,\theta_2\}$. If $0<\theta<\infty$, update $w_i'=w_i+\theta$ for $i\in X$ and $w_i'=w_i$ for $i\in\bar X$. Equivalently, reduced-cost differences are unchanged within each side of the cut, increased by $\theta$ on arcs from $X$ to $\bar X$, and decreased by $\theta$ on arcs from $\bar X$ to $X$. No kilter number worsens, and the algorithm returns to the primal phase. If $\theta=\infty$, the primal flow problem is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the selected out-of-kilter arc lies on no admissible circuit, form the set reachable from its head. Increase all node prices in that set by the smallest cut reduced-cost slack that can change a kilter state without worsening any kilter number. A finite step returns the method to the primal phase; an infinite step signals infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: q\in X,\quad p\in\bar X
z_{ij}=w_i-w_j
S_1=\{(i,j):i\in X,j\in\bar X,z_{ij}-c_{ij}<0,x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\}
S_2=\{(i,j):i\in\bar X,j\in X,z_{ij}-c_{ij}>0,x_{ij}\ge\ell_{ij}\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta<\infty\Rightarrow\text{a nonworsening dual update is made};\qquad \theta=\infty\Rightarrow\text{the primal problem is infeasible.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arcwise kilter characterization of minimum-cost optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient primal-dual optimality certificate for a bounded minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be any conserving flow and let \(w\in\mathbb Z^m\). For each existing arc define
\[
r_{ij}=w_i-w_j-c_{ij},\qquad v_{ij}=\max\{0,-r_{ij}\},\qquad h_{ij}=\max\{0,r_{ij}\}.
\]
Then \(x\) and \((w,h,v)\) are respectively primal and dual optimal if and only if, for every \((i,j)\in A\),
\[
r_{ij}<0\Rightarrow x_{ij}=\ell_{ij},\qquad
r_{ij}>0\Rightarrow x_{ij}=u_{ij},\qquad
r_{ij}=0\Rightarrow \ell_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}.
\]

w\in\mathbb Z^m.
\ell_{ij}\le u_{ij}\text{ and }r_{ij}=w_i-w_j-c_{ij}\text{ for every }(i,j)\in A.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ and }(w,h,v)\text{ are primal-dual optimal}\iff\text{ all stated arcwise sign and bound conditions hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite Out-of-Kilter Dual Step Certifies Flow Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut obstruction obtained when both sets defining the dual step length are empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
During a dual phase, let $X$ be the nodes reachable from the head of the selected out-of-kilter arc and let $\bar X=V\setminus X$. If $\theta=\infty$, equivalently $S_1=S_2=\varnothing$, then $x_{ij}\ge u_{ij}$ for every arc from $X$ to $\bar X$ and $x_{ij}\le\ell_{ij}$ for every arc from $\bar X$ to $X$, with at least one of these inequalities strict. Since the current flow is conserving, this implies
$\sum_{i\in X,j\in\bar X}u_{ij}-\sum_{i\in\bar X,j\in X}\ell_{ij}<0$.
No flow satisfying conservation and all lower and upper bounds can therefore exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If both cut sets used to compute the dual step are empty, the reachable-set cut has less total outgoing upper capacity than required incoming lower flow. This strict cut violation rules out every conserving flow satisfying the arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: Ax=0
X\cap\bar X=\varnothing,\quad X\cup\bar X=V
S_1=S_2=\varnothing
\theta=\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i\in X,j\in\bar X}u_{ij}<\sum_{i\in\bar X,j\in X}\ell_{ij}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\nexists\,\widehat x:\ A\widehat x=0,\ \ell\le\widehat x\le u.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Out-of-Kilter Extension for Bound-Infeasible Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalization to arcs with lower bounds and starting flows that may violate their bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arcs with bounds $l_{ij}\le u_{ij}$, the in-kilter conditions are $x_{ij}=l_{ij}\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge0$, $l_{ij}<x_{ij}<u_{ij}\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}=0$, and $x_{ij}=u_{ij}\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}\le0$; the kilter number is the magnitude of the flow change needed to reach this set at fixed reduced cost. Construct the generalized residual network arcwise: if $l_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}$, include $(i,j)$ with capacity $u_{ij}-x_{ij}$ and cost $c_{ij}$ when $x_{ij}<u_{ij}$, and $(j,i)$ with capacity $x_{ij}-l_{ij}$ and cost $-c_{ij}$ when $x_{ij}>l_{ij}$; if $x_{ij}<l_{ij}$, include a lower-infeasible arc $(i,j)$ of capacity $l_{ij}-x_{ij}$ and cost $c_{ij}$; if $x_{ij}>u_{ij}$, include an upper-infeasible arc $(j,i)$ of capacity $x_{ij}-u_{ij}$ and cost $-c_{ij}$. Feasible residual arcs use $k_{ij}=0$ for $c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge0$ and $k_{ij}=r_{ij}$ for $c_{ij}^{\pi}<0$. An infeasible residual arc's kilter number is the residual-capacity change needed to restore feasibility and optimality; in particular, for a lower-infeasible arc, $k_{ij}=l_{ij}-x_{ij}$ when $c_{ij}^{\pi}\ge0$ and $k_{ij}=u_{ij}-x_{ij}$ when $c_{ij}^{\pi}<0$. Lower- and upper-infeasible arcs have positive kilter numbers, and sending additional residual flow on them decreases those numbers. The ordinary out-of-kilter iteration then applies without first establishing a feasible flow and may start from $x=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonzero lower bounds, in-kilter status uses the lower bound, interior, and upper bound reduced-cost conditions. A generalized residual network includes ordinary feasible arcs and special lower- or upper-infeasible arcs. Their kilter numbers measure the change needed to recover feasibility and optimality, decrease when corrective residual flow is sent, and permit the usual out-of-kilter iteration to start from a possibly infeasible flow such as zero.
assumptions_latex: (i,j)\in A
l_{ij}\le u_{ij}
x\text{ satisfies flow conservation but may violate arc bounds}
c_{ij}^{\pi}\text{ is the reduced cost under potentials }\pi
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The generalized residual construction and kilter numbers allow the out-of-kilter iteration to begin without an initially bound-feasible flow, including from }x=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completeness of Kilter Unboundedness Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-cone and infinite-residual-cycle characterization of unbounded minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\ne\varnothing\), allowing infinite bounds. Then \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\) if and only if there exists \(d\) with \(Ad=0\), \(d_a\ge0\) whenever \(\ell_a\) is finite, \(d_a\le0\) whenever \(u_a\) is finite, and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Equivalently, for any feasible base flow, the residual arcs having infinite residual capacity contain a negative-cost directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible instance is unbounded below exactly when it has a negative-cost recession circulation, equivalently an all-infinite-residual-capacity negative cycle.
assumptions_latex: The finite network-flow feasible region is nonempty.
Arc bounds may be infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\iff\exists d\in\operatorname{rec}(P):c^{\mathsf T}d<0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Price-based preflow-push algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization, active-node selection, residual pushes, price rises, and stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain a valid pair $(x,p)$ such that $x$ is capacity-feasible, $p$ is integral,
\[g_1\le0,\qquad g_i\ge0\ (i\ne1),\]
and
\[p_1=N,\qquad p_N=0,\qquad 0\le p_i<N\ (i\ne1).\]
One initialization saturates all arcs leaving node $1$, assigns zero flow to all other arcs, and sets $p_1=N$ and $p_i=0$ for $i\ne1$. Select a node $i\ne N$ with $p_i<N$ and $g_i>0$; terminate if none exists. For a candidate forward arc $(i,j)$, increase $x_{ij}$ by
\[\delta=\min\{g_i,c_{ij}-x_{ij}\};\]
for a candidate backward arc $(j,i)$, decrease $x_{ji}$ by
\[\delta=\min\{g_i,x_{ji}\}.\]
If the candidate list is empty, set
\[p_i\leftarrow\min\{p_j+1\mid (i,j)\in\mathcal A,\ x_{ij}<c_{ij},\text{ or }(j,i)\in\mathcal A,\ x_{ji}>0\},\]
and resume scanning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a capacity-feasible preflow and valid integer node prices. Select a nonsink node having positive surplus and price below N, push surplus along a candidate residual arc toward a neighbor of price one less, and raise the node's price to the smallest eligible-neighbor price plus one when no candidate arc exists. Stop when no selectable node remains.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is a capacitated directed network with source }1\text{ and sink }N
(x,p)\text{ is initialized as the stated valid flow–price pair}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm performs the stated push and price-rise operations until no }i\ne N\text{ satisfies }p_i<N\text{ and }g_i>0.

assumptions_latex: A residual network, node prices \(p\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) are given.
At least one node has positive excess and can reach a deficit through residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each bid either pushes positive flow toward reducing excess or raises a price to create an \(\varepsilon\)-admissible residual arc; termination yields a feasible flow satisfying \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select an excess node \(i\). Among its outgoing residual arcs choose \((i,j)\) of minimum \(r_{ij}\), and let \(r^{(2)}_i\) be the second-smallest value, with \(+\infty\) allowed when no competitor exists. Adjust \(p_i\) so the chosen arc improves relative to its competitor by at least \(\varepsilon\), then push \(\delta=\min\{e_i,-e_j,u^x_{ij}\}\) when \(j\) is deficient, or the corresponding admissible positive amount under the variant's queue rule. Repeat until all node excesses vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excess nodes bid for residual arcs by changing prices and pushing flow, with each winning bid separated from alternatives by an epsilon margin.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: An iteration of the epsilon-relaxation method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow-push and price-rise iteration, including its saturated-cut exception and finite local termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\epsilon>0\) and maintain an \(\epsilon\)-CS pair \((x,p)\) with integral arc flows. Select a node \(i\) with \(g_i>0\); terminate if none exists. Repeatedly scan its candidate list. For an \(\epsilon^+\)-unblocked arc \((i,j)\), set \(x_{ij}\leftarrow x_{ij}+\min\{g_i,c_{ij}-x_{ij}\}\). For an \(\epsilon^-\)-unblocked arc \((j,i)\), set \(x_{ji}\leftarrow x_{ji}-\min\{g_i,x_{ji}-b_{ji}\}\). If the candidate list is empty, raise \(p_i\) to \[\bar p_i=\min\!\left\{\min_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A:x_{ij}<c_{ij}}(a_{ij}+p_j+\epsilon),\ \min_{(j,i)\in\mathcal A:b_{ji}<x_{ji}}(p_j-a_{ji}+\epsilon)\right\}.\] If both index sets are empty, the incident cut is saturated: stop the algorithm as infeasible when \(g_i>0\), and leave \(p_i\) unchanged and end the iteration when \(g_i=0\). With integral initial flows, supplies, and arc bounds, integrality is preserved, and each iteration terminates after finitely many operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method repeatedly pushes a positive node surplus along epsilon-unblocked incident arcs. When none is available, it raises the node price to the next value that unblocks an admissible arc. A saturated incident cut with positive surplus certifies infeasibility; with zero surplus it merely ends the iteration. Integral data preserve integral flows, and every iteration is finite.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon>0
(x,p)\text{ initially satisfies }\epsilon\text{-CS}
x\text{ is integral initially}
s_i,b_{ij},c_{ij}\in\mathbb Z
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The update preserves }\epsilon\text{-CS and flow integrality, handles the saturated-cut exception, and each iteration stops after finitely many operations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacitated Network, Feasible Flow, and Flow Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source, single-sink directed capacitated networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network is $N=(s,t,V,A,b)$, where $(V,A)$ is a digraph, $s\in V$ has indegree zero, $t\in V$ has outdegree zero, and $b:A\to\mathbb Z_+$ assigns a capacity to each arc. A flow is $f\in\mathbb R^{|A|}$ satisfying $0\le f(u,v)\le b(u,v)$ for every $(u,v)\in A$ and $\sum_{(u,v)\in A}f(u,v)=\sum_{(v,u)\in A}f(v,u)$ for every $v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}$. Its value is $|f|=\sum_{(s,u)\in A}f(s,u)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated network is a directed graph with a zero-indegree source, a zero-outdegree sink, and a positive-integer capacity on every arc. A feasible real-valued flow respects nonnegativity and capacities and conserves flow at every vertex other than the source and sink. Its value is the total flow leaving the source.
assumptions_latex: (V,A)\text{ is a digraph}
s\in V,\ \deg^-(s)=0
t\in V,\ \deg^+(t)=0
b:A\to\mathbb Z_+
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is feasible}\iff\bigl(0\le f(a)\le b(a)\ \forall a\in A\bigr)\land\bigl(\text{flow conservation holds on }V\setminus\{s,t\}\bigr),\quad |f|=\sum_{(s,u)\in A}f(s,u).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eligible arcs, valid flow–price pairs, and node surplus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State definitions for price-based preflow-push on a capacitated directed network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a capacity-feasible flow $x$, define
\[A(i,x)=\{(i,j)\in\mathcal A\mid x_{ij}<c_{ij}\}\cup\{(j,i)\in\mathcal A\mid x_{ji}>0\}.\]
The eligible neighbors $N(i,x)$ are the opposite endpoints of these eligible incident arcs. The candidate list of $i$ consists of eligible incident arcs whose other endpoint $j$ satisfies $p_i=p_j+1$. A pair $(x,p)$ is valid if
\[p_i\le p_j+1\qquad\text{for every }i\in\mathcal N\text{ and }j\in N(i,x).\]
The surplus of node $i$ is
\[g_i=\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}x_{ji}-\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eligible arcs are outgoing arcs with unused capacity and incoming arcs carrying positive flow. Candidate arcs additionally lead to a neighbor whose price is one less. A capacity-feasible flow and price vector are valid when each eligible neighbor's price is at least the node price minus one. Surplus is inflow minus outflow.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is capacity-feasible on }(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)
p=(p_i)_{i\in\mathcal N}\text{ is a node-price vector}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(i,x),\ N(i,x),\text{ candidate lists, validity of }(x,p),\text{ and }g_i\text{ are defined as displayed.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Node surplus, epsilon-unblocked arcs, and candidate lists
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific state definitions for epsilon-relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a flow \(x\), the surplus of node \(i\) is \[g_i=\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}x_{ji}-\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}+s_i.\] Given an \(\epsilon\)-CS pair \((x,p)\), an outgoing arc \((i,j)\) is \(\epsilon^+\)-unblocked when \(p_i=p_j+a_{ij}+\epsilon\) and \(x_{ij}<c_{ij}\). An incoming arc \((j,i)\) is \(\epsilon^-\)-unblocked at \(i\) when \(p_i=p_j-a_{ji}+\epsilon\) and \(b_{ji}<x_{ji}\). At an epsilon-complementary-slackness state, an unsaturated outgoing arc is epsilon-plus-unblocked when its price inequality is tight, and an incoming arc above its lower bound is epsilon-minus-unblocked when the corresponding reverse inequality is tight. These arcs form the node's candidate list.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Implicit node prices induced by arc-price values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auction-specific definition of node prices from upper and lower arc-price quantities during the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
During the algorithm, for every node $i\ne1$ there is a scalar $p_i$ such that
\[p_i=\bar p_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A\text{ with }x_{ij}>0,\]
and
\[p_i=\underline p_{ji}\quad\forall(j,i)\in\mathcal A\text{ with }x_{ji}<c_{ji}.\]
For the source,
\[p_1=\begin{cases}0,&x_{1j}=0\text{ for every }(1,j)\in\mathcal A,\\\bar p_{1j},&\text{otherwise, where }(1,j)\text{ is any arc with }x_{1j}>0.\end{cases}\]
The scalar $p_i$ is called the implicit price of node $i$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsource node, the implicit price is the common upper arc-price value on each positive-flow outgoing arc and the common lower arc-price value on each nonsaturated incoming arc. The source price is zero when all source outflows vanish and otherwise equals the upper price of any positive-flow source arc.

\text{The algorithm is in a state for which the displayed common-value properties hold}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral-Cost Exactness Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimality certificate from sufficiently small residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible circulation on an \(n\)-vertex network with integral arc costs. If some prices \(p\) make \((x,p)\) \(\varepsilon\)-optimal and \(0\le\varepsilon<1/n\), then \(x\) is a minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integral costs, residual epsilon-optimality below one over the vertex count certifies exact minimum cost.
assumptions_latex: The network has \(n\ge1\) vertices.
Arc costs are integral.
\(x\) is a feasible circulation.
\((x,p)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
\(0\le\varepsilon<1/n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{c^{\mathsf T}y:y\text{ is a feasible circulation}\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Cost Exactness Threshold

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure at the Uniform Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-cost witness showing that the strict inequality in the uniform exactness threshold cannot be replaced by equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\ge2\), consider a directed \(n\)-cycle of unit-capacity arcs, with one arc of cost \(-1\) and all other arcs of cost \(0\). The zero circulation is feasible and nonoptimal. Prices can be chosen so that every forward residual arc has reduced cost \(-1/n\); hence the zero circulation is \((1/n)\)-optimal despite not being minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral-cost negative cycle can make a nonoptimal circulation exactly one-over-n optimal, so the strict uniform threshold is necessary.
assumptions_latex: All cycle arcs have unit capacity.
The zero circulation is the tested flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon=1/n\not\Longrightarrow\text{exact optimality, even with integral costs}.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure at the Uniform Threshold

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Epsilon-Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate residual reduced-cost feasibility for a capacity-feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a capacity-feasible flow \(x\), node prices \(p\), and residual reduced costs \(\bar c_{ij}=c^x_{ij}+p_i-p_j\), the pair \((x,p)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal when \[\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every positive-capacity residual arc }(i,j).\] For \(\varepsilon=0\), this is exact residual reduced-cost optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow-price pair is epsilon-optimal when every available residual move has reduced cost at least minus epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) respects all arc bounds.
Residual arcs carry their signed linear costs.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{(i,j)\in E_x}\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: Positive-capacity residual arcs of the current flow.
Residual reduced cost under node prices.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Epsilon-Optimality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Cost Epsilon-Refinement Phase
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Push-relabel refinement of a capacity-feasible epsilon-optimal pseudoflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a capacity-feasible pseudoflow \(x\), prices \(p\), and excesses \(e=b-Ax\). Saturate residual arcs of negative reduced cost. Repeatedly select a positive-excess node; push on an outgoing negative-reduced-cost residual arc when one exists, and otherwise decrease its price until an outgoing residual arc becomes \(-\varepsilon\)-tight. With the reduced-cost sign convention \(\bar c_{ij}=c^x_{ij}+p_i-p_j\), saturation, pushes, and relabels preserve \(\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\). A completed phase has \(e=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epsilon refinement saturates negative arcs and alternates admissible pushes with price relabels until conservation is restored.
assumptions_latex: A feasible circulation exists.
The current pseudoflow respects all arc bounds.
The initial pair is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
Residual costs and price signs use the displayed convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e=0\Longrightarrow x\text{ is a feasible }\varepsilon\text{-optimal circulation}.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Cost Epsilon-Refinement Phase

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric Epsilon Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance schedule for integral linear minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an \(\varepsilon_0\)-optimal capacity-feasible pseudoflow-price pair and a correct refinement procedure, choose \(\alpha>1\), set \(\varepsilon_{k+1}=\varepsilon_k/\alpha\), and refine the preceding pair to the new tolerance in each phase. Stop after obtaining a feasible \(\varepsilon_k\)-optimal circulation with \(\varepsilon_k<1/|V|\). For integral arc costs, the final circulation is exactly optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric scaling repeatedly invokes epsilon refinement and stops below the integral-cost exactness threshold.
assumptions_latex: Arc costs are integral.
A correct refinement procedure produces a feasible pair at each completed phase.
A feasible circulation exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon_k<1/|V|\text{ and feasibility imply exact minimum cost}.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Epsilon Scaling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric-Scaling Phase Count
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance reductions needed to cross the integral-cost exactness threshold; excludes refinement work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon_0\alpha^{-k}\) with \(\alpha>1\), and let \(K\) be the least nonnegative integer such that \(\varepsilon_K<1/n\). Then \[K=\max\!\left\{0,\left\lfloor\log_\alpha(n\varepsilon_0)\right\rfloor+1\right\}.\] This counts scaling phases only and gives no bound on the work of a refinement phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric epsilon scaling uses logarithmically many tolerance reductions to pass below one over the vertex count, independently of the unresolved work per refinement.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon_0>0\).
\(\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon_0\alpha^{-k}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K=\max\{0,\lfloor\log_\alpha(n\varepsilon_0)\rfloor+1\}.

notation.meaning: First phase index with tolerance strictly below \(1/n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Scaling Phase Count

assumptions_latex: Residual reduced costs are \(r_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-p_j\), and initially \(r_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\) on every residual arc.
The current flow respects all arc bounds, although it may violate conservation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration maintains \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness; if it terminates with conservation, its objective is within the standard \(\varepsilon\)-dependent primal-dual gap, and exactness follows under an appropriate integral-cost threshold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-arc epsilon-relaxation with optional epsilon scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: While some node \(i\) has positive excess, push flow on an outgoing residual arc satisfying \(r_{ij}\le0\), respecting residual capacity and the chosen imbalance rule. If no such arc exists, let \(m_i=\min_{(i,j)}r_{ij}\) and relabel \(p_i\leftarrow p_i-(m_i+\varepsilon)\), making at least one outgoing residual arc have reduced cost \(-\varepsilon\). Continue until \(e=0\). In an epsilon-scaling implementation, reduce \(\varepsilon\) geometrically and restart relaxation from the preceding flow-price pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epsilon-relaxation alternates admissible residual pushes with price relabels that preserve approximate complementary slackness, then reduces epsilon across scaling phases.
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Relaxation Methods

knowledge_statements.title: Auction–Shortest-Path Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic residual-path hybrid for capacitated minimum-cost flow under epsilon complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible pseudoflow and node prices, select a node with positive excess and construct a residual path toward a node with negative excess. At each current node, traverse a residual arc minimizing reduced cost \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-p_j\). If no arc satisfies \(\bar c_{ij}\leq\varepsilon\), change the current node's price until at least one outgoing residual arc becomes epsilon-admissible. Upon reaching a deficit node, augment by the minimum of the source excess, terminal deficit, and residual capacities along the path. Repeat until all imbalances vanish; output the resulting feasible flow and prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly combine auction-style price changes with shortest reduced-cost residual-path construction, augmenting from excess nodes to deficit nodes until flow balance is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, with finite arc capacities and costs.
\(\varepsilon>0\), and the current pseudoflow satisfies capacity bounds.
\(\sum_{i\in V} b_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible when the procedure terminates with zero excess at every node.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward Auction Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided auction processing of supply excess in a residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A forward variant chooses only nodes having positive excess, sends flow on epsilon-admissible outgoing residual arcs, and otherwise raises or lowers the selected node price according to the adopted reduced-cost convention. Its progress guarantee requires every processed excess to reach some deficit through residual arcs after finitely many price changes. If an excess node lies in a residual set \(S\) from which no deficit is reachable, forward steps confined to \(S\) cannot restore balance; the method must invoke an infeasibility test, an artificial arc, or a complementary reverse phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward auction steps alone fail when trapped excess cannot reach any deficit in the residual network; explicit infeasibility or reverse processing is then required.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) obeys arc bounds but may violate node balance.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) containing positive net excess and no residual path to a deficit is a failure boundary for forward-only processing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the failure-taxonomy container, but the claimed progress guarantee and required remedies depend on the precise forward-auction variant and have no cited support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Termination and No-Path Behavior of the Shortest-Path Auction Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness when an origin-to-destination path exists and the precise nontermination boundary otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the shortest-path auction algorithm with origin \(s\) and destination \(t\), if at least one path from \(s\) to \(t\) exists, the algorithm terminates with a shortest such path. If no path from \(s\) to \(t\) exists, the algorithm never terminates and \(p_s\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an origin-to-destination path exists, the auction algorithm terminates with a shortest path. If none exists, it never terminates and the origin price tends to infinity.
assumptions_latex: s\text{ and }t\text{ are the origin and destination for the stated shortest-path auction algorithm.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\exists\text{ an }s\text{-}t\text{ path})\Rightarrow\text{termination with a shortest }s\text{-}t\text{ path};\quad(\nexists\text{ an }s\text{-}t\text{ path})\Rightarrow(\text{nontermination and }p_s\to\infty).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward Shortest-Path Auction Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration rule for the forward price-based shortest-path auction algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(i\) be the terminal node of the current path \(P\), and let \(m_i=\min_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}(a_{ij}+p_j)\). If \(p_i<m_i\), set \(p_i:=m_i\), contract \(P\) when \(i\ne s\), and continue. Otherwise choose \(j_i\in\arg\min_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}(a_{ij}+p_j)\), with ties broken arbitrarily, and extend \(P\) by \(j_i\). If \(j_i=t\), stop with \(P\) as the desired shortest path; otherwise continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the terminal node of the current path, raise its price to the minimum outgoing arc-cost-plus-successor-price value and contract the path when required. Otherwise extend the path through an outgoing minimizer. Stop when the destination is appended.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is the current path with terminal node }i.
\min_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}(a_{ij}+p_j)\text{ is defined.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: j_i=t\implies\text{the algorithm stops with }P\text{ designated as the shortest }s\text{-}t\text{ path.}

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Auction Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided auction processing of demand deficits using reversed residual orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reverse variant chooses only nodes having negative excess, traces admissible residual arcs backward toward positive excess, and changes prices when no admissible predecessor exists. Its progress guarantee requires each processed deficit to be reachable from some excess node in the residual graph after finitely many price changes. If a deficit node belongs to a set \(S\) having no incoming residual path from any excess, reverse steps confined to deficit processing cannot restore balance; the method must report infeasibility, introduce artificial feasibility arcs, or alternate with forward processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse-only auction processing fails when a deficit is unreachable from every excess in the residual network, requiring feasibility handling or a forward phase.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) obeys arc bounds but may violate node balance.
\(\varepsilon>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modified reverse auction for asymmetric assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-auction variant that preserves feasibility and the first two epsilon-complementary-slackness conditions while enforcing the unassigned-object price condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a feasible assignment \(S\) and \((\pi,p)\) satisfying \(\pi_i+p_j\ge a_{ij}-\epsilon\) for all \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\) and \(\pi_i+p_j=a_{ij}\) for all \((i,j)\in S\). Fix \(\lambda=\min\{p_j:j\text{ is assigned under the initial }S\}\). While an unassigned object \(j\) satisfies \(p_j>\lambda\), choose \(i_j\in\arg\max_{i\in B(j)}(a_{ij}-\pi_i)\), let \(\beta_j=\max_{i\in B(j)}(a_{ij}-\pi_i)\), and let \(\omega_j=\max_{i\in B(j),\,i\ne i_j}(a_{ij}-\pi_i)\), with \(\omega_j=-\infty\) when \(i_j\) is the sole member of \(B(j)\). If \(\lambda\ge\beta_j-\epsilon\), set \(p_j:=\lambda\). Otherwise set \(\delta=\min\{\beta_j-\lambda,\beta_j-\omega_j+\epsilon\}\), \(p_j:=\beta_j-\delta\), and \(\pi_{i_j}:=\pi_{i_j}+\delta\); assign \(j\) to \(i_j\) and unassign the object previously assigned to \(i_j\). Keep \(\lambda\) fixed and stop when no unassigned object has price greater than \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible assignment satisfying the first two epsilon-complementary-slackness conditions, fix the minimum initial assigned-object price. Repeatedly process an unassigned object priced above that threshold, either lowering its price to the threshold or assigning it to its best person while updating the person's potential and displacing the formerly assigned object. The threshold remains fixed, and the stopping condition enforces the third complementary-slackness condition.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is initially a feasible assignment}
\pi_i+p_j\ge a_{ij}-\epsilon\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A
\pi_i+p_j=a_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in S
\lambda=\min_{j:\,j\text{ assigned under the initial }S}p_j\text{ is fixed throughout}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each iteration preserves feasibility and the first two }\epsilon\text{-CS conditions; upon satisfying the stopping rule, }p_j\le\lambda\text{ for every unassigned }j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reverse-auction iteration for assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One reverse-auction iteration on a nonempty set of objects currently unassigned under the assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a nonempty set of objects unassigned under \(S\). For each \(j\in J\), choose \(i_j\in\arg\max_{i\in B(j)}\{a_{ij}-\pi_i\}\), define \(\beta_j=\max_{i\in B(j)}\{a_{ij}-\pi_i\}\), and define \(\omega_j=\max_{i\in B(j),\,i\ne i_j}\{a_{ij}-\pi_i\}\). If \(i_j\) is the only member of \(B(j)\), take \(\omega_j=-\infty\), or computationally a value much smaller than \(\beta_j\). Object \(j\) bids \(b_{i_jj}=\pi_{i_j}+\beta_j-\omega_j+\epsilon=a_{i_jj}-\omega_j+\epsilon\). For each person \(i\) receiving bids from \(P(i)\), set \(\pi_i:=\max_{j\in P(i)}b_{ij}\), remove any previous assigned pair incident to \(i\), and add \((i,j_i)\), where \(j_i\in P(i)\) attains that maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each currently unassigned object bids for its best admissible person using the difference between its best and second-best adjusted values plus epsilon. Each person accepts a highest bid, replaces any previous assignment, and updates its profit to that bid.

knowledge_statements.title: Price-War Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-polynomial bidding caused by near-indifference and a remote costly alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an assignment auction with \(n\) bidders and \(n\) objects. Each bidder values the first \(n-1\) objects at \(0\) and the last object at \(-M\), where \(M>0\). Under epsilon-sized price increments and an adverse admissible tie rule, bidders repeatedly displace one another among the first \(n-1\) objects until their prices approach the \(M\)-unit disadvantage of the last object. Thus the number of bids can scale as \(\Omega(M/\varepsilon)\). This price-war family precludes a strongly polynomial bound based only on \(n\) for that implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearly interchangeable preferred objects can provoke repeated displacement until their prices absorb a large cost gap, yielding order M/epsilon bids.
assumptions_latex: \(n\geq2\), \(M>0\), and \(0<\varepsilon<M\).
Bids increase a selected object's price by at least \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{bids}}=\Omega(M/\varepsilon)\) is possible under admissible tie breaking.

notation.meaning: value gap to the unattractive object

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits Price-War Regimes, but the claimed Omega(M/epsilon) bid bound depends on the exact bid increment and tie-breaking rules and has no authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex tableau identities and pivot-update complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the basis-complement identities defining a simplex tableau and the computational cost of updating it after a pivot selected by the specified simplex rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A':=\binom{-I}{A}\), \(b':=\binom0b\), and \(\bar c:=(c^\top,0)\). Let \(B\) consist of \(m\) indices such that \([A\ I]^B\) is nonsingular, let \(J\) be the complementary \(n\) indices, and put \(Q_B:=([A\ I]^B)^{-1}\). Then: (a) \(A'_J\) is nonsingular. (b) For \(x:=(A'_J)^{-1}b'_J\), \((b'-A'x)_J=0\), \((b'-A'x)_B=Q_Bb\), and \(c^\top x=\bar c^B Q_Bb\). (c) If \(y_B=0\) and \(y^\top A'=c^\top\), then \(y^\top=\bar c^B Q_B[A\ I]-\bar c\). (d) If \(i\in J\) and \(w\) satisfies \(A'_iw=-1\) and \(A'_{J\setminus\{i\}}w=0\), then \(A'_Bw=Q_B[A\ I]^i\). (e) For \(T_B:=\begin{pmatrix}Q_B[A\ I]&Q_Bb\\ \bar c^BQ_B[A\ I]-\bar c&c^\top x\end{pmatrix}\), if \(i\) and \(j\) are selected as prescribed by the referenced simplex-algorithm steps and \(B'\) is obtained from \(B\) by replacing \(j\) with \(i\), then \(B'\) and \(T_{B'}\) can be computed from \(B,T_B\) in \(O(m(n+m))\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular simplex basis determines the complementary system, residuals, objective value, dual vector, and pivot direction through explicit tableau identities. A pivot selected by the stated simplex rules updates the basis and tableau in O(m(n+m)) time.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb R^m,\quad c\in\mathbb R^n
A':=\binom{-I}{A},\quad b':=\binom0b,\quad \bar c:=(c^\top,0)
[A\ I]^B\text{ is nonsingular},\quad J:=\{1,\ldots,n+m\}\setminus B,\quad Q_B:=([A\ I]^B)^{-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A'_J\text{ is nonsingular; the stated primal, dual, residual, direction, and tableau identities hold; and a pivot satisfying the referenced simplex selection rules updates }T_B\text{ in }O(m(n+m))\text{ time}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Simplex Iteration and Conditional Optimality Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General primal-simplex algorithm and reduced-cost stopping certificate; no supplied candidate is its precise primary home.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization linear program in primal-simplex tableau form, begin with a primal-feasible basis. If a nonbasic variable \(s\) has reduced cost \(c_s<0\) and \(I_s=\{i:a_{is}>0\}\ne\varnothing\), select
\[
r\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{i\in I_s}\frac{b_i}{a_{is}}
\]
and pivot on \(a_{rs}\), thereby retaining primal feasibility. Repeat while such a pivot is selected. If a feasible basis is reached for which every nonbasic reduced cost is nonnegative, then that basis is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible basis for a minimization problem, enter a nonbasic variable with negative reduced cost and use the positive-entry minimum-ratio test to leave the basis. Each eligible pivot preserves feasibility. If the method reaches a feasible basis with all nonbasic reduced costs nonnegative, that basis is optimal; the extract does not establish finite termination or an anticycling rule.
assumptions_latex: \text{The linear program uses the stated primal-simplex minimization tableau convention.}
\text{The initial basis is primal feasible.}
c_s<0\quad\text{for each selected entering nonbasic variable }s
I_s=\{i:a_{is}>0\}\ne\varnothing\quad\text{for each performed pivot}
r\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{i\in I_s}\frac{b_i}{a_{is}}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\text{a feasible basis is reached and }\forall j\text{ nonbasic},\ c_j\ge 0\right)\Longrightarrow\text{that basis is optimal.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network Simplex Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-basis simplex procedure for minimum-cost network-flow problems, including artificial-variable initialization and terminal certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a basic feasible flow represented by a spanning tree rooted at \(r\), with basic flows \(\mathbf{x}_B\) and node dual variables \(\mathbf w\). At each iteration choose a nonbasic arc \((p,q)\) maximizing \(\delta_{ij}=w_i-w_j-c_{ij}\). If \(\delta_{pq}\le 0\), terminate with an optimal current flow; if an artificial variable remains positive, declare the original problem infeasible. Otherwise insert \((p,q)\), form its unique fundamental cycle, and let \(\Delta\ge0\) be the maximum feasible augmentation in the entering-arc orientation. If \(\Delta=+\infty\), terminate as unbounded, except that under big-\(M\), a positive artificial variable certifies infeasibility. If \(\Delta<+\infty\), augment by \(\Delta\), remove a blocking arc \((u,v)\), insert \((p,q)\), and shift all dual values in the component not containing \(r\) by \(\pm\delta_{pq}\), with the sign determined by whether that component contains \(q\) or \(p\); then repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with a rooted spanning-tree basic feasible flow and its node dual prices. Select a nonbasic arc having maximum reduced improvement. If its improvement is nonpositive, the flow is optimal, unless a positive artificial variable certifies infeasibility. Otherwise add the arc, augment as far as possible around the resulting unique cycle, and stop as unbounded if the augmentation is unlimited, subject to the big-M infeasibility exception. For a finite augmentation, remove a blocking arc, update the tree, flows, and dual prices on the detached component, and iterate.
assumptions_latex: \text{A minimum-cost network-flow problem is represented by a rooted spanning-tree basic feasible solution.}
\mathbf{x}_B\text{ and }\mathbf w\text{ are the basic flows and associated node dual variables.}
\delta_{ij}=w_i-w_j-c_{ij}\text{ is computed for every nonbasic arc }(i,j).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each iteration either certifies optimality or infeasibility, detects unboundedness, or performs a cycle augmentation and tree-basis pivot preserving the network-simplex iteration.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path construction of an initial transshipment basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies in the connected, uncapacitated transshipment setting with compatible total supply and demand; zero-flow basic arcs may be needed for degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a connected transshipment network have nonnegative origin supplies \(s_i\) and destination demands \(d_j\), with \(\sum_i s_i=\sum_j d_j\). Repeatedly select a path from an origin having residual supply to a destination having residual demand and send the largest amount permitted by those two residual quantities. A path may branch from a previously selected path, and intersecting paths may require reversal of flow on a common arc. Continue until all demands are satisfied. Select the basis paths without cycles and so that all nodes are connected, adding zero-flow arcs when necessary. This produces an initial basic feasible flow whose basis arcs form a connected acyclic spanning set, possibly with degenerate zero-flow basic arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a connected, balanced, uncapacitated transshipment network, repeatedly send as much as possible along a path from an origin with residual supply to a destination with residual demand. Choose the basis paths without cycles and connect every node, adding zero-flow arcs if necessary. The result is a possibly degenerate initial basic feasible flow with a tree-supported basis.
assumptions_latex: \text{The transshipment network is connected.}
s_i\ge 0,\quad d_j\ge 0
\sum_i s_i=\sum_j d_j
\text{The construction is in the uncapacitated transshipment setting described by the extract.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{An initial basic feasible flow exists whose basis arcs can be chosen as a connected acyclic spanning set, possibly including zero-flow arcs.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental-cycle coefficient procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded procedure for representing a nonbasic column in a spanning-tree network basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a spanning-tree basis \(T\) and a nonbasic arc \(e\), form the unique cycle \(C\subseteq T\cup\{e\}\) and orient it consistently with \(e\). For every basic arc \(f\in T\), set
\[
\lambda_f=\begin{cases}-1,&f\in C\setminus\{e\}\text{ and }f\text{ agrees with the cycle orientation},\\+1,&f\in C\setminus\{e\}\text{ and }f\text{ opposes the cycle orientation},\\0,&f\notin C.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\mathbf a_e=\sum_{f\in T}\lambda_f\mathbf a_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insert the nonbasic arc into the spanning-tree basis, find the resulting unique cycle, and orient that cycle with the nonbasic arc. Assign −1 to each basic cycle arc oriented with the cycle, +1 to each basic cycle arc oriented oppositely, and 0 to all other basic arcs; these coefficients represent the nonbasic column.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a spanning-tree basis}
e\notin T\text{ is a nonbasic arc}
\mathbf a_f\text{ denotes the incidence column of arc }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf a_e=\sum_{f\in T}\lambda_f\mathbf a_f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Free arcs, cycle-free solutions, and spanning-tree solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for feasible capacitated flows in network-simplex basis geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible flow $x$, an arc $(i,j)$ is free if $0<x_{ij}<u_{ij}$ and restricted if $x_{ij}\in\{0,u_{ij}\}$. The flow $x$ is cycle free if the network has no cycle composed entirely of free arcs. Given a spanning tree $T$, $(x,T)$ is a spanning-tree solution if every nontree arc is restricted; tree arcs may be free or restricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc is free when its flow is strictly between zero and capacity and restricted when it is at a bound. A feasible flow is cycle free when its free arcs contain no cycle. Relative to a spanning tree, it is a spanning-tree solution when every nontree arc is restricted.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is feasible}
0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in A
T\text{ is a spanning tree of the network}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (i,j)\text{ is free}\iff0<x_{ij}<u_{ij};\quad(i,j)\text{ is restricted}\iff x_{ij}\in\{0,u_{ij}\};\quad x\text{ is cycle free}\iff A_{\mathrm{free}}\text{ contains no cycle};\quad(x,T)\text{ is a spanning-tree solution}\iff A\setminus T\subseteq A_{\mathrm{restricted}}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spanning-tree structure and its associated flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation and classification of a minimum-cost-flow network-simplex basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spanning-tree structure is a partition $(T,L,U)$ of $A$ in which $T$ is a spanning tree, $L$ consists of nontree arcs fixed at $0$, and $U$ consists of nontree arcs fixed at capacity. Its associated flow is obtained by setting $x_{ij}=0$ on $L$, $x_{ij}=u_{ij}$ on $U$, and uniquely determining the flows on $T$ from the node-balance equations. The structure is feasible iff this flow satisfies every arc bound, optimal iff the associated flow is optimal, nondegenerate iff every tree arc is free, and degenerate otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network-simplex spanning-tree structure partitions the arcs into tree arcs, lower-bound nontree arcs, and upper-bound nontree arcs. Fixing the nontree flows at their indicated bounds and solving the balance equations uniquely determines the tree flows. Feasibility, optimality, and degeneracy are properties of this associated flow and its tree arcs.
assumptions_latex: A=T\mathbin{\dot\cup}L\mathbin{\dot\cup}U
T\text{ is a spanning tree}
L,U\subseteq A\setminus T
x_{ij}=0\ \forall(i,j)\in L
x_{ij}=u_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in U
x\text{ satisfies the node-balance equations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_T\text{ is uniquely determined};\quad (T,L,U)\text{ feasible}\iff0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in A;\quad (T,L,U)\text{ nondegenerate}\iff0<x_{ij}<u_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in T;\quad (T,L,U)\text{ optimal}\iff x\text{ is optimal}.

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-basis representation of a bounded network-simplex solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have connected underlying undirected graph, let \(A\) be its node-arc incidence matrix, and let \(T\subseteq E\) be a spanning tree. Assign each nontree arc \(e\in E\setminus T\) either \(x_e=l_e\) or \(x_e=u_e\). If \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\), then \(Ax=b\) uniquely determines the tree-arc vector \(x_T\). The resulting spanning-tree solution is feasible exactly when \(l_e\leq x_e\leq u_e\) for every \(e\in T\). A tree arc may lie at a bound, in which case the tree solution is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing every nontree arc at a bound uniquely determines the tree-arc flows; the tree solution is feasible exactly when all computed tree flows satisfy their bounds.
assumptions_latex: The underlying undirected graph of \(G=(V,E)\) is connected.
\(A\) is the node-arc incidence matrix of \(G\).
\(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\).
\(T\subseteq E\) is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{E\setminus T}\in\prod_{e\notin T}\{l_e,u_e\}\) uniquely determines \(x_T\), and feasibility is equivalent to \(l_T\leq x_T\leq u_T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic feasible flows are precisely spanning-tree solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the basic solutions of the capacitated flow-balance polyhedron by acyclicity of their strictly non-bound support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimum-cost-flow instance $(G,u,b,c)$, let
\[
P=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^{E(G)}:0\le x_e\le u(e)\ \forall e\in E(G),\quad \sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e=b(v)\ \forall v\in V(G)\right\}.
\]
The basic solutions of $P$ are precisely the spanning-tree solutions of $(G,u,b,c)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic solutions of the capacity-bounded flow-balance polyhedron are exactly the feasible flows whose strictly non-bound support contains no undirected cycle.
assumptions_latex: (G,u,b,c)\text{ is an instance of the minimum-cost-flow problem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:x\text{ is a basic solution of }P\}=\{x\in P:x\text{ is a spanning-tree solution}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network-simplex spanning-tree structure, feasibility, and potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the tree/bound partition, its associated balance flow, feasible and strongly feasible orientations, and its normalized tree potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(G,u,b,c)$ be a minimum-cost-flow instance with connected $G$. A spanning-tree structure is $(r,T,L,U)$ such that $r\in V(G)$, $E(G)=T\mathbin{\dot\cup}L\mathbin{\dot\cup}U$, $|T|=|V(G)|-1$, and $(V(G),T)$ is acyclic. Its associated $b$-flow satisfies $f(e)=0$ for $e\in L$, $f(e)=u(e)$ for $e\in U$, and, for $e=(v,w)\in T$ and the component $C_e$ of $(V(G),T\setminus\{e\})$ containing $v$,
\[
f(e)=\sum_{z\in C_e}b(z)+\sum_{a\in U\cap\delta^-(C_e)}u(a)-\sum_{a\in U\cap\delta^+(C_e)}u(a).
\]
The structure is feasible iff $0\le f(e)\le u(e)$ for every $e\in T$. A tree edge $(v,w)$ is downward when $v$ lies on the undirected $r$--$w$ path in $T$, and upward otherwise. The structure is strongly feasible iff $0<f(e)\le u(e)$ on every downward tree edge and $0\le f(e)<u(e)$ on every upward tree edge. Its associated potential is the unique $\pi:V(G)\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $\pi(r)=0$ and $c_\pi(e)=0$ for all $e\in T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network-simplex spanning-tree structure partitions the arcs into tree arcs and non-tree arcs fixed at their lower or upper bounds. The balance equations uniquely determine the tree flows. Feasibility imposes the capacity bounds; strong feasibility makes downward tree arcs positive and upward tree arcs strictly below capacity. The associated potential is normalized at the root and makes every tree arc's reduced cost zero.
assumptions_latex: (G,u,b,c)\text{ is a minimum-cost-flow instance}
G\text{ is connected}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (r,T,L,U)\text{ determines the stated associated }b\text{-flow }f\text{ and unique normalized potential }\pi,\text{ with feasibility and strong feasibility characterized by the stated inequalities.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network simplex algorithm from a strongly feasible tree structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes its stopping test, deterministic leaving-edge rule, basis update, primal augmentation, and potential update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a minimum-cost-flow instance $(G,u,b,c)$ and a strongly feasible spanning-tree structure $(r,T,L,U)$, compute its associated $b$-flow $f$ and potential $\pi$. Choose $e\in L$ with $c_\pi(e)<0$ or $e\in U$ with $c_\pi(e)>0$; if none exists, return $f$. Otherwise form the oriented fundamental circuit $C$ of $e$ when $e\in L$, or of $\overleftarrow e$ when $e\in U$, and set $\gamma:=c_\pi(e)$. Let $\delta:=\min_{a\in E(C)}u_f(a)$ and choose as blocking arc the last minimizer encountered while traversing $C$ from its peak. If this arc is $e_0$ or $\overleftarrow{e_0}$, replace $e_0$ by $e$ in $T$, place $e_0$ in $U$ or $L$ according to the blocking orientation, and augment $f$ by $\delta$ along $C$. For the component $X$ containing $r$ in $(V(G),T\setminus\{e\})$, add $\gamma$ to $\pi(v)$ for $v\notin X$ when $e\in\delta^+(X)$, and subtract $\gamma$ when $e\in\delta^-(X)$. Repeating these pivots terminates at an optimum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a strongly feasible spanning-tree structure, the network simplex method repeatedly selects a non-tree edge violating the reduced-cost sign condition, augments around its fundamental circuit up to the last blocking edge, exchanges that edge in the tree, and updates potentials on one side of the induced cut. If no violating edge exists, the current flow is optimal.
assumptions_latex: (G,u,b,c)\text{ is an instance of the minimum-cost-flow problem}
(r,T,L,U)\text{ is a strongly feasible spanning-tree structure}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stopping flow }f\text{ is an optimum solution.}

knowledge_statements.title: Forest-to-Tree Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate completion of an extreme flow's free-arc forest to a network-simplex tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have connected underlying undirected graph, let \(x\) be a basic feasible bounded flow, and let \(F=\{e:l_e<x_e<u_e\}\). Then \(F\) is a forest and there exists a spanning tree \(T\) satisfying \(F\subseteq T\subseteq E\). Declaring every arc outside \(T\) nonbasic at its current lower or upper bound represents the same flow \(x\) as a tree solution. Each added arc in \(T\setminus F\) is at a bound and is therefore a degenerate basic tree arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any basic flow's free-arc forest can be extended to a spanning tree without changing the flow; added tree arcs are degenerate.
assumptions_latex: The underlying undirected graph of \(G\) is connected.
\(x\) is a basic feasible solution of \(Ax=b,\ l\leq x\leq u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists T\text{ spanning tree}:F\subseteq T\) and \(x_e\in\{l_e,u_e\}\) for every \(e\in T\setminus F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis and Strong Feasibility for Bounded-Arc Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a bounded-arc network-simplex basis, its unique basic flow and tree-induced price vector, and rooted strong feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a minimum-cost flow problem with balance equations and bounds b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}, where b_{ij}<c_{ij} for every arc. A basis is a triple (T,L,U), where T is a spanning tree and L and U partition the non-tree arcs, with x_{ij}=b_{ij} on L and x_{ij}=c_{ij} on U. It uniquely determines the tree-arc flows from the balance equations. Specifically, if removing (i,j)\in T gives components T_i\ni i and T_j\ni j, then
x_{ij}=\sum_{n\in T_i}s_n-\sum_{(m,n)\in L:m\in T_i,n\in T_j}b_{mn}-\sum_{(m,n)\in U:m\in T_i,n\in T_j}c_{mn}+\sum_{(m,n)\in L:m\in T_j,n\in T_i}b_{mn}+\sum_{(m,n)\in U:m\in T_j,n\in T_i}c_{mn}.
The basis is feasible when this basic flow satisfies every arc bound. For a fixed root r and arbitrary p_r, it also determines prices
p_i=p_r-\sum_{(m,n)\in P_i^+}a_{mn}+\sum_{(m,n)\in P_i^-}a_{mn},
where P_i is the unique tree path from r to i. A feasible basis is strongly feasible if every tree arc at its lower bound is oriented away from r and every tree arc at its upper bound is oriented toward r.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a minimum-cost flow problem with strict lower and upper arc bounds, a basis consists of a spanning tree together with a designation of every non-tree arc as fixed at its lower or upper bound. The balance equations then uniquely determine all tree-arc flows, and tree costs determine node prices relative to a fixed root price. The basis is feasible if its induced flow obeys all bounds. It is strongly feasible if lower-bound tree arcs point away from the root and upper-bound tree arcs point toward it.
assumptions_latex: b_{ij}<c_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A
T\text{ is a spanning tree}
L\mathbin{\dot\cup}U=\mathcal A\setminus T
x_{ij}=b_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in L,\qquad x_{ij}=c_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in U
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (T,L,U)\text{ uniquely specifies a basic flow and a tree-induced price vector; strong feasibility is characterized by the stated rooted orientations of bound-active tree arcs.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual network simplex pivot rule, infeasibility certificate, and finiteness condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded minimum-cost flow represented by a spanning-tree structure satisfying reduced-cost optimality and node mass balance, although tree-arc bounds may be violated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a spanning-tree structure $(T,L,U)$ satisfying mass balance and the reduced-cost optimality conditions, with nontree arcs in $L$ and $U$ fixed at their lower and upper bounds. Select a bound-infeasible tree arc $(p,q)$ as the leaving arc and orient the cut $[S,\bar S]$ so that a cycle augmentation repairs its violation. Define $Q=((S,\bar S)\cap L)\cup((\bar S,S)\cap U)$ and $\theta_{ij}=c_{ij}^{\pi}$ for $(i,j)\in L$, while $\theta_{ij}=-c_{ij}^{\pi}$ for $(i,j)\in U$. If $Q=\varnothing$, the minimum-cost flow problem is infeasible. Otherwise choose $(k,l)\in\arg\min_{(i,j)\in Q}\theta_{ij}$, replace $(p,q)$ by $(k,l)$, update potentials, and augment around the induced cycle until $(p,q)$ reaches $u_{pq}$ when $x_{pq}>u_{pq}$ or reaches $0$ when $x_{pq}<0$. The pivot preserves mass balance and reduced-cost optimality, though another tree arc may become infeasible. If every pivot is nondegenerate and costs and flows are integral, each pivot increases the objective by at least one; since the objective is bounded above by $mCU$, the algorithm terminates finitely. A suitable dual perturbation can exclude degenerate pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual network simplex method keeps flow conservation and reduced-cost optimality while allowing tree arcs to violate their bounds. It removes an infeasible tree arc, chooses the eligible cut arc with minimum reduced-cost slack, and augments on the resulting cycle until the leaving arc reaches its violated bound. No eligible cut arc is an infeasibility certificate. Every nondegenerate integral pivot raises the objective by at least one, so an upper objective bound implies finite termination; dual perturbation can prevent degenerate pivots.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parametric network simplex algorithm and pseudopolynomial iteration bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source, single-sink minimum-cost flow with bounded arcs and nonnegative costs; multiple supply and demand nodes may first be reduced to this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with zero flow, a shortest-path tree $T$ rooted at $s$, $L=A\setminus T$, $U=\varnothing$, and potentials $\pi(j)=-d(j)$. Gradually increase $b'(s)=-b'(t)$ toward $b(s)=-b(t)$ while maintaining reduced-cost optimality. In each iteration augment by $\min\{\delta,\,b(s)-b'(s)\}$ on the unique tree path $P$ from $s$ to $t$, where $\delta=\min\{\min_{(i,j)\in\bar P}(u_{ij}-x_{ij}),\min_{(i,j)\in\underline P}x_{ij}\}$. If infeasibility remains, remove a blocking arc, let $[S,\bar S]$ be the resulting $s$-$t$ cut, set $Q=((S,\bar S)\cap L)\cup((\bar S,S)\cap U)$, and choose an entering arc minimizing $\theta_{ij}=c_{ij}^{\pi}$ on $L$ and $\theta_{ij}=-c_{ij}^{\pi}$ on $U$. If $Q=\varnothing$, the residual cut capacity is zero and the requested flow is infeasible; otherwise the dual pivot preserves optimality and enables further augmentation. Choosing the blocking arc closest to $s$ yields at least one positive augmentation every $n$ iterations and hence $O(nb(s))$ iterations for integral flow units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from zero flow and a shortest-path tree, then increase the required source-to-sink flow. Augment as far as possible on the current tree path; after a blocking arc is reached, remove it and perform a dual pivot using the eligible cut arc of minimum reduced-cost slack. Tree augmentations and pivots preserve optimality. An empty eligible set certifies that the requested flow exceeds the cut capacity. With the closest-to-source blocking rule and integral units, the implementation takes O(n b(s)) iterations.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ has one source }s\text{ and one sink }t
b(s)=-b(t)\ge 0
0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\quad((i,j)\in A)
c_{ij}\ge 0\quad((i,j)\in A)
T\text{ is initially a shortest-path tree rooted at }s
b(s)\text{ and flow increments are integral for the stated pseudopolynomial bound}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The method either obtains an optimal feasible flow of value }b(s)\text{ or certifies infeasibility, and the stated implementation uses }O(nb(s))\text{ iterations.}

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Status Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status update performed by one bounded network-simplex pivot, including the bound-flip case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a dual-infeasible nontree arc \(e\), oriented forward when \(x_e=l_e\) and backward when \(x_e=u_e\). Adding its undirected edge to the current spanning tree \(T\) determines a unique cycle. Increase flow by the largest \(\theta\geq0\) along the oriented cycle that preserves all arc bounds. If a tree arc \(f\in T\) is selected among the arcs attaining the limiting allowance, set \(T'=(T\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\), give \(e\) tree status, and give \(f\) the lower-bound or upper-bound status corresponding to the bound it reaches. If the entering arc \(e\) is the sole limiting arc, leave \(T\) unchanged and switch \(e\) directly from lower-bound to upper-bound status or from upper-bound to lower-bound status. The transition is degenerate when \(\theta=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augment around the cycle to the first bound. A limiting tree arc leaves and the entering arc joins the tree; if only the entering arc limits the step, it instead flips to the opposite bound and the tree is unchanged.
assumptions_latex: A feasible spanning-tree solution with tree \(T\) is available.
The nontree entering arc \(e\) has an improving residual orientation.
The augmentation allowance is computed for every arc on the induced cycle, including \(e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The updated flow remains feasible; either \(T'=(T\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\) for a limiting tree arc \(f\), or \(T'=T\) in a bound flip.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trees, Spanning Trees, and Feasible Tree Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Underlying undirected path and cycle terminology and the tree-supported flow concept used by network simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A path from \(u=w_1\) to \(v=w_k\) consists of arcs whose endpoints are \(w_i\) and \(w_{i+1}\). Adding an arc with endpoints \(w_1,w_k\) forms a cycle; in particular, two distinct parallel arcs form a cycle. A network is connected when every pair of nodes has a path and acyclic when it has no cycle. A tree is connected and acyclic. A spanning tree \(T\) of a network \(N\) contains all nodes of \(N\) and uses only arcs of \(N\). A feasible solution \(x\) is a feasible tree solution associated with \(T\) when \(x_{ij}=0\) for every \(ij\notin T\). Moreover, for every chosen node \(v_1\) of an \(n\)-node tree, the remaining nodes can be ordered \(v_2,\ldots,v_n\) so that each \(v_i\), \(i\geq2\), is incident with exactly one arc whose other endpoint is among \(v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\). Consequently, every \(n\)-node tree has exactly \(n-1\) arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree is a connected network without cycles, and a spanning tree contains every node of the original network. A feasible tree solution assigns zero flow outside its spanning tree. Rooting and ordering any n-node tree shows that each later node has exactly one arc to an earlier node, so the tree has n−1 arcs.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is an }n\text{-node tree for the ordering and cardinality conclusion}
x\text{ is feasible for the network-flow system when defining a feasible tree solution}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{ij}=0\ \forall ij\notin T,\qquad |A(T)|=n-1.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded transshipment flows represented by a spanning tree and fixed non-tree bound statuses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of a Tree-Induced Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed tree and balance vector determine a unique tree-supported solution, although that solution is not necessarily nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a tree on \(n\) nodes. Choose a node \(v_1\), order the remaining nodes as \(v_2,\ldots,v_n\), and order the tree arcs as \(e_2,\ldots,e_n\), where \(e_i\) is the unique arc joining \(v_i\) to an earlier node. After deleting the incidence row for \(v_1\) and applying these row and column orders, the truncated tree-incidence matrix \(B\) is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal. Hence \(B\) is nonsingular and, for every \(\widetilde b\), \[Bx^*=\widetilde b\] has a unique solution. Consequently, a feasible tree solution associated with a fixed tree is uniquely determined by that tree and the balance vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting one node row and ordering a rooted tree appropriately makes its incidence matrix triangular with a nonzero diagonal. It is therefore invertible, so a fixed tree and balance vector determine a unique tree-supported flow. The uniquely determined flow need not be nonnegative unless it is feasible.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a tree on }n\text{ nodes}
B\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}\text{ is its truncated incidence matrix}
\widetilde b\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ is nonsingular and }\exists!\,x^*\text{ such that }Bx^*=\widetilde b.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Computing Tree-Induced Flows by Leaf Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of the unique basic flow induced by a rooted network-simplex spanning-tree structure, including the capacitated initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(b'(i)=b(i)\) for every node and set \(x_{ij}=0\) for every \((i,j)\in L\). In the capacitated case, also set \(x_{ij}=u_{ij}\) for \((i,j)\in U\), update \(b'(i)\leftarrow b'(i)-u_{ij}\), and update \(b'(j)\leftarrow b'(j)+u_{ij}\). Repeatedly select a nonroot leaf \(j\) with predecessor \(i\). If its incident tree arc is \((i,j)\), set \(x_{ij}=-b'(j)\); if it is \((j,i)\), set \(x_{ji}=b'(j)\). Then set \(b'(i)\leftarrow b'(i)+b'(j)\) and delete \(j\).

Repeatedly eliminate a nonroot leaf and choose its incident tree-arc flow to satisfy the leaf balance. The resulting values are the flow induced by the spanning-tree structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Induced Potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node potentials normalized at one root and induced by zero reduced costs on tree arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a spanning tree of a connected directed graph with arc costs \(c_{ij}\). Choose a root \(r\) and impose \(\pi_r=0\). There is a unique potential vector \(\pi\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfying \[c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j=0\qquad((i,j)\in T).\] Equivalently, the potential of any node is obtained by summing signed tree-arc costs along its unique tree path from \(r\). Once these potentials are fixed, every arc \((i,j)\in A\) has the uniquely determined reduced cost \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rooted spanning tree uniquely determines node potentials by making every tree arc's reduced cost zero, and thereby determines all non-tree reduced costs.

\(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\) for every arc \((i,j)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalization \(\pi_r=0\) and the tree equalities uniquely determine \(\pi\) and all reduced costs \(\bar c\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Computing Tree-Induced Node Potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parent-before-child computation of node potentials from a rooted network-simplex basis tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\pi(1)=0\). Visit each nonroot node \(j\) after its predecessor \(i=\operatorname{pred}(j)\). If the tree arc is \((i,j)\in A\), set \(\pi(j)=\pi(i)-c_{ij}\); if it is \((j,i)\in A\), set \(\pi(j)=\pi(i)+c_{ji}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set the root potential to zero and visit parents before children. Subtract the cost for a parent-to-child arc and add the cost for a child-to-parent arc. This makes each oriented tree arc have zero reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a rooted network-simplex basis tree with root }1.
\text{Each nonroot node is visited after its predecessor.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall (p,q)\in T,\quad c_{pq}-\pi(p)+\pi(q)=0.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Tree Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between tree-induced basic flows, potentials, and bounded-flow optimality signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimum-cost bounded-flow problem, a spanning tree \(T\) together with a lower-or-upper status for each non-tree arc determines a basic flow \(x\) and, after one normalization, a potential vector \(\pi\). Tree arcs satisfy \(\bar c_a=0\). If \(x\) is primal feasible and every non-tree arc satisfies \[x_a=\ell_a\Rightarrow \bar c_a\ge0,\qquad x_a=u_a\Rightarrow \bar c_a\le0,\] then \(x\) and \(\pi\) satisfy complementary slackness and are respectively primal and dual optimal. Conversely, every nondegenerate optimal tree basis has these flow, potential, and reduced-cost sign relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree basis induces both a basic flow and node potentials; feasibility plus the appropriate reduced-cost signs gives primal-dual optimality.
assumptions_latex: The objective is \(\min\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a\) subject to balances and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
\(T\) is a spanning tree and each non-tree arc is assigned a bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal feasibility and the displayed reduced-cost signs imply primal-dual optimality; a nondegenerate optimal tree basis obeys the same correspondence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tree Prices and Tree-Determined Reduced Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of network-simplex prices from a feasible tree and invariance under additive price normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a root $r$ of a feasible tree $T$ and choose $p_r\in\mathbb R$ arbitrarily. For each node $i$, let $P_i$ be the unique tree path from $r$ to $i$, with forward- and backward-arc sets $P_i^+$ and $P_i^-$. Define
\[
p_i=p_r-\sum_{(m,n)\in P_i^+}a_{mn}+\sum_{(m,n)\in P_i^-}a_{mn}.
\]
Then $p_i-p_j=a_{ij}$ for every tree arc $(i,j)\in T$. All price differences are independent of the arbitrary value of $p_r$; hence, for every arc $(i,j)$, $r_{ij}=a_{ij}+p_j-p_i$ is uniquely determined by $T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an arbitrary root price and propagate prices along unique tree paths, subtracting an arc cost when traversing forward and adding it when traversing backward. Tree arcs then satisfy the price equations. Changing the root price adds a common constant, so price differences and reduced costs are unchanged and determined by the tree.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a feasible tree with root }r.
p_r\in\mathbb R\text{ is arbitrary}.
P_i\text{ is the unique simple path in }T\text{ from }r\text{ to }i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_i-p_j=a_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in T,\qquad r_{ij}=a_{ij}+p_j-p_i\text{ is independent of }p_r\text{ and uniquely determined by }T.
