knowledge_statements.title: Network Basis Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-algebraic characterization of bases of a reduced node–arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\) be the node–arc incidence matrix of a connected directed graph, and delete one row to obtain \(D'\). For any set \(B\subseteq A\) with \(|B|=|V|-1\), the square submatrix \(D'_B\) is nonsingular if and only if the undirected edges underlying \(B\) form a spanning tree. Consequently, simplex bases of the equality system \(D'x=b'\) are represented by spanning trees, while nonbasic arcs are fixed at bounds in the bounded-flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set of n−1 incidence columns is a linear-programming basis exactly when its underlying arcs form a spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: The underlying graph is connected.
One row is deleted from its node–arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D'_B\) is nonsingular if and only if \(B\) is a spanning tree.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Disconnected Network Basis Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise extension of the spanning-tree basis characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the node–arc incidence matrix of a directed graph with \(k\) connected components in its underlying undirected graph. Delete one row from each component to obtain a full-row-rank matrix \(D'\). For \(B\subseteq A\) with \(|B|=|V|-k\), the square matrix \(D'_B\) is nonsingular if and only if the underlying arcs of \(B\) form a spanning forest containing one tree in every connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a disconnected network, reduced-incidence bases are exactly component-spanning forests after one row is deleted per component.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and has \(k\) underlying connected components.
Exactly one incidence row is deleted from each component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D'_B\text{ is nonsingular}\iff B\text{ is a component-spanning forest}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network-Simplex Iteration with Lower and Upper Arc Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One primal network-simplex pivot from a strongly feasible bounded-arc basis, including its stopping certificate and invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a strongly feasible basis (T,L,U) with flow x, prices p, and reduced costs r_{ij}, choose a non-tree entering arc \bar e=(\bar i,\bar j) satisfying r_{\bar i\bar j}<0 when \bar e\in L or r_{\bar i\bar j}>0 when \bar e\in U. If none exists, x is primal optimal and p is dual optimal. Let C be the cycle in T+\bar e, oriented with \bar e when \bar e\in L and oppositely when \bar e\in U. Set
\delta=\min\left\{\min_{(i,j)\in C^-}(x_{ij}-b_{ij}),\ \min_{(i,j)\in C^+}(c_{ij}-x_{ij})\right\},
and let \widehat C contain all arcs attaining this minimum. Starting at the join of C and traversing C forward, choose as leaving arc e the first arc in \widehat C. Then \bar T=T+\bar e-e and
\bar x_{ij}=x_{ij}\ ((i,j)\notin C),\qquad \bar x_{ij}=x_{ij}+\delta\ ((i,j)\in C^+),\qquad \bar x_{ij}=x_{ij}-\delta\ ((i,j)\in C^-).
Update L and U according to the bounds attained. The entering and leaving arcs may coincide, in which case T is unchanged while that arc moves from one bound status to the other. The resulting basis remains strongly feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From a strongly feasible bounded-arc basis, enter a lower-bound non-tree arc with negative reduced cost or an upper-bound non-tree arc with positive reduced cost. Augment around its fundamental cycle until the first bound is reached, and use the first limiting arc encountered from the rooted cycle join as the leaving arc. The updated basis remains strongly feasible. If no eligible entering arc exists, the current flow and prices are primal and dual optimal. The entering arc may also leave immediately, changing only its bound status.
assumptions_latex: (T,L,U)\text{ is a strongly feasible basis with corresponding }x\text{ and }p
\bar e\in L\Rightarrow r_{\bar i\bar j}<0,\qquad \bar e\in U\Rightarrow r_{\bar i\bar j}>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Either no eligible entering arc exists and }(x,p)\text{ is primal-dual optimal, or the pivot produces another strongly feasible basis }(\bar T,\bar L,\bar U).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex with shortest-path pricing for multicommodity flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the demand-feasibility reduction, path-based LP, pricing oracle, pivot rule, and cycling boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with capacities $u_e\ge 0$ and commodities $(r_i,s_i,d_i)$, add an arc $r_i'r_i$ of capacity $d_i$ for every $i$. The prescribed-demand system is feasible if and only if the resulting maximum-flow objective attains $\sum_i d_i$. Equivalently, with $\mathcal P$ the union of all $(r_i,s_i)$-dipaths, solve $\max\{\sum_{P\in\mathcal P}x_P: \sum_{P\in\mathcal P}x_P\chi_e^P\le u_e\ (e\in E),\ x_P\ge0\}$. After adding arc slacks, initialize simplex with the identity slack basis. For a basis $B$, obtain dual prices from $y^TB=w_B$. If some $y_e<0$, its slack column may enter; otherwise, for every commodity find a shortest $(r_i,s_i)$-dipath under nonnegative arc costs $y_e$. The basis is optimal exactly when every such shortest-path cost is at least $1$; a path of cost below $1$ supplies an entering column. Determine the leaving variable by the usual minimum-ratio test. Unrestricted pivot choices may cycle, while a lexicographic leaving rule prevents cycling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a capacitated directed multicommodity-flow instance, adding one demand-capacity arc per commodity converts prescribed-demand feasibility into a maximum-flow test: feasibility holds exactly when the optimum equals total demand. The equivalent path-variable LP can be solved by simplex from the all-slack basis. Dual feasibility is checked directly for slack columns and by one shortest-path computation per commodity for path columns. If every shortest path has dual cost at least one, the current basis is optimal; otherwise, a cheaper path enters and the standard ratio test selects the leaving variable. Ordinary pivoting may cycle, whereas lexicographic selection prevents cycling.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is directed}
u_e\ge0\quad(e\in E)
d_i\ge0\quad(i=1,\ldots,k)
\mathcal P=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\mathcal P(r_i,s_i)
y\ge0\text{ when shortest-path pricing is invoked}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Demand feasibility}\iff z^*=\sum_{i=1}^k d_i;\qquad B\text{ is optimal}\iff \min_{P\in\mathcal P(r_i,s_i)}y^T\chi^P\ge1\ \forall i,\text{ subject also to }y_e\ge0\ \forall e.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unimodularity of every spanning-tree basis extracted from a reduced incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D'\) be a reduced node–arc incidence matrix and let \(T\) be a spanning tree. The tree-basis matrix \(D'_T\) has determinant \(1\) or \(-1\). Hence \(D'_T\) is unimodular, its inverse is integral, and \(D'_Tz=q\) has an integral solution whenever \(q\) is integral. More generally, every square subdeterminant of a node–arc incidence matrix belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\); thus the incidence matrix is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every spanning-tree incidence basis has determinant ±1, so its inverse is integral; node–arc incidence matrices are totally unimodular.
assumptions_latex: \(D'\) is obtained from a directed node–arc incidence matrix by deleting one row.
\(T\) is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det(D'_T)\in\{-1,1\}\), and \((D'_T)^{-1}\) has integer entries.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Basic Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of basic bounded flows under integral balances and arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(D'x=b'\) with integral balances \(b'\) and integral finite bounds \(\ell_a,u_a\). At a network basic solution, every nonbasic variable is fixed at one of its integral bounds, and the tree variables satisfy \[D'_Tx_T=b'-D'_Nx_N.\] The right-hand side is integral, while the tree-basis inverse \((D'_T)^{-1}\) is integral. Therefore every component of \(x_T\), and hence every component of the basic flow \(x\), is integral. In particular, every feasible basic solution of the bounded network-flow polyhedron is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral balances and bounds make every network basic flow integral because the spanning-tree basis has an integral inverse.
assumptions_latex: \(b'\), \(\ell\), and every finite component of \(u\) are integral.
The basic columns form a spanning tree.
Each nonbasic arc is fixed at a finite bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every component of the basic flow \(x\) is integral.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional basic flows when either balances or active bounds are nonintegral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For one arc \(a=(s,t)\) with \(0\le x_a\le1\), balances requiring \(x_a=\tfrac12\) give the unique basic feasible flow \(x_a=\tfrac12\). Fractional active bounds also suffice: take arcs \(a=(s,t)\) and \(e=(t,s)\), zero node balances, \(0\le x_a\le1\), and fix the nonbasic arc at \(x_e=\ell_e=u_e=\tfrac12\). The tree equation then gives \(x_a=\tfrac12\).

At least one balance or active nonbasic bound is nonintegral.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-time construction and integrality of tree-basis flow and potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the computation bounds for the associated flow and potential and preserves the distinct integrality hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a minimum-cost-flow instance $(G,u,b,c)$ and a spanning-tree structure $(r,T,L,U)$, its associated $b$-flow $f$ can be computed in $O(m)$ time and its associated potential $\pi$ in $O(n)$ time, where $m=|E(G)|$ and $n=|V(G)|$. Moreover, $f$ is integral whenever $b$ and $u$ are integral, and $\pi$ is integral whenever $c$ is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed network-simplex tree structure, the associated flow is computable in linear time in the number of edges and the associated potential in linear time in the number of vertices. Integral balances and capacities yield an integral flow, while integral costs yield an integral potential.

(r,T,L,U)\text{ is a spanning-tree structure}
m=|E(G)|,\quad n=|V(G)|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_f=O(m),\quad T_\pi=O(n);\qquad (b,u\text{ integral}\Rightarrow f\text{ integral}),\quad(c\text{ integral}\Rightarrow\pi\text{ integral}).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Network Simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-feasible tree pivots and bound flips for a bounded linear minimum-cost flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a primal-feasible tree basis with tree-induced flow \(x\) and potentials \(\pi\). Compute the reduced costs \(\bar c_a\) of the non-tree arcs. If every non-tree arc at its lower bound has \(\bar c_a\ge 0\) and every non-tree arc at its upper bound has \(\bar c_a\le 0\), output \(x\). Otherwise choose an arc violating the applicable sign condition and orient its fundamental cycle so that the entering arc moves away from its current bound in an improving direction. Let \(\theta\) be the largest step preserving every arc bound and update \(x\) by the corresponding cycle circulation. If a tree arc becomes limiting, remove a limiting tree arc and insert the entering arc; if the entering arc alone reaches its opposite bound first, keep the tree unchanged and change that arc's nonbasic bound status. Update the tree potentials after a basis exchange and repeat. Every iteration preserves balances and bound feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible tree flow, repeatedly move a reduced-cost-violating non-tree arc along its fundamental cycle. Exchange it with a limiting tree arc, or perform a bound flip if the entering arc reaches its opposite bound first, until the reduced-cost optimality conditions hold.
assumptions_latex: A primal-feasible tree basis is available.
The bounded minimum-cost flow problem is feasible and has a finite optimum.
A finite anti-cycling pivot rule is used for degenerate basis exchanges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every intermediate flow is primal feasible, and upon termination the returned flow is optimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Termination Under a Nonrepeating Pivot Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state convergence bound for primal network simplex in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite connected network with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) arcs, suppose primal network simplex starts from a primal-feasible tree basis and never repeats a complete basis state, consisting of its spanning tree and every nonbasic arc's active-bound status. Then it terminates after at most \(\tau(G)2^{m-n+1}-1\) state transitions, where \(\tau(G)\) is the number of spanning trees of the underlying graph; fixed or one-sided arc statuses can only reduce this bound. When no eligible nonbasic arc remains, the final feasible flow satisfies the reduced-cost sign conditions and is optimal. Without a nonrepetition rule, zero-step degenerate exchanges do not ensure finite termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonrepeating primal network-simplex rule terminates because only finitely many tree and bound-status states exist; uncontrolled degeneracy removes that guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite and its underlying graph is connected.
A primal-feasible tree basis is available.
The objective has a finite optimum.
Exact reduced costs and ratio tests are used.
Complete basis states are never repeated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{transitions}}\le \tau(G)2^{m-n+1}-1,\qquad \text{and the terminal flow is optimal}.

notation.meaning: number of spanning trees of the underlying graph

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic primal network-simplex iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One pivot or termination step for minimum-cost flow with nonnegative arc flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a strongly feasible tree $T$, its basic flow $x$ with $x_{ij}=0$ for $(i,j)
otin T$, and node prices $p$ satisfying $r_{ij}=a_{ij}+p_j-p_i=0$ on $T$, select an entering arc $ ar e=( ar i, ar j)
otin T$ with $r_{ ar i ar j}<0$. If no such arc exists, terminate with primal-optimal $x$ and dual-optimal $p$. Otherwise form the cycle $C$ in $T+ ar e$. If $C^-=\varnothing$, terminate and declare the problem unbounded; if $C^-
eq\varnothing$, select a leaving arc $e\in C^-$ by the strongly-feasible-tree pivot rule and replace $T$ by $ ar T=T+ ar e-e$, which is strongly feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a strongly feasible tree basis, its basic flow, and prices giving zero reduced cost on tree arcs. Enter a nontree arc of negative reduced cost. If none exists, the current flow and prices are primal and dual optimal. If the resulting cycle has no backward arc, the problem is unbounded. Otherwise apply the strongly feasible pivot rule to remove a backward arc and obtain a new strongly feasible tree.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a strongly feasible tree}
x_{ij}=0\quad\forall(i,j)\notin T
r_{ij}=a_{ij}+p_j-p_i=0\quad\forall(i,j)\in T
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration certifies optimality or unboundedness, or produces a strongly feasible pivoted tree }\bar T=T+\bar e-e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-basis pivot algorithm for minimum-cost flow.

While a nontree arc violates its optimality condition, choose it as the entering arc, determine a leaving arc, and update the tree, flow, and potentials. If the loop terminates, every nontree arc satisfies its optimality condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite termination and integrality of the strongly feasible network simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination, primal-dual optimality, and integrality guarantees for the stated minimum-cost-flow simplex method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Apply the stated simplex method to a minimum-cost flow problem with $x_{ij}\ge 0$, starting from a strongly feasible tree. If the problem is not unbounded, the method terminates after finitely many iterations with primal-optimal $x$ and dual-optimal $p$ having equal objective values. If every supply $s_i$ is integral, the returned primal solution is integral. If all arc costs $a_{ij}$ and the initial price of the root are integral, the returned dual solution is integral. If the problem is unbounded, the method verifies unboundedness after finitely many iterations.

children.top_down_role: Dual-feasible network pivoting for feasibility restoration.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Network Simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-feasible tree pivots that restore violated flow bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a tree basis whose reduced costs satisfy the lower-bound and upper-bound dual sign conditions, although some induced tree flow violates a bound. Choose a violating tree arc and delete it, producing a fundamental cut. Select a non-tree arc crossing that cut and change the potentials in the cut component until the selected arc's reduced cost reaches zero, choosing the minimum admissible dual step so that all other reduced-cost signs remain feasible. Insert that arc, recompute the tree-induced flow, and repeat. If no crossing arc can repair the chosen violation, the associated cut yields an infeasibility certificate; if all tree bounds become feasible, output the resulting optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain reduced-cost feasibility while exchanging arcs across a cut to repair bound violations; primal feasibility then certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: The initial tree basis is dual feasible.
Potential shifts and entering arcs are selected by the dual ratio test.
A finite anti-cycling rule resolves zero-step ties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method preserves dual feasibility and returns an optimal flow when primal feasibility is restored, or a cut certificate when repair is impossible.

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental-Cycle Pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacent tree-basis exchanges and bound flips induced by moving a non-tree arc around its fundamental cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be the current spanning tree and let \(e\notin T\) be a non-tree arc selected to move away from its current bound. The graph \(T\cup\{e\}\) contains a unique fundamental cycle \(C_e\). Choose the circulation direction on \(C_e\) that moves \(e\) away from that bound, and let \(d_a\in\{-1,0,1\}\) be its signed cycle vector. The largest feasible step is \[\theta^*=\min\left\{u_a-x_a:d_a>0\right\}\mathbin{\wedge}\min\left\{x_a-\ell_a:d_a<0\right\},\] where \(\wedge\) denotes the minimum of the two displayed quantities. Set \(x'=x+\theta^*d\). If a tree arc \(f\in C_e\cap T\) attains the limiting bound, then \(T'=T\cup\{e\}\setminus\{f\}\) is a spanning tree and represents the adjacent basis. If no tree arc is limiting because \(e\) reaches its opposite bound first, keep \(T'=T\) and change the nonbasic bound status of \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a non-tree arc identifies one fundamental cycle. Move along that cycle to the first bound, exchanging the entering arc with a limiting tree arc when one exists, or performing a bound flip when only the entering arc reaches its opposite bound.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a spanning tree representing a feasible bounded basic flow.
The selected non-tree arc \(e\) can move away from its current bound in the chosen cycle direction.
All residual capacities used to define \(\theta^*\) are interpreted in that direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update preserves balances and bounds; it produces either the spanning tree \(T'=T\cup\{e\}\setminus\{f\}\) for a limiting tree arc \(f\), or the unchanged tree with a bound flip of \(e\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Change Along a Fundamental Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost effect of the feasible cycle motion generated by one nonbasic arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let node potentials \(\pi\) make every tree arc have zero reduced cost, and let \(d\) be the signed fundamental-cycle circulation normalized by \(d_e=s\in\{+1,-1\}\) on its unique non-tree arc \(e\). For every feasible \(\theta\ge0\), \[c^{\mathsf T}(x+\theta d)-c^{\mathsf T}x=\theta c^{\mathsf T}d=\theta s\bar c_e.\] Thus \(s\bar c_e<0\) strictly improves the objective when \(\theta>0\), while a zero-step degenerate exchange leaves it unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fundamental-cycle step changes cost by its length times the entering arc's direction-adjusted reduced cost; a positive eligible step improves cost, while a zero step does not.
assumptions_latex: Costs are linear.
Tree potentials satisfy \(\bar c_a=0\) for every tree arc.
The cycle vector is normalized by \(d_e=s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta z=\theta s\bar c_e.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Feasible Tree Pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted-tree feasibility convention used to resolve degenerate network-simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the nonnegative transshipment form, root a feasible tree basis at a node \(r\). The basis is strongly feasible when every tree arc carrying zero flow is oriented toward \(r\) along its unique tree path. During a degenerate fundamental-cycle pivot, choose among the limiting tree arcs a leaving arc whose removal and replacement preserve this orientation condition; a consistent rooted ordering supplies a deterministic tie break. Starting from a strongly feasible tree and applying only such pivots keeps every subsequent tree strongly feasible. With the standard strongly-feasible leaving rule, a fixed entering-arc selection rule cannot cycle through the same sequence of tree bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Root the tree and require every zero-flow tree arc to point toward the root; preserving this condition during tied pivots controls degeneracy and cycling.
assumptions_latex: Flows are in nonnegative transshipment form.
A feasible rooted tree basis is maintained.
Degenerate leaving ties follow a fixed strongly-feasible rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every pivot preserves strong feasibility, and the prescribed deterministic rule prevents repetition of tree bases.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Last-blocking-arc rule for strongly feasible network-simplex pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leaving-arc selection, invariant preservation, finite termination, and the bounded-arc extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a strongly feasible basis tree and an entering arc \((p,q)\), let \(k\) be the first common node on the paths from \(p\) and \(q\) to the root. Orient the resulting fundamental cycle from \(k\) along the path to \(p\), through \((p,q)\), and back from \(q\) to \(k\). Among the blocking arcs, select the last one in this cycle order as the leaving arc. The new basis tree is strongly feasible. In a degenerate improving pivot with \(\delta_{pq}=z_{pq}-c_{pq}>0\), the dual values on the detached nonroot subtree decrease by \(\delta_{pq}\), while the remaining dual values are unchanged; hence a strictly decreasing dual potential prevents a basis tree from repeating and yields finite termination. For bounded arcs, require lower-bound-degenerate basic arcs to point toward the root and upper-bound-degenerate basic arcs to point away from it. The same leaving rule, including possible self-blocking by the entering arc, preserves strong feasibility and finite termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the entering arc's fundamental cycle, remove the last blocking arc. This preserves the strongly feasible orientation. Degenerate improving pivots strictly decrease a dual potential, preventing repeated basis trees and ensuring finite termination. The analogous rule applies to bounded arcs with opposite orientation requirements at lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a strongly feasible network-simplex basis tree before the pivot}
(p,q)\text{ is an enterable arc}
\delta_{pq}=z_{pq}-c_{pq}>0\text{ in the degenerate-pivot termination argument}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T'\text{ is strongly feasible, and repeated use of the rule gives finite network-simplex termination}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Feasible Trees and the Leaving-Arc Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root-relative orientation of zero-flow tree arcs and the corresponding leaving-arc selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a tree arc \(h=pq\), \(h\) is away from the root \(r\) in \(T\) if \(p\in R(T,h)\), and it is toward \(r\) otherwise. A tree \(T\) is strongly feasible if it determines a feasible flow \(x\) and every \(h\in T\) with \(x_h=0\) is away from \(r\). For an entering arc \(e\), the leaving-arc rule chooses \(h\) as the first reverse arc of \(C(T,e)\) satisfying \(x_h=\theta\).

A feasible tree is strongly feasible when every zero-flow tree arc points away from the root. The leaving-arc rule selects the first reverse cycle arc attaining the augmentation minimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial bound on consecutive degenerate strongly feasible pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stage-count bound for strongly feasible network-simplex pivots and the LRC specialization controlling stage length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_0,\ldots,T_M\) be strongly feasible basis trees in a sequence of consecutive degenerate pivots ending when optimality is recognized or the next pivot is nondegenerate. Let the common nondegenerate basic arcs form \(P\) components, and let \(L\) be the maximum number of degenerate arcs on a node-to-root path in \(T_M\). If \(S\) is the number of stages, then \(S\le L\le P-1\le m-1\); in particular, the stage count is no greater than the number of degenerate basic variables at the represented extreme point. Under the Least Recently Considered entering rule, each stage has at most \(n\) pivots, so the number of consecutive degenerate pivots is at most \(mn\). Finite anti-cycling alone does not imply such a polynomial stalling bound: when \(b=0\), all bases may represent the origin and exponentially many bases may be visited before optimality is recognized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consecutive run of degenerate strongly feasible pivots has at most L stages, where L is the largest number of degenerate arcs on a final-tree path to the root and is at most m−1. With the LRC entering rule, each stage has at most n pivots, giving an mn bound. Without stage-length control, finite but exponential stalling can still occur.
assumptions_latex: T_0,\ldots,T_M\text{ are strongly feasible basis trees connected by consecutive degenerate pivots}
L=\max_v\{\text{number of degenerate arcs on the }v\text{-to-root path in }T_M\}
\text{the LRC entering rule is used for the }mn\text{ bound}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\le L\le P-1\le m-1,\qquad N_{\mathrm{deg}}\le nS\le mn.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tie Rule Preserving Strong Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leaving-arc tie rule that preserves strong feasibility in network-simplex pivots, including degenerate pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $T$ be strongly feasible with root $r$ and flow $x$, let $\bar e=(\bar i,\bar j)$ be an entering arc, and let $C$ be the cycle formed by $T\cup\{\bar e\}$. Suppose $C^-\ne\varnothing$, set $\delta=\min_{(i,j)\in C^-}x_{ij}$, and let $\widehat C=\{(i,j)\in C^-:x_{ij}=\delta\}$. Let the join be the first node of $C$ lying on the unique tree path from $r$ to $\bar i$. Traverse $C$ in the direction of $\bar e$, starting from the join, and choose as leaving arc $e$ the first arc of $\widehat C$ encountered. Then $\bar T=T+\bar e-e$ is strongly feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an entering arc closes a cycle in a strongly feasible tree, consider the backward cycle arcs attaining the minimum flow. Starting at the cycle's join with the root-to-entering-tail path, traverse in the entering arc's direction and remove the first such candidate encountered. The resulting tree remains strongly feasible, including for a degenerate pivot.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is strongly feasible with root }r\text{ and flow }x.
\bar e=(\bar i,\bar j)\text{ is the entering arc and }C\text{ is the cycle in }T\cup\{\bar e\}.
C^-\ne\varnothing.
\delta=\min_{(i,j)\in C^-}x_{ij},\quad\widehat C=\{(i,j)\in C^-:x_{ij}=\delta\}.
e\text{ is the first arc of }\widehat C\text{ encountered when }C\text{ is traversed in the direction of }\bar e\text{ from the join}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar T=T+\bar e-e\text{ is strongly feasible}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Feasible Spanning Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent characterizations of strong feasibility for a rooted network-simplex spanning-tree structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\mathbf T,\mathbf L,\mathbf U)$ be a rooted spanning-tree structure for a minimum-cost-flow problem with integral data. The tree $\mathbf T$ is strongly feasible if every zero-flow tree arc points toward the root and every tree arc whose flow equals its capacity points away from the root. Equivalently, $\mathbf T$ is strongly feasible if a positive amount of flow can be sent from every node to the root along its tree path without violating any flow bound. If $\mathbf T$ is strongly feasible, then $(\mathbf T,\mathbf L,\mathbf U)$ is also called strongly feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a rooted spanning-tree structure for an integral minimum-cost-flow problem, a tree is strongly feasible when zero-flow tree arcs point toward the root and saturated tree arcs point away from it. Equivalently, every node can send a positive amount of flow to the root along its tree path without violating a flow bound.
assumptions_latex: (\mathbf T,\mathbf L,\mathbf U)\text{ is a rooted spanning-tree structure for a minimum-cost-flow problem with integral data}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf T\text{ is strongly feasible}\iff\left[\begin{array}{l}\text{every zero-flow tree arc points toward the root and every saturated tree arc points away from the root}\end{array}\right]\iff\text{a positive amount of flow can be sent from every node to the root along its tree path without violating any flow bound}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Feasible Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root-relative orientation condition for zero-flow tree arcs in the network simplex method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a root node $r$. A tree arc $(i,j)\in T$ is oriented away from $r$ if the unique simple path in $T$ from $r$ to $j$ passes through $i$. A feasible tree $T$ with corresponding flow $x$ is strongly feasible if every arc $(i,j)\in T$ with $x_{ij}=0$ is oriented away from $r$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a fixed root, a tree arc is oriented away from the root when its tail precedes its head on the unique path from the root to the head. A feasible tree is strongly feasible when every zero-flow tree arc is oriented this way.
assumptions_latex: r\text{ is a fixed root node}.
T\text{ is a feasible tree with corresponding flow }x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is strongly feasible}\iff\forall(i,j)\in T,\quad x_{ij}=0\Rightarrow(i,j)\text{ is oriented away from }r.

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Rule Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and restricted searches for an improving nonbasic arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization basis, define the eligible set \[E^- =\{a:x_a=\ell_a,\ \bar c_a<0\}\cup\{a:x_a=u_a,\ \bar c_a>0\}.\] Full pricing scans every non-tree arc and either returns an element of \(E^-\) or certifies optimal reduced-cost signs. Partial pricing scans a chosen subset; block pricing scans a cyclic partition; candidate-list pricing repeatedly scans a maintained list and refreshes it by a broader scan when exhausted. Restricted scans may select an improving arc but cannot certify optimality. Therefore any exact implementation must eventually perform a complete scan before declaring \(E^-=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing rules search all arcs, blocks, subsets, or candidate lists for a reduced-cost violation; only a complete scan can certify optimality.
assumptions_latex: The current basis and reduced costs are available.
Non-tree arcs are fixed at lower or upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any returned arc in \(E^-\) is eligible to enter, while optimality may be declared only after a complete scan proves \(E^-=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Eligible and Greatest-Violation Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection rules applied within a scanned set of bounded nonbasic arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scanned set \(S\) of nonbasic arcs, define \(v_a=-\bar c_a\) when \(x_a=\ell_a\) and \(v_a=\bar c_a\) when \(x_a=u_a\). An arc is eligible exactly when \(v_a>0\). First-eligible pricing returns the first eligible arc in a fixed scan order. Greatest-violation pricing returns an arc in \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in S}v_a\) when that maximum is positive; otherwise it reports that \(S\) contains no eligible arc. This report certifies global reduced-cost feasibility only when \(S\) is the complete nonbasic set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within a scanned set, pricing may choose the first eligible arc or the largest signed reduced-cost violation; failure on a restricted set is not a global optimality test.
assumptions_latex: Every arc in \(S\) is nonbasic and fixed at a lower or upper bound.
Current reduced costs \(\bar c_a\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_a>0\iff a\text{ is eligible},\qquad \max_{a\in S}v_a\le 0\iff S\text{ contains no eligible arc}.

notation.meaning: currently scanned set of nonbasic arcs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pricing Scan Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison cost when current reduced costs are directly accessible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If testing one nonbasic arc's active-bound reduced-cost sign takes \(O(1)\) time, first-eligible and greatest-violation scans over \(S\) take \(O(|S|)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space. A complete scan of \(m_N\) nonbasic arcs therefore costs \(O(m_N)\). First-eligible pricing can stop earlier, but a conclusive no-eligible-arc test must inspect all \(m_N\) arcs in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With stored reduced costs, pricing is linear in the scanned set, and a conclusive absence test is linear in all nonbasic arcs in the worst case.
assumptions_latex: Testing one arc's reduced-cost sign costs \(O(1)\).
Reduced-cost recomputation is not charged to the scan.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{scan}}(S)=O(|S|),\qquad T_{\mathrm{certificate}}=O(m_N).

notation.meaning: set scanned by the pricing rule

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cyclic from-node pricing rule and stalling bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entering-arc selection for network simplex when arcs are stored in groups indexed by their from-node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order the arcs by from-node. After an arc with from-node \(j\) enters, choose the best enterable arc with from-node \(j\); if none exists, scan the from-nodes cyclically in the order \(j+1,\ldots,m,1,\ldots,j-1\) and select the best enterable arc for the first node having one. Initialize with \(j=1\). When this pricing rule is combined with strongly feasible basis trees and the last-blocking-arc leaving rule, after a degenerate pivot from node \(p\), any arc from \(p\) that is then enterable would produce a nondegenerate pivot. Consequently, a stage contains at most \(m\) degenerate pivots. Since strong feasibility bounds the number of stages by \(L<m\), the number of consecutive degenerate pivots is at most \(mL<m^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group arcs by their tail node. Continue pricing at the previous tail, then scan tail nodes cyclically until an enterable arc is found. With strongly feasible trees and the last-blocking-arc rule, each stage has at most m degenerate pivots, and a consecutive degenerate run has at most mL, which is less than m².
assumptions_latex: \text{arcs are ordered by from-node}
\text{the best enterable arc is selected within each from-node group}
\text{strongly feasible basis trees and the last-blocking-arc leaving rule are maintained}
L<m\text{ bounds the number of stages}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{length}(\text{stage})\le m,\qquad N_{\mathrm{deg}}\le mL<m^2.

children.title: Leaving-Arc Rule Families

knowledge_statements.title: Leaving-Arc Rule Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ratio-test and tie-breaking rules for selecting a limiting tree arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After an entering arc defines a signed fundamental-cycle direction \(d\), compute \[\theta^*=\min\left(\min_{d_a>0}(u_a-x_a),\min_{d_a<0}(x_a-\ell_a)\right).\] Every tree arc attaining this minimum is a valid leaving candidate, because it reaches a bound at \(x'=x+\theta^*d\). If the minimizer is unique, it leaves. If several arcs tie, a basis-preserving family may use a fixed arc order, a lexicographic perturbation, or a rooted strongly-feasible rule. The selected candidate is deleted after the entering arc is inserted; deterministic anti-cycling rules must be applied consistently, including when \(\theta^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The leaving arc is a tree arc that first reaches a bound; fixed-order, lexicographic, or strongly-feasible rules resolve ties and degenerate pivots.
assumptions_latex: A feasible tree flow and an entering-arc cycle direction are given.
At least one tree arc limits movement on the fundamental cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deleting any limiting tree arc preserves feasibility and the tree-basis size; a consistent anti-cycling tie rule controls degenerate repetitions.

children.title: Multiple Pivoting

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Pivoting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic sequential interpretation of batched network-simplex pivots; exact named variants require source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible spanning-tree basis \(T\), flow \(x\), node potentials \(\pi\), and an ordered batch \(E=(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\) of candidate nonbasic arcs, process the arcs in order. Before processing \(e_j\), recompute its reduced cost and residual capacity relative to the current basis. If it remains dual-infeasible, add it to the tree, augment along its fundamental cycle by the largest bound-feasible amount, remove a blocking tree arc, and update \(T,x,\pi\); otherwise discard it. Stop after every candidate has been processed or an optimality test succeeds. The resulting basis is the output of one multiple-pivot major iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-pivot iteration selects several candidates, then applies valid ordinary network-simplex pivots sequentially, rechecking each candidate after earlier pivots change the basis.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is primal feasible for the arc bounds and balance equations.
\(T\) is a spanning-tree basis associated with \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{+}\) is feasible, and \(T^{+}\) is the basis obtained after at most \(k\) ordinary pivots.

notation.meaning: ordered batch of candidate entering arcs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but multiple-pivoting variants differ materially. The statement also assumes every eligible entry removes a blocking tree arc, omitting the possible bound-flip case. A dedicated algorithm source is required.

children.title: Block Pivoting
children.top_down_role: Pivot organizations restricted to localized arc or subtree blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Pivoting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-based candidate selection for a batched network-simplex iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the nonbasic arcs into ordered blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_q\). At a major iteration, scan the next block cyclically, compute current signed reduced costs, and retain its dual-infeasible arcs. Choose from them an ordered compatible subset \(S\). For each \(e\in S\), recompute eligibility and, when eligible, perform the ordinary fundamental-cycle network-simplex pivot. Advance to the next block after processing \(S\). If a complete pass through all blocks finds no dual-infeasible nonbasic arc, return the current feasible basis as optimal; otherwise continue from the updated basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block pivoting scans candidates in blocks, processes a compatible eligible subset, and declares optimality only after a complete block pass finds no improving arc.
assumptions_latex: The blocks satisfy \(\bigcup_{r=1}^{q}B_r=N\), where \(N\) is the set of nonbasic arcs.
Every executed pivot preserves primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A complete unsuccessful pass certifies the network-simplex reduced-cost optimality conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the block-scanning, compatibility, cycling, and optimality-pass conventions describe a particular unsourced variant.

children.title: Batch-Pivot Compatibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Joint Batch-Compatibility Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable structural and primal conditions for a proposed simultaneous network-simplex batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a spanning tree, let \(E^+\) and \(F^-\subseteq T\) be distinct entering and leaving arc sets with \(|E^+|=|F^-|\), and let \(d^j\) be signed fundamental-cycle circulations with proposed steps \(\theta_j\). Define \[T'=(T\cup E^+)\setminus F^-,\qquad x'=x+\sum_j\theta_jd^j.\] The batch is structurally and primal compatible exactly when \(T'\) is connected and has \(|V|-1\) edges and \(\ell\le x'\le u\). Flow balance needs no additional test because \(Bd^j=0\) for every cycle direction. If the directions are explicitly represented with total support size \(L\), these conditions can be checked in \(O(|V|+|E^+|+L)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proposed batch is compatible exactly when its joint exchanges leave a spanning tree and its summed cycle update respects every bound; conservation is automatic for cycle directions.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a spanning tree and \(x\) is balance-feasible.
Entering and leaving arcs are distinct within their respective sets.
Every \(d^j\) is a signed circulation on the fundamental cycle of its entering arc.
Cycle directions are explicitly available when the stated checking bound is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(T'\text{ is a tree and }\ell\le x'\le u\bigr)\iff\text{the proposed batch is a valid primal tree-basis update}.

notation.meaning: set of proposed leaving tree arcs
total number of explicitly represented nonzero cycle-direction entries

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Joint Batch-Compatibility Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Individual Pivot Feasibility Does Not Imply Batch Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-cycle interference in simultaneous pivot proposals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the current tree on vertices \(1,2,3\) contain arcs \(a=(1,2)\) and \(b=(2,3)\), each with current flow zero and capacity one. Add two distinct parallel nonbasic arcs \(e_1,e_2=(3,1)\) with sufficient capacity. Each fundamental-cycle augmentation of one unit increases the flows of \(a\), \(b\), and the selected \(e_j\), so either proposal is individually feasible; ties permit choosing \(a\) as the first leaving arc and \(b\) as the second. Applied simultaneously, the summed update assigns flow two to both \(a\) and \(b\), violating their capacities, while replacing both tree arcs by \(e_1,e_2\) isolates vertex \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two individually feasible pivots can overload shared tree arcs and jointly destroy the spanning tree, so individual ratio tests do not certify a batch.
assumptions_latex: Parallel directed arcs are permitted.
The two entering arcs have capacity at least one.
The current zero flow is a feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Individual pivot validity}\ \not\Rightarrow\ \text{joint batch compatibility}.

notation.meaning: shared tree arcs of the two fundamental cycles

knowledge_statements.title: Individual Pivot Feasibility Does Not Imply Batch Compatibility
Batch-Pivot Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-and-basis compatibility for simultaneous fundamental-cycle updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a spanning tree and let distinct nonbasic arcs \(e_j\) induce signed fundamental-cycle vectors \(d^j\). A proposed batch \(\{(e_j,f_j,\theta_j):1\le j\le k\}\), with leaving arcs \(f_j\in T\), is batch-pivot compatible when \[T'=T\cup\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}\setminus\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\] is a spanning tree and the simultaneous update \[x'=x+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\theta_jd^j\] satisfies every arc bound and every flow-balance equation. Pairwise edge-disjoint fundamental cycles, with each step individually bound-feasible, form a sufficient but not necessary compatibility test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivot batch is compatible when all exchanges jointly leave a spanning tree and the summed cycle augmentation remains feasible. Edge-disjoint cycles give a simple sufficient test.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a spanning tree and \(x\) is feasible.
Each \(d^j\) is the signed circulation of the fundamental cycle created by \(e_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T'\) is a valid tree basis and \(x'\) is primal feasible.

notation.meaning: signed fundamental-cycle direction for candidate j

knowledge_statements.title: Artificial-Root Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Star-tree initialization for zero-lower-bound transshipment form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network with node balances \(b_i\), using the convention that net outflow equals \(b_i\), add an artificial root \(r\). For every node \(i\), add \((i,r)\) with flow \(b_i\) when \(b_i>0\), add \((r,i)\) with flow \(-b_i\) when \(b_i<0\), and add either incident orientation with zero flow when \(b_i=0\). Set every original arc flow to zero. The artificial arcs form a star spanning tree on the augmented node set, and the assigned flows satisfy all original-node balances and the root balance because \(\sum_i b_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attach every node to an artificial root, directing and loading each artificial arc according to its imbalance. The resulting star is an immediately feasible auxiliary tree basis.
assumptions_latex: Original arcs have zero lower bounds.
Artificial arcs have sufficient capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented flow is feasible and the artificial arcs form an initial spanning-tree basis.

notation.meaning: prescribed net outflow at node i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Artificial-Star Degeneracy Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of the artificial-root star basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The basic artificial arc incident to node \(i\) carries \(|b_i|\). With lower bound zero and capacity \(u_i^{\rm art}\), the star basis is nondegenerate exactly when \(0<|b_i|<u_i^{\rm art}\) for every \(i\). Thus a zero balance or a tight artificial capacity makes the basis degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The artificial star is nondegenerate exactly when every artificial basic flow lies strictly between zero and its capacity.
assumptions_latex: Artificial arcs have lower bound zero.
The star arcs are precisely the basic arcs.
A basis is degenerate when a basic arc is at a bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The star basis is nondegenerate}\iff 0<|b_i|<u_i^{\rm art}\quad\forall i.

knowledge_statements.title: Big-Cost Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite big-cost realization of lexicographic Phase-One initialization for integral flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z(x)\) be the total flow on artificial arcs and \(g(x)\) the original-arc cost over the augmented feasible set. Assume all feasible flows are integral and the range of \(g\) is at most \(R\). Assign unit cost \(M\) to every artificial arc and retain original costs elsewhere, where \(M>R\). Then every minimizer of \(Mz(x)+g(x)\) first minimizes \(z(x)\); among solutions with minimum artificial flow, it minimizes \(g(x)\). Consequently, if the original network is feasible, every augmented optimum has zero artificial flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integral flows, an artificial-arc cost exceeding the entire possible original-cost range makes optimization lexicographically minimize artificial flow before the true objective.
assumptions_latex: Feasible augmented flows are integral.
\(R\ge \sup g-\inf g\) over the augmented feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}(Mz+g)\) minimizes \(z\) first and \(g\) second.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of a Range-Only Big Cost for Continuous Artificial Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite range domination without positive spacing between attainable artificial-flow totals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(M>R>0\) and choose \(0<\varepsilon<R/M\). If the augmented feasible image contains points with \((z,g)=(0,R)\) and \((z,g)=(\varepsilon,0)\), then \(M\varepsilon<R\). Minimizing \(Mz+g\) therefore prefers positive artificial flow although a zero-artificial-flow point exists. Thus \(M>R\) alone is insufficient when attainable values of \(z\) have no positive minimum separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous artificial flow, an arbitrarily small positive violation can buy a larger original-cost decrease, so a cost exceeding the original objective range need not implement lexicographic Phase One.
assumptions_latex: Artificial flow may take nondiscrete values.
The feasible image contains the two stated attainable points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M>R\ \not\Rightarrow\ \operatorname*{argmin}(Mz+g)\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}z\quad\text{without positive spacing of attainable }z.

notation.meaning: range bound for the original objective

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Big-M initialization for network simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of an initial strongly feasible tree using an artificial node and penalized artificial arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce a zero-supply node $0$. For each original node $i$, add $(i,0)$ when $s_i>0$ and add $(0,i)$ when $s_i\le 0$, assigning every artificial arc cost $M$. Initialize $x_{i0}=s_i$ for $s_i>0$, $x_{0i}=-s_i$ for $s_i\le 0$, and $x_{ij}=0$ on every original arc. The artificial arcs form a feasible spanning tree; rooted at $0$, its zero-flow arcs point away from the root, so it is strongly feasible. If $M$ is sufficiently large that every optimal solution assigns zero flow to all artificial arcs, restricting such a solution to the original arcs gives an optimal solution of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a zero-supply artificial root, connect positive-supply nodes to it and connect it to nonpositive-supply nodes, and charge cost M on every artificial arc. Routing each imbalance on its artificial arc and setting original-arc flows to zero gives a feasible, strongly feasible tree basis. If M is large enough to eliminate artificial flow at optimality, restriction to the original arcs yields an original optimum.
assumptions_latex: \overline{\mathcal A}=\{(i,0):s_i>0\}\cup\{(0,i):s_i\le 0\}
a_{ij}=M\quad\forall(i,j)\in\overline{\mathcal A}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The construction supplies an initial strongly feasible tree; if optimal artificial flows vanish for the chosen $M$, restriction gives an original-problem optimum.}

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Arc Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Removal of zero-flow artificial arcs after successful Phase One.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from an optimal Phase-One tree basis whose artificial arcs all carry zero flow. While an artificial arc is basic, delete it temporarily, obtaining a tree cut. If an original nonbasic arc crosses that cut, pivot the original arc into the basis and the artificial arc out with augmentation zero. Repeat until no basic artificial arc remains. Then delete all nonbasic artificial arcs. If the original arc columns span the balance space, this procedure yields an original-network tree basis; otherwise the remaining components expose the rank obstruction to such a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After Phase One reaches zero artificial flow, degenerate pivots replace basic artificial arcs with original cut-crossing arcs; all remaining artificial arcs are then deleted.
assumptions_latex: The Phase-One optimum has total artificial flow zero.
The augmented basis is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a feasible original-network basis whenever the original arc columns have full balance-space rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Phase-One Feasibility Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary optimization for restoring or disproving flow feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Augment the network with nonnegative artificial variables that make the balance equations and arc bounds feasible from a readily constructed basis. Minimize \[z=\sum_{a\in A_{m art}}x_a\] subject to the augmented constraints. If the optimum satisfies \(z^*=0\), discard the artificial variables and return the restricted flow as feasible for the original network. If \(z^*>0\), return the positive optimum together with an optimal dual solution of the auxiliary linear program; weak duality then certifies that no original feasible flow exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase One minimizes total artificial flow. Optimum zero supplies an original feasible flow; a positive optimum and its auxiliary dual solution certify infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The augmented auxiliary problem is feasible and bounded below.
Artificial variables exactly represent violations of the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*=0\) if and only if the original flow constraints are feasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-bound complementation using reversed-arc variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Use the incidence convention \(Bx=b\). For each selected arc \(a\in S\) satisfying \(0\le x_a\le u_a<\infty\), define \(y_a=u_a-x_a\) and represent \(y_a\) by the reversed incidence column \(-B_a\). Keep the other arc variables unchanged and denote the resulting variable vector and incidence matrix by \(x'\) and \(B'\). Then \[B'x'=b-\sum_{a\in S}u_aB_a,\qquad 0\le y_a\le u_a\quad(a\in S).\] The objective contribution of a replaced arc is \[c_ax_a=c_au_a-c_ay_a.\] Thus complementation is a bijective reformulation that exchanges the two bounds, reverses the incidence column and cost sign, shifts the balance vector, and adds a known objective constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing an upper-bounded flow and representing the complement on the reversed arc shifts node balances, negates that variable's cost, and adds a constant objective term. The complementary variable still has the equivalent upper bound.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite and uses the balance convention \(Bx=b\).
Each transformed arc satisfies \(0\le x_a\le u_a<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The substitutions \(y_a=u_a-x_a\) for \(a\in S\) give a feasibility-preserving bijection, and objective values differ by the constant \(\sum_{a\in S}c_au_a\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer-Lattice Preservation Under Upper Complementation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality behavior of finite-upper-bound complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y_a=u_a-x_a\), if \(u_a\in\mathbb Z\), then \(x_a\in\mathbb Z\) if and only if \(y_a\in\mathbb Z\). If \(u_a\notin\mathbb Z\), integral \(x_a\) corresponds to \(y_a\in u_a-\mathbb Z\), so requiring ordinary integrality of \(y_a\) is not equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper complementation preserves the ordinary integer lattice for an integral upper bound; a fractional upper bound translates the lattice.
assumptions_latex: The complemented upper bound is finite.
Integer feasibility is imposed on the original arc flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u_a\in\mathbb Z\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(x_a\in\mathbb Z\iff u_a-x_a\in\mathbb Z\bigr).

notation.meaning: translated integer lattice of the complemented variable

children.title: Lower-Bound Extensions

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound elimination by shifting each bounded flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite minimum-cost flow problem \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\;\ell\le x\le u\},\] assume every lower bound \(\ell_a\) is finite and set \(y=x-\ell\). Then \[By=b-B\ell,\qquad 0\le y\le u-\ell,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x=c^{\mathsf T}\ell+c^{\mathsf T}y.\] Hence translation by \(\ell\) is a bijection between feasible flows of the original instance and feasible flows of the zero-lower-bound instance. It preserves objective comparisons because the objectives differ by the constant \(c^{\mathsf T}\ell\). An infinite upper bound remains infinite after the shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting each finite lower bound converts flows to nonnegative variables, shifts node supplies by the incidence of the lower-bound vector, and changes objective values only by a constant. Infinite upper bounds remain infinite.
assumptions_latex: The network has finitely many arcs.
Each \(\ell_a\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\ell_a\le u_a\le+\infty\) for every arc \(a\).
The balance equations use the incidence convention \(Bx=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(x\mapsto y=x-\ell\) bijectively preserves feasibility and optimal solutions after the balance shift.

notation.meaning: upper-bound vector, possibly with infinite components

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Bound Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and reduced-cost conditions for bounded network-simplex bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc, let \(\bar c_a=c_a+B_a^{\mathsf T}\pi\). A bounded network-simplex basis consists of a spanning tree \(T\), tree flows determined by \(Bx=b\), and each nonbasic arc fixed at either \(\ell_a\) or \(u_a\). It is primal feasible when \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every arc. It is optimal precisely when \[\bar c_a\ge0\ \text{for every nonbasic arc at }\ell_a,\qquad \bar c_a\le0\ \text{for every nonbasic arc at }u_a.\] A violated inequality identifies the bound-to-bound direction in which that arc may enter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonbasic arcs sit at one bound. Optimality requires nonnegative reduced cost at a lower bound and nonpositive reduced cost at an upper bound.
assumptions_latex: The objective is minimization of a linear arc cost.
Tree-arc reduced costs are zero under the chosen potentials.
The current bounded tree solution is primal feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed signed reduced-cost inequalities are necessary and sufficient for optimality.

The tests \(\bar c_a\ge0\) at a lower bound and \(\bar c_a\le0\) at an upper bound apply only to nonfixed arcs; a fixed arc is exempt rather than required to satisfy both inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed arc cannot move and therefore has no reduced-cost sign restriction.

Arc \(a\) satisfies \(\ell_a=u_a\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Doubly and circular doubly linked lists
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional linked-list representation and its update costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A doubly linked list stores in each cell a data field, a predecessor link \(\mathrm{llink}\), and a successor link \(\mathrm{rlink}\). It can be traversed in either direction, and insertion or deletion at a known position requires \(O(1)\) time. Connecting the last cell's successor to the first cell and the first cell's predecessor to the last produces a circular doubly linked list, permitting traversal of the entire list from an arbitrary element. Pairwise disjoint lists over \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) can be represented by arrays \(\mathrm{first}\), \(\mathrm{llink}\), and \(\mathrm{rlink}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A doubly linked list gives every cell links to both its predecessor and successor. This permits traversal in either direction and constant-time insertion or deletion when the affected position is known. Linking the two ends creates a circular doubly linked list that can be traversed from any element. Multiple disjoint lists over elements 1 through n can share first, left-link, and right-link arrays.
assumptions_latex: \(\text{Each cell stores data, a predecessor link, and a successor link}\)
\(\text{The position at which an insertion or deletion occurs is known}\)
\(\text{For the shared-array representation, the lists are pairwise disjoint subsets of }\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{known\text{-}position\ insertion}}=T_{\mathrm{known\text{-}position\ deletion}}=O(1),\quad\text{and traversal is possible in both directions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singly linked-list representation and operation costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Array-based singly linked lists, including the shared-array representation of pairwise disjoint lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A singly linked list consists of cells having data and successor-link fields, together with an index \(\mathrm{first}\). The value \(\mathrm{first}=0\) denotes an empty list, and a zero successor marks the end of a nonempty list. Traversal and unsorted membership testing take linear time in the list length. Insertion at the front or after a known predecessor takes \(O(1)\) time. Deletion of the first element, or deletion after a known predecessor, takes \(O(1)\) time; if the predecessor must first be located, deletion takes \(O(n)\) time in the worst case. Pairwise disjoint lists \(\mathrm{LIST}(1),\ldots,\mathrm{LIST}(n)\) whose elements belong to \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) can share arrays \(\mathrm{first}[1..n]\) and \(\mathrm{link}[1..n]\), with constant-time insertion and deletion at a list front.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singly linked list stores data and a successor link in each cell, uses first to identify the initial cell, and uses zero to mark an empty list or the end of traversal. Scanning and membership testing are linear in the list length. Front insertion, insertion after a known predecessor, and deletion when the required predecessor is known are constant-time operations; finding an unknown predecessor can require a linear scan. Pairwise disjoint lists over elements 1 through n can share first and link arrays and support constant-time front updates.
assumptions_latex: \(\text{Each cell has a data field and one successor-link field}\)
\(\mathrm{first}=0\text{ denotes an empty list, and a zero successor denotes the end}\)
\(\mathrm{LIST}(1),\ldots,\mathrm{LIST}(n)\text{ are pairwise disjoint and contain elements from }\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{scan}}=O(n),\quad T_{\mathrm{front\ insertion}}=O(1),\quad T_{\mathrm{deletion\mid known\ predecessor}}=O(1),\quad T_{\mathrm{deletion\mid predecessor\ search}}=O(n)\text{ in the worst case.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Preorder-Label Ancestry Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-time ancestry testing in a threaded tree augmented with stable current preorder-position labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{pre}(z)\) be the stored current position of vertex \(z\) in the depth-first thread order, and let \(q(v)\) be the last vertex of the subtree rooted at \(v\). For all vertices \(u,v\), \[u\in V(T_v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{pre}(v)\le \operatorname{pre}(u)\le \operatorname{pre}(q(v)).\] Consequently, while these position labels and last-descendant pointers are current, ancestry and subtree membership are tested in \(O(1)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With current preorder positions stored, a vertex belongs to a subtree exactly when its position lies between the subtree root and its last descendant.
assumptions_latex: The thread order is a depth-first preorder of a finite rooted tree.
Each vertex stores its current preorder position.
\(q(v)\) is the final preorder vertex in the subtree rooted at \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Subtree membership is equivalent to containment in the corresponding preorder-position interval.

notation.meaning: stored current preorder position of vertex v
last preorder vertex in the subtree rooted at v

knowledge_statements.title: Preorder-Label Ancestry Test
Threaded-Tree Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth-first threaded encoding of a rooted network-simplex basis tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Root the basis tree at \(r\). A threaded-tree representation stores, for each node \(v\), its depth \(d(v)\), a thread pointer \(t(v)\) to the next node in depth-first preorder, and a last-descendant pointer \(q(v)\). The nodes of the rooted subtree of \(v\) are exactly the contiguous thread segment beginning at \(v\) and ending at \(q(v)\). Therefore a subtree can be enumerated by repeatedly following \(t\), without testing ancestry, and a pivot may splice the affected segment after updating its depths and boundary pointers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threaded tree links nodes in depth-first order and marks each subtree's last node, making every rooted subtree a contiguous list segment.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree rooted at \(r\).
The thread order is a depth-first preorder of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(T_v)=\{v,t(v),\ldots,q(v)\}\) as a contiguous preorder segment for every node \(v\).

notation.meaning: last preorder node in v's subtree

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and preorder-contiguity property are mathematically coherent, but the network-simplex threaded-tree fields and pivot-splicing claim have no cited source.

children.title: Predecessor-Tree Structures

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental-Path Extraction from Predecessors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a basis-tree path and lowest common ancestor from parent and depth fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given vertices \(u,v\), repeatedly replace the deeper current vertex by its predecessor until the current depths agree, and then replace both current vertices by their predecessors until they coincide at \(w\). Then \(w=\operatorname{lca}(u,v)\), and the recorded predecessor chains from \(u\) and \(v\) to \(w\) form the unique \(u\)-\(v\) path. If the rooted tree has height \(h\), the procedure uses \(O(h)\) predecessor steps and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space apart from the reported path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Depth leveling followed by simultaneous parent ascents finds the lowest common ancestor and recovers the unique tree path in time proportional to tree height.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite rooted tree with valid predecessor and depth fields.
\(d(z)=d(p(z))+1\) for every nonroot vertex \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique path between any two vertices is recoverable in \(O(h)\) predecessor steps.
knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental-Path Extraction from Predecessors
Predecessor-Tree Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parent-pointer encoding of a rooted network-simplex basis tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Root the basis tree \(T\) at \(r\). For every nonroot node \(v\), store its predecessor \(p(v)\), the tree arc \(a(v)\) joining \(p(v)\) and \(v\), its depth \(d(v)=d(p(v))+1\), and the orientation of \(a(v)\) relative to the parent-child direction. The unique path from \(v\) to \(r\) is recovered by repeated application of \(p\). Given the tree-arc costs and incidence columns, node potentials satisfying \(\bar c_{a(v)}=c_{a(v)}+B_{a(v)}^{\mathsf T}\pi=0\) are recovered recursively after fixing one root potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A predecessor tree stores each node's parent, parent arc, depth, and orientation. Parent pointers recover root paths and, given the tree-arc data and one root normalization, recursively determine node potentials with zero tree reduced costs.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree rooted at \(r\).
Each nonroot node has exactly one parent arc.
The cost and incidence column of every tree arc are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated predecessor pointers recover every unique root path and, after one root normalization, determine all node potentials satisfying zero reduced cost on the tree arcs.

notation.meaning: tree arc joining v to its parent
incidence column of the parent arc of v

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A predecessor encoding stores a parent arc, depth, and associated labels for each vertex in \(O(n)\) space; a root path can then be scanned in \(O(h)\) time. A threaded depth-first encoding additionally stores successor information, permitting enumeration of a rooted subtree of \(k\) vertices in \(O(k)\) time and constant-time access to its traversal boundary. Maintaining threading can require changing traversal links after a subtree move, whereas predecessor data localize ancestry information but do not provide contiguous subtree traversal. Thus the encodings exchange simpler structural updates against faster subtree-oriented access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Predecessor trees favor simple ancestry maintenance; threaded trees favor contiguous subtree traversal. Both use linear space, and their relative cost depends on the pivot operations performed.

children.title: Dynamic-Tree Network Simplex

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Dynamic-Tree Pivot Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-step tree-maintenance cost excluding entering-arc pricing and total simplex pivot count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the chosen dynamic-forest implementation performs each required path exposure, path aggregate, lazy path update, cut, and link in amortized time \(D(n)\). After an entering arc is known, the tree-maintenance portion of one network-simplex step uses a constant number of these operations and therefore costs \(O(D(n))\) amortized. In particular, an augmented link-cut tree supporting these aggregates with \(D(n)=O(\log n)\) gives \(O(\log n)\) amortized tree maintenance per selected entering arc. This bound excludes pricing and does not bound the number of simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With suitable logarithmic-time link-cut operations, the tree part of a selected step is logarithmic amortized time; pricing and total pivot count remain outside the bound.
assumptions_latex: The dynamic forest supports the stated path aggregates and lazy updates with operation cost \(D(n)\).
An entering arc has already been selected.
Only dynamic-forest work is charged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The amortized tree-maintenance cost per selected entering arc is \(O(D(n))\), and is \(O(\log n)\) for the stated augmented link-cut-tree implementation.

notation.meaning: amortized cost of one supported dynamic-forest operation

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Dynamic-Tree Pivot Cost

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut-Link Boundary for Bound Flips
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary on when a bounded-variable pivot changes the represented dynamic forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta_T\) be the minimum residual slack among tree arcs on the fundamental cycle and let \(\theta_e\) be the entering arc's residual distance to its opposite bound. If \(\theta_T\le\theta_e\), a limiting tree arc may be selected and the forest update is \(T'=T-f+e\), requiring \(\operatorname{cut}(f)\) and \(\operatorname{link}(e)\). If \(\theta_e<\theta_T\), the step is a bound flip: \(T'=T\), and performing a cut or link would incorrectly change the basis tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut and link are used only when a tree arc limits the augmentation; a strict entering-arc limit is a bound flip and leaves the forest unchanged.
assumptions_latex: The step length is the minimum of all directed residual slacks on the fundamental cycle.
A deterministic rule resolves ties involving tree arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dynamic-tree step has a tree-exchange branch and a no-forest-update bound-flip branch.

notation.meaning: minimum limiting slack among tree arcs
entering arc's slack to its opposite bound

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Link Boundary for Bound Flips

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Dynamic-Forest Pivot Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract dynamic-forest operations sufficient for the tree portion of a bounded network-simplex pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dynamic forest is sufficient for tree-pivot maintenance if it supports \(\operatorname{link}\), \(\operatorname{cut}\), exposure of the unique path between two vertices, addition of a signed flow increment along an exposed path, and retrieval of the minimum residual slack together with a limiting edge. With directional residual slacks stored for each tree edge, these operations determine and apply the tree-path portion of a fundamental-cycle augmentation after an entering arc is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Link, cut, path exposure, signed path updates, and path-minimum-with-argmin operations form a sufficient interface for dynamic-tree network-simplex pivots.
assumptions_latex: The current basis arcs form a tree.
Each tree edge stores the residual slack relevant to each traversal direction.
An entering non-tree arc has already been selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limiting tree edge and tree-path flow update can be obtained through dynamic-forest operations.

The dynamic-forest structure supports path aggregation, path updates, cuts, and links.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the dynamic forest with the arcs of \(T\), storing residual capacities and any additive flow labels needed on tree paths. For an eligible entering arc \(e\), expose the unique tree path joining its endpoints, determine the minimum residual capacity \(\theta\) on the directed fundamental cycle \(C_T(e)\), and add \(\theta\) units along that cycle. Select a limiting tree arc \(f\), execute \(\operatorname{cut}(f)\), and execute \(\operatorname{link}(e)\). Stop when no eligible non-tree arc exists; output the maintained flow and basis tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic forest exposes the entering arc's fundamental path, finds the limiting residual capacity, updates path flows, and performs the leaving-arc cut and entering-arc link.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Flow Maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal flow update for one bounded min-cost-flow network-simplex step, including tree-exchange and entering-arc bound-flip cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be the current flow, let \(C\) be the oriented fundamental cycle created by the entering non-tree arc \(e\), and let \(d_a\in\{-1,0,1\}\) be the signed incidence of each arc \(a\) on \(C\). Compute \[\theta=\min\!\left(\min_{a:d_a=1}(u_a-x_a),\;\min_{a:d_a=-1}(x_a-\ell_a)\right),\] with the minimum of an empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). Set \(x'_a=x_a+\theta d_a\) for \(a\in C\) and \(x'_a=x_a\) otherwise. If a tree arc attains the limiting value, select a limiting tree arc \(f\) using the prescribed tie rule and replace \(f\) by \(e\). If no tree arc is limiting and \(e\) reaches its opposite bound, retain the tree and change the bound status of \(e\). Output the resulting feasible flow and basis state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augment maximally around the entering arc's fundamental cycle. Exchange a limiting tree arc when one is reached; if only the entering arc reaches its opposite bound, retain the tree and update that arc's nonbasic bound status.
assumptions_latex: The current flow \(x\) satisfies all node balances and bounds \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\).
The entering non-tree arc \(e\) creates a unique fundamental cycle \(C\) in the basis tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update preserves node balances and arc bounds; it yields either a feasible tree exchange or a feasible nonbasic bound flip, according to which arc first limits the augmentation.

notation.meaning: fundamental cycle with a chosen augmentation orientation
lower and upper bounds of arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite Fundamental-Cycle Step Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a finite network-simplex flow update when every directed residual slack on an improving fundamental cycle is infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the step calculation gives \(\theta=+\infty\), no arc on the oriented fundamental cycle has a finite limiting residual slack. A finite pivot update and leaving arc therefore do not exist. If the chosen direction has strictly negative objective change per unit, then \(x+\alpha d\) is feasible for every \(\alpha\ge0\) and the minimum-cost-flow objective is unbounded below along that cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite cycle step is not a pivot: when the cycle direction strictly improves cost, it certifies unboundedness rather than producing an updated basis.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible and \(d\) is the signed incidence vector of the oriented fundamental cycle.
Every arc in the augmentation direction has infinite residual slack.
\(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x+\alpha d\) is feasible for all \(\alpha\ge0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}(x+\alpha d)\to-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Fundamental-Cycle Step Boundary

One entering arc replaces one leaving tree arc, splitting the old tree into two components.
