knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Delete the leaving tree arc and let \(S\) be either resulting component. For the entering arc \(e=(p,q)\), choose \(S\) so exactly one endpoint lies in \(S\), and define \[\delta=-\frac{\bar c_{pq}}{\mathbf 1_S(p)-\mathbf 1_S(q)}.\] Set \(\pi'_v=\pi_v+\delta\) for \(v\in S\) and \(\pi'_v=\pi_v\) otherwise. Reduced costs of tree arcs internal to either component are unchanged, and \(\bar c'_{pq}=0\); hence all arcs of the updated basis tree have zero reduced cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a tree exchange, shift all potentials on one detached component by one constant chosen to make the entering arc's reduced cost zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential Invariance under a Bound Flip
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-state response when a network-simplex step changes only an entering arc's nonbasic bound status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the entering non-tree arc reaches its opposite bound before any tree arc limits the cycle augmentation, the basis tree remains \(T'=T\). Setting \(\pi'=\pi\) therefore preserves \(\bar c'_a=0\) for every tree arc \(a\in T'\). No component potential shift, cut, or link is required; only the entering arc's nonbasic bound status changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure bound flip leaves the tree and its potentials unchanged, so every tree reduced cost remains zero.
assumptions_latex: Every arc of the current basis tree \(T\) has zero reduced cost under \(\pi\).
The entering arc alone limits the augmentation and the basis tree is retained.
Arc costs do not change during the step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T'=T\text{ and }\pi'=\pi\text{ preserve }\bar c'_a=0\text{ for every }a\in T'.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential Invariance under a Bound Flip

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((T,x,\pi)\) and a pivot pair \((e,f)\), first augment \(x\) on the fundamental cycle of \(e\) by the maximal feasible amount, selecting \(f\) among its limiting tree arcs. Form \(T'=T-f+e\). Using the two components of \(T-f\), shift potentials uniformly on one component so that the reduced cost of \(e\) becomes zero. Commit \((T',x',\pi')\) only after verifying node balances, arc bounds, the spanning-tree property of \(T'\), and zero reduced cost on every arc of \(T'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivot updates flow, tree structure, and potentials as one transaction, then checks primal feasibility and the defining tree reduced-cost invariant before committing the new state.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coupled Bound-Flip Transaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic basis-state maintenance when the entering arc reaches its opposite bound without a tree exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the entering non-tree arc \(e\) reaches its opposite bound before any tree arc limits the fundamental-cycle augmentation, set \(T'=T\), retain \(\pi'=\pi\), commit the feasible cycle-updated flow \(x'\), and reverse the nonbasic lower- or upper-bound status of \(e\). Before committing, verify node balances and arc bounds for \(x'\), unchanged spanning-tree structure, and zero reduced cost on every arc of \(T'\). No leaving arc, component potential shift, cut, or link occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bound flip, the coupled transaction updates the flow and entering arc's nonbasic status while leaving the tree and potentials unchanged.
assumptions_latex: The current state \((T,x,\pi)\) is consistent.
The entering arc alone limits the feasible cycle augmentation.
Arc costs do not change during the step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bound-flip branch produces a consistent state \((T,x',\pi)\) with the entering arc at its opposite nonbasic bound.

notation.meaning: basis tree, flow, and node potentials
entering non-tree arc that undergoes a bound flip

assumptions_latex: The modified instance has the same vertex set and admits a spanning-tree basis.
A previous basis tree and its associated state are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The previous basis is a valid warm start precisely when it remains structurally admissible; its flow and potentials may then be reused, projected, or repaired before ordinary pivots resume.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be the previous basis tree for \(I\). It is structurally admissible for \(I'\) if every arc of \(T\) exists in \(I'\), the underlying undirected edges of \(T\) form a spanning tree on the vertices of \(I'\), and each non-tree arc can be assigned to an allowed bound status. A full-state warm start is immediately feasible only if the reused flow also satisfies the new balances and bounds. Otherwise \(T\) is merely a structural warm start and requires primal repair before optimization pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old tree can seed a modified problem if it is still a spanning tree of available arcs. Its old flow is reusable only when new balances and bounds remain satisfied.

children.title: Basis Repair
children.top_down_role: Restoration of feasibility or valid basis structure after model changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Phase-I Feasibility Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary exact feasibility phase when no assignment on the repaired tree satisfies the modified balances and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the modified bounded-flow instance \(Mx=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), solve the auxiliary problem \[\min\ \mathbf 1^\top(s^++s^-)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Mx+s^+-s^-=b,\ \ell\le x\le u,\ s^+,s^-\ge0.\] The auxiliary problem is feasible whenever the arc-bound box is nonempty. Its optimum is zero if and only if the modified instance has a feasible flow. A zero-optimum basic solution may initialize subsequent basis construction; a positive certified optimum reports primal infeasibility rather than structural tree failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase I minimizes artificial node imbalance. Zero optimum is equivalent to feasibility of the modified bounded-flow instance; a positive optimum distinguishes primal infeasibility from failure merely to restore a tree.
assumptions_latex: The balance vector satisfies \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
Every arc has a nonempty bound interval \(\ell_a\le u_a\).
The auxiliary problem is solved exactly to certified optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{opt}_{\mathrm{I}}=0\iff\exists x:\ Mx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u.
knowledge_statements.title: Phase-I Feasibility Repair

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Retained-Forest Restoration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural repair of a previous tree after some of its arcs become unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Delete unavailable arcs from the old tree, obtaining a forest \(F\). Scan available arcs and add an arc whenever its endpoints lie in different components of the current forest. The procedure returns a spanning tree exactly when the underlying undirected graph of available arcs is connected; otherwise the remaining components certify structural repair failure. With a disjoint-set structure, the scan uses \(O(|E|\alpha(|V|))\) time in addition to output storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete invalid old-tree arcs and use available cross-component arcs to extend the retained forest. This succeeds exactly when the available graph is connected.
assumptions_latex: The retained valid arcs form a forest F on V.
Tree membership is interpreted in the underlying undirected network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns a spanning tree iff the available underlying graph is connected.}

notation.meaning: forest retained from the previous basis tree

knowledge_statements.title: Retained-Forest Restoration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tree-Flow Reconstruction Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-feasibility test after selecting a candidate tree and non-tree bound statuses during basis repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected directed network, let \(T\subseteq E\) be a spanning tree, and fix every \(a\in E\setminus T\) at an allowed bound value. If \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), the balance equations \(Mx=b\) uniquely determine \(x_T\). The candidate state is primal feasible if and only if \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a spanning tree and all non-tree bound values are fixed, balance uniquely determines the tree flows; their bound test is necessary and sufficient for primal feasibility of the candidate basis.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E) is connected and T is a spanning tree.
Every non-tree arc is fixed at an allowed lower- or upper-bound value.
The balance vector satisfies \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_T\text{ is unique, and the candidate basis is primal feasible exactly when }\ell_T\le x_T\le u_T.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Flow Reconstruction Test

assumptions_latex: The modified instance is feasible and its available arcs contain a spanning tree.
The reused state may violate tree structure, flow feasibility, or basis-state invariants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repair either returns an admissible feasible basis state for the modified instance or reports that the selected repair phase could not construct one.

notation.meaning: candidate tree and flow inherited from the previous instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic repair interface preceding network-simplex reoptimization; the Phase-I implementation is intentionally unspecified.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \((T_0,x_0)\), delete unavailable tree arcs and add available arcs joining distinct components until a spanning tree \(T\) is obtained; fail if this is impossible. Clamp non-tree flows to allowed bounds and solve the tree balance equations for the remaining basic flows. If some tree flow violates its bounds, invoke a finite Phase-I min-cost-flow procedure whose zero optimum is equivalent to primal feasibility. On success, compute tree potentials \(\pi\) from zero reduced costs on \(T\), assign non-tree bound states, and output \((T,x,\pi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair replaces invalid tree arcs, reconstructs flows from balance equations, uses a Phase-I procedure when bounds fail, and recomputes potentials before reoptimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Repair

children.title: Warm-Start Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Perturbation regimes determining whether a prior basis remains directly reusable.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural, primal, and optimality boundaries for carrying a bounded network-simplex state to a modified instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The old tree \(T\) is structurally reusable exactly when all its arcs remain available and its underlying undirected edges form a spanning tree on the updated vertex set. The old flow \(x\) is primally reusable exactly when it satisfies every updated node-balance equation and every updated bound \(\ell'_a\le x_a\le u'_a\). Define updated reduced costs by \(\bar c'_a=c'_a+\pi'_{i(a)}-\pi'_{j(a)}\), where potentials \(\pi'\) make every updated tree reduced cost zero. The feasible basis state remains optimal exactly when, for every non-tree arc with \(\ell'_a<u'_a\), an arc at its lower bound satisfies \(\bar c'_a\ge0\) and an arc at its upper bound satisfies \(\bar c'_a\le0\); a fixed non-tree arc with \(\ell'_a=u'_a\) imposes no reduced-cost sign condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree reuse fails when its arcs or spanning-tree structure are lost; flow reuse fails when an updated balance or bound is violated; optimality reuse fails when a nonfixed non-tree arc violates the reduced-cost sign required at its current bound. Fixed arcs impose no sign test.
assumptions_latex: The old state consists of a basis tree \(T\), a flow \(x\), node potentials, and non-tree bound statuses.
The modified bounded min-cost-flow instance specifies updated available arcs, costs \(c'_a\), bounds \(\ell'_a\le u'_a\), and node balances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of the structural, primal, or reduced-cost predicate identifies the corresponding boundary beyond which that portion of the old basis state cannot be reused without repair or reoptimization.

notation.meaning: updated reduced cost of arc a
updated lower and upper bounds of arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonbasic-Status Compatibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional validity condition for retaining the same bounded-variable tree basis after bounds change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the old tree basis and its nonbasic statuses to remain a valid basis state, every non-tree arc \(a\) must satisfy \(x_a=\ell'_a\) or \(x_a=u'_a\), and its retained lower- or upper-bound status must agree with that equality. If \(\ell'_a<x_a<u'_a\), the flow may remain feasible, but it is not represented by the same bounded-variable tree basis. A fixed arc with \(\ell'_a=u'_a=x_a\) may use either coincident-bound status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible old flow is not necessarily a reusable basis state: every non-tree arc must still lie at an updated bound with a compatible status. An interior non-tree flow invalidates direct basis reuse.
assumptions_latex: The old state uses a spanning-tree basis with every non-tree arc assigned a bound status.
The modified instance has bounds \(\ell'_a\le u'_a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) and the retained nonbasic statuses define a valid updated bounded-variable basis only if \(x_a\in\{\ell'_a,u'_a\}\) for every \(a\notin T\), with compatible statuses.

children.title: Pivot Cycling
children.top_down_role: Repeated basis-state behavior under network-simplex pivot selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Pivot Cycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-recurrence characterization of cycling in a deterministic network-simplex execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network-simplex execution cycles if there exist indices \(r<s\) such that \(B_r=B_s\), where equality includes the spanning-tree basis and every non-tree arc's lower-bound or upper-bound status. If entering and leaving choices are deterministic functions of this complete state, equality implies that the subsequent pivot sequence repeats. Cycling therefore yields an infinite execution without reaching a terminal reduced-cost condition, even though each repeated degenerate pivot may be locally admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cycling is recurrence of the complete basis state. Under deterministic state-based pivot choices, the same degenerate pivot sequence then repeats indefinitely without reaching termination.
assumptions_latex: The pivot rule permits degenerate pivots.
The complete algorithmic state \(B_k\) consists of the basis tree and every non-tree bound status, and pivot choices are deterministic functions of that state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cycling occurs when a positive-length pivot sequence returns to an identical complete basis state, causing deterministic state-based choices to repeat indefinitely.

notation.meaning: complete basis state after pivot k

children.title: Pivot Stalling
children.top_down_role: Extended sequences with negligible or absent progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Pivot Stalling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite or persistent zero-progress behavior, distinguished from exact recurrence of the basis state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For indices \(r\le s\), a network-simplex execution stalls on pivots \(r,\ldots,s\) if \(\theta_k=0\) for every \(k\) in that interval while the basis is not yet certified optimal. Consequently, \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) and \(z_{k+1}=z_k\) throughout the interval, although the basis trees may change. Persistent stalling means that such zero-progress intervals have unbounded length; unlike cycling, stalling does not require any complete basis state to recur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stalling is a run of zero-augmentation pivots before optimality. Flow and objective remain fixed while bases may change, so stalling need not be cycling.
assumptions_latex: The current basis is not certified optimal.
A sequence of admissible network-simplex pivots is performed, with augmentation \(\theta_k\), flow \(x_k\), and objective value \(z_k\) at iteration \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The execution stalls on an interval exactly when every pivot in that interval has zero augmentation; throughout that interval neither the primal flow nor its objective value changes.

notation.meaning: augmentation, primal flow, and objective value at iteration k

children.title: Degeneracy-Induced Failure Chain
children.top_down_role: Structural links through which degenerate bases can produce stalling or cycling.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Failure Chain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical failure chain linking degeneracy, zero progress, and recurrence in network-simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a degenerate basis, an eligible entering arc can have \(\theta_k=0\), so its pivot changes the basis but not the flow or objective; consecutive zero-augmentation pivots produce stalling. If during this zero-progress sequence there exist \(r<s\) with \(B_r=B_s\), deterministic state-based choices reproduce the intervening pivots and cause cycling. Degeneracy alone implies neither recurrence nor nontermination: a pivot rule with a strict anti-cycling ordering may permit zero-augmentation pivots while ensuring that no complete basis state is revisited.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy can cause zero-progress pivots and stalling. If a complete basis repeats under deterministic choices, stalling becomes cycling; a strict anti-cycling ordering can prevent recurrence.
assumptions_latex: Degenerate bases and zero-augmentation pivots are reachable.
Pivot choices are deterministic functions of the complete basis state unless a stated anti-cycling ordering is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy permits stalling, and recurrence of a complete basis state under deterministic state-based choices causes cycling; a strict anti-cycling ordering prevents the recurrence implication.

notation.meaning: complete basis state at iteration k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network-Simplex Degeneracy, Cycling, and the Finiteness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate iterations and the cycling obstruction to finite termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flow \(x\) determined by a tree \(T\) is degenerate if at least one arc of \(T\) carries zero flow. An iteration that changes the tree but not the flow is degenerate and can occur only when \(x\) is degenerate. Cycling is a return to the same tree after a sequence of degenerate iterations and can cause failure to terminate. If cycling does not occur, the method terminates because the number of different trees is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree flow is degenerate when some tree arc has zero flow. A tree-changing iteration that leaves the flow unchanged can occur only under degeneracy. Repeated degenerate iterations may cycle back to a prior tree and prevent termination; without cycling, the finite number of trees guarantees termination.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ determines a flow }x
\text{The number of different trees is finite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No cycling}\Longrightarrow\text{finite termination},\qquad \text{cycling can cause nontermination.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bland Least-Index Network-Simplex Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-LP specialization of Bland's finite anti-cycling rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Express the bounded network problem in a simplex form with a fixed total order on its variables, using complemented variables for upper-bound statuses when needed. At each iteration choose the least-index eligible entering variable and, among the minimum-ratio ties, the least-index eligible leaving variable. In exact arithmetic Bland's rule prevents basis recurrence; consequently a primal-feasible finite network LP whose optimum is attained reaches an optimal basis after finitely many pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bland's least-index entering and leaving choices prevent repeated network-LP bases and ensure finite termination from a primal-feasible start.
assumptions_latex: The network problem has a finite-dimensional linear-programming representation.
The initial basis is primal feasible and an optimum is attained.
A fixed variable order is used consistently.
Pivot tests use exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No basis recurs, and an optimal basis is reached after finitely many pivots.}
knowledge_statements.title: Bland Least-Index Network-Simplex Rule

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Feasible Rooted Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-specific feasibility invariant used by strongly feasible anti-cycling rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,x)\) be a feasible bounded-flow tree solution with root \(r\). It is strongly feasible if, for every \(v\ne r\), some \(\varepsilon_v>0\) can be sent from \(v\) to \(r\) along the unique signed tree path without violating any arc bound; equivalently, every path arc has positive residual capacity in the required traversal direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rooted tree solution is strongly feasible when every node can send a positive amount to the root along its tree path.
assumptions_latex: \((T,x)\) is a feasible bounded-flow tree solution.
A root \(r\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall v\ne r\ \exists\varepsilon_v>0:\ x+\varepsilon_v\chi_T^{v\to r}\in[\ell,u].

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate each admissible pivot with a lexicographic key formed from the entering-arc priority, the leaving-arc priority, and an infinitesimal perturbation \(\eta\) of the relevant bounds or supplies. Require the selected pivot to produce a strict lexicographic improvement of the perturbed primal or dual objective, including when the unperturbed step length is zero. Because a finite network has only finitely many spanning-tree bases and the lexicographic key strictly improves at every pivot, no basis can recur and cycling is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent ordering or lexicographic perturbation makes every pivot strictly improve an auxiliary order, preventing repeated bases and hence cycling.

children.title: Worst-Case Pivot Sequences
children.top_down_role: Adverse trajectories under network-simplex pivot strategies.

assumptions_latex: The pivot rule is a fixed deterministic network-simplex pricing and leaving-arc rule.
Arithmetic is exact, so the adverse behavior is combinatorial rather than numerical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule has no polynomial pivot bound on this family; its pivot count can grow exponentially with the instance size.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adverse exact-arithmetic trajectories for particular deterministic network-simplex pivot rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A worst-case pivot sequence for a specified network-simplex rule is a family of feasible minimum-cost flow instances \(\{I_n\}\) and initial tree bases \(\{T_n\}\) for which that rule uniquely determines a sequence of adjacent tree bases of length \(P(n)\). The adverse family is exponential when there exist constants \(a>1\) and \(n_0\) such that \(P(n)\ge a^n\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). Such a construction separates finite termination from polynomial pivot complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivot rule may terminate on every instance yet follow exponentially long, uniquely determined basis sequences on an adverse network family.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an exact nonbasic residual arc have \(\bar c_{ij}=-\delta<0\), where \(0<\delta\le\tau\). An admissible computed error of \(+\delta\) reports reduced cost zero and can suppress a valid entering arc. Likewise, if \(0<r_{ij}\le\tau\), an error of magnitude \(r_{ij}\) can report a saturated arc, while a flow error of the opposite sign can report a bound violation. Thus reliable basis feasibility and pricing require separation margins larger than the accumulated error or an exact corrective check.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced costs or residual slacks smaller than accumulated numerical error can have their signs reversed or erased, invalidating pricing and basis-feasibility decisions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacity-scaling maximum-flow algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical maximum-flow capacity scaling using successively halved residual-capacity thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $x:=0$ and $\Delta:=2^{\lfloor\log_2 U\rfloor}$. While $\Delta\geq1$, repeatedly choose an $s$-$t$ path $P$ in $G(x,\Delta)$, set $\delta:=\min\{r_{ij}:(i,j)\in P\}$, and augment $\delta$ units along $P$ until no such path remains; then replace $\Delta$ by $\Delta/2$. Return the final flow $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with zero flow and the largest power of two not exceeding the capacity bound U. At each scale, repeatedly augment by the bottleneck residual capacity of any source-to-sink path whose arcs all have residual capacity at least the current scale. When no such path remains, halve the scale, and return the flow after the final scale.

\text{arc capacities are nonnegative integers}
U\geq1\text{ bounds the arc capacities}
G(x,\Delta)\text{ contains residual arcs with }r_{ij}\geq\Delta
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is obtained by exhausting all }s\text{-}t\text{ augmenting paths at each scale }\Delta=2^{\lfloor\log_2U\rfloor},\ldots,1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic capacity-scaling algorithm for minimum-cost flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-capacity scaling procedure with reduced-cost shortest-path augmentations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x:=0\), \(\pi:=0\), and \(\Delta:=2^{\lfloor\log U\rfloor}\). While \(\Delta\geq1\), saturate each residual arc \((i,j)\) satisfying \(r_{ij}\geq\Delta\) and \(c_{ij}^{\pi}<0\), updating the flow and node imbalances. Set \(S(\Delta)=\{i\in N:e(i)\geq\Delta\}\) and \(T(\Delta)=\{i\in N:e(i)\leq-\Delta\}\). While both sets are nonempty, choose \(k\in S(\Delta)\) and \(\ell\in T(\Delta)\), compute reduced-cost shortest-path distances \(d\) from \(k\) in \(G(x,\Delta)\), take a shortest \(k\)-to-\(\ell\) path \(P\), update \(\pi:=\pi-d\), augment \(\Delta\) units along \(P\), and update \(x\), the two sets, and the thresholded residual network. After the phase, set \(\Delta:=\Delta/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with zero flow and potentials and the largest power-of-two scale not exceeding U. At each scale, saturate eligible negative-reduced-cost residual arcs. Then repeatedly send Δ units from a node with excess at least Δ to a node with deficit at least Δ along a reduced-cost shortest path in the Δ-residual network, updating the potentials and state. Halve Δ after each phase.
assumptions_latex: G(x,\Delta)=\{(i,j)\in G(x):r_{ij}\geq\Delta\}
S(\Delta)=\{i\in N:e(i)\geq\Delta\},\quad T(\Delta)=\{i\in N:e(i)\leq-\Delta\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure executes the scaling phases }\Delta=2^{\lfloor\log U\rfloor},2^{\lfloor\log U\rfloor-1},\ldots,1\text{ using thresholded shortest-path augmentations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scale-dependent imbalance sets and residual network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and phase properties used by the basic capacity-scaling algorithm for minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scale \(\Delta>0\), define \(S(\Delta)=\{i:e(i)\geq\Delta\}\), \(T(\Delta)=\{i:e(i)\leq-\Delta\}\), and let \(G(x,\Delta)\) be the subgraph of the residual network \(G(x)\) containing exactly the arcs with residual capacity at least \(\Delta\). In a \(\Delta\)-scaling phase, each augmentation starts in \(S(\Delta)\), ends in \(T(\Delta)\), and follows a shortest path in \(G(x,\Delta)\). Every arc in \(G(x,\Delta)\) satisfies the reduced-cost optimality condition, whereas arcs in \(G(x)\setminus G(x,\Delta)\) may violate it.

Augmentations run from S(Δ) to T(Δ) along shortest paths in that network. Reduced-cost optimality holds on retained arcs but may fail on excluded residual arcs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: ε-scaling ε-relaxation scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling implementation for integer arc costs with a terminal tolerance of $1/(N+1)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer $\theta>1$ and set $\epsilon^{k+1}=\max\{\epsilon^k/\theta,1/(N+1)\}$, starting with $p^0=0$ and $\epsilon^0$ equal to a fixed fraction of the arc-cost range $C=\max_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}a_{ij}$. In phase $k+1$, perturb each arc cost to a multiple $a_{ij}^k$ of $\epsilon^k$ satisfying $|a_{ij}^k-a_{ij}|\le\epsilon^k$, except that no correction is made in the final phase. Initialize $x_{ij}=b_{ij}$ if $p_i^k-p_j^k\le a_{ij}^k$ and $x_{ij}=c_{ij}$ otherwise, and run sweep $\epsilon^k$-relaxation, carrying its terminal prices and flow to the next phase. This initialization makes the admissible graph empty. There are $O(\log(NC))$ phases, and if the inherited prices satisfy $r\epsilon^k$-CS for a constant $r$ depending only on $\theta$, each phase takes $O(N^3)$ time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an integer scaling factor greater than one and repeatedly divide epsilon by it, stopping at 1/(N+1). Warm-start each phase with the preceding prices and flow, round arc costs to multiples of the current epsilon within an epsilon error, and initialize each arc at its lower or upper bound according to the current reduced-cost comparison. The resulting admissible graph is empty. The scheme uses O(log(NC)) phases, and each phase takes O(N cubed) time when the inherited prices have the stated constant-factor complementary-slackness guarantee.

a_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\text{ in the final phase}
\epsilon^{k+1}=\max\{\epsilon^k/\theta,1/(N+1)\}
|a_{ij}^k-a_{ij}|\le\epsilon^k
p^k\text{ satisfies }r\epsilon^k\text{-CS with a feasible flow, where }r=O_{\theta}(1)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Enhanced Capacity-Scaling Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost-flow procedure using abundant arcs, imbalance thresholds, reduced-cost shortest paths, potential updates, and scaling phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x:=0\), \(\pi:=0\), \(e:=b\), and \(\Delta:=\max_{i\in N}|e(i)|\). While some node has positive imbalance, set \(\Delta:=\max_i e(i)\) if \(\max_i e(i)\leq\Delta/(8n)\). At the start of the scaling phase, designate each nonabundant arc with \(x_{ij}\geq8n\Delta\) as abundant, update the abundant components, and reinstate the imbalance property. While some node \(k\) satisfies \(|e(k)|\geq(n-1)\Delta/n\), choose \(k,l\) satisfying either \(e(k)>(n-1)\Delta/n\) and \(e(l)<-\Delta/n\), or \(e(k)>\Delta/n\) and \(e(l)<-(n-1)\Delta/n\). Compute reduced-cost shortest-path distances \(d\) from \(k\), update \(\pi(i):=\pi(i)-d(i)\) for every \(i\), and augment \(\Delta\) units along a shortest residual path from \(k\) to \(l\). After the phase, set \(\Delta:=\Delta/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize zero flow and potentials, with imbalances equal to supplies and delta equal to the largest absolute imbalance. Each phase identifies abundant arcs and restores the imbalance property, then repeatedly sends delta units along reduced-cost shortest paths between qualifying excess and deficit nodes while updating potentials. Delta is halved after the phase.
assumptions_latex: G(x)\text{ is the current residual network on }n\text{ nodes}
e(i)\text{ denotes node imbalance and }\pi(i)\text{ denotes node potential}
\text{Reduced costs are used as residual-arc lengths}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{If the outer loop exits, then no }i\in N\text{ satisfies }e(i)>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Call \((f,p)\) \(\epsilon\)-optimal when every residual arc \((i,j)\) satisfies \(c^p_{ij}\ge-\epsilon\). Initialize prices and a tolerance \(\epsilon_0\) large enough for this condition. For a fixed constant \(\alpha>1\), set \(\epsilon_{k+1}=\epsilon_k/\alpha\), then apply a refinement routine that restores feasibility or controlled imbalance while producing an \(\epsilon_{k+1}\)-optimal pair. Repeat until the exact-optimality threshold is reached; for integral costs, a feasible pair with sufficiently small \(\epsilon\) can be converted to one with nonnegative residual reduced costs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fixed \(\epsilon\), select an active node \(v\) with \(e_f(v)>0\). If a residual arc \((v,w)\) is admissible, meaning \(c^p_{vw}<0\), push \(\delta=\min\{e_f(v),r_{vw}\}\) units along it. If no admissible outgoing residual arc exists, change \(p_v\) by the smallest permitted relabel amount that creates one while retaining \(c^p_{ij}\ge-\epsilon\) on every residual arc. Continue until no active node remains, then reduce \(\epsilon\) and begin the next refinement phase.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-cost translation and circuit balance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reduced costs, balanced circuits, and neutral costs and records their basic potential invariances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph cost function \(c\) and potential \(\pi:V\to\mathbb R\), define \(c_\pi(uv)=c(uv)-\pi(v)+\pi(u)\). Then \(c_\pi\) is conservative if and only if \(c\) is conservative, and an \(st\)-path minimizes \(c\)-cost if and only if it minimizes \(c_\pi\)-cost. Moreover, \(\pi\) is \(c\)-feasible if and only if \(c_\pi\ge 0\) on every arc. An undirected circuit is \(c\)-balanced when the costs of its edges in the two traversal directions are equal; in particular, a directed circuit is balanced exactly when its cost is zero. The function \(c\) is neutral when every circuit is balanced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating arc costs by potential differences preserves conservativity and the set of minimum-cost s–t paths. A potential is feasible exactly when every reduced cost is nonnegative. A circuit is balanced when its two directional cost totals agree, and a cost function is neutral when all circuits are balanced.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph}
c:A\to\mathbb R
\pi:V\to\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_\pi\text{ is conservative}\iff c\text{ is conservative};\quad P\text{ is }c\text{-minimum}\iff P\text{ is }c_\pi\text{-minimum};\quad \pi\text{ is }c\text{-feasible}\iff c_\pi\ge0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-cost flow relaxation algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Main control procedure using potential and flow adjustments to eliminate positive node excess.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x:=0\) and \(\pi:=0\). While some node \(s\) has \(e(s)>0\), set \(S:=\{s\}\). If \(e(S)>r(\pi,S)\), call \(\operatorname{adjust\text{-}potential}\). Repeatedly select a residual arc \((i,j)\in(S,\bar S)\) with \(c_{ij}^{\pi}=0\); if \(e(j)\ge0\), set \(\operatorname{pred}(j):=i\) and add \(j\) to \(S\). Stop this search when \(e(j)<0\) or \(e(S)>r(\pi,S)\). In the latter case call \(\operatorname{adjust\text{-}potential}\); otherwise call \(\operatorname{adjust\text{-}flow}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from zero flow and potentials, repeatedly grow a set from a positive-excess node along zero-reduced-cost residual arcs. Adjust potentials when the set excess exceeds its residual threshold; otherwise augment flow when a negative-excess node is reached. Continue until no node has positive excess.
assumptions_latex: e(v)\text{ denotes node imbalance under the current pseudoflow}
r(\pi,S)\text{ is the residual threshold used by the relaxation method}
c_{ij}^{\pi}\text{ is the reduced cost of residual arc }(i,j)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure terminates its outer loop only when }\nexists s\text{ with }e(s)>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential-adjustment and flow-adjustment procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two update procedures used by the minimum-cost flow relaxation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\operatorname{adjust\text{-}potential}\), send \(r_{ij}\) units on every arc \((i,j)\in(S,\bar S)\) with \(c_{ij}=0\), set \(\alpha:=\min\{c_{ij}^{\pi}:(i,j)\in(S,\bar S),\ r_{ij}>0\}\), and update \(\pi(i):=\pi(i)+\alpha\) for every \(i\in S\). For \(\operatorname{adjust\text{-}flow}\), trace predecessor indices to obtain the directed path \(P\) from \(s\) to \(j\), set \(\delta:=\min\{e(s),-e(j),\min_{(i,j)\in P}r_{ij}\}\), augment \(\delta\) units along \(P\), and update imbalances and residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The potential update saturates specified zero-cost arcs leaving the current set and raises all potentials in the set by the smallest positive-residual outgoing reduced cost. The flow update augments along the predecessor path by the minimum of the source excess, destination deficit, and path residual capacity.
assumptions_latex: S\subseteq V\text{ is the current searched node set}
r_{ij}\text{ is the current residual capacity}
c_{ij}^{\pi}\text{ is the current reduced cost}
P\text{ is the predecessor path from a node }s\text{ with }e(s)>0\text{ to a node }j\text{ with }e(j)<0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi(i)\leftarrow\pi(i)+\alpha\ (i\in S)\quad\text{or}\quad x\leftarrow x+\delta\chi_P,\ \delta=\min\{e(s),-e(j),\min_{a\in P}r_a\}.

children.title: Augment-Relabel Variants
children.top_down_role: Cost-scaling variants organized around complete admissible residual paths.

assumptions_latex: The pseudoflow is \(\epsilon\)-optimal and has at least one node with positive excess.
Every augmentation uses a residual path whose internal arcs satisfy the phase's admissibility rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each operation either decreases source excess by a positive amount or changes a price according to the relabel rule while preserving the phase invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic augment-or-relabel schema within an epsilon-optimal cost-scaling phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an active node \(s\). Search the admissible residual subgraph for a directed path \(P\) from \(s\) to a node \(t\) with negative imbalance. If such a path exists, augment \(\delta=\min\{e_f(s),-e_f(t),r_f(P)\}\) along every arc of \(P\). Otherwise relabel a reached node or reached set by the smallest price change permitted by the \(\epsilon\)-optimality invariant, rebuild the admissible subgraph, and continue. Stop the phase when every node has zero imbalance, and output the resulting \(\epsilon\)-optimal flow-price pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Send excess along an admissible residual path to a deficit; if no such path exists, relabel reached nodes and resume the search.
knowledge_statements.title: Augment-Relabel Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic path augmentation is plausible, but admissibility, relabel scope, progress, and termination vary among augment-relabel algorithms and require an exact variant and authoritative source.

children.title: Partial Augment-Relabel Variants
children.top_down_role: Cost-scaling variants using incomplete admissible residual paths.

assumptions_latex: The current pseudoflow and prices satisfy the phase's \(\epsilon\)-optimality invariant.
A partial search begins at an active node and explores only admissible residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every partial operation preserves the phase invariant and either performs a positive augmentation or exposes a boundary on which a valid relabel can act.

notation.meaning: set reached by the partial admissible search

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract partial-search variant; its intended stopping and relabel conventions require identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start an admissible residual search from an active node, maintaining a reached set \(S\) and a partial path \(P\). Stop the search before full path completion when the prescribed event occurs, such as reaching a deficit, saturating the current bottleneck, or exhausting admissible arcs leaving \(S\). In the first two cases augment \(\delta>0\) along the available portion of \(P\); in the last case relabel an eligible node or the set \(S\). Retain valid search information, discard invalidated arcs, and repeat until the phase has no active node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial augment-relabel method interrupts path search at a defined event, then augments the available segment or relabels the blocked search region.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Augment-Relabel Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The listed stopping events do not define a single partial augment-relabel algorithm, and augmenting an incomplete path segment is not justified without a specified imbalance invariant.

children.title: Path-Completion Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions distinguishing complete augmentation from partial-path processing.

assumptions_latex: An admissible residual search starts at a node with positive excess.
The phase invariant specifies which residual arcs are admissible and which price changes are valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A completion regime is valid only if every incomplete search ends in augmentation, a valid relabel, or a certificate that no phase-active source remains.

notation.meaning: residual capacity of the path prefix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for completing or terminating paths in augment-relabel cost scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A path-completion regime must prescribe one of three outcomes after each admissible search: extend \(P\) until it reaches a deficit node; augment when a bottleneck of residual capacity \(r_f(P)>0\) is fixed; or stop with a reached set \(S\) having no admissible outgoing residual arc and apply a valid relabel to \(S\). It must forbid an unchanged restart from the same state. Consequently, each completion attempt must strictly reduce an imbalance, saturate a residual arc, enlarge the reached set, or change a price by a positive amount.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path regime must end each search by augmenting, enlarging the search, or making a valid positive relabel; unchanged restarts provide no progress guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Path-Completion Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed alternatives are an abstract progress template rather than a sourced path-completion regime. Validity and finite progress depend on precise admissibility, relabel, and state-retention rules.

knowledge_statements.title: Double Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity and reduced-cost scales are decreased jointly for integral minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have integral capacities and costs. Initialize a feasible circulation \(x\), potential \(p\), capacity scale \(\Delta\), and cost tolerance \(\varepsilon\). At each phase, use residual augmentations and price updates on arcs with residual capacity at least \(\Delta\), maintaining \(c_p(a)=c(a)+p(u)-p(v)\ge-\varepsilon\). After restoring this invariant, reduce one or both scales geometrically. Stop when \(\Delta<1\) and \(\varepsilon<1/|V|\); output \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double scaling restores flow and reduced-cost invariants while geometrically decreasing capacity and cost scales; sufficiently small terminal scales yield an optimal circulation.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and admits a feasible circulation.
Capacities and costs are integral.
Each phase restores feasibility and \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(x\) is a minimum-cost circulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Improve-Approximation Procedure for Double Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow-augmentation subprocedure within the double-scaling minimum-cost-flow algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \operatorname{improve\text{-}approximation}(\epsilon,x,\pi):\quad x\mathrel{:=}0;\ \text{compute node imbalances};\ \pi(j)\mathrel{:=}\pi(j)+\epsilon\ \forall j\in N_2;\ \Delta\mathrel{:=}2^{\lfloor\log U\rfloor}.\ \text{While an active node exists, set }S(\Delta)=\{i\in N_1\cup N_2:e(i)\geq\Delta\}.\ \text{While }S(\Delta)\neq\varnothing,\ \text{choose }k\in S(\Delta),\ \text{find an admissible path }P\text{ from }k\text{ to some }l\text{ with }e(l)<0,\ \text{augment }\Delta\text{ units on }P,\ \text{and update }x\text{ and }S(\Delta).\ \text{Then set }\Delta\mathrel{:=}\Delta/2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set the flow to zero and compute node imbalances, increase each potential on N2 by epsilon, and initialize Delta to the largest indicated power of two based on U. While an active node exists, repeatedly augment Delta units along an admissible path from a node with imbalance at least Delta to a node with negative imbalance. Update the flow and eligible-node set, and halve Delta after each scaling phase.
assumptions_latex: (\epsilon,x,\pi)\text{ is an input accepted by the procedure}
U\text{ is such that }2^{\lfloor\log U\rfloor}\text{ is defined}
N_1,N_2,e(\cdot),\text{ active nodes, and admissible paths are defined by the surrounding double-scaling framework}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure applies successive }\Delta\text{-scaled admissible-path augmentations according to the stated loop until no active node remains.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible circulation \(x\), its finite residual graph \(G_x\), and a target \(\varepsilon'\ge 0\), compute a potential \(p':V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(c(a)+p'(u)-p'(v)\ge-\varepsilon'\) for every residual arc \(a=(u,v)\). Such a potential exists if and only if every directed residual cycle \(C\) satisfies \(c(C)/|C|\ge-\varepsilon'\). It may be computed by solving the difference constraints \(p'(v)-p'(u)\le c(u,v)+\varepsilon'\); infeasibility is certified by a residual cycle of mean cost below \(-\varepsilon'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Price refinement tightens reduced-cost inequalities without changing the flow. It succeeds exactly when no residual directed cycle violates the target mean-cost tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible circulation.
\(G_x\) is finite.
\(\varepsilon'\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A refining potential exists if and only if every directed residual cycle \(C\) satisfies \(c(C)/|C|\ge-\varepsilon'\).

children.title: Global Price Updates

knowledge_statements.title: Global Price Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path labels shift prices at many vertices simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\ell(u,v)=c_p(u,v)+\varepsilon\ge0\) on every residual arc, and choose a nonempty target set \(T\). Let \(d(v)\) be the shortest \(\ell\)-length of a residual path from \(v\) to \(T\). For every finitely labeled vertex set \(p'(v)=p(v)+d(v)\). Then each residual arc \((u,v)\) with finite endpoint labels satisfies \(\ell'(u,v)=\ell(u,v)+d(u)-d(v)\ge0\). Output \(p'\) and the arcs having zero updated slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global update uses residual shortest-path labels to shift many prices while preserving reduced-cost feasibility and exposing zero-slack arcs.
assumptions_latex:
\(c_p(a)
\ge-\varepsilon\) on every residual arc.
Shortest-path distances are finite on the updated vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update preserves \(c_{p'}(a)\ge-\varepsilon\) between updated vertices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For distances from each vertex to the target, shortest-path optimality gives \(d(u)\le \ell(u,v)+d(v)\). With the stated reduced-cost convention, preserving nonnegative slack requires the opposite potential shift, \(p'=p-d\), rather than \(p'=p+d\). A source is needed to establish the intended orientation and convention.

children.title: Local–Global Update Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conditions favoring localized price correction or network-wide price restoration.

knowledge_statements.title: Local–Global Update Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid regimes combine single-vertex relabeling with simultaneous global price updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a pseudoflow \(x\), potential \(p\), and invariant \(c_p(a)\ge-\varepsilon\) on residual arcs. A local step changes one active vertex price by the maximal amount allowed by its incident inequalities and then pushes on admissible arcs. When a fixed trigger occurs, perform a global shortest-path price update and resume local steps. Stop when all imbalances vanish. If every update preserves the invariant, pushes respect residual capacities, and active vertices are selected fairly, the output is feasible and \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime uses local relabels ordinarily and occasional global price updates, preserving reduced-cost feasibility until all flow imbalances disappear.
assumptions_latex: Local and global updates preserve \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.
Pushes respect residual capacities.
Active-vertex selection is fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(x\) is feasible and \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local relabel amount, admissibility rule, global-update convention, trigger, and termination mechanism are not specified precisely. Fair active-vertex selection alone does not establish finite termination or the claimed output.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum Mean Cycle-Canceling Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost flow algorithm based on minimum-mean residual cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a feasible flow \(x\). At each iteration, select a minimum-mean directed cycle \(W\) in the residual network \(G(x)\). If its mean cost is negative, augment the maximum possible flow around \(W\), update the residual network, and repeat. If its mean cost is nonnegative, terminate; then \(G(x)\) has no negative-cost cycle and \(x\) is a minimum-cost flow. The algorithm is strongly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible flow, repeatedly augment maximally around a negative minimum-mean residual cycle. A nonnegative minimum mean certifies optimality. The algorithm is strongly polynomial, assuming the required arithmetic on input data can be performed.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is a feasible flow}
W\text{ is a minimum-mean directed cycle in }G(x)
\text{the computational model permits the required additions and subtractions on input data}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu(W)\ge 0\implies x\text{ is a minimum-cost flow};\qquad \text{the algorithm is strongly polynomial in }n\text{ and }m.

children.title: Minimum-Mean-Cycle Canceling
children.top_down_role: Strongly polynomial cycle selection through mean-cost structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Mean-Cycle Canceling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle canceling always selects a minimum-mean residual directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite capacitated directed network with arc costs \(c:A\to\mathbb{Q}\), and start with a feasible circulation \(x\). If its residual graph \(G_x\) has no directed cycle, output \(x\). Otherwise compute a directed residual cycle \(C\) minimizing \(c(C)/|C|\). If \(c(C)\ge0\), output \(x\). If \(c(C)<0\), set \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)\), augment \(\delta\) units around \(C\), update \(G_x\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment by the bottleneck amount around a minimum-mean negative residual cycle. Stop when no negative residual cycle exists; the resulting circulation is minimum-cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
Arc capacities and costs are rational.
The network admits an initial feasible circulation \(x\).
Every selected residual cycle consists of arcs with positive residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon stopping, \(x\) is a minimum-cost circulation.

children.title: Cycle-Cancellation Phases

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Cancellation Phases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A phase removes residual cycles violating a fixed mean-cost threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(\varepsilon>0\) and a feasible circulation \(x\). While the residual graph contains a directed cycle \(C\) with \(c(C)/|C|<-\varepsilon\), augment around \(C\) by \(\delta=
\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)\), then update the residual graph. Stop when no violating cycle remains. Each step preserves feasibility and strictly decreases cost. The phase output therefore satisfies \(c(C)/|C|\ge-\varepsilon\) for every residual directed cycle \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed tolerance, cancel bottleneck flow around sufficiently negative residual cycles until every remaining cycle mean meets the threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible circulation.
Selected cycles have positive residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every residual cycle after the phase has mean cost at least \(-\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Tightening Phases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A price-tightening phase converts a residual cycle-mean bound into arcwise reduced-cost inequalities without changing the flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible circulation in a finite network, and suppose every directed cycle \(C\) in its residual graph satisfies \(c(C)/|C|\ge-\varepsilon\). Solve the residual difference constraints \(p(v)-p(u)\le c(u,v)+\varepsilon\) for all residual arcs \((u,v)\). The resulting potential \(p:V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(c_p(u,v)=c(u,v)+p(u)-p(v)\ge-\varepsilon\) on every residual arc, while \(x\) remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A price-tightening phase solves residual difference constraints to obtain prices enforcing the target reduced-cost tolerance on every residual arc without changing the circulation.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible circulation in a finite network.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
Every directed residual cycle \(C\) satisfies \(c(C)/|C|\ge-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The phase returns a potential \(p\) satisfying \(c_p(a)\ge-\varepsilon\) on every residual arc.

children.title: Cancellation–Tightening Alternation
children.top_down_role: Structural coordination between the two phase types.

knowledge_statements.title: Cancellation–Tightening Alternation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal cancellation and dual tightening alternate while decreasing a common tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize a feasible circulation \(x\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and reduction factor \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Set \(\varepsilon'=
\alpha\varepsilon\); cancel residual cycles whose mean cost is below \(-\varepsilon'\), then solve the residual difference constraints to obtain prices satisfying \(c_p(a)\ge-\varepsilon'\). Replace \(\varepsilon\) by \(\varepsilon'\) and repeat. For integral costs, stop once \(\varepsilon<1/|V|\). The final feasible circulation has no negative-cost residual cycle and is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method alternates cycle cancellation with price tightening at decreasing tolerances; an integral-cost stopping threshold yields exact optimality.
assumptions_latex: Costs are integral.
Each cancellation phase terminates.
Each tightening system is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(\varepsilon<1/|V|\), the feasible circulation \(x\) is minimum-cost.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integral-cost threshold is mathematically plausible after a valid cycle-mean phase, but no source supports this exact alternation framework, arbitrary reduction factor, or termination of its cancellation subphases.

children.title: Cycle-Canceling View

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Canceling View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual negative cycles certify nonoptimality, while nonnegative residual reduced costs certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible circulation in a finite capacitated network, and let \(G_x\) be its residual graph. If a directed residual cycle \(C\) has \(c(C)<0\), then \(C\), together with \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)>0\), is a certificate that \(x\) is not optimal; augmenting \(\delta\) units around \(C\) decreases the objective by \(\delta c(C)\). If \(G_x\) has no negative-cost directed cycle, a potential \(p:V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(c_p(a)\ge0\) on every residual arc is an optimality certificate for \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative residual cycle certifies an improving augmentation. Absence of negative residual cycles, equivalently a feasible nonnegative reduced-cost potential, certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible circulation in a finite capacitated network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The circulation \(x\) is optimal if and only if \(G_x\) has no negative-cost directed cycle.

children.title: Cut-Canceling View
children.top_down_role: Dual organization of cost improvement through cut structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Canceling View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A cut-supported potential shift changes only reduced costs crossing that cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\) satisfy \(c_p(a)\ge0\) on residual arcs, and choose \(S\subset V\). For \(\alpha\ge0\), define \(p'=p+
\alpha\mathbf 1_S\). Reduced costs are unchanged off the cut, increase by \(\alpha\) on arcs leaving \(S\), and decrease by \(\alpha\) on arcs entering \(S\). Hence the largest feasible shift is \(\alpha^*=
\min\{c_p(u,v):(u,v)\in
delta^-(S)\}\), with the minimum over an empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). A finite maximal shift makes at least one entering residual arc tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut update shifts all prices on one side together; the minimum entering-arc slack determines the largest shift preserving reduced-cost feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(c_p(a)\ge0\) for every residual arc.
\(S\) is a proper nonempty vertex subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(0\le\alpha\le\alpha^*\) preserves nonnegative residual reduced costs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-shift calculation is plausible under the stated orientation, but the displayed cut notation has lost the backslash in \(\delta^-(S)\), and no source establishes that this operation is the intended Cut-Canceling View rather than a generic dual price shift.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle–Cut Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle augmentations and cut potential shifts are orthogonal primal–dual directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cycle directions span circulation changes, cut directions arise from potential changes, and the two subspaces are orthogonal under the signed incidence pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
Arc and cut incidence vectors use the same orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker B\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{im}B^{\mathsf T}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cycle-space/cut-space orthogonality claim is standard, but several intended commands in the statement and notation have lost their backslashes, so the displayed formulas do not express the claimed vectors. A specific source locator is also required.

children.title: Strongly Polynomial Frameworks

children.title: Tardos Combinatorial Framework
children.top_down_role: Strong polynomiality from bounded combinatorial matrix structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Tardos Combinatorial Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-program complexity depends on the constraint matrix rather than numerical objective and right-hand-side magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,
x\ge0\}\) with integral \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), rational \(b,c\), and \(\Delta_A\) the largest absolute determinant of a square submatrix of \(A\). The Tardos framework solves the problem using a number of arithmetic operations polynomial in \(m\), \(n\), and \(\log(1+\Delta_A)\), independent of the encoding lengths of \(b\) and \(c\). Consequently, for matrix families with polynomially bounded \(\Delta_A\), including fixed-subdeterminant combinatorial families, the operation bound is strongly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tardos-type linear programming bounds depend on dimensions and subdeterminants of the constraint matrix, not on the magnitudes of costs or right-hand sides.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is integral.
\(b\) and \(c\) are rational.
The linear program has a well-defined feasibility and boundedness status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The arithmetic-operation count is \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,
log(1+\Delta_A))\), independently of the sizes of \(b\) and \(c\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative Tardos theorem locator is essential because the exact dependence on subdeterminants, the meaning of strong polynomiality, and the distinction between arithmetic-operation and bit complexity require qualification. The displayed \(\log\) command is also malformed.

knowledge_statements.title: Orlin Minimum-Cost Flow Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural outline of the excess-scaling and contraction framework; exact implementation details require source review.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed minimum-cost-flow instance with integral supplies, capacities, and linear arc costs. An Orlin-type framework maintains a pseudoflow \(x\), node excesses \(e_v\), residual reduced costs, and a scale \(\Delta>0\). Within a \(\Delta\)-phase it transfers flow from nodes having excess of order \(\Delta\) to deficit nodes while preserving the prescribed reduced-cost invariant. Arcs certified to carry flow large relative to the remaining imbalance are contracted. A phase ends by reducing \(\Delta\); contraction or exhaustion of active excess supplies graph-size progress. When all excesses vanish, the maintained optimality invariant certifies that \(x\) is a minimum-cost feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The framework combines excess scaling with contraction of sufficiently abundant arcs, ensuring graph-size progress until feasibility and the maintained cost-optimality invariant coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has integral finite input data and admits a feasible flow.
Residual reduced costs are maintained under a valid primal-dual optimality invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination with \(e_v=0\) for every \(v\in V\) yields a minimum-cost feasible flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Pivot Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for strongly polynomial pivot-and-contraction organizations in network-flow algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of rational network-flow instances, a pivot framework is strongly polynomial when there is a polynomial \(p\) such that every instance on \(n\) vertices and \(m\) arcs performs at most \(p(n,m)\) pivots, contractions, and other arithmetic operations, independently of the numerical magnitudes of capacities, supplies, and costs. Each pivot must be selectable by comparisons and arithmetic on represented data, and every intermediate number must have encoding length polynomial in the input encoding length. Contraction may reduce the active graph, but its expansion must recover a feasible solution with the same objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires graph-size bounds on pivots and contractions, controlled intermediate encodings, and an objective-preserving expansion of contracted solutions.
assumptions_latex: The input network and all numerical data are rational and finitely encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The framework is strongly polynomial exactly when the stated operation and encoding bounds hold.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity guarantees polynomial in numerical magnitudes rather than necessarily in their binary encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integral minimum-cost-flow instance with \(n=|V|\) vertices and \(m=|A|\) arcs, and let \(M\) bound the absolute values of its capacities, supplies, and costs. An algorithm has a pseudo-polynomial complexity guarantee if its running time is bounded by a polynomial \(q(n,m,M)\). Such a bound is polynomial when the numerical data are encoded in unary, but it need not be polynomial in their binary encoding length, which depends on \(\log(1+M)\). Bounds polynomial in the total transported quantity are also pseudo-polynomial guarantees when that quantity can be exponentially large relative to its binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-polynomial guarantee is polynomial in graph size and numerical magnitudes, but need not be polynomial in the binary input length.
assumptions_latex: All capacities, supplies, and costs are integral and finitely encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound of the form \(q(n,m,M)\) is pseudo-polynomial and, by itself, does not imply a running-time bound polynomial in the binary input length.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity regime polynomial in the complete encoded input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the binary encoding length of a rational minimum-cost-flow instance, including its graph, capacities, balances, and costs. An algorithm is weakly polynomial, or polynomial-time in the ordinary bit model, if its number of bit operations is bounded by a polynomial in \(L\). Equivalently for standard encodings, its bound may depend polynomially on \(n\), \(m\), and logarithms of numerical magnitudes. Such dependence distinguishes it from a strongly polynomial algorithm, whose arithmetic-operation count is independent of those magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly polynomial algorithm has bit complexity polynomial in the full binary input length, including logarithms of all numerical values.
assumptions_latex: The instance uses a standard finite binary encoding of rational data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm is weakly polynomial when its bit complexity is bounded by \(\operatorname{poly}(L)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-polynomiality criterion for rational minimum-cost-flow algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational minimum-cost-flow algorithm is strongly polynomial if, on every network with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) arcs, it performs at most \(p(n,m)\) arithmetic operations and comparisons for some polynomial \(p\), independently of the numerical values and encoding lengths of capacities, balances, and costs. In addition, the encoding length of every intermediate number is bounded by a polynomial in the input encoding length. Consequently, under the standard bit model, the overall bit complexity is polynomial while the combinatorial operation count depends only on graph dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly polynomial algorithm uses a graph-size polynomial number of arithmetic operations and keeps every intermediate number polynomially encoded.
assumptions_latex: The network data are rational and represented in binary.
Arithmetic operations and comparisons are counted in the standard strong-polynomial model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operation count is bounded by \(p(n,m)\), and intermediate encoding lengths remain polynomial in the input length.

notation.meaning: polynomial operation bound depending only on graph dimensions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent optimality criteria for nonnegative m-flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the zero-lower-bound, infinite-upper-bound minimum-cost m-flow model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(f\equiv0\) and \(g\equiv\infty\), and let \(x\ge0\) be an \(m\)-flow. The following are equivalent: (i) \(x\) is a cheapest feasible \(m\)-flow; (ii) its residual digraph \(D_x\) contains no negative directed circuit; (iii) there exists \(\pi:V\to\mathbb R\) such that \(c_\pi(uv)\ge0\) for every \(uv\in A\), with \(c_\pi(uv)=0\) whenever \(x(uv)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative m-flow is minimum-cost exactly when its residual digraph has no negative directed circuit, equivalently when a potential gives nonnegative reduced costs and every positive-flow arc has zero reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: \(f\equiv0\)
\(g\equiv\infty\)
\(x\ge0\) is an \(m\)-flow
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is minimum-cost}\iff D_x\text{ has no negative di-circuit}\iff\exists\pi\;[c_\pi(uv)\ge0\ \forall uv\in A,\ x(uv)>0\Rightarrow c_\pi(uv)=0].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit deficit and m-flow optimality deficit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a quantitative measure of nonconservativity and its use in residual-circuit cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a subdigraph \(D'=(V,A')\), its deficit is the least \(\varepsilon_{D'}\ge0\) such that \(c^+(e)=c(e)+\varepsilon_{D'}\) is conservative on \(D'\). Equivalently, \(\varepsilon_{D'}=\max\{0,-\mu(D',c)\}\), where \(\mu\) is the minimum directed-circuit mean. A verifying potential \(\pi\) satisfies \(c_\pi(e)\ge-\varepsilon_{D'}\) for every \(e\in A'\); if \(D'\) is deficient, some directed circuit \(C\) satisfies \(c_\pi(e)=-\varepsilon_{D'}\) for every \(e\in C\). For a nonnegative \(m\)-flow \(x\), define \(\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon_{D_x}\), with \(\varepsilon(x)=0\) for optimal \(x\). Thus \(x\) is optimal exactly when \(\varepsilon(x)=0\); otherwise a negative residual circuit can be cancelled to improve \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The deficit is the smallest uniform arc-cost increase that removes every negative directed circuit, or the negative of the minimum circuit mean when that mean is negative. Applied to a flow's residual graph, it is zero exactly at optimality; a positive deficit exposes a negative circuit along which the flow can be improved.
assumptions_latex: \(D'=(V,A')\subseteq D^*\)
\(c:A'\to\mathbb R\)
\(x\ge0\) is an \(m\)-flow when defining \(\varepsilon(x)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon_{D'}=\inf\{\varepsilon\ge0:c+\varepsilon\text{ is conservative on }D'\}=\max\{0,-\mu(D',c)\}\), and \(\varepsilon(x)=0\iff x\text{ is optimal}\); if \(\varepsilon(x)>0\), \(D_x\) contains an improving negative di-circuit.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility and cost normalization for uncapacitated m-flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies when lower bounds vanish, upper bounds are infinite, and the total prescribed imbalance is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\widetilde m(V)=0\), \(f\equiv0\), and \(g\equiv\infty\). Then an \(m\)-flow function is feasible exactly when it satisfies \(x\ge 0\), and feasibility requires and is guaranteed by \(\widetilde m(X)\ge0\) for every \(X\subseteq V\) with \(\delta_D(X)=0\). If a directed circuit \(C\) has \(\widetilde c(C)<0\), the feasible-flow objective is unbounded below. Otherwise \(c\) is conservative and admits a feasible potential \(\pi\); replacing \(c\) by the equivalent reduced cost \(c_\pi(uv)=c(uv)-\pi(v)+\pi(u)\) makes every arc cost nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With zero lower bounds, infinite upper bounds, and zero total imbalance, feasibility reduces to nonnegativity together with the Hoffman closed-set condition. A negative-cost directed circuit makes the objective unbounded below; otherwise a potential transforms the costs into an equivalent nonnegative cost function.
assumptions_latex: \(\widetilde m(V)=0\)
\(f\equiv0\)
\(g\equiv\infty\)
\(c:A\to\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible}\iff x\ge0\), subject to \(\widetilde m(X)\ge0\) whenever \(\delta_D(X)=0\); moreover \(\widetilde c(C)<0\Rightarrow\inf\{cx:x\text{ feasible}\}=-\infty\), while conservative \(c\) is equivalent to a nonnegative reduced-cost function \(c_\pi\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Convex Network Flow Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a convex optimization model over graph flows and identifies nonseparable costs and joint side constraints as departures from pure separable network structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A general convex network flow problem has the form
\[\min\{f(x):x\in F\},\]
where \(F\) is a convex set of flow vectors on a graph and \(f\) is convex on \(F\). The function \(f\) may couple several arc flows, and \(F\) may impose side constraints that jointly restrict several arc flows, for example through a shared resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general convex network flow problem minimizes a convex function over a convex set of graph flows. The objective may couple multiple arc flows, and the feasible set may include joint side constraints such as shared-resource restrictions.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is a convex set of flow vectors on a graph}
f\text{ is convex on }F

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential optimality criterion for polyhedral convex minimum-cost flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient potential certificate for feasible flows in MCFP_3, plus characterization of all feasible optima sharing the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \({\rm MCFP}_3\), suppose that \(f\) and all \(f_a\) are polyhedral convex. A feasible flow \(\xi:A\to\mathbf R\) is optimal if and only if there exists \(p:V\to\mathbf R\) such that \(\xi(a)\in\arg\min f_a[\delta p(a)]\) for every \(a\in A\) and \(\partial\xi\in\arg\min f[-p]\). If a potential \(p\) satisfies these conditions for an optimal flow \(\xi\), then a feasible flow \(\xi'\) is optimal if and only if \(\xi'(a)\in\arg\min f_a[\delta p(a)]\) for every \(a\in A\) and \(\partial\xi'\in\arg\min f[-p]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For MCFP_3 with polyhedral convex costs, a feasible flow is optimal exactly when a vertex potential simultaneously certifies every arcwise tilted minimization and the tilted boundary minimization. Once a potential certifies one optimum, those same conditions characterize every other feasible optimum.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is polyhedral convex}
f_a\text{ is polyhedral convex}\quad(a\in A)
\xi:A\to\mathbf R\text{ is feasible}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi\text{ is optimal}\iff\exists p\in\mathbf R^V:\bigl[(\forall a\in A)\ \xi(a)\in\arg\min f_a[\delta p(a)]\bigr]\land[\partial\xi\in\arg\min f[-p]],\text{ and a certifying }p\text{ gives the analogous equivalence for every feasible }\xi'.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Separable Convex-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous capacitated flow with an extended-real separable convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) have node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), balance vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), and arc bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\). A continuous separable convex-cost flow problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^A}\ \sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=b,\qquad \ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\ \ (a\in A),\]
where every \(\phi_a:[\ell_a,u_a]\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex. Flow variables are real; neither the balances nor feasible flows are required to be integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This model minimizes a sum of convex arc costs over real flows satisfying conservation and arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(\{x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty.
Each arc cost is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex on its interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any minimizer \(x^\star\) is an optimal continuous separable convex-cost flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Optimality and Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic global consequences of convexity for the continuous model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the feasible flow set and \(\Phi(x)=\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)\). Because \(F\) and \(\Phi\) are convex, every finite-valued local minimizer of \(\Phi\) on \(F\) is global. If \(\Phi\) is strictly convex on \(F\cap\operatorname{dom}\Phi\), then an attained finite optimum is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite local optimum is global, and strict convexity on the effective feasible set makes an attained optimum unique.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is convex.
Each \(\phi_a\) is convex.
For uniqueness, \(\Phi\) is strictly convex on \(F\cap\operatorname{dom}\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star\text{ finite local minimum}\Rightarrow x^\star\text{ global minimum},\qquad \Phi|_{F\cap\operatorname{dom}\Phi}\text{ strictly convex}\Rightarrow |\operatorname*{argmin}_F\Phi|\le1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Continuous Convex-Cost Optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment for finite bounds and a nonempty effective feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^A:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\). If \(F\ne\varnothing\), all arc bounds are finite, every \(\phi_a\) is proper and lower-semicontinuous on \([\ell_a,u_a]\), and some \(\bar x\in F\) satisfies \(\sum_a\phi_a(\bar x_a)<+\infty\), then \(\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)\) attains a finite minimum on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finite arc bounds, lower-semicontinuous proper costs, and at least one finite-cost feasible flow, the continuous model has an optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(F\ne\varnothing\).
\(-\infty<\ell_a\le u_a<+\infty\) for every arc.
Each \(\phi_a\) is proper and lower-semicontinuous.
There exists \(\bar x\in F\cap\operatorname{dom}\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)\ne\varnothing\) and the minimum is finite.
