knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary Slackness for Separable Convex-Cost Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines arcwise complementary slackness and its equivalent arcwise Lagrangian-minimizer characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a continuous separable convex-cost flow problem, a flow-price pair \((x,p)\) satisfies complementary slackness if, for every arc \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\),
\[x_{ij}\in X_{ij},\qquad f_{ij}^{-}(x_{ij})\le p_i-p_j\le f_{ij}^{+}(x_{ij}).\]
Equivalently, for every arc,
\[f_{ij}(x_{ij})-(p_i-p_j)x_{ij}=\min_{z_{ij}\in X_{ij}}\left\{f_{ij}(z_{ij})-(p_i-p_j)z_{ij}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow-price pair satisfies complementary slackness when each arc flow is admissible and the corresponding node-price difference lies between the arc cost's left and right slopes. Equivalently, each arc flow minimizes its arcwise Lagrangian term.
assumptions_latex: f_{ij}\text{ is a convex arc-cost function on }X_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A
p\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal N}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A:\ \left[x_{ij}\in X_{ij},\ f_{ij}^{-}(x_{ij})\le p_i-p_j\le f_{ij}^{+}(x_{ij})\right]\iff x_{ij}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in X_{ij}}\left\{f_{ij}(z)-(p_i-p_j)z\right\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Separable Convex-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral capacitated flow with nondecreasing discrete marginal arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\), \(B\), and integral vectors \(b,\ell,u\) be given. An integer separable convex-cost flow problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb Z^A}\ \sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=b,\qquad \ell_a\le x_a\le u_a.\]
For each arc, \(\phi_a:\{\ell_a,\ldots,u_a\}\to\mathbb R\) is discretely convex: its forward differences \(d_a(k)=\phi_a(k)-\phi_a(k-1)\) satisfy \(d_a(k+1)\ge d_a(k)\) wherever both sides are defined. Thus successive integral units on an arc have nondecreasing marginal cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This model minimizes separable discrete-convex costs over integral flows, with each arc’s successive unit costs nondecreasing.
assumptions_latex: The balance and bound data are integral.
At least one integral flow satisfies conservation and the bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal solution lies in \(\mathbb Z^A\) and minimizes the stated separable discrete-convex objective.

notation.meaning: cost of the kth marginal unit on arc a

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Convex-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous network flow with finite convex piecewise-linear arc costs described by breakpoints and nondecreasing slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) have node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), balance vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), and finite arc bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\). A piecewise-linear convex-cost flow problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^A}\ \sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=b,\qquad \ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\ \ (a\in A),\]
where each \(\phi_a:[\ell_a,u_a]\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, convex, and linear on each interval of a finite breakpoint partition. Equivalently, the successive segment slopes of each \(\phi_a\) are nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This model minimizes separable convex piecewise-linear arc costs over real flows satisfying conservation and bounds.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(\{x\in\mathbb R^A:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty.
Each arc cost has finitely many linear segments and nondecreasing successive slopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed optimization problem is a continuous piecewise-linear convex-cost flow model.

notation.meaning: convex piecewise-linear cost on arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Segment-Arc Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact continuous linear-flow representation using one capacity-limited parallel arc per linear segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi\) on \([\ell,u]\) have breakpoints \(\ell=\beta_0<\beta_1<\cdots<\beta_m=u\) and segment slopes \(c_1\le\cdots\le c_m\). Replace the arc by parallel arcs \(j=1,\ldots,m\) having capacities \(\beta_j-\beta_{j-1}\) and linear unit costs \(c_j\). For every \(x\in[\ell,u]\), \[\min\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m c_jy_j:\sum_jy_j=x-\ell,\ 0\le y_j\le\beta_j-\beta_{j-1}\right\}=\phi(x)-\phi(\ell).\] After shifting the lower-bound flow in the node balances and adding the constant \(\phi(\ell)\), the expanded linear network has the same feasible aggregate flows and optimal objective values as the original arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex piecewise-linear arc is represented exactly by capacity-limited parallel segment arcs with nondecreasing linear costs.
assumptions_latex: The breakpoint partition is finite.
Segment slopes are nondecreasing.
Only aggregate flow through the replacement interacts with the rest of the network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum expanded linear cost equals \(\phi(x)-\phi(\ell)\) for every feasible aggregate flow \(x\).

notation.meaning: flow on replacement segment arc j

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth-Cost Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable convex arc costs and their marginal-cost optimality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) have node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), balance vector \(b\), arc bounds \([\ell_a,u_a]\), and separable objective \(\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\). The model is in the smooth-cost regime when every \(\phi_a\) is convex and continuously differentiable on an open interval containing \([\ell_a,u_a]\). Each marginal-cost function \(\phi_a'\) is then nondecreasing. A feasible flow \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if there exists \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) such that
\[0\in \phi_a'(x_a^\star)+(B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_a+N_{[\ell_a,u_a]}(x_a^\star)\qquad(a\in A),\]
where \(N_{[\ell_a,u_a]}(x_a^\star)\) is the normal cone of the bound interval at \(x_a^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convex arc costs have nondecreasing marginal derivatives, and optimality is characterized by derivative stationarity with node potentials and bound normal cones.
assumptions_latex: The set \(\{x\in\mathbb R^A:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty.
Every arc cost is convex and continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of its bound interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible \(x^\star\) is optimal exactly when the displayed potential-based stationarity condition holds.

notation.meaning: normal cone of the arc-bound interval

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth-Cost Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex arc costs that are nondifferentiable at permitted interior flow values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) have node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), balance vector \(b\), arc bounds \([\ell_a,u_a]\), and finite convex arc costs \(\phi_a:[\ell_a,u_a]\to\mathbb R\). The model is in the nonsmooth-cost regime when at least one \(\phi_a\) is not differentiable at a point in \((\ell_a,u_a)\). Marginal information is then represented by the convex subdifferential. A feasible flow \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if there exists \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) such that
\[0\in \partial\phi_a(x_a^\star)+(B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_a+N_{[\ell_a,u_a]}(x_a^\star)\qquad(a\in A).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth convex-cost regime contains an arc cost with an interior kink; subgradients replace derivatives in the potential-based optimality condition.
assumptions_latex: The set \(\{x\in\mathbb R^A:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty.
Every arc cost is finite and convex on its bound interval.
At least one arc cost is nondifferentiable at an interior point of its bound interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality is characterized by the displayed subgradient, potential, and normal-cone inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A kink where derivative-only marginal-cost conditions cease to be defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the convex arc cost \(\phi(x)=|x|\) on \([-1,1]\). It is differentiable for \(x\ne0\), with \(\phi'(x)=-1\) for \(x<0\) and \(\phi'(x)=1\) for \(x>0\), but \(\phi'(0)\) does not exist. Hence any optimality test requiring a single marginal derivative fails at a feasible flow using \(x=0\). The correct replacement is the subdifferential \(\partial\phi(0)=[-1,1]\); stationarity holds whenever the negative reduced potential difference belongs to this interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a convex kink, a single marginal derivative is unavailable; the interval of subgradients supplies the valid optimality condition.
assumptions_latex: The feasible arc interval contains \(0\).
The arc cost is \(\phi(x)=|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Derivative-only stationarity is undefined at \(x=0\), whereas subgradient stationarity remains valid because \(\partial\phi(0)=[-1,1]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Fenchel Representation, Attainment Equivalence, and Dual Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General one-dimensional convex-duality result for a closed convex function on an interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ be closed and convex, and define $q(t)=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)-tx\}$. Then
\[
\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\{q(t)+tx\}=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in X,\\+\infty,&x\notin X.\end{cases}
\]
For every $x\in X$ and $t\in\mathbb{R}$, the following are equivalent: $tx=f(x)-q(t)$; $x$ attains the infimum defining $q(t)$; and $t$ attains the displayed supremum at $x$. If, for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$, the infimum defining $q(t)$ is uniquely attained at $x(t)$, then $q$ is real-valued and differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$, with $q'(t)=-x(t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex real-valued function on an interval, its concave dual q recovers the function through a supremum, with value positive infinity outside the interval. Equality, primal attainment, and dual attainment are equivalent. If every defining infimum has a unique minimizer x(t), then q is finite and differentiable everywhere and its derivative is minus x(t).
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{ is an interval}
f:X\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is closed and convex}
q(t)=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)-tx\}
\text{For the differentiability conclusion, }\forall t\in\mathbb{R}\text{ the infimum is uniquely attained at }x(t)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\{q(t)+tx\}=f(x)\text{ for }x\in X\text{ and }+\infty\text{ otherwise};\quad tx=f(x)-q(t)\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in X}(f(y)-ty)\iff t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{s\in\mathbb{R}}(q(s)+sx);\quad q'(t)=-x(t)\ \forall t\in\mathbb{R}\text{ under unique attainment}.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal-Cost Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous and discrete convex arc costs reconstructed from monotone marginal costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u>0\). For a finite closed convex cost \(\phi:[0,u]\to\mathbb R\), define the right derivative \(g(t)=\phi_+'(t)\) for \(0\le t<u\). The function \(g\) is nondecreasing and
\[\phi(x)=\phi(0)+\int_0^x g(t)\,dt\qquad(0\le x\le u),\]
with the endpoint integral understood in the usual limiting sense when necessary. For an integer cost \(\phi:\{0,\ldots,u\}\to\mathbb R\), define \(d(k)=\phi(k)-\phi(k-1)\). Discrete convexity is equivalent to \(d(1)\le\cdots\le d(u)\), and
\[\phi(k)=\phi(0)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}d(j)\qquad(0\le k\le u).\]
Thus continuous or discrete convex arc costs are represented by their nondecreasing marginal costs together with the additive constant \(\phi(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex continuous arc cost or a discrete-convex integer arc cost equals its initial value plus accumulated nondecreasing marginal costs.
assumptions_latex: In the continuous case, \(u>0\) and \(\phi\) is finite, closed, and convex on \([0,u]\).
In the discrete case, \(u\) is a positive integer and the forward differences of \(\phi\) are nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The marginal data and \(\phi(0)\) uniquely reconstruct \(\phi\) through the displayed integral or sum.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Arc Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral separable convex costs with finite arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replace every arc \(a=(i,j)\) by parallel arcs \((a,k)\), \(k=1,\ldots,u_a\), each having capacity \(1\) and linear unit cost \(d_{a,k}\). For an aggregate integer flow \(z_a\), impose \(z_a=\sum_{k=1}^{u_a}y_{a,k}\) with \(y_{a,k}\in\{0,1\}\). Then
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{u_a}d_{a,k}y_{a,k}:\sum_{k=1}^{u_a}y_{a,k}=z_a,\ y_{a,k}\in\{0,1\}\right\}=\sum_{k=1}^{z_a}d_{a,k}=\phi_a(z_a)-\phi_a(0).
\]
Thus the integral flows of the expanded network aggregate to exactly the feasible integral flows of the original network, and minimizing expanded linear cost solves the original convex-cost flow problem up to the constant \(\sum_a\phi_a(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral discretely convex arc cost is represented exactly by integral flows on unit-capacity parallel arcs whose ordered linear costs are its marginal increments.
assumptions_latex: The arc flow is integral: \(x_a\in\{0,\ldots,u_a\}\), where \(u_a\in\mathbb Z_+\).
Each arc cost \(\phi_a\) is discretely convex: \(d_{a,k}:=\phi_a(k)-\phi_a(k-1)\) is nondecreasing in \(k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering boundary for independent parallel-segment linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two unit-length sequential segments with slopes \(s_1=1\) and \(s_2=0\), the intended cost is \(\phi(z)=z\) on \([0,1]\) and \(\phi(z)=1\) on \([1,2]\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Using the Lagrangian \(L(x,p)=\Phi(x)+p^T(b-Bx)\), minimization over \(x\) gives the concave dual function
\[
q(p)=b^Tp-\Phi^*(B^Tp)=b^Tp-\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a).
\]
Consequently the dual problem is \(\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^V}q(p)\). Under the stated qualification, its supremum equals the primal infimum. If both optima are attained, \(x\) and \(p\) are optimal exactly when \(Bx=b\) and \(B^Tp\in\partial\Phi(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex conjugate of an arc cost is
\[
\phi_a^*(s)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\{sx-\phi_a(x)\}.
\]
Because \(\phi_a\) is proper, closed, and convex, it has the biconjugate representation
\[
\phi_a(x)=\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\{sx-\phi_a^*(s)\}.
\]
Moreover, equality in the Fenchel inequality \(\phi_a(x)+\phi_a^*(s)\ge sx\) holds exactly when \(s\in\partial\phi_a(x)\), equivalently \(x\in\partial\phi_a^*(s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each closed convex arc cost is the supremum of affine functions determined by its convex conjugate.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Conjugate Representations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Biconjugacy Requires Closed Convex Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of exact recovery by the affine-supremum representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper extended-real function \(f\) on a finite-dimensional space, \(f^{**}\) is its lower-semicontinuous convex envelope and satisfies \(f^{**}\le f\). Exact recovery \(f^{**}=f\) holds exactly when \(f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex. Thus a nonclosed or nonconvex arc cost is replaced by its closed convex relaxation rather than represented exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without closed convexity, biconjugacy recovers the closed convex relaxation rather than necessarily the original arc cost.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a proper extended-real function on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{**}=\operatorname{clconv}f\le f\), with equality exactly for lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separable Conjugate Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space conjugacy of the aggregate arc-cost function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite arc set and \(\Phi(x)=\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\), separability gives
\[
\Phi^*(s)=\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a^*(s_a).
\]
If the arc costs are proper, closed, and convex, then
\[
s\in\partial\Phi(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s_a\in\partial\phi_a(x_a)\ \text{for every }a.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of the separable network cost is the sum of its arc conjugates, and the subgradient relation decomposes arcwise.
assumptions_latex: The arc set is finite.
Each \(\phi_a\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi^*(s)=\sum_a\phi_a^*(s_a)\) and \(s\in\partial\Phi(x)\iff(\forall a)\ s_a\in\partial\phi_a(x_a)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Conjugate Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every primal-feasible \(x\) and potential vector \(p\), Fenchel inequalities give
\[
\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)+\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a)-b^Tp\ge0.
\]
Since \(Bx=b\), this gap equals the sum of the nonnegative arcwise gaps \(\phi_a(x_a)+\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a)-(B^Tp)_ax_a\). It vanishes exactly when
\[
(B^Tp)_a\in\partial\phi_a(x_a)\quad\text{for every }a\in A,
\]
equivalently \(x_a\in\partial\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a)\). Under strong duality and attainment, these relations characterize primal-dual optimal pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal arc flows and node potentials correspond through equality in every arcwise Fenchel inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual–Conjugate Correspondence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Construct \(R_x\) by giving each original arc \(a=(i,j)\) a forward residual arc of weight \(\phi'_{a,+}(x_a)\) when \(x_a<u_a\), and a reverse residual arc \((j,i)\) of weight \(-\phi'_{a,-}(x_a)\) when \(x_a>l_a\). Then \(x\) is optimal exactly when every directed cycle \(C\) in \(R_x\) satisfies
\[
\sum_{e\in C}w_x(e)\ge0.
\]
Thus absence of a negative marginal residual cycle is a finite, locally checkable optimality certificate; a negative cycle supplies a feasible improving circulation direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible convex-cost flow is optimal exactly when its one-sided marginal residual network has no negative directed cycle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Marginal Cycles Do Not Imply Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a zero first-order cycle and a flat optimal direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take two parallel arcs from \(s\) to \(t\), require \(x_1+x_2=1\), impose \(0\le x_1,x_2\le1\), and set \(\phi_1(z)=\phi_2(z)=z^2\). The unique optimum is \(x_1=x_2=1/2\). The residual cycle that increases one arc and decreases the other has marginal weight \(2x_1-2x_2=0\), although every nonzero feasible displacement \((\delta,-\delta)\) increases the objective by \(2\delta^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-weight marginal cycle need not yield another optimum because positive curvature may make every nonzero displacement costly.
assumptions_latex: Two parallel arcs carry one unit in total and have quadratic costs on \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is unique although its marginal residual network contains a zero-weight directed cycle.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A node-potential vector \(p\in\mathbb R^V\) certifies optimality of \(x\) when every residual arc \((i,j)\in R_x\) obeys
\[
w_x(i,j)+p_i-p_j\ge0.
\]
Summing these inequalities around any directed residual cycle cancels the potentials and yields a nonnegative cycle weight. Conversely, if \(R_x\) has no negative directed cycle, shortest-path distances from a super-source provide such potentials. Hence the potential inequalities are equivalent to the marginal residual-cycle certificate and are directly verifiable arc by arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node prices certify optimality when every available marginal residual move has nonnegative reduced cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Cost Potential Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Verification and Construction of Potential Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-graph checking and construction of marginal reduced-cost potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(p\), scan every residual arc and test \(w_x(i,j)+p_i-p_j\ge0\). This takes \(O(|R_x|)\) arithmetic comparisons. To construct a potential, initialize every vertex label to zero and apply Bellman--Ford relaxation to the difference constraints \(p_j\le p_i+w_x(i,j)\). The procedure either returns feasible labels or a negative directed cycle, in \(O(|V||R_x|+|V|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supplied potential is checked by one residual-arc scan; Bellman–Ford constructs one or returns a negative-cycle witness.
assumptions_latex: The marginal residual network is finite and all residual weights are explicitly available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Potential verification uses \(O(|R_x|)\) tests, and Bellman--Ford constructs a potential or negative-cycle witness in \(O(|V||R_x|+|V|)\) time.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a Concave Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's concave-function convention: an upper affine support vector is called a subgradient; it is often called a supergradient elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave and let \(x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A vector \(s\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x^*\) if \[f(x)\le f(x^*)+s^\top(x-x^*)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] The set of all such vectors is the subdifferential \(\partial f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the source's convention for concave functions, s is a subgradient at x* when the affine function through f(x*) with slope s globally upper-bounds f. All such vectors form the subdifferential.

x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a Finite Minimum of Affine Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the concave subdifferential using the slopes of the affine pieces active at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge1\), \(h_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(f_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and define \[Z(p)=\min_{1\le i\le m}\bigl(h_i+f_i^\top p\bigr),\qquad E(p)=\{i:Z(p)=h_i+f_i^\top p\}.\] For every \(p^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\), each \(f_i\) with \(i\in E(p^*)\) belongs to \(\partial Z(p^*)\), and \[\partial Z(p^*)=\operatorname{conv}\{f_i:i\in E(p^*)\}.\] Thus \(s\in\partial Z(p^*)\) if and only if \(s\) is a convex combination of the active slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite pointwise minimum of affine functions, each active slope is a concave subgradient, and the full subdifferential is exactly the convex hull of the active slopes.

p^*\in\mathbb{R}^n
Z(p)=\min_{1\le i\le m}(h_i+f_i^\top p)
E(p)=\{i:Z(p)=h_i+f_i^\top p\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Nondifferentiability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued imbalance formula at conjugate kinks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose each \(\phi_a^*\) is finite and continuous on a neighborhood of \((B^Tp)_a\). Then for \(q(p)=b^Tp-\sum_a\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a)\),
\[
\partial^+q(p)=\{b-Bx:x_a\in\partial\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a)\ \forall a\}.
\]
Thus \(q\) is differentiable at \(p\) exactly when this set is a singleton. Arcwise differentiability is sufficient but not necessary, because distinct arcwise selections may have the same node imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At conjugate kinks the dual imbalance is set-valued; differentiability survives exactly when all admissible selections produce the same imbalance.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\phi_a^*\) is finite and continuous near the evaluated price difference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\) is differentiable at \(p\) if and only if \(\{b-Bx:x_a\in\partial\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a)\}\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Nondifferentiability Boundary

children.title: Primal Uniqueness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings governing uniqueness of optimal flows.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(F:=\{x:Bx=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty and convex.
The objective \(\Phi(x)=\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)\) is strictly convex on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a minimizer of \(\Phi\) over \(F\) exists, it is unique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of the full arc-flow vector, not merely its cost.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.2 Network Flow Problems with Convex Cost p. 16
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\Phi\) is strictly convex on the feasible set \(F\), then the convex-cost flow problem has at most one minimizer. More generally, uniqueness follows when for every two distinct feasible flows \(x,y\in F\) and every \(t\in(0,1)\),
\[
\Phi(tx+(1-t)y)<t\Phi(x)+(1-t)\Phi(y).
\]
It is sufficient that every \(\phi_a\) be strictly convex on its feasible interval, but strict convexity is only required along nonzero feasible circulation directions that can connect two points of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity along every feasible flow direction makes an attained optimal arc-flow vector unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Uniqueness Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Convexity Is Sufficient but Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of the standard strict-convexity uniqueness criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a network have a one-dimensional feasible circulation set identified with \(F=[0,1]\). For \(\Phi(x)=x\), the objective is affine rather than strictly convex, yet its unique minimizer is \(x^*=0\). On the same feasible set, \(\Phi(x)=0\) makes every point optimal. Thus failure of strict convexity neither forces nor excludes nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-strictly-convex flow objective may have one optimum or many, depending on its interaction with the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The network admits a nontrivial one-dimensional feasible circulation interval \(F=[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict convexity on feasible directions is sufficient but not necessary for primal uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Convexity Is Sufficient but Not Necessary

children.title: Dual Uniqueness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings governing uniqueness of optimal price certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Uniqueness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential uniqueness after removing incidence-matrix gauge freedom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each weakly connected component \(K\), the balance condition \(\sum_{i\in K}b_i=0\) and the identity \(B^T(p+c\mathbf 1_K)=B^Tp\) make the dual objective invariant under addition of a constant on \(K\). Fixing one node potential per component defines a normalized potential space \(P\). If
\[
D(p)=\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a)-b^Tp
\]
is strictly convex on \(P\), then any attained minimizer of \(D\), equivalently any maximizer of \(q=-D\), is unique in \(P\). Without normalization, all optimal potentials are precisely the componentwise constant translates of that normalized optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When supply is balanced in every component, strict convexity of the normalized negative-dual objective yields a unique potential modulo componentwise additive constants.
assumptions_latex: For every weakly connected component \(K\), the supplies satisfy \(\sum_{i\in K}b_i=0\).
The normalized dual domain \(P\) fixes one potential in each weakly connected component of the network.
The convex function \(D(p):=\sum_a\phi_a^*((B^Tp)_a)-b^Tp\) is strictly convex on \(P\).
A dual minimizer exists in \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized optimal potential \(p^*\) is unique, and the unnormalized optimal potentials are exactly its componentwise constant translates.

notation.meaning: A weakly connected component of the network

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalized Potentials Need Not Be Unique
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of price uniqueness when the normalized negative dual has a flat direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take two nodes joined by one arc, zero balance \(b=0\), capacity interval \([0,1]\), and extended cost \(\phi(x)=\delta_{[0,1]}(x)\). Then \(\phi^*(s)=\max\{0,s\}\). With one node potential fixed and the remaining price difference denoted by \(p\), the normalized negative-dual objective is \(D(p)=\max\{0,p\}\), up to reversing the incidence sign. Every \(p\le0\) minimizes \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge normalization alone does not ensure unique prices; a capacity-indicator cost leaves a ray of normalized dual optima.
assumptions_latex: The incidence orientation is chosen so that the arc price difference is \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}D=(-\infty,0]\), so the normalized dual optimum is not unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Potentials Need Not Be Unique

children.title: Curvature–Uniqueness Interface
children.top_down_role: Dependence of primal or dual uniqueness on curvature properties.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature Implications Are Not Reversible Without Stronger Hypotheses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinctions among strict convexity, strong convexity, smoothness, and dual curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strict convexity alone does not imply Lipschitz differentiability of the conjugate: \(f(x)=x^4\) is strictly convex, while \(\nabla f^*(s)\) is not Lipschitz near zero. Strong convexity alone does not imply strict convexity of the conjugate: for \(f(x)=\frac{\mu}{2}x^2+\delta_{[0,\infty)}(x)\), \(f^*(s)=\frac{(\max\{s,0\})^2}{2\mu}\), which is smooth but constant on \(( -\infty,0]\). Incidence gauge directions additionally prevent unnormalized dual uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict curvature, strong curvature, smoothness, and dual uniqueness are distinct; the reciprocal conclusions require the stated quantitative and rank hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither strict primal convexity nor strong primal convexity alone supplies all dual curvature and uniqueness conclusions.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Implications Are Not Reversible Without Stronger Hypotheses

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal Curvature–Smoothness Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional curvature transfer between the primal cost and normalized price dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be proper and closed. If \(\Phi\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \(\Phi^*\) is differentiable with \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(q(p)=b^Tp-\Phi^*(B^Tp)\) has a gradient with Lipschitz constant at most \(\|B\|^2/\mu\). The primal problem has at most one attained minimizer. Conversely, if \(\Phi\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb R^A\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, then \(\Phi^*\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex. On a normalized potential space \(P\) where \(B^T|_P\) is injective, \(D(p)=\Phi^*(B^Tp)-b^Tp\) is strongly convex with modulus at least \(\sigma_{\min}(B^T|_P)^2/L\), so an attained normalized dual optimum is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong primal curvature yields a smooth dual; globally smooth primal costs yield curvature and uniqueness of the normalized dual.
assumptions_latex: All spaces are finite-dimensional.
For the converse, \(\Phi\) is differentiable on the full arc space and \(\nabla\Phi\) is globally \(L\)-Lipschitz.
The normalized space \(P\) removes componentwise incidence gauge freedom.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong primal curvature gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla q)\le\|B\|^2/\mu\); primal \(L\)-smoothness gives normalized dual strong convexity at least \(\sigma_{\min}(B^T|_P)^2/L\).

notation.meaning: Strong-convexity modulus of the primal cost
Lipschitz constant of the primal gradient

knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Curvature–Smoothness Interface

assumptions_latex: The arc costs are proper, closed, and convex on the relevant domains.
Potential vectors are normalized so that \(B^T\) is injective on the potential space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong primal curvature yields dual smoothness, while sufficiently smooth primal costs yield dual curvature and hence normalized dual uniqueness.

notation.meaning: Strong-convexity modulus of the primal objective
Gradient Lipschitz constant of the primal objective

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\Phi\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then the primal minimizer is unique and \(\Phi^*\) is differentiable with \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz gradient; consequently \(q(p)=b^Tp-\Phi^*(B^Tp)\) is differentiable with Lipschitz gradient. Conversely, if \(\Phi\) is differentiable and its gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \(\Phi^*\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex. Hence
\[
p\mapsto\Phi^*(B^Tp)-b^Tp
\]
is strictly convex on any normalized potential space on which \(B^T\) is injective, yielding uniqueness of an attained normalized dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal strong convexity produces dual smoothness; primal smoothness can produce normalized dual curvature and uniqueness.

children.title: Linear Network-Expansion Methods
children.top_down_role: Reduction of convex costs to expanded minimum-cost-flow networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Network-Expansion Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit-capacity reduction for integral separable convex-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite directed network with integral node supplies, integral capacities, and marginal increments, perform the following operations. For each arc \(a\), create unit-capacity parallel copies \((a,k)\) of linear cost \(d_{a,k}\), for \(k=1,\ldots,u_a\). Solve the resulting linear minimum-cost-flow problem. If it is feasible, choose an integral optimal expanded flow \(y\) and output
\[
x_a=\sum_{k=1}^{u_a}y_{a,k}
\]
for every original arc. Because the marginal costs are nondecreasing, an optimal integral expanded solution uses the cheapest required copies, so its cost is \(\sum_a(\phi_a(x_a)-\phi_a(0))\). If the expanded problem is infeasible, return its infeasibility certificate; the original integral convex-cost flow problem is then infeasible as well.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integral supplies and capacities, expand each convex arc into unit-capacity marginal arcs, solve linear minimum-cost flow, and either aggregate an integral optimum or report infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The directed network is finite, every node supply is integral, and the supplies sum to zero in each weakly connected component.
Every arc has integral capacity \(u_a\), its flow is restricted to \(\{0,\ldots,u_a\}\), and its discretely convex cost \(\phi_a\) is available through nondecreasing marginal increments.
The expanded network size \(\sum_a u_a\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the expanded problem is feasible, aggregation returns an optimal integral convex-cost flow using \(\sum_a u_a\) parallel arcs; otherwise the method returns an infeasibility certificate valid for the original problem.

notation.meaning: Marginal cost of the kth unit on arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compressed Segment-Expansion Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-flow reduction using explicitly supplied piecewise-linear segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc \(a\) with breakpoints \(0=t_{a,0}<\cdots<t_{a,r_a}=u_a\) and nondecreasing slopes \(s_{a,1}\le\cdots\le s_{a,r_a}\), replace it by \(r_a\) parallel arcs having capacities \(t_{a,j}-t_{a,j-1}\) and linear costs \(s_{a,j}\). Solving the resulting linear minimum-cost-flow problem and aggregating parallel flows returns an optimum of the original piecewise-linear convex-cost problem, up to \(\sum_a\phi_a(0)\), or establishes its infeasibility. The expansion contains \(\sum_a r_a\) arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expand each explicitly piecewise-linear convex arc by its segments, solve one linear minimum-cost-flow problem, and aggregate the parallel flows.
assumptions_latex: Every arc cost is finite, convex, and piecewise linear on its capacity interval.
Breakpoints and segment slopes are explicitly supplied.
The resulting linear minimum-cost-flow instance is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method returns an exact optimum or a valid infeasibility conclusion using \(\sum_a r_a\) expanded arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Cycle Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-augmentation version for separable discrete-convex integral circulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc, give an available forward residual unit cost \(\Delta_a^+(x_a)=\phi_a(x_a+1)-\phi_a(x_a)\) and an available backward residual unit cost \(\Delta_a^-(x_a)=\phi_a(x_a-1)-\phi_a(x_a)\). Repeatedly find a directed cycle \(C\) of negative total marginal cost in \(R_x\), augment one unit around \(C\), and update the affected marginal costs. Stop when no negative directed cycle remains. Discrete convexity makes \(\Delta_a^+(x_a)\) nondecreasing in \(x_a\) and makes \(\Delta_a^-(x_a)\) nonincreasing in \(x_a\); the resulting negative-cycle optimality criterion certifies global optimality of the final feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment one flow unit around a negative marginal-cost residual cycle. For an integral separable discrete-convex circulation, absence of such a cycle certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: The directed network is finite, arc flows and bounds are integral, and each separable arc cost \(\phi_a:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\) is discrete convex.
The current circulation \(x\) satisfies flow conservation and all arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method terminates at an optimal integral circulation when the marginal residual network contains no negative-cost directed cycle.

notation.meaning: Marginal residual network at flow x
Forward and backward one-unit residual costs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Line Search on a Marginal Residual Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiunit variant for an integral discrete-convex circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a directed residual cycle at a feasible integral circulation \(x\), and let \(\bar\delta\) be the largest feasible integer augmentation. The restricted objective \[F_C(\delta)=\sum_a\phi_a\bigl(x_a+\delta(\chi_C)_a\bigr),\qquad \delta\in\{0,\ldots,\bar\delta\},\] is discrete convex. Choosing \(\delta^*\in\arg\min F_C\) and replacing \(x\) by \(x+\delta^*\chi_C\) preserves feasibility and does not increase cost. Marginal costs must be updated as marginal breakpoints are crossed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chosen residual cycle can be augmented by exact discrete-convex line search, batching unit updates while respecting changing marginal costs.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible integral circulation with separable discrete-convex costs.
\(C\) is a directed residual cycle at \(x\).
\(\bar\delta\) is the feasible integer augmentation limit along \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_C(\delta^*)\le F_C(0), and \(x+\delta^*\chi_C\) is feasible.

notation.meaning: Signed original-arc incidence vector of cycle C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Price-Feasible Unit Marginal-Path Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive shortest-path method under a reduced-cost invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an integral pseudoflow \(x\) and node prices \(p\) such that every available marginal residual arc has nonnegative reduced cost. While the target balance vector is unmet, choose a node requiring one additional unit of net outflow and a node requiring one additional unit of net inflow. If a residual path joins them, compute a minimum reduced-cost path, update prices by shortest-path distances, augment one unit on the resulting tight path, and update the affected forward and backward marginal costs. Discrete convexity preserves nonnegative reduced costs after the marginal update. When all target balances are met, the resulting feasible flow satisfies the marginal reduced-cost optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under nonnegative marginal reduced costs, repeatedly send one unit along a shortest residual path and update prices until the prescribed balances are met.
assumptions_latex: Arc bounds and target balances are integral.
Arc costs are separable and discrete convex.
The initial pseudoflow and prices satisfy nonnegative reduced costs on all available marginal residual arcs.
Each selected excess-to-deficit pair is connected by a residual path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each augmentation preserves the reduced-cost invariant; upon attaining the target balances, the flow is optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Price-Feasible Unit Marginal-Path Augmentation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Reachability Cut for Unmet Balances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasibility certificate for marginal path augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the current bounded integral pseudoflow has unmet target balances. If no marginal residual path leads from any node requiring additional net outflow to any node requiring additional net inflow, then the set of vertices reachable from the former nodes defines a residual cut across which no admissible correction can carry the required net amount. The target balance equations and arc bounds are therefore infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If residual reachability cannot connect remaining excess requirements to deficit requirements, the reachable-set cut certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The current pseudoflow respects all arc bounds.
Target balances remain unmet.
No required-outflow node reaches a required-inflow node in the residual graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual reachable-set cut certifies infeasibility of the target balances under the arc bounds.

notation.meaning: Set reachable from nodes with remaining outflow requirement
Residual network at the current pseudoflow

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Reachability Cut for Unmet Balances

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit Marginal-Path Augmentation Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-dependent bound for the unit-augmentation variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) units of balance must be installed from a price-feasible starting pseudoflow, the unit marginal-path method performs at most \(F\) augmentations. With a shortest-path routine of cost \(T_{\mathrm{sp}}(n,m)\) per augmentation, its path-search work is \(O(F\,T_{\mathrm{sp}}(n,m))\), apart from marginal and price updates. This is generally pseudopolynomial when \(F\) is binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit path method uses at most one shortest-path augmentation per installed flow unit and is generally pseudopolynomial in binary input size.
assumptions_latex: Each augmentation installs one unit of the remaining target balance.
The total number of units to install is \(F<\infty\).
One shortest-path computation costs \(T_{\mathrm{sp}}(n,m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method uses at most \(F\) augmentations and \(O(F\,T_{\mathrm{sp}}(n,m))\) path-search work.

notation.meaning: Total number of balance units installed

knowledge_statements.title: Unit Marginal-Path Augmentation Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Label-Setting Failure Without Price Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity witness against Dijkstra-style search with negative marginal costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider unit-capacity residual arcs \(s\to a,s\to b,a\to b,b\to t\) with marginal costs \(2,1,-3,1\). The path \(s\to a\to b\to t\) costs \(0\), while \(s\to b\to t\) costs \(2\). A label-setting routine that permanently settles \(b\) at distance \(1\) before processing \(a\) can return the latter path and an invalid price update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative marginal arc can make a settled-label shortest-path search return a nonminimum path even with unit capacities.
assumptions_latex: Every displayed residual arc has capacity one.
The routine permanently settles an extracted vertex.
No prices making all residual reduced costs nonnegative are supplied.
knowledge_statements.title: Label-Setting Failure Without Price Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant-Marginal Batched Path Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Batched price-feasible path augmentation over an interval in which every used marginal cost remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a price-feasible integral pseudoflow has a tight residual path \(P\) from a node with remaining outflow requirement to a node with remaining inflow requirement. Let \(\Delta\) be the largest positive integer bounded by both endpoint requirements, every residual capacity on \(P\), and the number of consecutive units for which each residual arc used by \(P\) retains its current marginal cost. Then augmenting \(\Delta\) units on \(P\) is equivalent to \(\Delta\) successive valid unit augmentations along that unchanged tight path. It preserves the bounds and nonnegative reduced marginal costs, and at least one endpoint requirement, residual capacity, or constant-marginal interval becomes tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight marginal path can carry a maximal batch while endpoint requirements, residual capacities, and all used marginal costs remain unchanged.
assumptions_latex: Arc bounds, target balances, and the current pseudoflow are integral.
Arc costs are separable and discrete convex.
All available marginal residual arcs initially have nonnegative reduced cost.
Every residual arc of the selected path remains zero reduced-cost throughout the chosen constant-marginal interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'=x+\Delta\chi_P\text{ is bound-feasible and price-feasible, and the batch equals }\Delta\text{ valid unit augmentations}.

notation.meaning: Largest batch not crossing an endpoint, capacity, or marginal-cost breakpoint.
Signed original-arc incidence vector of the residual path.

assumptions_latex: The network has integral supplies and demands, integral arc bounds, and separable discrete-convex arc costs.
A bounded integral pseudoflow \(x\) is maintained, possibly with nonzero node imbalance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successive marginal path augmentations eliminate all node imbalance; subsequent absence of negative marginal cycles certifies optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum Derivative-Length Path Optimality Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient first-order optimality condition under the preceding nonnegative, differentiable convex, monotone, side-constraint-free multicommodity-flow assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume nonnegative multicommodity flows, only conservation and nonnegativity constraints, and a convex continuously differentiable objective that is componentwise nondecreasing. knowledge_statements.title: Cycle–Path Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-direction decomposition underlying mixed path-and-cycle algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_x\) be the marginal residual digraph of a bounded integral pseudoflow \(x\), let \(B_x\) be its node-arc incidence matrix, and let \(d\ge0\) be an integral residual-arc flow respecting all residual capacities. The residual flow \(d\) can be decomposed into incidence vectors of directed residual cycles and directed residual paths, with path endpoints accounting for the nonzero entries of \(B_xd\). Consequently, if \(B_xd=0\), cycle augmentations suffice. If \(B_xd\ne0\), path augmentations transfer imbalance between their endpoints, while cycle components change cost without changing imbalance. A cycle–path selection regime may therefore use paths to restore prescribed balances and cycles to improve cost at fixed balances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral residual correction decomposes into imbalance-carrying directed paths and balance-preserving directed cycles, supporting algorithms that use paths for feasibility and cycles for cost improvement.
assumptions_latex: A finite marginal residual digraph \(H_x\) of a bounded integral pseudoflow \(x\) is given.
The vector \(d\) is a nonnegative integral flow on the residual arcs and respects every residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Path components account for the imbalance vector \(B_xd\), while cycle components preserve balances; if \(B_xd=0\), cycles alone suffice.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace each original arc \(a\) by \(u_a-\ell_a\) unit-capacity parallel arcs whose linear costs are the successive discrete marginal values of \(\phi_a\). Discrete convexity orders these values nondecreasingly, so an optimal linear flow on \(G'\) selects a prefix of the marginal units and maps to an optimal convex-cost flow. The expanded network has \(|V|\) vertices and \(U\) unit arcs, up to the original lower-bound transformation. Thus any polynomial linear-flow algorithm yields a running time polynomial in \(|V|\), \(|E|+U\), and expanded-data length, which can be exponential in \(\log U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Convex-Cost Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-length criterion distinguishing polynomial frameworks from unit enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary-encoded separable convex-cost flow instance, call a framework polynomial only when its number of cost-oracle evaluations and unit-cost arithmetic operations is bounded by a polynomial in \(|V|\), \(|E|\), and the binary input length \(L\), and every intermediate number has encoding length polynomial in \(L\). A running-time bound polynomial only in the numerical range \(U=\sum_{a\in E}(u_a-\ell_a)\) does not meet this condition. Scaling, aggregated marginal searches, or compact convex optimization can meet the condition only when their termination, oracle complexity, and intermediate encoding lengths are polynomially bounded in \(|V|\), \(|E|\), and \(L\), without constructing all \(U\) marginal units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-cost network-flow framework is polynomial only when its work and intermediate encodings are polynomial in the binary input length, rather than merely polynomial in the numerical flow range.
assumptions_latex: Arc bounds, balances, and convex-cost descriptions have finite binary encoding length \(L\).
Marginal values or suitable convex-cost subgradients can be evaluated in time polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomiality requires oracle use, arithmetic work, and intermediate encoding lengths polynomial in \(|V|\), \(|E|\), and \(L\), independently of the numerical value of \(U\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Evaluation Oracles Do Not Determine Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation boundary for polynomial-time claims about discrete convex-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound polynomial in the number of calls to an abstract value, comparison, or marginal-cost oracle does not by itself imply polynomial bit complexity. Such a conclusion additionally requires polynomial-time oracle evaluation, polynomial encoding length for every oracle answer and intermediate number, and a polynomially decodable output representation. Without these requirements, one oracle call may hide superpolynomial computation or return a superpolynomial-length value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomially many abstract cost-oracle calls are not a polynomial-time guarantee unless oracle evaluation, numeric encodings, intermediate values, and output decoding are polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: Convex costs are accessed through an oracle rather than an explicit unit-marginal list.
Complexity is measured in the binary input model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{poly}(n,m,L)\text{ oracle calls}\not\Longrightarrow\operatorname{poly}(n,m,L)\text{ bit time without oracle and encoding guarantees}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative of a Separable Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise convex-analysis representation in arc-indexed notation, including the source's convention for an indeterminate sum of infinite terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(x)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}f_{ij}(x_{ij}),
\]
where each $f_{ij}$ is closed and convex on an interval $X_{ij}$, and let $x_{ij}\in X_{ij}$. Then
\[
f'(x;y)=\sum_{\{(i,j):y_{ij}>0\}}f_{ij}^{+}(x_{ij})y_{ij}+\sum_{\{(i,j):y_{ij}<0\}}f_{ij}^{-}(x_{ij})y_{ij}.
\]
Here $f_{ij}^{+}$ and $f_{ij}^{-}$ denote the right and left derivatives. The formula remains valid under the convention $+\infty-(+\infty)=+\infty$. In particular, if $f_{ij}^{+}(x_{ij})=+\infty$ for some component with $y_{ij}>0$, then that component points outside its interval for every $\alpha>0$, and hence $f'(x;y)=+\infty$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a separable closed convex function, positive direction components use right derivatives and negative direction components use left derivatives. The source resolves a positive-infinity-minus-positive-infinity ambiguity by assigning it positive infinity. An infinite right derivative in a positive direction forces the perturbed point outside the domain and makes the total directional derivative positive infinity.
assumptions_latex: f(x)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}f_{ij}(x_{ij})
f_{ij}\text{ is closed and convex on the interval }X_{ij}
x_{ij}\in X_{ij}\text{ for every }(i,j)\in\mathcal A
y\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal A}
(+\infty)-(+\infty):=+\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotropic programming problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General continuous separable convex optimization over a linear subspace, with network-flow and linearly constrained specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A monotropic programming problem is \(\min\{\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(x_j):x\in S,\ x_j\in X_j\ (j=1,\ldots,n)\}\), where every \(X_j\subseteq\mathbb R\) is a nonempty interval, every \(f_j:X_j\to\mathbb R\) is closed and convex, and \(S\) is a linear subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\). Choosing \(S\) as a graph's circulation subspace recovers the zero-supply form of separable convex network flow. A separable convex program with \(Ax=b\) is equivalently represented using an artificial variable \(z\) subject to \((x,z)\in\{(x,z):Ax-z=0\}\) and \(z\in\{b\}\). Linear and separable convex-quadratic programs are special cases; a quadratic objective \(x^{\mathsf T}C^{\mathsf T}Cx\) can be made separable by introducing \(y=Cx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotropic program minimizes a sum of closed convex one-variable functions over intervals while requiring the complete vector to lie in a linear subspace. It contains separable convex circulation models and can represent separable convex equality-constrained programs by adding fixed artificial variables.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb N
X_j\subseteq\mathbb R\text{ is a nonempty interval for }j=1,\ldots,n
f_j:X_j\to\mathbb R\text{ is closed and convex for }j=1,\ldots,n
S\leq\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(x_j):x\in S,\ x_j\in X_j\right\}\text{ is a monotropic programming problem and has the stated special-case representations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycle Feasible-Direction Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-cycle descent with a feasibility-preserving line search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: From a feasible flow \(x^k\), select a directed residual cycle having negative total current marginal cost. Let \(d^k\) be its signed circulation direction and let \(\alpha_{\max}\) be the largest bound-feasible step. Choose \(0<\alpha_k\le\alpha_{\max}\) by exact line search or a sufficient-decrease rule and set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k\). If no negative marginal cycle exists, stop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method follows a negative marginal residual cycle and line-searches within its residual capacity.
assumptions_latex: The initial flow is feasible.
Arc costs are differentiable and convex.
A positive sufficient-decrease step is selected whenever a negative cycle exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iterate is feasible, every accepted step decreases the objective, and any finite stopping point is optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Feasible-Direction Descent

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible Directions as Residual Circulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network representation of tangent directions at a bounded feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=\{x:Ax=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\) and \(x\in F\), a first-order feasible direction satisfies \(Ad=0\), \(d_a\ge0\) at a nonfixed lower bound, and \(d_a\le0\) at a nonfixed upper bound. Representing positive and negative components by forward and backward residual arcs turns \(d\) into a nonnegative residual circulation, hence a conic combination of directed residual-cycle directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangent directions of a bounded flow polytope are residual circulations and decompose into directed cycles.
assumptions_latex: The current flow satisfies \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every first-order feasible direction is a conic combination of directed residual-cycle directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Directions as Residual Circulations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected-Gradient Feasible-Flow Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonasymptotic convergence of a feasibility-preserving first-order network method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x:Bx=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\) be nonempty and let \(f\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Starting from \(x^0\in F\), define \[x^{k+1}=\Pi_F\!\left(x^k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x^k)\right).\] Every iterate is feasible, and for every minimizer \(x^*\in F\) and \(k\ge1\), \[f(x^k)-f(x^*)\le\frac{L\|x^0-x^*\|^2}{2k}.\] The projection subproblem is a convex quadratic network-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected gradient preserves flow feasibility and attains the standard one-over-k objective rate for smooth convex costs.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty and closed.
\(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
A minimizer exists in \(F\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible-flow polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Gradient Feasible-Flow Rate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Summable-Step Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent without an adequate step rule need not reach the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize \(f(x)=x\) over \(F=[0,1]\), start at \(x^0=1\), and choose \(d^k=-1\). With \(\alpha_k=2^{-k-2}\), every iterate is feasible and strictly improves the objective, but \(\sum_{k\ge0}\alpha_k=1/2\), so \(x^k\to1/2\), which is not optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible descent with summable steps can converge to a nonoptimal point despite strict improvement at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x^{k+1})<f(x^k)\text{ for every }k,\qquad x^k\to1/2\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{[0,1]}f.
knowledge_statements.title: Summable-Step Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network Conditional-Gradient Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-preserving conditional-gradient variant whose direction subproblem is linear minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x:Ax=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\) be nonempty and compact, let \(f\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(F\), and let \(D=\sup_{x,y\in F}\|x-y\|\). At iteration \(k\), compute \[s^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in F}\nabla f(x^k)^{\mathsf T}s\] by a linear minimum-cost-flow subproblem and set \(x^{k+1}=(1-\eta_k)x^k+\eta_k s^k\). With \(\eta_k=2/(k+2)\), every iterate is feasible and, for \(k\ge1\), \[f(x^k)-f(x^*)\le\frac{2LD^2}{k+2}.\] The gap \(g(x)=\max_{s\in F}\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(x-s)\) satisfies \(f(x)-f(x^*)\le g(x)\), and \(g(x)=0\) exactly at global optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional gradient solves a linear minimum-cost-flow direction problem, preserves feasibility by convex averaging, and has the standard one-over-k smooth-convex rate and gap certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty and compact.
\(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(F\).
A minimizer \(x^*\in F\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x^k)-f(x^*)\le 2LD^2/(k+2)\quad(k\ge1),\qquad f(x)-f(x^*)\le g(x).

notation.meaning: Euclidean diameter of the feasible-flow polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Conditional-Gradient Method

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(F=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), and \(F\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Descent Property for Monotropic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a uniformly separating feasible-subspace direction when a feasible point exceeds the optimal value by more than the stated epsilon gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be primal feasible. If, for some \(\epsilon>0\), \(\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(x_j)>f^*+n\epsilon\), then there exists \(d\in S\) such that \(t^{\prime}d<0\) for every \(t\in B_\epsilon(x)\), and \(d\) is an \(\epsilon\)-descent direction at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a primal-feasible point is more than n epsilon above the optimum, there is a direction in the feasible subspace having strictly negative inner product with every vector in the epsilon-subgradient box; this direction is an epsilon-descent direction.

\epsilon>0

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists d\in S\;\forall t\in B_\epsilon(x):\ t^{\prime}d<0,\qquad d\text{ is an }\epsilon\text{-descent direction at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dualizing \(Ax=b\) with prices \(p\) gives \[g(p)=p^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_a\inf_{\ell_a\le z\le u_a}\bigl(\phi_a(z)-(A^{\mathsf T}p)_az\bigr).\] Let \(x_a(p)\) be the unique scalar minimizer in the corresponding term. Then \(g\) is concave and differentiable, with \(\nabla g(p)=b-Ax(p)\). Hence a dual ascent method updates node prices using the imbalance induced by independently optimized arc flows. A zero gradient yields a primal-feasible Lagrangian minimizer and therefore a primal-dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separable arc minimization defines a smooth price dual whose gradient is node imbalance; dual ascent adjusts prices until the induced arc flow is feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge-Fixed Dual Newton Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Damped Newton iteration exploiting the weighted-Laplacian Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Where the Laplacian Hessian formula applies, compute \(d\) from \[A\operatorname{diag}\!\bigl(\phi_a''(x_a(p))^{-1}\bigr)A^{\mathsf T}d=b-Ax(p)\] with one price gauge per connected component, and set \(p^+=p+\alpha d\), choosing \(0<\alpha\le1\) to increase the dual and remain in the smooth regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth-dual Newton update solves a gauge-fixed weighted Laplacian system driven by node imbalance.
assumptions_latex: The dual is twice differentiable at the current price.
A price gauge is fixed on every connected component.
The step length preserves the smooth regime and produces dual ascent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonsmooth Dual Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of classical smooth-dual updates when arc minimizers are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an arcwise Lagrangian subproblem has multiple minimizers at \(p\), the induced flow need not be unique and the dual need not be differentiable there. The possible imbalance vectors \(b-Ax\) are supergradients, but no unique gradient or classical Newton Hessian exists without regularization or a selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonunique arc minimizers can make the price dual nonsmooth and invalidate ordinary gradient and Newton formulas.
assumptions_latex: At least one scalar Lagrangian arc subproblem has multiple minimizers at \(p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Hessian as a Weighted Network Laplacian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order structure of the smooth node-price dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every induced arc minimizer is interior and \(\phi_a''(x_a(p))>0\), then \[\nabla^2g(p)=-A\operatorname{diag}\!\bigl(\phi_a''(x_a(p))^{-1}\bigr)A^{\mathsf T}.\] Thus \(-\nabla^2g(p)\) is a weighted graph Laplacian whose nullspace contains the vectors constant on each connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative smooth-dual Hessian is a weighted network Laplacian with the usual additive price gauge.
assumptions_latex: Every induced arc minimizer is interior.
Each arc cost is twice differentiable with positive second derivative at the induced flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: -\nabla^2g(p)\text{ is a positive-semidefinite weighted network Laplacian.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Convergence of Smooth Dual Gradient Ascent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global rate under uniform smoothness and strong concavity after fixing the price gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix one price gauge on each connected component. Suppose the concave dual \(g\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly concave on a convex invariant region containing a maximizer \(p^*\), where \(0<\mu\le L\). Then \(p^{k+1}=p^k+L^{-1}\nabla g(p^k)\) satisfies \[g(p^*)-g(p^k)\le(1-\mu/L)^k\bigl(g(p^*)-g(p^0)\bigr),\] and \(\nabla g(p^k)=b-Ax(p^k)\) converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform smoothness and strong concavity give linear convergence of gauge-fixed dual gradient ascent and vanishing node imbalance.
assumptions_latex: A price gauge is fixed on each connected component.
\(g\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly concave on an invariant convex region.
The dual maximum is attained in that region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(p^*)-g(p^k)\le(1-\mu/L)^k\bigl(g(p^*)-g(p^0)\bigr).

notation.meaning: Strong-concavity constant on the gauge-fixed space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inexact Coordinate Relaxation with Relative Surplus Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inexact node-price relaxation controlled by a relative residual parameter, including its positive-tolerance existence boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\delta\in[0,1)\). For a selected node \(i\) with \(g_i(p)\neq0\), change only \(p_i\) to obtain \(\bar p\) such that \[g_i(p)>0\Rightarrow 0\leq g_i(\bar p)\leq\delta g_i(p),\qquad g_i(p)<0\Rightarrow\delta g_i(p)\leq g_i(\bar p)\leq0.\] The case \(\delta=0\) gives exact coordinate relaxation. For \(\delta>0\), the required price adjustment is possible without assuming that either every arc lower endpoint is finite or every arc upper endpoint is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Change one node price so that its surplus does not change sign and its magnitude is reduced by at least the factor delta. Delta zero gives the exact step. With positive delta, the adjustment exists without the preceding global finite-lower-endpoint or finite-upper-endpoint assumption.

g_i(p)\neq0
\bar p_j=p_j\quad\text{for every }j\neq i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative Cycle Optimality Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality characterization for the stated constraint-separable convex network-flow problem using all simple cycles unblocked at the candidate flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the constraint-separable convex network-flow problem, and suppose \(f\) is continuously differentiable on the entire ambient space and convex on the feasible set. A vector \(x^*\) is optimal if and only if it is feasible and, for every simple cycle \(C\) unblocked with respect to \(x^*\), \[\sum_{(i,j)\in C^+}\frac{\partial f(x^*)}{\partial x_{ij}}-\sum_{(i,j)\in C^-}\frac{\partial f(x^*)}{\partial x_{ij}}\ge 0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the constraint-separable convex network-flow problem, a candidate flow is optimal exactly when it is feasible and every simple cycle along which flow can be adjusted has a nonnegative signed sum of objective partial derivatives.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is a vector for the constraint-separable convex network-flow problem}
f\text{ is continuously differentiable on the entire ambient space}
f\text{ is convex on the feasible set}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Coordinate Relaxation for a Differentiable Network Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-specific coordinate ascent in node-price variables, including its complementary-slackness stopping test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a price vector \(p\), if \(g_i(p)=0\) for every node \(i\), terminate: \(p\) is dual optimal, and the unique flow \(x\) satisfying CS together with \(p\) is primal optimal. Otherwise, choose any node \(i\) with \(g_i(p)\neq0\), change only \(p_i\), and obtain \(\bar p\) maximizing \(q\) along that coordinate, so that \(g_i(\bar p)=0\). Successive iterations increase the dual-function value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every node surplus is zero, the prices are dual optimal and the unique complementary-slackness flow is primal optimal. Otherwise, change one node price with nonzero surplus until that surplus is zero, thereby maximizing the dual function along that coordinate.
assumptions_latex: q\text{ is the differentiable dual function and }g_i(p)\text{ is its partial derivative with respect to }p_i
\text{The flow }x\text{ satisfying CS together with }p\text{ is unique}
\text{The required exact coordinate adjustment is well defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall i,\ g_i(p)=0\right)\Rightarrow\left(p\text{ is dual optimal and }x\text{ is primal optimal}\right);\quad \text{otherwise choose }i\text{ with }g_i(p)\neq0\text{ and set }\bar p_{-i}=p_{-i},\ g_i(\bar p)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a bounded pseudoflow \(x\), node prices \(p\), and the invariant \(\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\) on every marginal residual arc. Select a node with positive excess. If it has a residual outgoing arc attaining the best price-adjusted marginal cost within tolerance \(\varepsilon\), push as much flow as permitted toward that arc's head. Otherwise change the selected node's price until at least one outgoing residual arc becomes admissible. Update the forward and backward marginal costs after each push. Stop when every node has its prescribed balance; optionally reduce \(\varepsilon\) and restart from the current flow and prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex auction alternates admissible marginal-flow pushes with node repricing, preserving approximate complementary slackness until feasibility and the desired tolerance are reached.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Per-Node Bound on Auction Price Rises
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite price-update bound for the generic convex auction algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r\geq0\). Suppose the initial price vector \(p^0\) satisfies \(r\epsilon\)-CS together with some feasible flow vector \(x^0\), and each price rise increases the selected node's price by at least \(\beta\epsilon\), where \(\beta\in(0,1)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Duality-Gap Bound under Epsilon-Complementary Slackness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual gap bound and limiting result for separable convex-cost flow-price pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x(\epsilon),p(\epsilon))\) satisfy \(\epsilon\)-CS with \(x(\epsilon)\) feasible, and let \(\xi(\epsilon)\) be any flow vector satisfying exact CS together with \(p(\epsilon)\), without requiring flow conservation for \(\xi(\epsilon)\). Then \[0\leq f(x(\epsilon))-q(p(\epsilon))\leq \epsilon\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}\left|x_{ij}(\epsilon)-\xi_{ij}(\epsilon)\right|.\] If all dual arc-cost functions \(q_{ij}\) are real-valued, then \[\lim_{\epsilon\to0}\left(f(x(\epsilon))-q(p(\epsilon))\right)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible epsilon-CS flow-price pair has a nonnegative primal-dual gap bounded by epsilon times its arcwise distance from any exact-CS comparison flow using the same prices. The comparison flow need not conserve flow. If every dual arc-cost function is real-valued, the gap tends to zero with epsilon.

x(\epsilon)\text{ is feasible}
\xi(\epsilon)\text{ satisfies exact CS together with }p(\epsilon)

\text{For the limiting conclusion, all }q_{ij}\text{ are real-valued}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Candidate Lists for Convex Auction Flow Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc eligibility bands used to organize flow changes in a convex auction iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\epsilon>0\), \(\beta\in(0,1)\), and an \(\epsilon\)-CS flow-price pair \((x,p)\). The candidate list of node \(i\) is the union of \[L^+(i)=\{(i,j)\in\mathcal A:(1-\beta)\epsilon<p_i-p_j-f_{ij}^+(x_{ij})\leq\epsilon\}\] and \[L^-(i)=\{(j,i)\in\mathcal A:-(1-\beta)\epsilon>p_j-p_i-f_{ji}^-(x_{ji})\geq-\epsilon\}.\] Equivalently, relative to \(\Gamma_{ij}=\{(x_{ij},t_{ij})\in\mathbb R^2:f_{ij}^-(x_{ij})\leq t_{ij}\leq f_{ij}^+(x_{ij})\}\), the flow-price point lies in the indicated strip between offsets \((1-\beta)\epsilon\) and \(\epsilon\) above or below \(\Gamma_{ij}\). At the right endpoint of \(X_{ij}\), \(f_{ij}^+=+\infty\), so outgoing membership in \(L^+(i)\) is impossible; analogously, incoming membership in \(L^-(i)\) is impossible at the left endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive epsilon, beta strictly between zero and one, and an epsilon-CS pair, a node's candidate list contains outgoing and incoming arcs whose price-derivative discrepancies lie in the specified epsilon bands. The characteristic-curve description is equivalent. Endpoint infinite derivatives exclude the corresponding candidate-list membership.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon>0
\beta\in(0,1)
(x,p)\text{ satisfies }\epsilon\text{-CS}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{CandidateList}(i)=L^+(i)\cup L^-(i)\text{ with the stated strict and weak bounds; the relevant domain endpoints exclude the corresponding memberships.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((x,p)\) satisfies \(\varepsilon\)-relaxation when \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-p_j\ge-\varepsilon\) for every available marginal residual arc \((i,j)\). Price terms telescope on a directed residual cycle, so every simple cycle has marginal cost at least \(-n\varepsilon\). If marginal costs are integral and \(0<\varepsilon<1/n\), every cycle cost is an integer strictly greater than \(-1\), hence nonnegative. The marginal negative-cycle criterion then certifies that the feasible flow \(x\) is exactly optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate reduced-cost inequalities bound every residual cycle. With integral costs and tolerance below the reciprocal of the vertex count, they certify exact optimality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed price refinement using one-unit marginal residual arcs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose signs so that auction prices and relaxation potentials satisfy \(q_i=-p_i\). Then comparing auction net values is equivalent to comparing reduced marginal costs \(c_{ij}+p_i-p_j\). Assigning or transferring flow to an arc whose net value is within \(\varepsilon\) of best is exactly an admissible relaxation push. Raising an auction price until another choice becomes competitive is the corresponding relaxation relabel. Thus both descriptions generate the same flow-price transitions, modulo tie breaking and additive translation of all prices, and preserve identical \(\varepsilon\)-complementary-slackness inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a sign change in node prices, auction bids and repricing coincide with relaxation pushes and relabels, preserving the same approximate optimality conditions.
