knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Log-Barrier Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-start logarithmic-barrier method for bounded convex network flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite bounds and \(\mu>0\), minimize \[F_\mu(x)=\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)-\mu\sum_a\bigl(\log(x_a-\ell_a)+\log(u_a-x_a)\bigr)\] subject to \(Ax=b\). Starting from a strictly feasible flow, use damped equality-constrained Newton steps that preserve \(\ell<x<u\); after meeting an inner residual tolerance, reduce \(\mu\) and warm-start the next barrier problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method follows the bound-barrier central path with feasibility-preserving Newton steps and decreasing barrier parameters.
assumptions_latex: All arc bounds are finite.
A strictly feasible flow exists.
Each arc cost is convex and twice differentiable on the open interval.
Each barrier subproblem is solved to the prescribed residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\mu\downarrow0\) and inner residuals vanish, the produced feasible objective values approach the optimum under attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Log-Barrier Path Following

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-Barrier Central-Path Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier-parameter stopping bound with two finite bounds per arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an exact central-path point for a differentiable convex objective, the lower- and upper-bound multipliers satisfy complementarity products equal to \(\mu\). With two finite bounds per arc, the resulting primal-dual gap is \(2|A|\mu\). Approximate central points require their feasibility and stationarity residual errors to be added to this bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two logarithmic bound barriers per arc give a central-path primal-dual gap of two times the arc count times the barrier parameter.
assumptions_latex: All arc bounds are finite and strict feasibility holds.
The optimum is finite and attained.
The objective is differentiable at the central-path point.
The stated equality applies to an exact central-path point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_\mu)-f^*\le 2|A|\mu.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Barrier Central-Path Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Feasibility Boundary for Primal Log Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization boundary of the direct primal barrier formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\{x:Ax=b,\ell<x<u\}=\varnothing\), the direct primal logarithmic barrier has no feasible point even when the closed-bound problem is feasible. Initialization then requires a phase-one embedding, facial reduction, or a primal-dual self-dual formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed-bound feasibility is insufficient for a direct primal log-barrier method; strict feasibility or an embedding is required.
assumptions_latex: The closed-bound problem is feasible.
No balance-feasible flow satisfies every finite bound strictly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The direct primal logarithmic-barrier path is empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Feasibility Boundary for Primal Log Barriers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier Newton System and Network Schur Complement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network linear algebra of a primal barrier step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(H=\nabla^2F_\mu(x)\) positive diagonal, the equality-constrained Newton equations have coefficient matrix \[\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}.\] Eliminating the arc direction yields a node system with coefficient \(AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\), a weighted graph Laplacian; after fixing one multiplier gauge per connected component, the arc direction follows by back-substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating arc directions from the barrier KKT equations yields a weighted Laplacian system in node multipliers.
assumptions_latex: The current flow is strictly inside every bound.
The barrier Hessian is positive diagonal.
Redundant balance rows are removed or multiplier gauges are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each Newton direction reduces to a weighted-Laplacian solve and arcwise back-substitution.
knowledge_statements.title: Barrier Newton System and Network Schur Complement

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell<x<u\}\) contains a strictly feasible point.
Every arc cost is convex and twice continuously differentiable on its open bounded interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Following approximate minimizers of the barrier problems as \(\mu\downarrow0\) yields primal solutions approaching the optimal convex-cost flow value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal equality-constrained logarithmic-barrier path-following framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), minimize over \(Ax=b\) the barrier objective \[F_\mu(x)=\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)-\mu\sum_a\bigl(\log(x_a-\ell_a)+\log(u_a-x_a)\bigr).\] Starting from a strictly feasible point, compute damped Newton directions in the null space of \(A\), equivalently by solving the associated weighted network KKT system, and use a step preserving \(\ell<x<u\). Once the Newton residual meets the prescribed inner tolerance, reduce \(\mu\) and warm-start the next barrier problem. Stop when the barrier duality-gap bound and residual tolerances are at most the requested accuracy, and output the current feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network interior-point method follows logarithmic-barrier minimizers using feasibility-preserving Newton steps and reduces the barrier parameter until the target optimality gap is reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Network Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The barrier construction fits the interior-point leaf, but no source is supplied for the network KKT formulation, convergence of approximate barrier minimizers, or the invoked barrier duality-gap stopping bound. Those conditions and the treatment of finite bounds require authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hardness of the Unrestricted Nonconvex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity boundary supplied by the fixed-charge subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The separable nonconvex-cost flow class contains fixed-charge network flow, whose arc costs may have the form \(\phi_a(0)=0\) and \(\phi_a(x)=F_a+c_ax\) for \(0<x\le u_a\), with \(F_a>0\). Consequently, solving unrestricted separable nonconvex-cost flow is NP-hard under standard binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unrestricted separable nonconvex-cost flow is NP-hard because it contains fixed-charge network flow.
assumptions_latex: Capacities, balances, and cost parameters are finitely and binary encoded.
Positive fixed charges are permitted in the arc-cost representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Unrestricted separable nonconvex-cost flow is NP-hard.}\)

notation.meaning: fixed charge for using arc a
variable unit cost on arc a

review_flags: Published source locator for the fixed-charge hardness reduction remains desirable.
knowledge_statements.title: Hardness of the Unrestricted Nonconvex Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvex Arc-Cost Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable network flow in which convexity fails on at least one arc; coupled objectives and side constraints are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a):Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), the arc-cost regime is nonconvex if some \(\phi_a\) is not convex on its feasible interval. Equivalently, for some arc \(a\), points \(s,t\in[\ell_a,u_a]\), and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), \[\phi_a(\lambda s+(1-\lambda)t)>\lambda\phi_a(s)+(1-\lambda)\phi_a(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable flow has nonconvex arc costs when at least one arc cost violates the convex chord inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(Bx=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\) are the underlying network constraints.
The objective is arc-separable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least one arc cost violates convexity on its feasible interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Arc-Cost Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Monotone Marginal Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural feature lost when a differentiable arc cost is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a differentiable function \(\phi:I\to\mathbb R\) is nonconvex on an interval \(I\), then \(\phi'\) is not nondecreasing on \(I\). Thus there exist \(s<t\) in \(I\) with \(\phi'(s)>\phi'(t)\), and residual marginal costs derived from this arc need not be monotone as its flow increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable nonconvex arc cost has nonmonotone marginal costs, so convex-flow monotone-marginal reasoning no longer applies.
assumptions_latex: \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) is an interval.
\(\phi\) is differentiable but not convex on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi'\) is not nondecreasing on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Monotone Marginal Costs
Nonconvex Arc Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-parallel-arc example where arcwise nonconvexity separates local and global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two parallel arcs from source to sink carrying one unit in total. Let the first-arc flow be \(x\in[0,1]\), the second-arc flow be \(1-x\), and the total cost be \(h(x)=x^2-3x^3+x^4\). The function \(h\) is nonconvex on \([0,1]\). Moreover, \(x=0\) is a strict one-sided local minimizer because \(h(x)>h(0)=0\) for every sufficiently small \(x>0\), whereas \(h(1)=-1<h(0)\). Thus local marginal or residual optimality cannot, without convexity, certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex arc cost can admit a locally optimal feasible flow whose cost exceeds that of a distant feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=0\) is locally minimizing but not globally minimizing.

notation.meaning: flow on the first parallel arc

review_flags: Exact published locator for the counterexample and local-to-global failure is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically consistent and fits the failure-boundary container, but no inspectable source supports the local-to-global failure claim.

children.title: Coupled Arc Costs
children.top_down_role: Loss of separability and local residual representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Convex Optimality Certificate for Coupled Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replacement for arc-local reduced-cost certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Bx=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\), let \(F\) be proper closed convex, and assume a standard relative-interior qualification for \(F+\delta_P\). A feasible \(x^*\) is optimal exactly when \[0\in\partial F(x^*)+N_P(x^*).\] Equivalently, there exist node multipliers \(p\) and nonnegative bound multipliers \(\lambda,\mu\) such that \[0\in\partial F(x^*)+B^{\mathsf T}p-\lambda+\mu,\] with \(\lambda_a(x_a^*-\ell_a)=0\) and \(\mu_a(u_a-x_a^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled convex flow retains a global subgradient/KKT certificate, although it generally lacks independent arc-local reduced costs.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex.
A relative-interior qualification ensures the displayed multiplier form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}F(x)\iff0\in\partial F(x^*)+N_P(x^*).

notation.meaning: Normal cone of the feasible-flow set at the candidate.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Convex Optimality Certificate for Coupled Costs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shared-Load Quadratic Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete convex objective with a nonzero mixed derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On an open set in \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(F(x_1,x_2)=(x_1+x_2)^2\). Its Hessian is positive semidefinite, so \(F\) is convex, but \(\partial^2F/(\partial x_1\partial x_2)=2\). Hence it cannot equal \(\phi_1(x_1)+\phi_2(x_2)\) there for twice-differentiable scalar functions \(\phi_1,\phi_2\), whose mixed derivative would be zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared-load quadratic is convex but not decomposable into independent arc costs.
assumptions_latex: \((x_1,x_2)\) ranges over a nonempty open set.
Any asserted scalar decomposition is twice differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\ne\phi_1+\phi_2\text{ on the open set}.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Load Quadratic Coupling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Flow with Coupled Arc Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex network-flow model without an arcwise-separable objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A coupled convex-cost flow problem has the form \[\min\{F(x):Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\},\] where \(F:\mathbb R^A\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper convex but need not satisfy \(F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\). Feasibility retains network structure, while objective values and marginal changes may involve several arcs jointly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled convex-cost flow preserves network feasibility but permits a jointly dependent convex objective.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper and convex.
The feasible set is defined by network conservation and arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ need not decompose into independent scalar arc costs}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Flow with Coupled Arc Costs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Arcwise Lagrangian Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of independent scalar subproblems after dualizing conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dualizing \(Bx=b\) with node prices \(p\) yields \[\inf_{\ell\le x\le u}\bigl(F(x)-(B^{\mathsf T}p)^{\mathsf T}x\bigr).\] Additive arc separability makes this infimum split into scalar arc subproblems. For a genuinely coupled \(F\), the split generally fails, and the price-induced flow must be obtained from a coupled convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node prices do not generally split a coupled objective into independent arc minimizations.
assumptions_latex: Conservation is dualized by node prices.
\(F\) is genuinely nonseparable on the feasible box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Arcwise scalar Lagrangian minimization is not valid in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Arcwise Lagrangian Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Fixed Arc-Local Residual Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivatives of a coupled objective depend on the whole current flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is differentiable, the first-order cost of a feasible circulation direction \(d\) at \(x\) is \(\nabla F(x)^{\mathsf T}d\). For nonseparable \(F\), \(\partial F(x)/\partial x_a\) may depend on coordinates \(x_b\) with \(b\ne a\). Thus a residual arc cannot generally be assigned an exact marginal-cost function determined solely by its own flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under coupling, an arc's marginal cost can depend on other arc flows, invalidating independent arc-local residual costs.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is differentiable near the current flow.
\(F\) is not arc-separable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_aF(x)\text{ may depend on }x_b\text{ for }b\ne a.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Fixed Arc-Local Residual Costs
Coupled Arc Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex coupling can invalidate an exact decomposition into independent arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On two arc variables \((x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R^2\), let \(F(x_1,x_2)=(x_1-x_2)^2\). This cost is convex but cannot be represented on any open set as \(F(x_1,x_2)=\phi_1(x_1)+\phi_2(x_2)\): its mixed derivative is \(\partial^2F/(\partial x_1\partial x_2)=-2\), while every twice-differentiable separable representation has zero mixed derivative. Consequently, the exact marginal cost of changing one arc depends on the other arc flow, so fixed arc-local residual costs do not represent the coupled objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a convex objective may lose arc separability, making each arc’s exact marginal cost depend on flows elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: \((x_1,x_2)\) ranges over an open subset of \(\mathbb R^2\).
\(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) are twice differentiable if such a decomposition is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\neq\phi_1+\phi_2\) on every nonempty open set.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the separability boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex nonseparability example is precise and fits the container, but it has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Side-Constrained Convex Flows
children.top_down_role: Additional constraints that destroy pure network structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality with Side-Constraint Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT certificate showing how genuine side constraints enlarge the node-potential certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each \(\phi_a\) is proper, closed, and convex, the side-constrained problem has a finite feasible point, and a convex constraint qualification ensuring KKT necessity holds. A feasible finite-cost flow \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if there exist node potentials \(\pi\), equality multipliers \(\lambda\), and inequality multipliers \(\mu\ge0\) such that \[0\in\partial\phi_a(x_a^\star)+(B^{\mathsf T}\pi+C^{\mathsf T}\lambda+D^{\mathsf T}\mu)_a+N_{[\ell_a,u_a]}(x_a^\star)\quad(a\in A),\] and \(\mu_i((Dx^\star)_i-q_i)=0\) for every side inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a suitable constraint qualification, side constraints require additional KKT multipliers; node potentials alone generally do not certify optimality.
assumptions_latex: Each arc cost is proper, closed, and convex.
The problem has a finite feasible point.
A constraint qualification ensuring KKT necessity holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality is equivalent to primal feasibility, stationarity, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness with side-constraint multipliers.

notation.meaning: multipliers for side equalities and inequalities
normal cone of the arc-bound interval

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality with Side-Constraint Multipliers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Side-Constrained Convex Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A separable convex-cost flow augmented by constraints not expressible solely as node balances and individual arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A side-constrained convex flow has the form \[\min_x\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=b,\quad \ell\le x\le u,\quad Cx=d,\quad Dx\le q,\] where every \(\phi_a\) is convex and at least one row of \(C\) or \(D\) is nonredundant and is neither a node-balance equation nor a single-arc bound. The model remains convex, but its constraint system is not purely an incidence system with box bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A side-constrained convex flow adds genuine linear coupling constraints to a separable convex network-flow model.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\phi_a\) is convex.
At least one added constraint is nonredundant and is not merely a balance equation or arc bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is convex but is not a pure incidence-matrix flow problem.

notation.meaning: matrices of additional equality and inequality constraints

knowledge_statements.title: Side-Constrained Convex Flow
Side-Constrained Convex Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An additional linear constraint can destroy the integral network-flow structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two parallel source-to-sink arcs with continuous flows \(x_1,x_2\geq0\), unit demand \(x_1+x_2=1\), and any convex objective, for example the zero function. Adding the side constraint \(x_1=x_2\) leaves the unique feasible flow \((x_1,x_2)=(1/2,1/2)\). Hence, although the underlying network and its demand have integral data, the side-constrained feasible set has no integral point. Pure network-flow integrality and algorithms relying on the unaugmented incidence structure therefore do not transfer automatically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A side constraint can force fractional flows despite integral network data, eliminating the usual network-flow integrality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_1,x_2)=(1/2,1/2)\) is the unique feasible flow.
review_flags: A source explicitly documenting this side-constraint integrality boundary is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly shows that an added side constraint can eliminate integral feasible flows, but no inspectable source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Side-Constrained Convex Network-Flow Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a convex network-flow model with additional convex inequality constraints beyond arc-domain and flow-conservation constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a network $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$, a side-constrained convex network-flow problem has the form
\[
\min_x f(x)
\]
subject to
\[
x_{ij}\in X_{ij}\quad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal A,
\]
\[
\sum_{\{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A\}}x_{ij}-\sum_{\{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A\}}x_{ji}=s_i\quad\forall i\in\mathcal N,
\]
and
\[
g_t(x)\le 0\quad(t=1,\ldots,r),
\]
where each $X_{ij}$ is an interval of the real line and $f,g_1,\ldots,g_r$ are convex functions of $x$. The inequalities $g_t(x)\le 0$ are called side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A side-constrained convex network-flow problem minimizes a convex function subject to interval restrictions on arc flows, flow-conservation equations at the nodes, and finitely many additional convex inequalities called side constraints.
assumptions_latex: X_{ij}\subseteq\mathbb R\text{ is an interval for every }(i,j)\in\mathcal A
f\text{ is convex in }x
g_t\text{ is convex in }x\text{ for }t=1,\ldots,r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The inequalities }g_t(x)\le 0,\quad t=1,\ldots,r,\text{ are side constraints added to the arc-interval and flow-conservation constraints.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Side-Constrained Network Flow Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies how additional coupling and integrality restrictions produce discrete network optimization models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A discrete side-constrained network flow model augments flow-conservation equations and arc-flow bounds with constraints coupling flows on different arcs and with integrality restrictions on some or all arc variables; a common special case is
\[x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.\]
Such restrictions yield combinatorial optimization problems even when the underlying network objective is linear or convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete network optimization models add cross-arc coupling constraints and integer restrictions to the usual flow-conservation and arc-bound constraints. Binary arc flows are an important special case, and the resulting models include many combinatorial optimization problems.

\text{additional constraints may couple distinct arc flows}
x_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\text{ for designated arcs, possibly }x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Convex-Flow Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable convex-cost flow with real-valued arc variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), let \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), and let \(\ell,u\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\})^A\) satisfy \(\ell_a\leq u_a\) for every \(a\in A\). The continuous convex-flow problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^A}\left\{\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a):Bx=b,\ \ell_a\leq x_a\leq u_a\text{ for every }a\in A\right\}.\]
Each \(\phi_a:[\ell_a,u_a]\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Feasible flows and perturbations are real-valued; no integrality restriction is imposed on \(x\), even when \(b,\ell,u\) are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous convex flow minimizes separable convex arc costs over real-valued flows satisfying conservation equations and arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a directed graph and \(B\) is its node-arc incidence matrix.
\(b\in\mathbb R^V\) and \(\ell_a\leq u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).
\(\phi_a\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \([\ell_a,u_a]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is optimized over a convex subset of \(\mathbb R^A\).

notation.meaning: directed graph with node set V and arc set A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient existence condition within the continuous regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every arc interval is compact, the continuous feasible-flow set is nonempty, and the lower-semicontinuous separable objective is finite at some feasible flow, then the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite closed arc bounds and a proper lower-semicontinuous objective guarantee attainment on a nonempty feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(-\infty<\ell_a\le u_a<+\infty\) for every arc.
The feasible set is nonempty.
The separable objective is lower semicontinuous and finite at some feasible flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Domains Need Not Attain Their Infimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment boundary within continuous convex flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two oppositely directed arcs between two nodes, zero balances, unrestricted arc flows, cost \(e^t\) on one arc and zero on the other. Conservation forces both arc flows to equal a common \(t\in\mathbb R\). The objective has infimum \(0\) as \(t\to-\infty\), but no feasible flow attains it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex objective on an unbounded continuous-flow domain can have a finite unattained infimum.
assumptions_latex: The feasible circulation contains the unrestricted common-flow direction \(t\in\mathbb R\).
The objective along that direction is \(e^t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf f=0\text{ but }\operatorname*{argmin}f=\varnothing.

notation.meaning: common flow on the two-arc circulation

children.title: Integral Convex-Flow Regime
children.top_down_role: Structural behavior of convex flows restricted to integral variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Convex-Flow Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable discrete-convex cost flow with integer arc variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), let \(b\in\mathbb Z^V\), and let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^A\) satisfy \(\ell_a\leq u_a\) for every \(a\in A\). The integral convex-flow problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb Z^A}\left\{\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a):Bx=b,\ \ell_a\leq x_a\leq u_a\text{ for every }a\in A\right\}.\]
For every \(a\in A\), the function \(\phi_a\) is defined on \([\ell_a,u_a]\cap\mathbb Z\), and its forward differences \(\Delta\phi_a(k)=\phi_a(k+1)-\phi_a(k)\) are nondecreasing wherever they are defined. Thus convexity is interpreted discretely, and feasible augmentations change flow by integral amounts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral convex flow minimizes separable costs with nondecreasing discrete marginal costs over integer-valued flows satisfying conservation equations and arc bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous–Integral Transfer Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous convex optima need not themselves be feasible integral flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take two parallel arcs carrying total demand one, with \(x_1+x_2=1\), \(x_1,x_2\geq0\), and objective \(x_1^2+x_2^2\). Over real flows, strict convexity gives the unique optimum \((x_1,x_2)=(1/2,1/2)\) with value \(1/2\). Under the additional restriction \((x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\), the only feasible flows are \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), each with value \(1\). Thus network integrality does not imply that a nonlinear continuous convex optimum is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly convex continuous flow may have a unique fractional optimum even though integral feasible flows exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{cont}}=1/2<1=z_{\mathrm{int}}\).

children.title: Generalized-Flow Feasibility

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Flow Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility with arc gains and lower-bound node requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each directed arc \(a=(i,j)\) have gain \(\gamma_a>0\), capacity \(u_a\geq0\), and sent flow \(x_a\). Define node excess by
\[e_v(x)=\sum_{a=(i,v)}\gamma_a x_a-\sum_{a=(v,j)}x_a.\]
For a requirement vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), a generalized flow is feasible when \(0\leq x_a\leq u_a\) for every arc and \(e_v(x)\geq b_v\) for every node. An arc sending \(x_a\) units consumes that amount at its tail and delivers \(\gamma_a x_a\) at its head.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-flow feasibility requires capacities and gain-adjusted node excesses meeting all prescribed lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_a>0\)
\(u_a\geq0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq x\leq u\) and \(e(x)\geq b\).

notation.meaning: required minimum excess at node v

children.title: Generalized Circulation

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gain-adjusted balance equalities, including the zero-demand circulation case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a directed gain network, a generalized circulation with prescribed balance vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) is a vector \(x\) satisfying \(\ell_a\leq x_a\leq u_a\) and
\[\sum_{a=(i,v)}\gamma_a x_a-\sum_{a=(v,j)}x_a=b_v\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.\]
The pure generalized-circulation case has \(b=0\). Unlike ordinary circulation, the total amount arriving along an arc may differ from the amount sent, so the equations need not reduce to ordinary flow conservation unless all gains equal one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized circulation satisfies capacity bounds and gain-adjusted balance equations at every node; pure circulation uses zero balances.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\gamma_a<\infty\)
\(\ell_a\leq u_a\)

children.title: Generalized-Flow Maximization

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Flow Maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum gain-adjusted delivery to a designated sink under finite capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(t\in V\) be a designated sink, let \(s_v\geq0\) be available external supply at each \(v\neq t\), and define \(e_v(x)\) by gain-adjusted inflow minus sent outflow. The generalized-flow maximization problem is
\[\max\left\{e_t(x):0\leq x_a\leq u_a,\ e_v(x)\geq-s_v\text{ for every }v\neq t\right\}.\]
Its objective measures the quantity delivered to \(t\) after applying all traversed arc gains; finite capacities prevent unlimited use of amplifying arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-flow maximization sends available supplies through gain arcs to maximize gain-adjusted excess delivered at a chosen sink.
assumptions_latex: \(t\in V\) is designated as the sink.
\(s_v\geq0\) for \(v\neq t\).
\(0\leq u_a<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_t(x)\) is maximized over the stated feasible generalized flows.

children.title: Minimum-Cost Generalized Flow

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Generalized Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost optimization subject to gain-adjusted balance equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given arc costs \(c_a\in\mathbb R\), gains \(\gamma_a>0\), bounds \(\ell_a\leq u_a\), and prescribed balances \(b_v\), the minimum-cost generalized-flow problem is
\[\min_x\left\{\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a:\ell_a\leq x_a\leq u_a,\ \sum_{a=(i,v)}\gamma_ax_a-\sum_{a=(v,j)}x_a=b_v\text{ for every }v\in V\right\}.\]
Costs are charged per unit sent on an arc, while the receiving node obtains the gain-scaled quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-cost generalized flow minimizes sending costs while satisfying capacities and gain-adjusted node balances.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_a>0\)
\(\ell_a\leq u_a\)
\(c_a,b_v\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) minimizes \(\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a\) over the gain-feasible balance system.

notation.meaning: cost per unit sent on arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc-multiplier semantics in generalized network flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the gain-or-loss transmission rule used by the minimum-cost generalized-flow model and identifies its unit-multiplier specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a generalized network flow, every arc $(i,j)$ has a positive multiplier $\mu_{ij}>0$. Sending one unit of flow from $i$ on arc $(i,j)$ causes $\mu_{ij}$ units to arrive at $j$. If $\mu_{ij}=1$ for every arc, this generalized model specializes to the ordinary minimum-cost flow model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each arc in a generalized network flow has a positive multiplier. One unit sent from the tail of an arc delivers the multiplier's number of units at its head. If every multiplier is one, the model becomes ordinary minimum-cost flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Minimum-Cost Flow Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility, capacity feasibility, supplies and demands, and the possible use of infinite bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a directed graph $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ and scalars $a_{ij},b_{ij},c_{ij}$ and $s_i$, the minimum-cost flow problem is
\[\min_x\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}a_{ij}x_{ij}\]
subject to
\[\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}x_{ji}=s_i\quad(\forall i\in\mathcal N),\qquad b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad(\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A).\]
A flow satisfying both families is feasible; one satisfying only the arc bounds is capacity-feasible. The instance is feasible exactly when a feasible flow exists. Negative $s_i$ represents demand $-s_i$. When explicitly allowed, some lower bounds may equal $-\infty$ or upper bounds may equal $+\infty$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize total linear arc cost subject to prescribed flow divergence at every node and lower and upper bounds on every arc. A feasible flow satisfies both conservation and capacity constraints, while a capacity-feasible flow satisfies only the bounds. An instance is feasible precisely when such a feasible flow exists. Positive node imbalance is supply, negative imbalance is demand, and explicitly designated arc bounds may be infinite.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is a directed graph}
a_{ij},b_{ij},c_{ij},s_i\in\mathbb R
b_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}a_{ij}x_{ij}:\operatorname{div}_i(x)=s_i\ \forall i,\ b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separable Convex-Cost Network Flow Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the continuous convex arc-separable flow model with general convex interval domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given convex functions $f_{ij}:X_{ij}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ and convex intervals $X_{ij}\subseteq\mathbb R$, the separable convex-cost network flow problem is
\[\min_x\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}f_{ij}(x_{ij})\]
subject to
\[\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}x_{ji}=s_i\quad(\forall i\in\mathcal N),\qquad x_{ij}\in X_{ij}\quad(\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A).\]
A standard domain is $X_{ij}=[b_{ij},c_{ij}]$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable convex-cost network flow problem minimizes the sum of one convex cost function per arc, subject to prescribed node-flow balances and membership of each arc flow in a convex interval, such as a lower-and-upper-bound interval.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted-Link Representation of Two-Nonzero-per-Column LPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The generalized-network interpretation uses arbitrary incident coefficients as flow multipliers; it does not require a normalized directed-arc sign pattern. Columns with no nonzero entries contribute to no nodal balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\) and \(|\operatorname{supp}(a_j)|\le 2\) for every column \(a_j\). In \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), associate each row \(p\) with a node. A column having two nonzero entries defines a link between the corresponding nodes, while a column having one nonzero entry defines a link incident to that node. At each incidence \((p,L_j)\), use \(A_{pj}\) as the multiplier of flow \(x_j\). Then \(Ax=b\) is exactly the system of weighted nodal-balance equations \(\sum_{j:\,p\in L_j}A_{pj}x_j=b_p\) for \(p=1,\ldots,m\). This weighted-link LP is termed a generalized network or network flow with gains problem in the source formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-row-rank equality-form nonnegative LP with at most two nonzero entries per column can be represented as a weighted-link network: rows become nodes, one- or two-entry columns become incident links, and the column coefficients become incidence multipliers. The LP equalities are exactly the resulting weighted nodal-balance equations.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
\operatorname{rank}(A)=m
|\operatorname{supp}(a_j)|\le 2\quad\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
b\in\mathbb{R}^m,\quad c\in\mathbb{R}^n
x\ge 0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax=b\iff \sum_{j:\,p\in L_j}A_{pj}x_j=b_p\quad\forall p\in\{1,\ldots,m\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Loss Cycle Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-product classification under the weakly lossy convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0<\gamma_a\le1\) for every arc, then for every directed cycle \(C\), \(\gamma(C)=1\) exactly when every arc of \(C\) has unit gain; any strict-loss arc on \(C\) implies \(\gamma(C)<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under weak lossiness, a cycle preserves quantity exactly only when all its arcs have unit gain.

\(C\) is a directed cycle.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Loss Cycle Classification
Lossy Generalized Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gain networks in which no arc increases transported quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized network is lossy when every arc gain satisfies \(0<\gamma_a\leq1\), with \(\gamma_a<1\) for at least one arc if strict lossiness is intended. Sending \(x_a\geq0\) on arc \(a\) delivers \(\gamma_ax_a\leq x_a\) at its head. Consequently, along any directed walk \(P\), a quantity transported without intermediate injection is multiplied by \(\gamma(P)=\prod_{a\in P}\gamma_a\leq1\); in particular, no directed cycle has multiplicative gain exceeding one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a lossy generalized network every arc weakly diminishes flow, so every walk and cycle has gain at most one.

\(x_a\geq0\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone-Cycle Amplification Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-product condition within the proposed arc-amplifying convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a directed cycle. If \(\gamma_a\ge1\) for every \(a\in C\) and \(\gamma_{a_0}>1\) for some \(a_0\in C\), then \(\gamma(C)=\prod_{a\in C}\gamma_a>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle of nonlossy arcs is amplifying when at least one arc has gain above one.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a directed cycle.
Every arc of \(C\) has gain at least one.
At least one arc of \(C\) has gain greater than one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma(C)>1.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Cycle Amplification Test
Amplifying Generalized Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gain networks containing at least one quantity-increasing arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized network is amplifying when it contains an arc \(a\) with gain \(\gamma_a>1\). Sending \(x_a>0\) units on that arc delivers \(\gamma_ax_a>x_a\) units at its head. This arc-level condition does not by itself imply an amplifying directed cycle: a directed cycle \(C\) amplifies repeated circulation precisely when its multiplicative gain \(\gamma(C)=\prod_{a\in C}\gamma_a\) exceeds one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An amplifying network has a gain-above-one arc, but an amplifying cycle exists only when a cycle’s gain product exceeds one.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_a>0\) for every \(a\in A\).
\(x_a\geq0\)

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generalized networks containing loss, neutral, and amplification arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-gain network is a generalized network whose arc set has the partition \[E^-:=\{e\in E:\gamma_e<1\},\qquad E^0:=\{e\in E:\gamma_e=1\},\qquad E^+:=\{e\in E:\gamma_e>1\},\] where \(E^-\), \(E^0\), and \(E^+\) are all nonempty. Sending \(x_e\geq0\) units from the tail of \(e=(i,j)\) removes \(x_e\) units at \(i\) and delivers \(\gamma_e x_e\) units at \(j\). Thus one network simultaneously permits attenuation, conservation, and amplification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Change Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between residual vectors and bound-preserving changes under tail-based units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_e^+\) and \(z_e^-\) be nonnegative amounts on the forward and reverse residual copies of an original arc \(e\), within their respective residual capacities. Define \[\Delta x_e=z_e^+-\frac{z_e^-}{\gamma_e}.\] Then \(0\leq x+\Delta x\leq u\), and, writing \(A_{\gamma_x}\) for the generalized incidence matrix of the residual arcs, \[A_\gamma\Delta x=A_{\gamma_x}z.\] For linear costs, \[c^{\mathsf T}\Delta x=\sum_e c_ez_e^+-\sum_e\frac{c_e}{\gamma_e}z_e^-,\] which is the residual-vector cost. Conversely, every bound-preserving change \(\Delta x\) has such a representation by using only the forward copy when \(\Delta x_e\geq0\) and only the reverse copy when \(\Delta x_e<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual vectors encode exactly all bound-preserving arc changes, with matching generalized imbalance and objective change.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) satisfies \(0\leq x\leq u\).
Every gain \(\gamma_e\) is positive.
Residual capacities and costs use the immutable seed's tail-unit convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual vectors and bound-preserving changes correspond under \(\Delta x_e=z_e^+-z_e^-/\gamma_e\), preserving generalized imbalance and linear cost change.

notation.meaning: amounts on the forward and reverse residual copies
generalized incidence matrix of the residual network

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Change Correspondence

assumptions_latex: \(x\) satisfies \(0\leq x_e\leq u_e\) on every arc \(e\), with \(0<u_e\leq+\infty\).
Every original arc has gain \(\gamma_e>0\) and linear cost \(c_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Forward and reverse residual arcs encode every bound-preserving infinitesimal change of one original arc.

notation.meaning: current flow and upper capacity on arc e
gain and cost on arc e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual quantities are measured at the tail of each residual arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generalized residual network \(G_x\) contains, for every original arc \(e=(i,j)\), a forward residual arc \(e^+=(i,j)\) when \(x_e<u_e\), with capacity \(u_e-x_e\), gain \(\gamma_e\), and cost \(c_e\). When \(x_e>0\), it also contains a reverse residual arc \(e^-=(j,i)\), with capacity \(\gamma_e x_e\), gain \(1/\gamma_e\), and cost \(-c_e/\gamma_e\). Sending \(\delta\) units on \(e^-\) means replacing \(x_e\) by \(x_e-\delta/\gamma_e\), so the induced node-excess change agrees with generalized-flow conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each usable arc has a forward residual copy; each positive-flow arc has a gain-reciprocal reverse copy whose capacity and cost use tail-based units.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Residual Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tail-unit reverse capacity, reciprocal gain, and scaled reverse cost are internally consistent, but these convention-sensitive formulas require a specialized source.

children.title: Generalized Node-Label Representations
children.top_down_role: Gain-aware node labels used to express price information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge Invariance of Generalized Node Labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common rescaling and logarithmic translation of a positive node labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any positive labeling \(\mu\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{V}\) and scalar \(a>0\), set \(\mu'_i=a\mu_i\). Then \[\gamma_{ij}^{\mu'}=\gamma_{ij}\frac{a\mu_i}{a\mu_j}=\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}.\] Equivalently, for \(p_i=\log\mu_i\), replacing \(p\) by \(p+(\log a)\mathbf 1\) preserves every label difference, represented gain, and tight arc. Thus one normalization such as \(\mu_r=1\) or \(p_r=0\) may be imposed without changing the represented gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common positive rescaling changes no represented gain; in logarithmic coordinates it is translation by a constant, so one reference label may be normalized.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_{ij}>0\) for every arc and \(\mu_i>0\) for every node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma^{a\mu}=\gamma^{\mu}\), and common-scalar normalization preserves all represented-gain inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Invariance of Generalized Node Labels

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and every \(\gamma_e>0\).
Each node label satisfies \(\mu_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive node labeling represents gains equivalently by scaled gains or additive log-lengths.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative labels and their logarithmic additive representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized node-label representation assigns \(\mu_i\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) to every \(i\in V\). For an arc \((i,j)\), its represented gain is \[\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}:=\gamma_{ij}\frac{\mu_i}{\mu_j}.\] Equivalently, setting \(p_i:=\log\mu_i\) and \(\ell_{ij}:=-\log\gamma_{ij}\) gives \[\log\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}=p_i-p_j-\ell_{ij}.\] Thus the multiplicative condition \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}\leq1\) is the additive difference inequality \(p_i-p_j\leq\ell_{ij}\), while equality identifies an arc tight under the labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive node labels rescale each gain by the tail label divided by the head label; logarithms convert this into a difference-constraint representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Node-Label Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplicative and logarithmic representations are algebraically consistent and fit the representation leaf, but no source is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composition and Invertibility of Relabeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic group law for positive diagonal changes of node units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_{\mu}\) denote the relabeling \(x_{ij}\mapsto x_{ij}/\mu_i\) and \(\gamma_{ij}\mapsto\gamma_{ij}\mu_i/\mu_j\), together with the corresponding transformations of capacities, costs, and balances. For positive vectors \(\mu,
u\), \[R_{
u}(R_{\mu}(x,\gamma))=R_{\mu\odot
u}(x,\gamma),\] where \((\mu\odot
u)_i=\mu_i
u_i\). Hence \(R_{\mu}\) is invertible with inverse \(R_{\mu^{-1}}\). Relabelings whose label vectors differ by a common scalar induce the same transformed gains, though their other unit-dependent quantities are correspondingly rescaled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal relabelings compose by componentwise multiplication and are inverted by reciprocal labels; common label scaling leaves transformed gains unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu,\nu\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{V}\).
All quantities use the tail-unit convention of the immutable relabeling seed.

notation.meaning: relabeling by positive node vector mu

knowledge_statements.title: Composition and Invertibility of Relabeling

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a generalized flow on \(G=(V,E)\).
The scaling vector satisfies \(\mu\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{V}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relabeling conjugates generalized balances by positive diagonal scaling and preserves every directed cycle-gain product.

notation.meaning: relabeling vector and its diagonal matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive diagonal change of units at generalized-flow nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every arc \(e=(i,j)\), define \[x_e^{\mu}:=\frac{x_e}{\mu_i},\qquad \gamma_e^{\mu}:=\gamma_e\frac{\mu_i}{\mu_j}.\] If \(A_\gamma x=b\), then the relabeled quantities satisfy \(A_{\gamma^{\mu}}x^{\mu}=D_\mu^{-1}b\). Capacities transform as \(u_e^{\mu}=u_e/\mu_i\), and linear costs as \(c_e^{\mu}=c_e\mu_i\), preserving \(c^{\mathsf T}x\). For every directed cycle \(C\), cancellation of node labels yields \(\prod_{e\in C}\gamma_e^{\mu}=\prod_{e\in C}\gamma_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relabeling changes node units, flows, gains, capacities, and costs consistently while preserving balances, objective values, and every directed cycle-gain product.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Relabeling Transformations

children.title: Label Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compatibility boundaries for node labels within generalized residual networks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible-Label Construction by Difference Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a nonamplifying label or a gain-cycle obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\ell_{ij}=-\log\gamma_{ij}\). Form a difference-constraint graph having an arc \(j\to i\) of length \(\ell_{ij}\) for every original arc \(i\to j\), and add a source with zero-length arcs to all vertices. Bellman--Ford either returns a negative directed cycle, corresponding to an original directed cycle \(C\) with \(\prod_{e\in C}\gamma_e>1\), or returns distances \(p\) satisfying \(p_i-p_j\leq\ell_{ij}\). In the latter case \(\mu_i=e^{p_i}\) is gain-feasible. In a real-arithmetic model this requires \(O(|V||E|)\) relaxation evaluations on the augmented graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic difference-constraint algorithm either constructs a feasible positive label or returns an amplifying directed cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite.
Every gain satisfies \(\gamma_e>0\).
Logarithms and exact comparisons are available in the stated real-arithmetic complexity model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns either \(\mu>0\) with \(\gamma_{ij}\mu_i\leq\mu_j\) for every arc or a directed cycle \(C\) with \(\Gamma(C)>1\).

notation.meaning: negative logarithm of the arc gain

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Label Construction by Difference Constraints
Label Feasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility of labels that make all represented gains nonamplifying.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive label \(\mu\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{V}\) is gain-feasible when \[\gamma_{ij}\mu_i\leq\mu_j\qquad\text{for every }(i,j)\in E.\] Such a label exists if and only if every directed cycle \(C\) satisfies \[\Gamma(C):=\prod_{e\in C}\gamma_e\leq1.\] Under logarithms, this is the feasibility criterion for the difference constraints \(p_i-p_j\leq-\log\gamma_{ij}\). A cycle with \(\Gamma(C)>1\) is therefore a finite, directly checkable obstruction to this label regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Labels making every rescaled gain at most one exist exactly when every directed cycle has gain product at most one.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph.
Every arc gain satisfies \(\gamma_e>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible positive label exists exactly when no directed cycle has gain product greater than one.

notation.meaning: multiplicative gain of directed cycle C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-network labeling algorithm for maximum flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inner-loop guard is normalized to the mathematically coherent interpretation: scan while the list is nonempty and the sink remains unlabeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible flow $x$ in a capacitated network with source $s$ and sink $t$, clear all labels, label $s$, and maintain a list initially containing $s$. While the list is nonempty and $t$ is unlabeled, remove a labeled node $i$ and label every previously unlabeled node $j$ with $r_{ij}>0$, recording $\operatorname{pred}(j)=i$. If $t$ becomes labeled, trace the predecessor chain to obtain an augmenting path $P$, set $\delta=\min\{r_{ij}:(i,j)\in P\}$, augment by $\delta$, update residual capacities, and repeat. Stop when $t$ cannot be labeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible source–sink flow, search the positive-capacity residual network from the source using predecessor labels. Whenever the sink is reached, augment by the minimum residual capacity on the resulting path and repeat; stop when the sink is unreachable.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a capacitated network with source }s\text{ and sink }t.
x\text{ is a feasible flow and }r_{ij}\text{ denotes residual capacity.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure repeatedly performs bottleneck augmentations until }t\text{ is unreachable from }s\text{ in }G(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Labeling Maximum-Flow Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes augmentation from an integral feasible flow and the optimality certificate obtained when the sink cannot be labeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x=(x_{ij})$ be an integral feasible $s$-$t$ flow with arc capacities $c_{ij}$. Label $s$ permanently and scan labeled nodes in the residual network: label an unlabeled $j$ from $i$ through a forward arc $(i,j)$ when $x_{ij}<c_{ij}$, with $\delta_j=\min\{c_{ij}-x_{ij},\delta_i\}$, or through a backward arc $(j,i)$ when $x_{ji}>0$, with $\delta_j=\min\{x_{ji},\delta_i\}$. If $t$ is labeled, follow predecessor labels to obtain an augmenting path, augment by $\delta_t$, erase all labels except that of $s$, and repeat. If all labeled nodes have been scanned without labeling $t$, then $x$ is a maximum flow, and the labeled vertices $S$ together with the unlabeled vertices $T$ define a minimum-capacity $s$-$t$ cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from any integral feasible flow, label and scan vertices reachable from the source by positive residual-capacity arcs. Whenever the sink is labeled, recover the predecessor path and augment by its residual bottleneck, then restart the labeling. If scanning ends without labeling the sink, the current flow is maximum and the labeled versus unlabeled vertices form a minimum cut.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is a directed capacitated network with source }s\text{ and sink }t.
x=(x_{ij})\text{ is an integral feasible flow satisfying }0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\notin S\text{ after exhaustive residual labeling}\implies x\text{ is a maximum flow and }(S,V\setminus S)\text{ is a minimum-capacity }s\text{-}t\text{ cut}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Traversability and source-reachability labeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the mixed-graph definition with the stated labeling procedure for a digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed graph $M$ is traversable if, for every ordered pair $(u,v)$ of vertices, it contains a forward $uv$-path. This specializes to strong connectivity for digraphs and connectivity for undirected graphs. For a digraph $D=(V,A)$ and source $s$, initialize $s$ as REACHED, every other vertex as NON-REACHED, and every vertex as UNSCANNED. Repeatedly scan a reached, unscanned vertex $u$; for each newly reached out-neighbor $v$, store the predecessor arc $uv$. Stop when no reached vertex remains unscanned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed graph is traversable when every ordered vertex pair is joined by a forward path; this is strong connectivity for digraphs and ordinary connectivity for undirected graphs. The labeling search starts at a source, repeatedly scans reached vertices, and records the arc by which each new vertex is reached.
assumptions_latex: $M$ is a mixed graph for the traversability definition
$D=(V,A)$ is a finite digraph with source $s\in V$ for the labeling procedure
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns reached-vertex labels and predecessor arcs rooted at }s.

children.top_down_role: Label and gain-cycle obstructions to feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Feasibility Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity Farkas separation certificate for generalized balance feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bounded generalized-flow system \(A_\gamma x=b\), \(0\leq x\leq u\), is infeasible if and only if there exists a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfying \[y^{\mathsf T}b>\sum_{e\in E}u_e\bigl[(A_\gamma^{\mathsf T}y)_e\bigr]_+.\] Such a vector is a finite, directly checkable generalized feasibility obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded generalized-flow balance system is infeasible exactly when a node vector values the demand more highly than every capacity-bounded generalized arc flow can be valued.
assumptions_latex: \(A_\gamma\) is the generalized incidence matrix of a finite network.
The feasibility system is \(A_\gamma x=b\) with finite bounds \(0\leq x\leq u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed strict inequality is a verifiable certificate that the bounded generalized-flow system is infeasible, and such a certificate exists whenever the system is infeasible.

children.title: Generalized Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Gain-aware replacements for ordinary cut and reduced-cost certificates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Generalized-Flow Linear-Programming Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit dual program underlying the gain-aware reduced-cost certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:A_\gamma x=b,\ 0\leq x\leq u\},\] with finite \(u\), an equivalent dual is \[\max_{\pi\in\mathbb R^V,\ q\geq0}\ b^{\mathsf T}\pi-u^{\mathsf T}q\quad\text{subject to}\quad A_\gamma^{\mathsf T}\pi-q\leq c.\] Writing \(r=c-A_\gamma^{\mathsf T}\pi\), the gap for primal- and dual-feasible points is \[c^{\mathsf T}x-(b^{\mathsf T}\pi-u^{\mathsf T}q)=x^{\mathsf T}(r+q)+(u-x)^{\mathsf T}q\geq0.\] Equality is equivalent to \(x_e(r_e+q_e)=0\) and \((u_e-x_e)q_e=0\) for every arc, and eliminating \(q\) gives the immutable seed's reduced-cost sign conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded generalized-flow LP has a node-potential and upper-bound-multiplier dual; zero primal-dual gap is equivalent to the gain-aware reduced-cost certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(A_\gamma x=b\) is finite-dimensional.
Every upper bound \(u_e\) is finite.
The primal is feasible and has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal and dual feasibility imply weak duality, while zero gap is necessary and sufficient for mutual optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Generalized-Flow Linear-Programming Dual

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:A_\gamma x=b,\ 0\leq x\leq u\}\).
All capacities are finite and all data are real.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The flow \(x\) is optimal if and only if a node potential satisfying the displayed gain-aware sign conditions exists.

notation.meaning: gain-aware reduced cost of arc e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost, bounded generalized-flow optimality via LP reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gain-aware optimality certificate for a feasible flow \(x\) is a vector \(\pi\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). For each arc \(e=(i,j)\), define \[r_e:=c_e-(A_\gamma^{\mathsf T}\pi)_e=c_e+\pi_i-\gamma_e\pi_j.\] The certificate conditions are \[x_e=0\Rightarrow r_e\geq0,\qquad 0<x_e<u_e\Rightarrow r_e=0,\qquad x_e=u_e\Rightarrow r_e\leq0.\] A feasible \(x\) is globally optimal if and only if such \(\pi\) exists. These conditions are linear-programming complementary slackness expressed through the generalized incidence columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible generalized flow is optimal exactly when node potentials give nonnegative reduced costs at lower bounds, zero inside bounds, and nonpositive costs at upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Optimality Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduced-cost signs are the correct bounded-LP optimality conditions and the certificate content kind fits, but the exact generalized-flow formulation lacks a source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-Cost Sufficiency Conditions for Minimum-Cost Generalized Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A node-potential certificate sufficient for global optimality of a feasible capacitated generalized flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x^*$ be feasible, and let $c_{ij}^{\pi}=c_{ij}-\pi(i)+\mu_{ij}\pi(j)$. If there exists a node-potential vector $\pi$ such that, for every arc $(i,j)$, $0<x_{ij}^*<u_{ij}$ implies $c_{ij}^{\pi}=0$, $x_{ij}^*=0$ implies $c_{ij}^{\pi}\geq0$, and $x_{ij}^*=u_{ij}$ implies $c_{ij}^{\pi}\leq0$, then $x^*$ is an optimal solution of the generalized network-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible generalized flow is optimal if node potentials exist such that each interior-flow arc has zero reduced cost, each arc at zero flow has nonnegative reduced cost, and each arc at capacity has nonpositive reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is feasible}
\exists\pi\;\forall(i,j)\in A:\ c_{ij}^{\pi}=c_{ij}-\pi(i)+\mu_{ij}\pi(j)
0<x_{ij}^*<u_{ij}\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}=0
x_{ij}^*=0\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}\geq0
x_{ij}^*=u_{ij}\Rightarrow c_{ij}^{\pi}\leq0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is an optimal solution of the generalized network-flow problem.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmented Forest Structures, Feasibility, and Reduced Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for augmented-forest states in the capacitated generalized network-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $A=\mathbf F\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathbf L\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathbf U$, where $\mathbf F$ is a good augmented forest. This triple is an augmented forest structure. Set $x_{ij}=0$ for $(i,j)\in\mathbf L$ and $x_{ij}=u_{ij}$ for $(i,j)\in\mathbf U$. The generalized node-balance equations uniquely determine the flow on the arcs in $\mathbf F$. The structure is feasible when this induced flow satisfies the lower and upper bounds on every arc in $\mathbf F$, and infeasible otherwise. A feasible structure is nondegenerate when $0<x_{ij}<u_{ij}$ for every $(i,j)\in\mathbf F$, and degenerate otherwise. It is optimal when its associated flow is an optimal solution of the generalized network-flow problem. Given node potentials $\pi$, the reduced cost of arc $(i,j)$ is $c_{ij}^{\pi}=c_{ij}-\pi(i)+\mu_{ij}\pi(j)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An augmented forest structure partitions the arcs into good augmented-forest arcs, arcs fixed at zero, and arcs fixed at capacity. The balance equations uniquely determine the forest-arc flows. Feasibility requires those flows to obey their bounds; nondegeneracy requires them to lie strictly between their bounds; and optimality means that the associated flow solves the generalized network-flow problem. Reduced cost incorporates the arc gain and node potentials.
assumptions_latex: A=\mathbf F\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathbf L\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathbf U
\mathbf F\text{ is a good augmented forest}
x_{ij}=0\quad((i,j)\in\mathbf L)
x_{ij}=u_{ij}\quad((i,j)\in\mathbf U)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The balance equations uniquely induce the flow on }\mathbf F,\text{ with feasibility, degeneracy, and optimality defined as above, and }c_{ij}^{\pi}=c_{ij}-\pi(i)+\mu_{ij}\pi(j).

notation.meaning: oriented multiplicative gain around cycle C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-incidence bases represented by forests with one augmentation per component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An augmented forest consists of an undirected forest \(F\) of selected arc columns together with exactly one augmentation in each connected component: either one node-unit column, or one additional arc that creates a unique cycle \(C\). In the second case orient the traversal of \(C\), using \(\gamma_e\) when traversing an arc forward and \(\gamma_e^{-1}\) when traversing it backward, and require \(\Gamma(C)\neq1\). The square matrix formed from the columns indexed by \(F\cup Q\) is nonsingular if and only if every component has exactly one such augmentation and each augmented cycle satisfies this nonunit-gain condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized-flow basis is represented by forest components, each augmented by one root column or by one extra arc forming a nonunit-gain cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-Forest Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asserted augmented-forest nonsingularity characterization depends on the precise extended matrix containing node-unit columns and on specialized terminology; neither is sourced or fully specified.

children.title: Augmented-Forest Flows
children.top_down_role: Primal flow information induced by augmented-forest structures.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the nonsingular basis matrix represented by an augmented forest.
Nonbasic arc variables are fixed at specified lower or upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented-forest flow is the unique basic solution obtained by solving the generalized balance equations on the forest and its augmentations.

notation.meaning: generalized right-hand side after fixing nonbasic variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal basic solution associated with a nonsingular augmented forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix every nonbasic variable \(x_N\) at one of its bounds and set \(\widehat b:=b-A_Nx_N\). The augmented-forest flow is the unique vector \(x_B\) satisfying \[Bx_B=\widehat b,\qquad x_B=B^{-1}\widehat b.\] On a rooted-tree component, its entries can be determined by eliminating leaves toward the augmenting node column. On a unicyclic component, tree elimination leaves one scalar cycle equation; its coefficient is nonzero precisely because \(\Gamma(C)\neq1\). The resulting full vector \(x=(x_B,x_N)\) is primal feasible exactly when every basic component also obeys its prescribed bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After nonbasic flows are fixed, the augmented forest uniquely determines all basic flows; feasibility additionally requires those values to respect their bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-Forest Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear-algebraic basic-flow representation is plausible, but its augmented-forest interpretation and elimination claims depend on the unsourced basis convention.

children.title: Augmented-Forest Potentials
children.top_down_role: Dual price information induced by augmented-forest structures.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a nonsingular augmented-forest basis matrix.
\(c_B\) contains the objective coefficients of its basic columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented forest determines a unique node-potential vector satisfying zero reduced cost on every basic column.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual basic solution induced by augmented-forest columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The augmented-forest potential is the unique vector \(\pi\) solving \[B^{\mathsf T}\pi=c_B,
\qquad \pi=B^{-\mathsf T}c_B.\] Hence every basic arc \(e=(i,j)\) has zero reduced cost \(c_e+\pi_i-\gamma_e\pi_j=0\). A selected node-unit column fixes the potential at its augmented node to that column's cost. In a unicyclic component, propagating the arc equations around the unique cycle determines the remaining scalar potential because \(\Gamma(C)\neq1\). Reduced costs of nonbasic arcs are then obtained from the same gain-aware formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic costs and the augmented forest uniquely determine node potentials, making every basic reduced cost zero and defining reduced costs on nonbasic arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-Forest Potentials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual equation is correct for a square nonsingular basis, but the node-unit and unicyclic augmented-forest interpretations require specialized evidence.

children.title: Flow–Potential Compatibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Arc Exception to Bound-Sign Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrects the overlapping lower- and upper-bound implications when an arc has equal bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with reduced cost r_e, the lower-bound rule r_e\ge0 and upper-bound rule r_e\le0 apply only to nonfixed variables. If \ell_e=u_e, the variable admits no feasible local displacement and bound complementarity imposes no sign restriction on r_e. Thus the disjoint rule is r_e\ge0 at a nonfixed lower bound, r_e=0 in the strict interior, r_e\le0 at a nonfixed upper bound, and no sign condition for a fixed arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed arc has no reduced-cost sign requirement; lower-, interior-, and upper-bound tests apply only to nonfixed arcs with disjoint bound statuses.
assumptions_latex: x_e\in[\ell_e,u_e].
r_e\text{ is the reduced cost in a minimization formulation}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell_e=u_e\Longrightarrow r_e\text{ is unrestricted by bound complementarity}.

notation.meaning: Gain-aware reduced cost of arc e.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Arc Exception to Bound-Sign Tests

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is the augmented-forest basic flow and \(\pi\) its associated potential.
The model is a bounded linear-cost generalized flow with finite capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal bounds together with the gain-aware reduced-cost signs are equivalent to compatibility and certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual compatibility for a bounded augmented-forest basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An augmented-forest flow-potential pair \((x,\pi)\) is compatible when \(A_\gamma x=b\), \(0\leq x\leq u\), and, for every arc \(e=(i,j)\), \[r_e:=c_e+\pi_i-\gamma_e\pi_j\] satisfies \[x_e=0\Rightarrow r_e\geq0,
\qquad 0<x_e<u_e\Rightarrow r_e=0,
\qquad x_e=u_e\Rightarrow r_e\leq0.\] The basis equations already imply \(r_e=0\) for every basic arc \(e\in B\). Therefore compatibility is checked by primal bounds on basic flows and the appropriate reduced-cost signs on nonbasic arcs; when both hold, \((x,\pi)\) is a primal-dual optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An augmented-forest flow and potential are compatible when the flow respects balances and bounds and every reduced cost has the complementary sign required by its bound status.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow–Potential Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility conditions match bounded-LP complementary slackness when lower and upper bounds are distinct. As written, finite capacities permit \(u_e=0\), where the displayed implications overlap and incorrectly force zero reduced cost; the source or assumptions must resolve this boundary case.

children.title: Good Augmented-Forest Structures
children.top_down_role: Augmented forests possessing the structural features needed for basis interpretations.

assumptions_latex: The augmented directed graph is \(\bar G=(V,\bar E)\), and every arc \(a\in\bar E\) has gain \(\gamma_a>0\).
An augmented forest \(F\subseteq\bar E\) has exactly one undirected cycle in each weakly connected component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is good if and only if \(\Gamma(C)\ne 1\) for the unique cycle \(C\) of every component.

notation.meaning: Gain product around an oriented cycle, using reciprocal gains against its orientation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unicyclic-component interpretation of an augmented forest; the project-specific convention requires confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an oriented traversal of a cycle \(C\), define \(\Gamma(C)=\prod_{a\in C}\gamma_a^{\sigma_a}\), where \(\sigma_a=1\) when the traversal follows arc \(a\) and \(\sigma_a=-1\) otherwise. An augmented forest \(F\) is called good when every weak component of \((V,F)\) is unicyclic and its unique cycle \(C\) satisfies \(\Gamma(C)\ne1\). Equivalently, the generalized-incidence columns indexed by each component of \(F\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unicyclic augmented forest is good when the gain product around every component’s unique cycle is not one, equivalently making its generalized-incidence columns independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Good Augmented-Forest Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is plausible under the stated full generalized-incidence convention, but no inspectable source establishes the project-specific meaning of an augmented forest, the term “good,” or the claimed linear-independence equivalence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmented Trees, Extra Cycles, and Good Augmented Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of the augmented-forest structures used for generalized network flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G^a=(N^a,T^a)$ be a subgraph of $G=(N,A)$, where $N^a\subseteq N$ and $T^a\subseteq A$. It is an augmented tree when its arcs comprise a spanning tree on $N^a$ together with one additional arc $(\alpha,\beta)$, called the extra arc, and it has a designated root. Adding the extra arc to the spanning tree creates exactly one cycle, called the extra cycle; any arc of that cycle may be designated as the extra arc. The augmented tree is good when its extra cycle is lossy or gainy, equivalently not breakeven. An augmented forest $G^f=(N,F)$ is a collection of node-disjoint augmented trees spanning all nodes of $G$, and it is good when each component is a good augmented tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An augmented tree is a rooted spanning tree on a selected node set plus one extra arc. The extra arc creates a unique extra cycle. The tree is good when that cycle is lossy or gainy rather than breakeven. An augmented forest consists of node-disjoint augmented trees spanning every graph node and is good when every component is good.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)
N^a\subseteq N
T^a\subseteq A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^a\text{ is an augmented tree exactly when it is a rooted spanning tree on }N^a\text{ plus one extra arc; }G^f\text{ is good exactly when every component has a nonbreakeven extra cycle.}

assumptions_latex: The generalized-flow polyhedron is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^{E}:A_\gamma x=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).
The generalized incidence matrix \(A_\gamma\) has full row rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A basis is an arc set \(B\subseteq E\) with \(|B|=r\) and \(\det A_{\gamma,B}\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_\gamma\in\mathbb R^{r\times E}\) have full row rank. A linear-programming basis is a set \(B\subseteq E\) of \(r\) arcs such that the square matrix \(A_{\gamma,B}\) is nonsingular. After every nonbasic variable \(x_a\), \(a\notin B\), is fixed at either \(\ell_a\) or \(u_a\), the basic vector is uniquely determined by \(A_{\gamma,B}x_B=b-A_{\gamma,E\setminus B}x_{E\setminus B}\). The basis is feasible precisely when \(\ell_B\le x_B\le u_B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis selects a nonsingular square set of generalized-incidence columns; fixing all other variables at bounds uniquely determines the basic variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Characterization by Free-Column Independence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-variable LP geometry specialized to the generalized-incidence formulation; it does not characterize independent sets as augmented forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:A_\gamma x=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}, let \operatorname{rank}(A_\gamma)=r, and define I(x)=\{a\in E:\ell_a<x_a<u_a\}. A feasible x is a vertex of P if and only if the columns A_{\gamma,I(x)} are linearly independent. Equivalently, I(x) extends to a size-r basis B, all variables outside B are at bounds, and A_{\gamma,B} uniquely determines x_B.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible bounded generalized flow is a vertex exactly when the columns belonging to its strictly non-bound arcs are independent; equivalently, those columns can be extended to a feasible LP basis.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x:A_\gamma x=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\ne\varnothing.
\operatorname{rank}(A_\gamma)=r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\iff A_{\gamma,I(x)}\text{ has linearly independent columns}.

notation.meaning: Variables strictly between their bounds at x.

assumptions_latex: For each arc \(a=(i,j)\), its column has entries \(-1\) at \(i\), \(\gamma_a>0\) at \(j\), and zero elsewhere.
The selected set \(B\) contains exactly \(|V|\) arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_{\gamma,B}\) is nonsingular exactly when every component of \((V,B)\) is unicyclic and has cycle gain different from \(1\).

Oriented gain product of a cycle.

Then \(A_{\gamma,B}\) is nonsingular if and only if every weak component of \((V,B)\) contains equally many vertices and arcs and its unique undirected cycle \(C\) has oriented gain product \(\Gamma(C)\ne1\). Thus the linear-programming bases are exactly the good augmented forests under this matrix convention.
